# Majmu' al-Fatawa - Tome 20

## Page 9829

VOLUME TWENTY
THE BOOK OF THE PRINCIPLES OF ISLAMIC JURISPRUDENCE
PART TWO:
ADHERENCE TO A SCHOOL OF LAW

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.

All praise belongs to Allah alone, and may blessings and peace be upon him after whom there is no prophet.

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said:

All praise belongs to Allah. We praise Him, seek His help and forgiveness, believe in Him, and place our trust in Him. We extol Him with the praise He deserves, and we seek refuge in Allah from the evil within ourselves and from our evil deeds. Whoever Allah guides, none can lead astray; and whoever He leads astray, none can guide.

We bear witness that none is worthy of worship except Allah alone, with no partner. And we bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, whom He sent before the Hour as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner, one who calls to Allah by His permission, and an illuminating lamp. He sent him with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion, and Allah is sufficient as a witness. Through him, He guided people out of error, taught them out of ignorance, gave them sight after blindness, and led them away from misguidance. Through him, He opened deaf ears, blind eyes, and veiled hearts. May Allah bestow abundant blessings and peace upon him, his family, and his Companions.

To proceed:

Allah, glory be to Him, has made His noble Self known to us through what He has told us in

---

## Page 9830

His mighty Book and through the words of His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. For this purpose He revealed the Books and sent the messengers.

Allah Most High says:

“He has ordained for you the religion He enjoined upon Noah,” down to His words, “turns to Him.”

He also says:

“Ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: ‘Have We appointed gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?’”

And Allah Most High says:

“We never sent a messenger before you without revealing to him: ‘There is no god worthy of worship except Me, so worship Me.’”

It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“We prophets have one religion, but our laws differ.”

All the messengers thus agree upon the religion they share, both in the fundamentals of belief and knowledge—such as faith in Allah, His messengers, and the Last Day—and in the fundamentals of practice, such as the general deeds mentioned in Surahs al-An‘ām, al-A‘rāf, and Banī Isrā’īl. These include His words:

“Say, ‘Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you: do not associate anything with Him’”—the three verses;

“Say, ‘My Lord has commanded justice. Direct your faces towards Him at every place of worship’”—the verse;

“Say, ‘My Lord has only forbidden shameful deeds, whether openly or in secret’”—the verse;

“Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him”—through to the end of the injunctions;

and His words:

“Say, ‘This is my way: I call to Allah with clear insight’”—the verse.

Calling to Allah and worship encompass the utmost love for Allah and the utmost humility before Him. Whoever humbles himself before Him without love is not a worshipper. Rather, He must be the ultimate object of love; thus one must not love

---

## Page 9831

anything except for His sake. Whoever associates another with Him in these two respects has not devoted true love to Him and is thus a polytheist; his association of partners diminishes the reality of that love. As Allah Most High says:

“Yet among people are those who take others as equals to Allah, loving them as they love Allah”—the verse.

Love entails humility and obedience. Islam means submitting to Allah alone, not to anyone else. Whoever submits to Him and to another is a polytheist, while whoever refuses to submit to Him is arrogant. Both are contrary to Islam. The heart can only be sound through worshipping Allah alone, and fully realizing this fulfils the prophetic call.

Calling to Allah is an expression of love. It means calling people to believe in Him and in what His messengers brought, accepting their reports as true and obeying their commands. Calling to this is part of calling to Allah Most High. Likewise, forbidding what Allah and His Messenger hate is part of calling to Allah.

Calling to Allah also includes the servant doing what Allah and His Messenger love and abandoning what Allah and His Messenger hate, in both inward and outward words and deeds, in accordance with what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, conveyed concerning Allah’s names and attributes, and concerning creation at large, such as the Throne, the Footstool, the angels, and the prophets; and that Allah and His Messenger should be dearer to him than anything else.

---

## Page 9832

Calling to Allah is obligatory upon those who follow the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, namely his community. Allah has described them in these terms, as in His words, Most High:

“Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet,”

through to His words:

“the successful.”

This passage concerns him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Concerning them, Allah says:

“You are the best community brought forth for mankind”—the verse.

And He says:

“The believing men and believing women are allies of one another; they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong”—the verse.

This duty rests upon the community as a whole. It is a collective obligation: when some fulfil it, the others are relieved of it. As Allah says:

“Let there be among you a group calling to goodness”—the verse.

Thus, the community collectively takes his place in calling to Allah. On this basis, their consensus constitutes authoritative proof. When they disagree about anything, they refer it back to Allah and His Messenger.

With this established, every believer must love what Allah and His Messenger love and hate what Allah and His Messenger hate, as indicated in His Book. No one may make anyone other than the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the foundational authority in religion, nor make religious pronouncements except on the basis of the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Whoever sets up an individual—whoever he may be—and bases allegiance and hostility on agreement with him in word and deed is

“among those who divided their religion and became sects”—the verse.

If a man acquires religious understanding and cultivates his conduct according to the way of a group of believers—for example, by following imams and shaykhs—he may not make his exemplar and his companions the standard, showing allegiance to those who agree with them

---

## Page 9833

and showing hostility to those who disagree with them. A person should therefore train himself to cultivate inward understanding in his heart and act upon it, for this serves as a restraint. What lies hidden in hearts becomes apparent in times of trial.

No one may advocate a position, believe in it, or engage in conflict over it merely because it is the position of his companions. Rather, he should do so because it is something Allah and His Messenger have commanded or conveyed, and thus constitutes obedience to Allah and His Messenger. The caller should give priority to the evidence they cite from the Quran, for it is light and guidance. Next, he should place the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as the imam of all imams, followed by the statements of the imams.

The caller’s situation falls into one of two cases:

First: he either exercises independent scholarly judgment or follows the judgments of others. The one exercising independent judgment examines the writings of the early scholars from the first three generations, then gives preference to whichever view deserves preference.

Second: the follower follows the early generations, since the earlier generations are better than those that came after them.

With this established, we say, as our Lord has commanded us:

“Say: We believe in Allah,”

through to His words:

“Muslims.”

We enjoin what He has commanded us and forbid what He has prohibited us, as stated explicitly in His Book and conveyed through His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. As He, Most High, says:

“Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it”—the verse.

Thus, the rulings of this religion rest upon three foundations: the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus.

## Page 9834

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked about the meaning of scholarly consensus: May a scholar exercising independent judgment disagree with them? What does it mean? Is the statement of a Companion authoritative evidence?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah.

Consensus means that the Muslim scholars agree upon a ruling. Once the Muslim community’s consensus on a ruling is established, no one may depart from it, for the community does not agree upon misguidance. However, in many matters some people suppose that a consensus exists when this is not the case; rather, the opposing view has stronger support in the Book and the Sunnah.

As for the statements of individual imams, such as the four leading jurists and others, these constitute neither binding evidence nor consensus, as the Muslims agree. Indeed, it is established that these imams—may Allah be pleased with them—forbade people to follow their judgments uncritically. They instructed them, whenever they found a view more strongly supported by the Book and the Sunnah than their own, to adopt what the Book and the Sunnah indicated and leave aside their statements. For this reason, it has always been the practice of the leading followers of the four imams, whenever

---

## Page 9835

it became clear to them that the Book or the Sunnah supported a position contrary to that of the imam they followed, to follow that evidence. One example concerns the distance at which prayers may be shortened. Since fixing this at three days’ travel or sixteen parasangs was a weak position, some scholars among Ahmad’s followers and others held that prayers could be shortened on journeys shorter than that, such as the journey from Mecca to ‘Arafah. It is established that the people of Mecca shortened their prayers with the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—at Minā and ‘Arafah.

Likewise, some followers of Mālik, Abū Hanīfah and Ahmad held that pronouncing three divorces together is forbidden and an innovation, because, in their understanding, the Book and the Sunnah supported only that conclusion. They thus disagreed with their imams. Some followers of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī and Abū Hanīfah held that ritually impure oil could be washed, contrary to the position of the four imams. Some followers of Abū Hanīfah held that people could be made to swear oaths invoking divorce, contrary to the position of the four imams. Indeed, Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr stated that a consensus had been reached against this.

Some followers of Mālik and others held that whoever swears an oath invoking divorce is to offer expiation for his oath, and likewise whoever swears an oath invoking emancipation. The same view was also held by some followers of

---

## Page 9836

Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfi‘ī. They said that whoever says, “Divorce is binding upon me,” does not thereby effect a divorce, nor does anyone who swears an oath using this formula. This is also reported from Abū Hanīfah himself.

Some scholars held that whoever swears an oath invoking divorce does not thereby effect a divorce, nor is he required to offer expiation. It is established from the Companions and the leading Successors that, when someone swears an oath invoking emancipation, emancipation does not become binding upon him; rather, expiation for an oath suffices. The positions of the four imams differ from this. This applies all the more to oaths invoking divorce. Accordingly, some leading Successors held that an oath invoking divorce does not effect a divorce, treating it instead as an oath requiring expiation.

This differs from actually effecting a divorce: if undertaken in the manner prescribed by Islamic law, it takes effect by the unanimous agreement of the Muslim community, and no expiation is due, likewise by their unanimous agreement. Indeed, no expiation applies to effecting a divorce at all; expiation pertains specifically to swearing oaths.

When Muslims disagree over a matter, they must refer their disagreement to Allah and the Messenger. Whichever of the two positions is supported by the Quran and the Sunnah must be followed. One example is the position that distinguishes between making a vow, emancipating a slave or effecting a divorce, and swearing an oath invoking any of these. This distinction is supported by the Quran, the Sunnah, the statements of the Companions and analogical reasoning. Allah mentions the ruling on divorce in His words, Exalted is He:

“When you divorce women”

and He mentions the ruling on oaths in His words:

“Allah has prescribed for you release from your oaths.”

It is established in the authentic hadith collections that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said: “Whoever swears

---

## Page 9837

an oath and then sees that another course is better, let him do what is better and expiate his oath.”

Whoever assigns one ruling to oaths invoking these matters and another to making vows, emancipating slaves and effecting divorce holds a position consistent with the Quran and the Sunnah. Whoever treats the two alike has contradicted the Quran and the Sunnah. Anyone who supposes that there is a consensus on this does so according to the extent of his knowledge, because he knows of no disagreement concerning it. Yet how could the Muslim community agree upon a weak position outweighed by stronger evidence, unsupported by any sound proof, when the Quran, the Sunnah, the reports from the Companions and sound analogy all contradict it?

There are three forms of wording:

A formula that effects divorce, such as saying, “You are divorced.” This is not an oath, by unanimous agreement.

An oath formula, such as saying, “Divorce is binding upon me: I will certainly do such-and-such.” This is an oath formula, by unanimous agreement.

A conditional formula, such as saying, “If you commit adultery, you are divorced.” In this case, if he intends the divorce to take effect when the condition is met—that is, if he wishes to effect the divorce if she commits adultery

---

## Page 9838

and not remain married to an adulteress—then this effects divorce and is not an oath. But if he intends to deter and restrain her, without intending to divorce her if she commits adultery, then this is an oath, by unanimous agreement.

Section

As for the statements of the Companions, if they became widely known and were not challenged during their lifetime, they constitute authoritative evidence according to the vast majority of scholars. If the Companions disagreed, the matter in dispute must be referred back to Allah and the Messenger. Scholars unanimously agree that the statement of some Companions is not authoritative evidence when other Companions oppose it.

If one of them expressed a view, none expressed a contrary view, and it did not become widely known, its authority is disputed. The majority of scholars accept it as evidence, including Abū Hanīfa, Mālik, Ahmad—according to the well-known position reported from him—and al-Shāfi'ī in one of his two positions. Indeed, in his later works, al-Shāfi'ī relies on such statements as evidence in several places. Nevertheless, some people say that this was his earlier position.

## Page 9839

He was asked about independent reasoning, inference from evidence, imitation, and following others.

He replied:

Invalid, blameworthy imitation means accepting another person’s statement without proof. Allah Most High says:

“When it is said to them, ‘Follow what Allah has revealed,’ they say, ‘Rather, we follow what we found our forefathers following.’ Even though their forefathers understood nothing and were not guided?”

This is in al-Baqara; similar passages occur in al-Mā’ida and in Luqmān:

“Even if Satan were inviting them…”

And in al-Zukhruf:

“He said, ‘Even if I bring you better guidance than what you found your forefathers following?’”

And in al-Sāffāt:

“Indeed, they found their forefathers astray.”

“So they rush in their footsteps.”

And He says:

“On the Day their faces are turned about in the Fire, they will say, ‘If only we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!’”

“And they will say, ‘Our Lord, we obeyed our masters and our great ones, and they led us astray from the path.’”

And the following verses.

And He says:

“When those who were followed disown those who followed them, and they see the punishment, and all ties between them are severed.”

And He says:

“The weak will say to those who were arrogant, ‘We were your followers; will you then relieve us of any share of the Fire?’”

And in the other verse:

“Anything of Allah’s punishment.”

And He says:

“So that they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection

---

## Page 9840

and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge.”

This following and imitation which Allah condemns amounts to following one’s desires, whether because of custom and lineage, as in following one’s forefathers, or because of authority, as in following prominent people, masters, and the arrogant. It resembles a person’s imitation of his father, his master, or someone who holds authority over him. This occurs with someone who is not yet independent, namely a child. His religion is that of his mother; if she is absent, it is that of his ruler and his father. If the latter is absent, as in the case of a foundling, his religion is that of those responsible for him—namely, the inhabitants of the town where he lives. Once he reaches maturity and can speak for himself, however, he is either grateful or ungrateful. Allah has made clear that one must turn away from this imitation and instead follow what Allah has revealed to His messengers, for they are Allah’s proof through whom He has left His creation without excuse.

The discussion of imitation concerns two matters: whether it is valid or invalid as evidence, and whether it is sanctioned or not under religious law. As for the first, the imitation in question yields no knowledge. The person being imitated may be right or wrong, and the imitator does not know whether he is right or wrong. Thus, he gains neither confidence nor reassurance. If, however, he knows that the person he imitates is right

---

## Page 9841

—as when following the Messenger or those whose agreement constitutes consensus—then he follows on the basis of proof: his knowledge that the person followed possesses knowledge. This is not the imitation under discussion. Such imitation is obligatory, because it is known that the Messenger is protected from error and that those whose agreement constitutes consensus are protected from error. As for imitating a scholar where this is permissible, it is comparable to following evidence that yields a strong presumption, such as solitary reports and analogical reasoning. The imitator considers it highly probable that the scholar exercising independent judgment is correct, just as he considers it highly probable that an informant is truthful. There is, however, a difference between following a transmitter and following an opinion, which will be discussed elsewhere, Allah willing.

Following a transmitter is obligatory because he alone possesses knowledge of what he reports. An opinion, by contrast, can be arrived at through the same means by which its holder arrived at it. Moreover, errors in transmission are unlikely, since accurately preserving a report is easy; hence reports have been transmitted on the authority of women and ordinary people. Errors in reasoning, by contrast, are frequent because its methods are subtle and numerous. This is the accepted practice among those who permit accepting a report even when it is possible to consult the person on whose authority it is transmitted, but do not permit accepting an interpretation when it is possible to ascertain the evidence.

As for the former accepted practice, the scholars agree upon it. Hence they require following a report, whereas no one requires a person capable of examining the evidence to imitate a scholar. They differ only over whether doing so is permissible, since that person can acquire knowledge through the same means by which the scholar acquired it. This, then, is a general outline.

---

## Page 9842

As for the details, we say:

People adopt two opposite extremes regarding the examination of evidence and imitation. Some require everyone to examine the evidence even in subtle questions, whether fundamental or subsidiary. Others forbid anyone from examining the evidence in subtle questions, both fundamental and subsidiary. The best course is the middle one.

---

## Page 9843

He was also asked:

“Is everyone who exercises independent reasoning correct, or is only one correct and the rest mistaken?”

He replied:

This question has been discussed at length elsewhere, together with the disagreement concerning it. It has also been explained that the word “error” may mean sin, or it may mean lack of knowledge. If the former is intended, then everyone who exercises independent reasoning and fears Allah to the best of his ability is correct, for he is obedient to Allah and is neither sinful nor blameworthy. If the latter is intended, some who exercise independent reasoning may be granted knowledge hidden from others. This may be knowledge of the reality of the matter which, had another person become aware of it, he would have been obliged to follow.

However, that obligation is waived for him because he is unable to fulfill it, and he receives a reward for his effort in reasoning. But the one who reaches the correct conclusion receives two rewards, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith whose authenticity is agreed upon:

“When a judge exercises independent judgment and is correct, he receives two rewards; when he exercises independent judgment and errs, he receives one reward.”

---

## Page 9844

And the word khata’ (“error”) is used of both deliberate and unintentional acts. Allah Most High says:

“Do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Surely killing them is a grievous sin.”

Most reciters read khit’an, patterned like rid’an and ‘ilman. Ibn ‘Āmir read khata’an, patterned like ‘amalan, corresponding to the word khata’ in His saying:

“It is not for a believer to kill another believer, except by mistake.”

Ibn Kathīr read khitā’an, patterned like hijā’an. Ibn Razīn read khatā’an, patterned like sharāban. Al-Hasan and Qatādah read khat’an, patterned like qatlan. Al-Zuhrī read khitā, without a hamzah, patterned like ‘idan.

Al-Akhfash said: “Khatā–yakhta’u means ‘to sin’; it does not have the meaning of akhta’a, which refers to something done unintentionally. For something done deliberately, one says khattaytu (‘I sinned’), whereas for something done unintentionally, one says akhta’tu (‘I erred’).”

Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī likewise said: “Khata’ means sin. One says khatā–yakhta’u when someone sins, and akhta’a–yukhti’u when someone departs from what is correct.”

Ibn al-Anbārī said likewise concerning His saying:

“By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us, and we were indeed sinners.”

The commentators, including Ibn ‘Abbās and others, explained this as meaning: “We were guilty of sin in our treatment of you.” It is indeed as they said, for they also said:

“Our father, ask forgiveness for our sins; we were indeed sinners.”

Likewise, al-‘Azīz said to his wife:

“Ask forgiveness for your sin; you were indeed one of the sinners.”

Ibn al-Anbārī explained that this is why khāti’īn (“sinners”) was chosen rather than mukhti’īn (“those who err”), even though akhta’a is more common in people’s speech than khatā–yukhtī: khatā–yukhtī, whose active participle is khāti’, means being sinful, whereas akhta’a–yukhti’u means departing from what is correct

---

## Page 9845

without committing a sin.

He said:
“Your servants err, while You are a Lord
who has charge of death and all that is decreed.”

Al-Farrā’ said: “Khata’ means sin. Al-khatā, al-khatā, and the lengthened form al-khatā’: three linguistic forms.”

I say:
Khata’ is used of deliberate acts, just as it is used of unintentional acts, according to Ibn ‘Āmir’s reading. Thus, someone who acts unintentionally may be told akhta’ta (“you erred”), just as he may be told khattayta (“you erred”). The word khatī’ah (“sin”) is derived from this. Examples include the words of Allah Most High:

“Because of their sins they were drowned,”

and the words of the magicians:

“We hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins, since we were the first to believe.”

Another example is His saying in the authentic divine hadith:

“My servants, you sin by night and day, and I forgive all sins. So seek My forgiveness, and I will forgive you.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Mūsā reported that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) used to say in his supplication:

“O Allah, forgive my sin, my ignorance, my excesses in my affairs, and whatever You know better than I do. O Allah, forgive what I have done in jest and in earnest, unintentionally and deliberately; all of these are found in me.”

The two Sahīh collections also relate from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), the following exchange:

“Tell me, what do you say during your silence between the opening takbīr and the recitation?”

He replied: “I say: ‘O Allah, distance me from my sins as You have distanced the east from the west. O Allah, cleanse me of my sins as a white garment is cleansed of dirt. O Allah, wash away my sins with water, snow, and hail.’”

---

## Page 9846

Those who say, “Every scholar exercising independent judgment is correct, and such a scholar cannot be in error,” and object to saying that such a scholar has erred—as well as many ordinary people—dislike saying of a great imam that he erred or that his statement was mistaken. This is because the term is used for sin, as in Ibn ‘Āmir’s reading: “Indeed, it is a grave sin.” Moreover, the verb akhta’a, yukhti’u (“to err”) is used of someone acting deliberately, as in His saying:

“My servants, you sin by night and day, and I forgive all sins. So seek My forgiveness, and I will forgive you.”

Thus, the terms khata’ (“error”) and akhta’a (“to err”) may encompass both kinds of action, while also being used specifically for unintentional acts. The term khatī’ah (“sin”), however, is used only for sinful conduct.

The usual usage distinguishes khata’ (“error”) from deliberate action, as Allah Most High says:

“It is not for a believer to kill another believer except by mistake,”

and so on to the end of the verse. He then says:

“But whoever kills a believer intentionally—his recompense is Hell.”

The jurists have explained that error falls into two categories: error in carrying out an action and error in what one intends.

The first is when someone intends to shoot at something that may lawfully be shot at, such as game or a target, but his shot goes astray. This entails expiation and blood money.

The second is when someone errs in what he intends because he lacks knowledge, just as his error in the former case results from a lack of

---

## Page 9847

physical ability. This is when someone shoots a person whom he believes it lawful to kill, although that person’s life is protected—as when someone kills a man in the ranks of the unbelievers, only to discover that he was a Muslim. Errors in knowledge belong to this category. Hence, according to one of the two scholarly opinions, no blood money is due in this case, because the act was one he was commanded to perform, unlike the first case.

Allah Most High also says:

“There is no blame upon you for what you do by mistake, but only for what your hearts deliberately intend.”

He thus distinguishes between the two kinds. Allah Most High also says:

“Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake.”

It is established in the Sahīh that Allah Most High said:

“I have done so.”

Thus, the terms khata’ (“error”) and akhta’a (“to err”), when used without qualification, encompass unintentional action. When mentioned alongside forgetfulness or contrasted with deliberate action, they refer unequivocally to unintentional action. With a contextual indication, however, they may denote deliberate action, or both deliberate and unintentional action, as in Ibn ‘Āmir’s reading and in the divine hadith—if its wording is as most hadith scholars transmit it: tukhti’ūna (“you sin”), with a u-vowel on the initial letter.

As for the designation khāti’ (“sinner”), it occurs in the Quran only in reference to sin, in the sense conveyed by khatī’ah (“sin”), as in His saying:

“And seek forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were among the sinners.”

And His saying:

“Allah has certainly favored you over us, and we were indeed sinners.”

And His saying:

“O our father, seek forgiveness for our sins; indeed, we were sinners.”

And His saying:

“None but sinners will eat it.”

---

## Page 9848

Once this is clear, every jurist exercising independent judgment is correct—neither sinful nor mistaken—if “error” is understood to mean sin, in accordance with Ibn ‘Āmir’s reading. No error, in this sense, proceeds from a jurist exercising independent judgment. This is what those who say, “Every jurist exercising independent judgment is correct,” intended. They maintain that error and sin are inseparable: for them, the word “error” is equivalent to “sin,” in accordance with Ibn ‘Āmir’s reading. They acknowledge that some knowledge beyond his ability to attain remains hidden from him, but they do not call this an error, since it was not required of him. They may, however, call it an error in a relative sense: he has missed something which, had he known it, he would have been obliged to follow, and which would then have constituted Allah’s ruling applicable to him.

However, the Companions, the four Imams—may Allah be pleased with them—and the majority of the early generations apply the word “error” to what is unintentional, even when it involves no sin. The Quran and Sunnah explicitly use it this way in several places. Thus, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“When a judge exercises independent judgment and is correct, he receives two rewards; when he exercises independent judgment and errs, he receives one reward.”

More than one Companion, including Ibn Mas‘ūd, said:

“I shall give my own considered opinion on this matter. If it is correct, it is from Allah; if it is mistaken, it is from me and Satan. Allah and His Messenger are free of it.”

In the case of the woman whom ‘Umar summoned and who consequently miscarried, ‘Uthmān and ‘Abd al-Rahmān—may Allah be pleased with them both—told him, “You were acting to discipline her, and no liability rests upon you.” ‘Alī then said:

“If they exercised independent judgment, they erred; if they did not exercise independent judgment, they have given you dishonest counsel.”

---

## Page 9849

Ahmad draws a distinction in this matter. If an issue is addressed by an authentic hadith with no evidence opposing it, anyone who follows a weak hadith or the opinion of a Companion is mistaken. If two authentic hadiths address the issue, he considers which carries greater weight and follows it, without declaring someone who follows the other mistaken. If no scriptural text addresses the issue, he exercises independent judgment, saying:

“I do not know whether I have reached the truth or missed it.”

Thus, he distinguishes between cases where there is a text that must be followed and cases where there is not. If someone follows one text while remaining unaware of another text addressing the issue, Ahmad does not call him mistaken, because he has done what was required of him.

This distinction, however, concerns determining who is in error. Some people say, “I do not categorically declare my opponent mistaken in matters open to independent judgment.” Others say, “I categorically declare him mistaken.” Ahmad distinguishes between cases, and this is the correct approach. Even when he categorically judges someone mistaken in the sense of lacking knowledge, he does not categorically judge him sinful. The latter judgment applies only to someone known not to have exercised independent judgment.

The reality is that a text may remain unknown to a jurist exercising independent judgment, who has no means of learning of it, although he would have been obliged to follow it had he known it. Because it remained unknown to him, he followed another text that had been abrogated or whose scope had been restricted. He has thereby done what was required of him to the best of his ability, like those who prayed facing Jerusalem after that direction of prayer had been abrogated but before they learned of the abrogation.

This is because, according to the soundest view, a scriptural ruling does not become binding upon those legally accountable until they have the opportunity to learn of it. Another view holds that it takes effect in the sense of requiring the act to be made up, but not

---

## Page 9850

in the sense of incurring sin. A third view holds that this applies to an initial scriptural ruling, but not to one that abrogates an earlier ruling. All three views are found in the school of Ahmad and elsewhere.

Accordingly, if a jurist exercising independent judgment has not heard certain abrogating texts or texts whose scope has been restricted, and has had no means of learning of them, their ruling is not binding upon him. He is obeying Allah by acting upon the abrogated or general text and incurs no sin in doing so.

There are three views on this point:

One holds that he must follow the underlying ruling, and that if he errs, he is mistaken before Allah and, with respect to the ruling, has failed to do what he was commanded. Yet those who hold this view also say that he incurs no sin. This is contradictory, for anyone who fails to do what he has been commanded is sinful. How, then, can he fail to do what he was commanded without being sinful?

Another view holds that he was never commanded to follow the underlying ruling; it is not a ruling applicable to him, nor has he mistaken Allah’s ruling. Allah has no underlying ruling applicable to him other than the one he has reached. Nor may he be described as mistaken, for in their view, error necessarily entails sin. Yet they concede that, had he known that ruling, he would have been obliged to act upon it, and it would have been applicable to him. The dispute is therefore one of terminology. By prohibiting the use of this expression, however, they have contravened the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Companions. Moreover, their statement that there is no underlying ruling is mistaken. Rather, Allah’s underlying ruling

---

## Page 9851

is what is stated in the abrogating and specific texts. However, he is not obliged to act upon it until he is able to learn of it; his inability therefore exempts him from that obligation.

Another view holds that Allah’s ruling applicable to him was the underlying ruling, but once he exercised independent judgment and came to believe that a particular conclusion was most likely Allah’s ruling, Allah’s ruling applicable to him changed, and he was now commanded to follow that conclusion.

The correct view is what Ahmad and others have stated: he must exercise independent judgment. That is his obligation; he is not obliged to arrive at the underlying ruling if he is unable to do so. He is required only to exercise independent judgment. If he neglects to do so, he sins. If he exercises independent judgment but is unable to ascertain the underlying ruling, he is not commanded to follow it while unable to do so. Nevertheless, he is commanded to follow it, and it is Allah’s ruling applicable to him, on condition that he is able to do so.

Anyone who says that it is Allah’s underlying ruling in this sense has spoken truthfully. If he exercises independent judgment and Allah makes the underlying truth clear to him, he receives two rewards, as Allah Most High says:

“So We gave Solomon understanding of it.”

We do not say that Allah’s ruling applicable to him changed, such that before exercising independent judgment he was commanded to follow the underlying truth, but afterwards he was commanded to follow what he believed to be correct. Rather, he has always been commanded to exercise independent judgment and fear Allah as much as he can. He was indeed commanded to follow the truth, but on condition that he was able to do so. If he is unable, he is not commanded to do so. He is commanded to exercise independent judgment; if that leads him to a different view, he must act

---

## Page 9852

upon it—not because he was commanded to follow that particular view, but because Allah commanded him to act according to the conclusions of his independent judgment and what he could ascertain. Since that view was all he could arrive at, he is commanded to follow it because it lies within his capacity, not because of the view itself.

This is like people who exercise independent judgment to determine the direction of prayer and then pray facing four different directions. Only one has correctly faced the direction of prayer, yet all have done what they were commanded to do, and none incurs sin. The obligation to ascertain the precise direction is waived for those unable to determine it. Each person is instead obliged to exercise independent judgment to the extent of his ability and face what he consequently believes to be the direction of the Kaaba. He is commanded to follow what is actually correct, but on condition that he can ascertain it. He is also commanded to follow what he believes to be correct and within his capacity. When he arrives at that view, it becomes binding upon him not because the Lawgiver—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—has specifically prescribed it, but because it is what he is capable of.

However, if he is following a text and its abrogating text has not reached him, he is commanded to continue following it until he learns of the abrogating text. The abrogated ruling was Allah’s ruling applicable to him, both inwardly and outwardly, and this is not accepted until the abrogating text has reached him.

As for general wording whose scope has been restricted, it may be said that the Lawgiver did not intend to include the excluded case, but the person believed that He intended to include it because he was unaware of the restriction. The same may be said of texts abrogated before the independent jurist became obliged to act upon them, such as texts abrogated during the lifetime of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—whose abrogation remained unknown to some people, although the text abrogated by them had reached the person concerned. It cannot be said that the abrogated text

---

## Page 9853

had a ruling applicable to him, both inwardly and outwardly, as was said of those whose obligation to face the direction of prayer applied both inwardly and outwardly before its abrogation. Rather, it should be said: whoever has not received the abrogating text but has received the other text must follow it and act upon it. Accordingly, the rulings applicable to independent jurists differ according to their ability to ascertain the evidence. For someone unable to ascertain the stronger evidence, such as an abrogating text or one restricting the scope of a general text, Allah’s ruling is that he act upon the evidence he has been able to ascertain. Even if stronger, conflicting evidence actually exists, he is not obliged to follow it unless he is able to ascertain it.

Likewise, if a verse admits two meanings, and one of them is not apparent to a particular person, who recognizes only what is not apparent to another, he must act upon the evidence that has led him to that meaning, even though someone else must act upon the evidence that has led him to the other meaning. Each has fulfilled his obligation. Yet Allah’s ruling in reality is one, with the obligation to follow it conditional upon ability.

If it is said, “But Allah also commanded that person to do what he did,” the response is: He did not command that particular act as such. Rather, He commanded him to fear Allah as much as he could and to act according to what was apparent to him; and nothing but this was apparent to him. He is therefore commanded to do it insofar as it falls within the general category of what is within the independent jurist’s ability, known to him, and apparent to him—not on account of that particular act in itself.

Thus, whoever says, “He was not commanded to do it,” is correct. And whoever says, “He was commanded to do it insofar as it was what he was able to do, what he knew, what was apparent to him, and what the evidence indicated to him,” is correct.

---

## Page 9854

as when two witnesses testify before a judge but are mistaken in their testimony. He is commanded, as a general rule, to judge according to their testimony; he has not been commanded to rule otherwise in this particular case. Hence the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“You bring your disputes before me, and some of you may present your arguments more eloquently than others. I judge only according to what I hear. If I award anyone something that rightfully belongs to his brother, let him not take it, for I am only allotting him a piece of the Fire.”

Thus, when one litigant’s evidence becomes apparent to him while the other has not presented his evidence, he has acted according to what was apparent to him. Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. He is obedient to Allah in fulfilling his own duty within the limits of his ability and knowledge, not because Allah has commanded that particular ruling in itself. Allah does not command falsehood, injustice, or error, but He does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. This encompasses prophetic judgments and judgments based on reports.

The independent jurist who errs receives a reward because he intended to reach the truth and sought it to the best of his ability, judging only on the basis of evidence. This is like a judge ruling on the basis of a litigant’s admission of a liability, although that liability may subsequently have been discharged through release or payment, without evidence of this being established. Likewise, he may rule that someone is free of liability upon taking an oath, although that person may have incurred a liability through borrowing, purchasing, or some other transaction, without evidence of this being established. Judgment may also be given in favour of the person in possession upon his taking an oath, although ownership may have passed from him to someone else, or he may be holding the property as a usurper, without evidence of this being established.

---

## Page 9855

The same applies to general evidence: an independent jurist may rule according to its general purport without having received the evidence that qualifies it; or according to a text that has been abrogated without his knowing it; or he may adopt an analogy that appears to establish equivalence, although the case in question has a legally significant distinguishing feature that he has been unable to discern. The significance of that distinction may be established by a text that has not reached him, or it may consist in a subtle characteristic.

In short, he is rewarded for following the truth to the best of his ability through independent reasoning, even if the actual truth contradicts his conclusion and would have a greater claim to be followed had he been able to ascertain it. But he was unable to do so. His case is therefore like that of those who strive to determine the direction of the Kaaba.

The same applies to anyone who performs a prohibited act of worship without knowing of the prohibition, provided that it belongs to a generally prescribed category of worship. An example is someone who prays at prohibited times, having learned of the general command to pray but not of the prohibition. Another is someone who relies on specific evidence that is outweighed by stronger evidence, as did a number of the early Muslims who prayed two units after the afternoon prayer because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, had prayed them. Other examples include prayers concerning which weak or fabricated hadiths have been transmitted, such as the Alfiyyah prayer of mid-Shaʿbān, the prayer at the beginning of Rajab, and the prayer of glorification, which Ibn al-Mubārak permitted, as well as other such prayers.

If such a prayer falls within the general recommendation to pray, and the person has not received evidence establishing its prohibition, he is rewarded for it—even if it is prohibited in a respect unknown to him, owing to its being an innovation adopted as an established observance for which people gather every year. This is like introducing a sixth prayer. Thus, if someone wished to perform such a prayer without a hadith to support it, he would not be entitled to do so. But when the hadith was transmitted, he believed it to be authentic and was mistaken in that; such a person is forgiven

---

## Page 9856

for his error and is rewarded for performing an act within a generally prescribed category of worship. The same applies to someone who fasts on the day of Eid without knowing of the prohibition.

This differs from acts whose very category has not been prescribed, such as shirk (associating partners with Allah). There is no reward for this, even though Allah does not punish the person who commits it until the message has reached him. As Allah Most High says:

“We never punish until We have sent a messenger.”

Yet although He does not punish him, the person receives no reward for this. Rather, it is as Allah Most High says:

“And We will turn to whatever deeds they did and make them scattered dust.”

Ibn al-Mubārak said: “These are deeds performed for other than Allah.” Mujāhid said: “These are deeds that were not accepted.” Allah Most High also says:

“The deeds of those who disbelieve in their Lord are like ashes swept away by a fierce wind,”

to the end of the verse. Their deeds are therefore invalid and carry no reward. If the Messenger forbids them from these acts and they do not desist, they are punished. Punishment for them is thus conditional upon the Messenger’s conveying the prohibition. Their inherent invalidity, however, is because they have not been commanded. Every act of worship that has not been commanded must therefore be forbidden.

If someone knows that it is forbidden and performs it, he deserves punishment; if he does not know, he does not deserve punishment. If he believes it to have been commanded, and it belongs to a generally prescribed category of worship, he is rewarded for it. But if it belongs to the category of shirk, nothing within that category has been commanded, although some people may suppose that certain forms of it have been commanded.

Such a person does not qualify as an independent jurist, because an independent jurist must follow evidence from revealed law, and these practices can have no such evidence. He may, however, perform them through the sort of reasoning exercised by someone like him: namely, following the shaykhs and scholars who have done so. Those who performed them may have done so because they found them beneficial, or because of a fabricated hadith they heard.

If the proof establishing the prohibition has not been made clear to these people, they are not punished. As for reward, their reward may consist in their being better than others of their kind. But reward for drawing near to Allah cannot be attained through such deeds.

---

## Page 9857

Section

Forgiven errors in independent reasoning occur in both categories of questions—those concerning transmitted reports and those concerning knowledge—as has been explained at length in several places. For example, someone may believe something to be established on the evidence of a verse or hadith, while remaining unaware of other evidence that counters that conclusion and clarifies the intended meaning. Such is the case of someone who believes that Isaac was the son to be sacrificed, based on a hadith he believes to be authentic; or someone who believes that Allah cannot be seen because He says:

“Vision does not encompass Him,”

and:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation or from behind a veil.”

Similarly, Ā’ishah cited these two verses to deny that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had seen Allah, although they support that conclusion only through the generality of their wording.

---

## Page 9858

And likewise, some of the Successors are reported to have held that Allah cannot be seen and to have interpreted His words:

“Some faces on that Day will be radiant,”

“looking at their Lord,”

as meaning that they will be awaiting their Lord’s reward, as reported from Mujāhid and Abū Sālih.

Or someone may believe that the deceased is not punished on account of the weeping of the living, because he believes that His words:

“No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another,”

indicate this, and that this takes precedence over a narrator’s report because hearing is susceptible to error. This was the belief of a group among the earlier and later generations.

Or someone may believe that the deceased cannot hear the living addressing them, because he believes that His words:

“Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear,”

indicate this.

Or someone may believe that Allah does not marvel, as Shurayh believed, because he holds that marvelling arises only from ignorance of the cause, whereas Allah is exalted above ignorance.

Or someone may believe that ʿAlī is the best of the Companions, because he believes the hadith of the bird to be authentic, and that “the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘O Allah, bring me the one most beloved to You among Your creation, to eat some of this bird with me.’”

Or someone may believe that anyone who spies for the enemy and informs them of the military expedition of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace

---

## Page 9859

is a hypocrite—as ʿUmar believed concerning Hātib, saying, “Let me strike off this hypocrite’s head.”

Or someone may believe that anyone who becomes angry in defense of some hypocrites is a hypocrite—as Usayd ibn Hudayr believed concerning Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah, saying, “You are a hypocrite arguing on behalf of the hypocrites.”

Or someone may believe that certain words or verses are not part of the Quran because they have not been established for him through reliable transmission. Thus, a number of the early generations reportedly rejected certain wordings of the Quran. One of them rejected:

“Your Lord has decreed,”

saying, “It is actually: ‘Your Lord has enjoined.’” Another rejected His words:

“When Allah took the covenant of the prophets,”

saying, “It is actually ‘the covenant of the Children of Israel.’” This is also how it appears in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh. Another rejected:

“Have those who believe not yet realized,”

maintaining that it is actually: “Has it not become clear to those who believe?”

Likewise, ʿUmar objected to Hishām ibn al-Hakam when he found him reciting Surah al-Furqān differently from the way he himself recited it. Similarly, some of the early generations objected to certain reciters’ use of readings unfamiliar to them, until ʿUthmān united them upon the standard codex.

Likewise, some among the earlier and later generations denied that Allah wills acts of disobedience, believing this to mean that Allah loves them, is pleased with them, and commands them. Another group denied

---

## Page 9860

that Allah wills acts of disobedience, because they—people from among the earlier and later generations—thought that willing could only mean willing to create them. They knew that Allah is the Creator of all things, and that whatever He wills comes to pass, while whatever He does not will does not come to pass. The Quran uses the word “will” in both senses, but each group recognized one meaning and denied the other.

Another example is the man who said to his family:

“When I die, burn me, then scatter me in the sea. By Allah, if Allah has power over me, He will punish me as He punishes no one else in all creation.”

Similar examples are those mentioned by some of the early generations concerning His words:

“Does he think that no one has power over him?”

And concerning the words of the disciples:

“Can your Lord send down to us a table spread with food from heaven?”

Likewise, the Companions who asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Will we see our Lord on the Day of Resurrection?” did not know that they would see Him. Many people do not know this, either because the hadiths have not reached them or because they think those reports are false and erroneous.

## Page 9861

Section

Allah has distinguished between the periods before and after the coming of the message in certain designations and rulings, while treating them alike in others. This is evidence against both groups: those who say that actions are neither good nor bad, and those who say that people deserve punishment, on either of the two views.

As for the first position, Allah called them wrongdoers, transgressors and corrupters, as in His words:

“Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.”

And His words:

“And when your Lord called Moses, ‘Go to the wrongdoing people—the people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear Allah?’”

And His words:

“Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and divided its people into factions, oppressing one group among them, slaughtering their sons and sparing their women. Indeed, he was one of the corrupters.”

Thus, He described Pharaoh and his people as wrongdoers, transgressors and corrupters. These are designations that condemn actions, and condemnation applies only to evil, bad actions. This shows that actions can be bad and blameworthy before the Messenger comes to people. Yet they do not deserve punishment until the Messenger has come to them, for Allah says:

“We never punish until We have sent a messenger.”

Likewise, He relates that Hūd said to his people:

“Worship Allah; you have no

---

## Page 9862

god other than Him. You are nothing but fabricators.” Thus, He described them as fabricators before issuing a ruling that they would contravene, because they had set up another god alongside Allah. The designation “polytheist” therefore applies before the coming of the message: a person associates partners with his Lord, sets others equal to Him, takes other gods alongside Him and assigns rivals to Him before the Messenger comes. This establishes that these designations precede the message. Likewise, the terms “ignorance” and “the state of ignorance” apply: one may speak of a state of ignorance and describe someone as ignorant before the Messenger comes. Punishment, however, does not apply before then.

As for turning away from obedience, as in His words:

“He neither believed nor prayed, but denied and turned away,”

this can only occur after the Messenger comes. An example is His statement about Pharaoh:

“But he denied and disobeyed.”

This was after the Messenger had come to him, as Allah Most High says:

“He showed him the greatest sign, but he denied and disobeyed.”

And He says:

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger.” (1).

Were al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasā’ī, Ibn Mājah, Abū Dāwūd al-Tayālisī, al-Dārimī, al-Bazzār, al-Dāraqutnī, al-Bayhaqī, Ibn Khuzaymah and Abū Ya‘lā al-Mawsilī independent jurists who did not follow the authority of any of the imams, or did they follow the authority of others? Did any of them adhere to the school of Abū Hanīfah?

“From Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd, from Ibrāhīm ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hārith al-Taymī, from ‘Ā’ishah,”

and the following is found in al-Bukhārī:

can it be said that the latter is more authentic than the former in the Muwatta’?

If a hadith appears in al-Bukhārī with one chain of transmission and in the Muwatta’ with another, can it be said that the version in al-Bukhārī is more authentic? As for Abū Dāwūd al-Tayālisī, he predates all of these. in mindfulness of Allah, they roam through His dominion and return to their owners bearing choice insights, without any scholar imparting knowledge to them.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

## Page 9868

sin and righteousness stir within people’s hearts, what, then, of someone for whom Allah is his hearing and sight, and who has Him in his heart?

Ibn Masʿūd said:

“Sin takes hold of hearts.”

We have already explained that falsehood brings doubt, while truth brings reassurance. Thus, a truthful report puts both the soul and the heart at ease. Moreover, Allah created His servants with an innate disposition toward the truth. If this disposition remains unaltered, it perceives things as they really are, rejecting what is wrong and recognizing what is right.

ʿUmar said:

“Truth is clear and cannot escape a discerning person.”

If the innate disposition is genuinely sound and illuminated by the light of the Quran, things become manifest to it as they really are, in those distinguishing features. The darkness of ignorance is dispelled from it, and it sees matters directly, although they remain hidden from others.

In the Sunan collections, the Musnad, and elsewhere, al-Nawwās ibn Samʿān reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah sets forth a parable: a straight path, with two walls along its sides. In the walls are open doors, and over the doors hang curtains. A caller calls at the entrance to the path, and another caller calls from above the path. The straight path is Islam; the hanging curtains are Allah’s boundaries; and the open doors are the things Allah has forbidden. Whenever a servant wishes to open one of those doors, the caller calls out to him: ‘O servant of Allah, do not open it, for if you open it, you will enter it.’ And the caller at the entrance to

---

## Page 9869

the path is the Book of Allah; and the caller above the path is Allah’s admonisher in the heart of every believer.”

In this great hadith—which brings immense benefit to whoever understands it, if granted divine guidance, and spares him the need for much other knowledge—the Prophet explained that there is an admonisher in the heart of every believer. Admonition consists of commands and prohibitions, encouragement and warning. When the heart is filled with piety, matters become clear and manifest to it, unlike a desolate, darkened heart.

Hudhayfah ibn al-Yamān said:

“In the believer’s heart is a shining lamp.”

An authentic hadith states:

“The Dajjāl has ‘disbeliever’ written between his eyes, which every believer will read, whether literate or illiterate.”

This indicates that the believer perceives what others do not, especially during trials, and that the true character of anyone who lies and fabricates statements about Allah and His Messenger becomes apparent to him. The Dajjāl is the most deceitful of Allah’s creatures, even though Allah causes tremendous events and unsettling displays of deception to occur at his hands, to the point that those who see him are beguiled by him. Yet Allah exposes these things to the believer, so that he becomes convinced of their falsehood and futility.

The stronger faith becomes in the heart, the more clearly matters are disclosed to it, and the better it distinguishes what is true from what is false. The weaker faith becomes, the weaker this discernment grows. It is like the difference between a bright lamp and a dim lamp in a dark house.

For this reason, one of the early generations said, concerning Allah’s words:

“Light upon light”:

“It refers to the believer who speaks wisdom that accords with the truth, even though he has heard no transmitted report concerning it. Then, when he hears a transmitted report concerning it, it becomes light

---

## Page 9870

upon light.”

The faith in the believer’s heart thus accords with the light of the Quran. Sometimes inspiration in the heart takes the form of statements and knowledge, and of supposing that a particular statement is false, that a particular action is invalid, or that one thing carries greater weight or is more correct than another.

An authentic hadith reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Among the nations before you were people who were inspired. If there is any such person in my community, it is Umar.”

Such a person is one who receives inspiration and is addressed inwardly. Umar never said of anything, “I think it is such and such,” without its proving to be as he thought. They believed that tranquility spoke through his heart and tongue.

Furthermore, if matters pertaining to the created world may be disclosed to a believing servant because of the strength of his faith—whether with certainty or conjecture—then religious matters are all the more readily disclosed to him, since he has a greater need for their disclosure. Evidence concerning things arises in the believer’s heart that he is usually unable to express, for not everyone can articulate the meanings within his heart.

When a liar speaks in the presence of a truthful person, the latter recognizes his falsehood from the tenor of his words. A strong sense of faith-born modesty then comes over him, preventing him from speaking out; inwardly, however, he has already taken precautions against the liar. He may nevertheless hint at the falsehood or state it explicitly, out of fear of Allah and compassion for Allah’s creatures, so that they beware of transmitting the liar’s account or acting upon it.

---

## Page 9871

Many believers endowed with spiritual insight receive from Allah an inward awareness that a certain food is unlawful, or that a certain man is a disbeliever, an evildoer, a man who tolerates sexual immorality in his household, someone who engages in sodomy, a wine seller, a singer, or a liar—without any outward evidence, but through what Allah casts into their hearts. Conversely, He places in a believer’s heart love for someone and an awareness that he is one of Allah’s allies, that a certain man is righteous, that a certain food is lawful, and that a certain statement is true. Such things must not be considered far-fetched in the case of Allah’s believing, God-fearing allies.

The story of al-Khidr and Moses belongs to this category: al-Khidr knew those particular circumstances through what Allah had disclosed to him. This is a vast subject whose detailed treatment would be lengthy. We have drawn attention here to some valuable insights that will lead you to understand what lies beyond them.

Section: A comprehensive discussion of conflicts between good deeds, between evil deeds, or between the two
