> (1, 2) Blank in the original.

---

## Page 9950

The twentieth point:

Allah, Exalted is He, sent the messengers and revealed the scriptures concerning knowledge and action, bringing good words and righteous deeds, guidance and the religion of truth. All this involves positive content in belief and action. In matters of belief, He commanded detailed beliefs concerning Allah’s names and attributes and everything else one needs concerning promises of reward and threats of punishment. In matters of action, He commanded diverse forms of inward and outward worship. As for negation, the scriptures expressed it in general terms and prohibited whatever undermines what is commanded. Thus, the divine scriptures and the laws of the messengers abound in affirmations concerning what one is to know and do.

As for the negationists among the philosophical thinkers and their like, negation and prohibition predominate among them. Their beliefs are dominated by denial: “Not such-and-such, not such-and-such, not such-and-such…”

In matters of action, censure and abstention predominate, taking the form of corrupt asceticism and corrupt scrupulousness: “He does not do this, he does not do that, he does not do that…” Yet they offer no righteous deeds for a person to perform that would benefit him and keep him from harmful, corrupt deeds. Thus, most of those who follow their paths are idle and inactive, given to negation in both their beliefs and their actions.

---

## Page 9951

The followers of the messengers, by contrast, possess knowledge, guidance, righteousness, and goodness in their beliefs and deeds. It is thus clear that command and affirmation predominate in what the messengers brought, whereas prohibition and negation predominate in the way of the disbelieving negationists and their like. This is among the clearest proofs of the superiority of command and affirmation over prohibition and negation.

The twenty-first point:

Negation and prohibition cannot stand independently; they must be preceded by something affirmed and a command. Command and affirmation, by contrast, can stand independently. This is because a person cannot conceive of the nonexistent from the outset, nor direct his intention toward it from the outset. I have established this earlier and explained that a person can conceive of the nonexistent only through conceiving of what exists. If he cannot conceive of it, then he is even less able to intend it, for intention and will are preceded by awareness and conception.

This dependence is more pronounced in intention and will than in awareness and knowledge. A person can conceive of both the existent and the nonexistent and make statements about them. As for willing the nonexistent, this is not conceivable in every respect. Rather, willing a thing’s nonexistence consists in hating and disliking it. A person either wills a thing’s existence, wills its nonexistence, or wills neither its existence nor its nonexistence. The first is the fundamental form of will and love.

As for the second—willing its nonexistence—it consists in hating and disliking it, which is preceded by conceiving of what is hated and disliked. Thus, hatred and dislike of a thing, which entail refraining from it—the aim of the one issuing the prohibition and what is required of the person addressed by it—are derivative in two respects:

---

## Page 9952

in that conceiving of it depends on conceiving of what is loved, willed, and commanded; and in that intending its nonexistence—which is hatred and dislike of it—depends on willing the existence of what is commanded, which is loving and willing it.

This is because a person may know that something does not exist and report its nonexistence, as when we say: “I bear witness that there is no deity but Allah”; “There is no prophet after Muhammad”; “The Messiah is neither a deity nor a lord”; or “That is the Book in which there is no doubt.” Further examples include such statements as: “The mountain is not ruby, nor is the sea mercury,” and the like. These negative declarative statements are negative propositions. Without conceiving of the negation and the subject of that negation, a person could not assert the negation and make the judgment. He must therefore conceive of both the negation and its subject, as in conceiving of the mountain and the ruby.

What is negated is pure nonexistence. Yet the human soul, which is aware, knows, and perceives through its faculties and instruments, has neither found nonexistence, nor comprehended it, nor encountered it, nor sensed it through any of its inward or outward senses. It has been aware only of what exists. But once it becomes aware of something existent, the intellect and imagination begin to posit within the soul things derived from those existing things: either combinations of them or things resembling them.

Thus, a person perceives a ruby and a mountain, then combines them in his imagination into a mountain of ruby. He knows what prophethood is and knows the period following Muhammad’s being sent as a messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—then imagines a prophet in that later period. And he knows God and the divinity established for Allah, Lord of

---

## Page 9953

the worlds, then imagines that divinity existing in other beings. The believer then denies what has thus been posited: divinity in anyone other than Allah Most High, and prophethood in anyone after Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The disbeliever, however, may believe that what has been posited actually exists. He thus attributes divinity to the sun, the moon, the stars, the angels, the prophets or some of them, the righteous or some of them, other human beings, or idols fashioned as representations of some of these deities taken besides Allah, glorified be He.

The point is that a person cannot conceive of something’s nonexistence or report it without first conceiving of something existent, using it as the basis for an analogy, and thereby positing something else. He then negates what has been posited by analogy with it, then affirms it. The derivative thing posited by analogy depends upon the original that serves as the basis of the analogy and the supposition. Nonexistence can therefore be conceived of only through analogy, comparison, and derivation—not independently, as a directly apprehended reality or an original basis.

Although certain existing things can be conceived of in this world by people—or by some of them—only through analogy or comparison, some existing things are nevertheless perceived in their reality and actual existence, while others are perceived through analogy or comparison, as with things perceived in dreams. As for what does not exist, it can be perceived only through analogy or comparison, since it has no reality that a living, perceiving being can apprehend or that conscious beings can encounter directly. For the reality of each thing in the external world is identical with its essence. As for the essences and realities posited in the mind, they may have an actual reality in external, concrete existence in the world, or they may not.

---

## Page 9954

And the same holds for intention, love, and will in two respects:

First, loving or hating an object—whether sought and loved or disliked and hated—is inconceivable without some prior awareness of it. Awareness of what exists is primary, while awareness of what does not exist is derivative; this applies all the more to the love and hatred that follow such awareness.

Second, a person loves only what suits him and accords with his nature, bringing him pleasure and delight. His soul is neither suited nor akin to sheer nonexistence and pure negation. In sheer nonexistence he finds neither pleasure nor joy, neither blessing nor bliss, no good whatsoever, and certainly no benefit. Indeed, loving sheer nonexistence is like the absence of love, and taking pleasure in sheer nonexistence is like the absence of pleasure. How can something that is nothing at all contain any benefit, pleasure, or good?

Rather, his soul loves what brings it benefit and pleasure: milk at birth, for example, and other foods; then the pleasures of sexual intimacy and the like; then the pleasures of honour, leadership, and similar things; and then the pleasures of reason, knowledge, and faith. He also loves what wards off harm, such as clothing, dwellings, and the good things that shield him from his foes—heat and cold, harmful human beings, harmful animals, and so forth. Thus, he loves the existence of what benefits him and the absence of what harms him. What benefits him is necessarily something that exists, as explained above. As for what harms him, sometimes

---

## Page 9955

it means the absence of what benefits him, for most of what harms him consists in the absence of what benefits him. Such absence is addressed only by securing the presence of what benefits him. At other times, something that exists harms him; he hates nothing about it except the harm it causes him, which consists in depriving him of pleasure or causing him suffering.

If it is said:

“What you have stated faces an objection: from beginning to end, the Quran commands piety and urges it, so much so that nothing is mentioned in the Quran more frequently. It is Allah’s counsel to the earlier and later generations, the hallmark of His allies, and the first call of the prophets and of those who attain the good end and occupy the seat of honour—among its many other attributes.

“Piety means refraining from what is prohibited. Sahl ibn ‘Abd Allāh said:

‘Both the righteous and the wicked perform good deeds, but only one truly steadfast in faith can persevere in abstaining from sins.’

“There is more praise of scrupulousness and those who practise it, and of asceticism and its adherents, than space here permits us to recount. Yet all this comes down to refraining from forbidden acts, disliked acts, and unnecessary indulgence in permissible things. These are more akin to the category of things one is instructed to refrain from than to the category of things one is commanded to do. People recount virtues and merits of those who practise such scrupulousness that they do not recount of others.”

---

## Page 9956

We reply:

This objection rests on two things: ignorance of the true nature of piety, scrupulousness, and asceticism; and ignorance of why these are praiseworthy.

First, we say:

Who said that piety consists merely in refraining from evil deeds? Rather, piety—as earlier and later generations have explained it—means doing what you have been commanded to do and refraining from what you have been forbidden. Thus, when strife broke out, Talq ibn Habīb said, “Protect yourselves against it through piety.” They asked, “What is piety?”

He replied:

“To obey Allah, guided by light from Allah, hoping for Allah’s reward; and to refrain from disobeying Allah, guided by light from Allah, fearing Allah’s punishment.”

Allah Most High says in the longest surah of the Quran:

“Alif Lām Mīm.”

“This is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for the pious.”

“Those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them.”

And so the passage continues. He thus describes the pious as carrying out what is commanded: faith and righteous deeds, including establishing prayer and giving zakah. He also says:

“O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, so that you may become pious.”

And He says:

“Righteousness does not consist in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets, and give wealth, despite their love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveller

---

## Page 9957

and those who ask, and for freeing slaves; establish prayer and give zakah; fulfil their pledges when they make them; and are patient in hardship, suffering, and battle. Those are the ones who are true, and those are the pious.”

This is a momentous verse of immense significance, among the greatest verses of the Quran and the most comprehensive in addressing the matters of religion. It has been reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about the qualities of faith, whereupon this verse was revealed. In al-Tirmidhī, Fātimah bint Qays reports that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “There is a due upon wealth besides zakah,” and recited this verse.

It indicates several things:

First, Allah declares that those who do these things are the pious, and most of these things consist of commanded actions.

Second, He declares that these things constitute righteousness, and that those who practise them are truthful—that is, in saying, “We believe.” Most of them involve actively performing commanded deeds. Thus, carrying out what is commanded is more integral to righteousness, piety, and faith than merely not doing what is forbidden.

It is by virtue of these three descriptions that Paradise is merited, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, and indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire.”

And He says:

“Or should We treat the pious like the wicked?”

“Indeed, the pious will be amid gardens and rivers.”

And He says:

“Is one who is a believer like one who is defiantly disobedient? They are not equal.”

The verse also indicates that these qualities mentioned in it are obligatory, for He

---

## Page 9958

declares that those who practise them are truthful in what they say and are the pious. Truthfulness is obligatory, as is faith. The obligation of dues besides zakah is also indicated by His words:

“So recite whatever is easy of it, establish prayer, give zakah, and lend Allah a good loan. Whatever good you send ahead for yourselves, you will find it with Allah, better and greater in reward.”

And His words to the Children of Israel:

“If you establish prayer, give zakah, believe in My messengers and support them, and lend Allah a good loan.”

And His words:

“You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love.”

And His words:

“Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbour who is related to you, the neighbour who is unrelated, the companion at your side, the traveller, and those whom your right hands possess.”

And His words:

“Give relatives their due, and the needy and the traveller,”

in the surahs Subhān and al-Rūm.

Giving relatives their due means maintaining ties of kinship; giving the needy their due means feeding the hungry; and giving the traveller his due means offering hospitality to guests. Spending on freeing slaves includes securing the release of captives, while giving to orphans is a form of feeding the poor. In al-Bukhārī, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Visit the sick, feed the hungry, and free the captive.”

And in the hadith upon which Ahmad based his ruling:

“If the beggar were truthful, no one who turned him away would prosper.”

Furthermore, the messengers—such as Noah, Hūd, Sālih, and Shuayb—began their call, as related in Surah Hūd, with:

“Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him.”

And in al-Shuarā:

---

## Page 9959

“Will you not fear Allah?”

“So fear Allah and obey me.”

Allah Most High also says:

“But righteousness is in one who fears Allah.”

And He says:

“Yes, whoever fulfils his covenant and fears Allah—indeed, Allah loves those who fear Him.”

And He says:

“Fulfil your treaty with them until the end of its term. Indeed, Allah loves those who fear Him.”

And He says:

“As long as they remain true to you, remain true to them. Indeed, Allah loves those who fear Him.”

He has thus made clear that fulfilling covenants is part of the piety that Allah loves. Fulfilling covenants encompasses everything commanded, for an obligation arises either from revealed law or from a stipulation, and all of this involves performing a commanded act. It constitutes fulfilment of the covenant with Allah and covenants with His servants.

Taqwā (piety) means either fearing Allah or guarding against His punishment, as He says:

“So fear the Fire whose fuel is people and stones.”

“And fear the Fire prepared for the disbelievers.”

Thus, taqwā means guarding against what is feared by doing what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden, though it consists more in the former. This is called taqwā because neglecting what is commanded and doing what is forbidden is a means of safety from Allah’s censure, displeasure, and punishment. Its motivating force is therefore fear of sin. This differs from an act that brings benefit but whose omission causes no harm: that is a recommended act, which one may either perform or leave undone. He therefore described this as taqwā to make clear that it is obligatory and that the person concerned exposes himself to punishment by abandoning taqwā.

Secondly, we say: wherever taqwā is used to mean refraining from what is forbidden—if that interpretation is adopted—as in His words:

“Cooperate in righteousness and piety,”

concerning which some of the early Muslims said, “Righteousness means doing what you have been commanded, and piety means avoiding what you have been forbidden,” it is always coupled

---

## Page 9960

with doing what is commanded, just as He mentions righteousness alongside it, and as in Noah’s words:

“Worship Allah, fear Him, and obey me.”

This is because such piety necessarily entails doing what is commanded.

Thirdly, we say: most people may perform some of what is commanded, but only the truly sincere refrain from what is forbidden, as Sahl said. This is because the soul has an inclination towards what is commanded, whereas refraining from what is forbidden requires opposing one’s desires and striving against oneself. It is therefore harder and more demanding, and few practise it. No one can do so without also doing what is commanded. Piety cannot be conceived as action [and] abstention alone. Whoever abandons associating partners with Allah, following misleading desires, and pursuing forbidden pleasures must necessarily perform many commanded deeds that keep him from these things. Their piety thus preserves the good deeds they have been commanded to perform and protects them from sins that harm them. This differs, for example, from someone who does both what he is commanded and what he is forbidden: committing forbidden acts corrupts whatever commanded deeds it corrupts, so that they do not remain intact for him.

This is why the ultimate good outcome belongs to piety, as Allah Most High says:

“And the ultimate good outcome belongs to piety.”

“And the ultimate good outcome is for those who fear Allah.”

“And if you are patient and fear Allah, their plotting will not harm you at all.”

Those who fear Allah are like someone who eats wholesome food and avoids harmful foods: his body becomes healthy, and his eventual condition is sound. Someone who lacks piety, however, is like a person who mixes different foods: although he gains nourishment from them, those mixtures may cause him

## Page 9961

illnesses that are either harmful or fatal. Even so, no reasonable person would say that his need for, and benefit from, avoiding harmful foods is greater than his need for, and benefit from, wholesome foods. Rather, his need for and benefit from the foods he eats are greater than the benefit he derives from those he avoids. If he ate no food whatsoever, he would certainly perish. If, however, he eats both wholesome and harmful foods, there may be hope for his safety, but also fear for his life. If he eats wholesome foods and avoids harmful ones, he enjoys health and safety.

The first case is comparable to someone who abandons what he has been commanded to do. The second is comparable to someone who does both what is commanded and what is forbidden: someone who mixes righteous deeds with evil ones. The third is comparable to the person of piety who does what he has been commanded and avoids what he has been forbidden. Piety is therefore of such great importance because it combines safety with honour, not because it brings safety alone. In the Hereafter there is no abode other than Paradise or Hell: whoever is saved from Hell enters Paradise, and whoever is not granted bliss is punished. No human being is left without either punishment or bliss.

Reflect on this: every quality that Allah has commanded or praised necessarily involves doing what is commanded, either as an integral part of it or as its necessary consequence. Such qualities are praised for securing good rather than evil, and reward rather than punishment.

Likewise, scrupulousness and renunciation, as prescribed in Islam, are forms of the piety it prescribes. Some people, however, have misunderstood this. As for the prescribed and recommended scrupulousness with which Allah sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, it is the caution exercised by one who fears

---

## Page 9962

that something may lead to blame and punishment, in the absence of an overriding consideration.

This includes performing obligatory acts and doubtful acts that appear to be obligatory, and avoiding prohibited acts and doubtful acts that appear to be prohibited. If disliked acts are included, I would say: “We fear that it may lead to deficiency and punishment.” Obligatory scrupulousness, however, means guarding against what leads to blame and punishment: performing what is obligatory and avoiding what is prohibited. The difference between the two concerns matters whose obligatory status is uncertain—whether they are obligatory or not—and matters whose prohibition is uncertain—whether they are prohibited or not. Refraining from what is unquestionably lawful is not scrupulousness, nor is performing what is unquestionably not required.

My qualification, “in the absence of an overriding consideration,” addresses cases in which a person can avoid something clearly prohibited or doubtful only by abandoning a good deed whose standing in Islamic law is greater than that of avoiding that evil. An example is someone who refuses to follow a sinful imam and consequently abandons Friday prayer, congregational prayer, Hajj and military campaigns. Likewise, a person may be able to perform a clear or possible obligation only by committing an evil more sinful than leaving that obligation unfulfilled. An example is someone who cannot fulfil the duties of enjoining right and forbidding wrong with respect to those in authority except through fighting that causes greater harm than the harm caused by the ruler’s injustice.

The basis for scrupulousness concerning doubtful matters is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The lawful is clear, and the unlawful is clear. Between them are doubtful matters which many people do not know. Whoever avoids doubtful matters safeguards his honour and his religion, and whoever falls into doubtful matters falls into

---

## Page 9963

the unlawful, like a shepherd grazing his flock around a protected pasture who is liable to enter it.” This is recorded in the two Sahīh collections.

In the Sunan collections are his sayings:

“Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt.”

“Righteousness is that with which the soul is at ease and the heart is tranquil.”

In one narration in Sahīh Muslim, he says:

“Righteousness is good character, and sin is what troubles your conscience, even if people give you their rulings.”

“He saw a date on his bed and said: ‘Were it not that I fear it might be a date given in charity, I would have eaten it.’”

As for obligatory acts… (1)

However, errors concerning scrupulousness arise in three ways.

The first is that many people believe it consists in abstention. They therefore see scrupulousness only in avoiding the unlawful, not in fulfilling obligations. This afflicts many religiously observant and scrupulous people. You may see someone scrupulously avoiding a lie or a dirham of doubtful provenance because it comes from a wrongdoer’s wealth or an invalid transaction. He also scrupulously avoids inclining towards wrongdoers on account of religious innovations, and towards those given to immorality in worldly affairs.

Yet he neglects duties incumbent upon him, whether individual obligations or collective obligations that have become his personal responsibility: maintaining ties of kinship; fulfilling the rights of neighbours, the needy, companions, orphans and travellers; and fulfilling the rights of Muslims, those in authority and people of knowledge. He also neglects enjoining right

---

## Page 9964

and forbidding wrong, striving in Allah’s cause, and other duties incumbent upon him that benefit people in their religious and worldly affairs. Or he performs these duties not as worship of Allah Most High, but merely as an imposed obligation or the like.

Such scrupulousness may lead a person into grave religious innovations. The scrupulousness of the Khawārij, the Rāfidah, the Mu‘tazilah and others like them is of this kind. They scrupulously avoided injustice and what they believed to be injustice, such as associating with those they considered wrongdoers, until they abandoned major obligations: Friday and congregational prayers, Hajj, striving in Allah’s cause, sincere counsel to Muslims and compassion towards them. Those practising this kind of scrupulousness were censured by the leading scholars, including the four imams, and their case came to be discussed in expositions of the creed of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah.

The second source of error concerns unsound beliefs. When someone performs obligatory and doubtful acts, and refrains from forbidden and doubtful acts, his belief that something is obligatory or forbidden must rest on evidence from the Quran and Sunnah and on knowledge, not personal inclination. Many people feel an aversion to certain things because of habit or similar influences, which reinforces their belief that those things are forbidden or doubtful. Some harbour illusions and false suspicions, and these suspicions rest upon misguided scrupulousness. Such a person is among those of whom Allah Most High says:

“They follow nothing but conjecture and what their souls desire.”

This is the condition of those afflicted by obsessive doubts concerning ritual impurities. Their misguided scrupulousness combines a measure of religiosity with weakness of intellect and knowledge. The same applies to the scrupulousness of people who consider most people’s wealth unlawful

---

## Page 9965

or doubtful, or who regard all of it in this way. Some have gone so far as to deem it lawful for a ruler, on the grounds that he is entitled to it, and to hold that a thief’s hand should not be cut off for stealing it, nor should rulings concerning usurped property be applied to it. Imams such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others condemned these people’s conduct and censured those who go to excess in scrupulousness.

Muslim narrated in his Sahīh that ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘Those who go to excess are ruined.’ He repeated this three times.”

Much of the scrupulousness practised by the people of religious innovation belongs to this category. Indeed, the scrupulous refusal of Jews, Christians and other disbelievers to fulfil the obligations of Islam belongs to this category. So too does their scrupulous avoidance of things they themselves declared forbidden, although Allah Most High had not forbidden them—a practice Allah Most High censured in the Quran—such as the animals called bahīrah, sā’ibah, wasīlah and hām.

Another example is the scrupulousness censured by the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith recorded in the Sahīh. When he availed himself of certain concessions and learned that some people had scrupulously abstained from those things, he said:

“What is the matter with men who scrupulously abstain from things in which I avail myself of concessions? By Allah, I hope to be the one among them who knows Allah best and fears Him most.” In another narration: “The one who fears Him most and knows His limits best.”

The hadith about the man who kissed his wife is another such example. Thus, a devout person who practises scrupulousness needs extensive knowledge of the Quran and Sunnah, and understanding

---

## Page 9966

of religion. Otherwise, his misguided scrupulousness may do more harm than good, as has happened among disbelievers and people of religious innovation, including the Khawārij, the Rāfidah and others.

The third consideration: a countervailing factor of greater weight.

This is more difficult than the preceding consideration. Something may have a harmful aspect that calls for avoiding it. A scrupulous person notices this but overlooks the greater good that weighs against it. The converse is subject to the same principle. It has become clear that someone who regards scrupulousness as abstention alone, includes within it the conduct of people who have good intentions but lack insight into their religion, and disregards the greater good they have forfeited through their scrupulousness, has missed more of the religion of Islam than he has grasped. Indeed, he may find fault with people who are closer to salvation and happiness. This principle is of great benefit in cases of this kind and others like them.

It benefits those whose scrupulousness is deficient or misguided, as well as those whose renunciation of worldly things is deficient or misguided. For the renunciation prescribed by Allah and His Messenger consists in having no desire for superfluous permissible things that bring no benefit. Forgoing superfluous permissible things that bring no religious benefit is renunciation, not scrupulousness. There is no doubt that craving and desire for this worldly life and its wealth and power are harmful. Al-Tirmidhī narrated that Ka‘b ibn Mālik said:

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Two hungry wolves let loose in a sheepfold are no more destructive to it than a man’s craving for wealth and honour is to his religion.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “This is a good and authentic hadith.” Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, condemned craving

---

## Page 9967

for wealth and honour—the latter meaning leadership and authority—and stated that this corrupts religion as much as, or more than, two hungry wolves ravage a sheepfold. This shows that such craving is condemned precisely because it corrupts religion, which consists of faith and righteous deeds. Giving up this craving therefore serves righteous action. These two things are mentioned in Allah’s words:

“My wealth has availed me nothing. My authority has vanished from me.”

They are also the two things Allah mentions in Sūrat al-Qasas. He begins it with the account of Pharaoh and describes his exaltation on earth—that is, leadership, honour and authority. Then, towards its end, He mentions Qārūn and the wealth he had been given. He describes the ultimate fate of the authority of the one and the wealth of the other, then says:

“That abode of the Hereafter We assign to those who desire neither superiority on earth nor corruption.”

Such were the ways of Pharaoh and Qārūn. Accumulating wealth without spending it where one is commanded to, and acquiring it through improper means, are forms of corruption. Likewise, when someone seeks authority for himself without justice or right, he can attain it only through corruption and wrongdoing.

But simply possessing authority and wealth, when used to seek Allah’s countenance, uphold the truth and attain the abode of the Hereafter, and as an aid to obeying Allah—without the heart’s love for Allah, His Messenger and striving in His cause growing weak, as was the case with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Abū Bakr and ‘Umar, and without being distracted from remembering Allah—is among the greatest blessings Allah Most High bestows upon His servant, provided these conditions are met. Yet rarely does

---

## Page 9968

one find a person of authority or wealth without finding that he is sluggish in obeying and loving Allah, discourages others from doing so, follows his own desires in using what Allah has given him, and shrinks from warfare, fighting in Allah’s cause, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. Through these traits, he earns humiliation and blame in this world and the Hereafter.

Allah Most High said to His Prophet and his Companions:

“Do not lose heart or grieve, for you will have the upper hand.”

He thus declares that they have the upper hand, yet they desire neither superiority on earth nor corruption. Allah Most High also says:

“So do not lose heart and call for peace while you have the upper hand, and Allah is with you.”

“Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for Paradise.”

And He says:

“Do not entrust the foolish with your wealth, which Allah has made a means of support for you.”

Honour and wealth are therefore neither praised nor condemned unconditionally. Rather, whatever helps one obey Allah is praiseworthy. This may even be obligatory, when it is indispensable for fulfilling obligatory duties, or it may be recommended. It is praiseworthy only when accompanied by this intention. Whatever is used to disobey Allah or to hinder the fulfilment of obligations is blameworthy and forbidden. Its merit is diminished when it distracts from recommended deeds or leads to disliked acts.

And Allah knows best. As stated in the hadith:

“Whoever seeks this wealth to be independent of others, to refrain from begging, and to provide assistance to his vulnerable neighbour, the widow and the needy will meet Allah Most High with his face shining like the moon on the night when it is full. But whoever seeks it to show off and boast

---

## Page 9969

and to outdo others in wealth will meet Allah while He is angry with him.”

He also said:

“The trustworthy, truthful merchant will be with the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs and the righteous.”

And he said:

“How excellent is good wealth for a righteous man!”

Know that scrupulousness does not benefit a person or earn him a reward unless he fulfils the command to be sincere. With regard to scrupulousness expressed in doing what is commanded, this is clear: Allah Most High accepts only deeds done for His sake. As for refraining from what is forbidden—which some people call scrupulousness—if a person refrains from sins for a reason other than seeking Allah’s pleasure, he is not rewarded for refraining, although he is not punished for those sins. If he refrains for Allah’s sake, he is rewarded. This can only arise from the hope for Allah’s mercy or fear of His punishment that resides in his heart. Hope for His mercy and fear of His punishment are positive states that one is commanded to cultivate. Thus, scrupulousness is only a righteous deed when accompanied by the commanded acts of hope and fear. Mere abstention, as an absence of action, carries no reward.

As for renunciation, which is the opposite of desire, it is praised without qualification, while desire is condemned for leading one to neglect working for the Hereafter. Allah Most High says:

“Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment—We will repay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be shortchanged.”

“Those are the ones who will have nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire.”

And He says:

“Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter—We will increase his harvest. And whoever desires the harvest of this world—We will give him some of it, but he will have no share in the Hereafter.”

And He says:

“Whoever desires the fleeting life of this world—We hasten for him therein whatever We will

---

## Page 9970

for whomever We choose. Then We appoint Hell for him, where he will burn, condemned and banished.”

Whoever does not seek the Hereafter in word and deed, in preference, love, longing and devotion, will have no share in the Hereafter and gain no benefit in this worldly life. Rather, he is an unbeliever, accursed, distracted and tormented. Yet his renunciation of this world may afford him some immediate relief, although such renunciation is not sanctioned by the revealed law. He may also suffer from missing out on worldly pleasures. If he does not renounce them, however, he finds no relief in this regard.

Thus, whether someone renounces this world to find worldly ease or pursues it to obtain its pleasures, neither is engaged in a righteous deed or deserves praise for it according to the revealed law. Nevertheless, one course may sometimes be more advantageous in worldly terms, and the other at other times, just as one craft may be preferable to another, or one trade to another. Worldly pleasures are generally attained only through some effort. At times, the pleasure of foregoing them may outweigh the effort of pursuing them; at other times, the effort of pursuing them may be preferable to the pleasure of foregoing them. There is therefore no praise for abandoning this world unless it is for the sake of working for the Hereafter, just as there is no praise for pursuing it unless it is for the sake of working for the Hereafter.

It is thus established that merely renouncing this world deserves no praise, just as desiring it deserves no praise. Rather, praise is due to seeking Allah and the Hereafter, while blame attaches to the desire for this world that prevents one from seeking them, as explained above and as expressed in the words of Allah Most High:

“If you desire the life of this world and its adornment, then come: I will provide for you and release you graciously.”

“But if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the Hereafter, then Allah has prepared a tremendous reward for those of you who do good.”

For this reason, those with spiritual understanding customarily call such a person a seeker and aspirant;

---

## Page 9971

for all goodness begins with seeking Allah, His Messenger and the Hereafter. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Actions are judged only by intentions.”

It is thus established that obligatory renunciation consists in abandoning whatever [distracts one] from the obligatory pursuit of Allah and the Hereafter, while recommended renunciation consists in abandoning whatever distracts one from the recommended deeds of those brought near to Allah and those steadfast in truth.

It therefore becomes clear, in three respects, that the purpose of renunciation is to fulfil what has been commanded:

First: Were it not that this world distracts from worshipping Allah and seeking the Hereafter, renouncing it would not have been prescribed. Rather, renouncing it and not renouncing it would be equal, or one or the other would be preferable on worldly grounds.

Second: Suppose there were two people, one seeking both the Hereafter and this world, and the other renouncing both this world and the Hereafter. The first would be a praiseworthy believer, and the second an accursed unbeliever, even though the second renounces this world while the first seeks it. What distinguishes the first, however, is that he fulfils something commanded while committing something forbidden, whereas the second does not fulfil that command. It is thus established that fulfilling the command to seek the Hereafter is beneficial, while renunciation without fulfilling this command is of no benefit.

Third: What the Quran and Sunnah praise is seeking the Hereafter; the person they condemn is the one who abandons the pursuit of the Hereafter and becomes preoccupied with seeking this world

---

## Page 9972

instead. As for praising the abandonment of this world in itself, this is found neither in Allah’s Book nor in the Sunnah of His Messenger. Do not be swayed by how often people condemn this world on grounds unrelated to religion. Most ordinary people condemn it only because they have not obtained what they wanted from it. It has never afforded anyone untroubled happiness, however much he may have gained from it. No home has ever been filled with joy without also being filled with tears.

Sensible people therefore condemn the ignorant who place their trust in this world and imagine that their authority, wealth and enjoyment of its pleasures will endure. Yet they themselves still need its necessities, and most of them seek the very things in it that they condemn. Their condemnation of this world is, in reality, a worldly condemnation prompted by its worldly harms. It resembles sensible people’s condemnation of commerce or a craft that brings no profit but only toil, or your condemnation of keeping company with someone who harms you without benefiting you, as in marrying an ill-tempered woman, and similar matters whose harm and benefit concern this world alone.

There is no doubt that whatever causes harm in this world is blameworthy if it brings no benefit in the Hereafter, such as wasting wealth or undertaking arduous acts of worship that neither Allah nor His Messenger has commanded. Whatever brings benefit in this world is blameworthy if it causes harm in the Hereafter, such as enjoying forbidden pleasures and satisfying forbidden desires. The same applies to permissible pleasures and desires if they weaken a person’s resolve and hold him back in matters concerning the Hereafter and his pursuit of it. Whatever is harmful both in this world and in the Hereafter is evil and hardship. Whatever is beneficial in the Hereafter is praiseworthy, even if it causes harm in this world, such as sacrificing lives and wealth

---

## Page 9973

in jihad in Allah’s cause. The same applies to what causes no harm in this world, such as many acts of worship. Whatever is beneficial both in this world and in the Hereafter is also praiseworthy. There are thus seven categories:

Whatever is beneficial in the Hereafter is praiseworthy, whether it causes harm in this world, brings benefit, or neither benefits nor harms. Whatever is harmful in the Hereafter is blameworthy, whether it brings benefit in this world, causes harm, or neither benefits nor harms.

Three categories remain: what is beneficial in this world without being harmful in the Hereafter, and what is harmful in this world without being beneficial in the Hereafter. The beneficial is praiseworthy, and the harmful is blameworthy.

There are two views concerning the third category. One holds that it merits neither praise nor blame; the other holds that it is blameworthy.

Most of people’s condemnation of this world is not because it distracts them from the Hereafter, but because of the harm they suffer in it. It is indeed blameworthy in that respect. The strongest grounds for condemning it, however, are that it distracts from the Hereafter. Yet a person may count his misfortunes and forget his blessings. He may condemn many things because of some harm he suffers, although they contain many benefits that he fails to mention. Such condemnation is a form of fretfulness and panic, as

---

## Page 9974

the Exalted says:

“Indeed, mankind was created anxious:
when evil touches him, impatient,
and when good touches him, withholding—
except those who pray.”

What is truly blameworthy is whatever distracts one from the obligatory deeds that benefit one in the Hereafter. Whatever distracts from recommended deeds that benefit one there constitutes a shortcoming. Also blameworthy is whatever brings more harm than benefit in the Hereafter. These three principles settle the matter. Thus, it is clear that what is praiseworthy in this world may lie either in the presence of something or in its absence.

Errors may arise in renunciation, just as they do in scrupulousness:

First, some people renounce things that benefit them without causing harm, thereby neglecting obligatory or recommended acts—as when someone abstains from marriage to women, from meat, and the like. Yet the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “But I fast and break my fast; I marry women and eat meat. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.”

Second, a person’s renunciation may lead him to commit prohibited acts—as when someone forgoes wealth or benefits lawfully available to him, then needs them and obtains them unlawfully, begs from people in a forbidden manner, or looks expectantly to them; such expectation is disliked.

Third, some renounce things out of laziness, idleness, and a desire for ease, rather than to seek the abode of the Hereafter through righteous deeds and beneficial knowledge. For when a servant is given to renunciation but remains idle, he becomes utterly corrupt. Such people cultivate neither this world nor the Hereafter, as stated by

---

## Page 9975

‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd:

“I dislike seeing a man idle, occupied neither with the affairs of this world nor with those of the Hereafter.”

Such people are among the people of the Fire, as indicated by the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh from ‘Iyād ibn Himār, who reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “The people of Paradise are of five kinds.” Among them he mentioned “the weak man who lacks the judgment to restrain himself—those among you who merely follow others, seeking neither family nor wealth.”

Anyone whose renunciation leads him to abandon commanded good deeds—in which case what he abandons is better than his renunciation—or to commit forbidden sins or lapse into laziness and idleness is among “the greatest losers in their deeds,” “those whose efforts are wasted in this worldly life while they think they are doing good.”

Whoever renounces what distracts him from his obligations or leads him into forbidden acts is among those who follow a middle course, the people of the right. Whoever renounces what distracts him from recommended deeds and higher ranks is among those who are foremost, taking the lead in goodness.

This is a brief summary of renunciation. It has become clear that the primary aim is to do what has been commanded, since renunciation helps one to do so. This is the point intended here. And Allah knows best.

The twenty-second point:

Good deeds are a cause of things being made lawful, both in religious law and in the created order, while sins are a cause of things being forbidden in both respects. Prohibition may serve as protection or as punishment, while making things lawful may bring abundance or serve as punishment and a trial. Allah Most High says:

Thus, He permitted livestock to them while they refrained from treating hunting as lawful—that is, while believing it to be forbidden and abstaining from it.

Allah thus perfected the religion by prescribing the obligations He prescribed, the last of which was Hajj, and by prohibiting the forbidden things mentioned in this verse. This was in terms of His legislation. As for His action—His granting strength, assistance, and victory—the disbelievers despaired of overcoming our religion, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed the pilgrimage prescribed in Islam. ## Page 9979

I have also written in my treatment of “Covenants and Contracts”—on religious covenants among the general principles, and on worldly contracts among the principles of jurisprudence—and in the Book of Vows, that when something is already obligatory under Islamic law, and a servant vows to perform it, makes a covenant with Allah to do so, pledges himself to the Messenger or the ruler to do so, or joins others in a mutual oath to do so, these covenants and solemn pledges impose a second obligation, distinct from the obligation established by the original command alone. The act thus becomes obligatory on two grounds: whoever neglects it deserves both the punishment due to someone who breaks a covenant or solemn pledge and that due to someone who disobeys Allah and His Messenger. This is the correct analysis.

Some jurists of Ahmad’s school say that when someone vows to perform an obligatory act, its status remains unchanged after the vow, unlike a vow to perform a recommended act. This is not correct. If a vow makes a recommended act obligatory, then it is all the more capable of imposing an obligation to perform an already obligatory act. This does not amount to bringing about what already exists. Rather, these are two obligations of different kinds, each with a legal effect distinct from the other. An example is a grandmother who is both one’s maternal grandmother’s mother and one’s paternal grandfather’s mother: she possesses two grounds of entitlement, each of which entitles her to one-sixth.

Likewise, some jurists of Ahmad’s school say that conditions inherent in a contract cannot validly be stipulated, or may even invalidate it. Some jurists of al-Shāfiʿī’s school have gone so far as to say that if someone says, “I give her to you in marriage on the terms Allah has commanded—keeping her on honorable terms or letting her go with kindness,” the marriage is invalid because he has stipulated divorce within it. This is

---

## Page 9980

utterly unsound reasoning. The obligations arising from contracts become binding only because the contracting parties bind themselves to them. A contract expressed without qualification has a recognized meaning; when they express it without qualification, they thereby bind themselves to what is understood from it.

An obligation arising from a contract is binding by virtue of that contract, just as an obligation arising from a vow is binding by virtue of that vow. The Lawgiver did not impose it in the first instance; rather, He commanded the fulfillment of contracts, just as He commanded the fulfillment of vows. Thus, if a contract has an obligation known from its unqualified wording, or the contracting parties recognize its imposition through specific wording, this constitutes mentioning the particular after the general. The obligation has thus been imposed twice, or has been given a specific basis of obligation that dispenses with the general one.

There are parallels to this in the Quran, such as His saying:

“Whoever is an enemy to Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel and Michael—then Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers.”

And His saying:

“And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, son of Mary.”

And His saying:

“Guard strictly the prayers, especially the middle prayer.”

And His saying:

“Say to your wives, your daughters, and the women of the believers.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, Allah commands justice, kindness, and giving to relatives, and forbids indecency, wrongdoing, and oppression.”

And His saying:

“Those who break Allah’s covenant after its solemn confirmation.”

For Allah proclaimed His covenant, which He commanded them to observe, after taking their solemn pledge to fulfill it. Thus, both grounds are combined in it: that of the covenant and that of the solemn pledge.

## Page 9983

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

People disagree over whether commanding something also entails commanding its necessary requirements, and whether it entails prohibiting its opposite, although they agree that the commanded act cannot be performed without fulfilling its necessary requirements and refraining from its opposite. (*)

The disagreement arises because someone who commands an act may not intend its necessary requirements or the avoidance of its opposite. Thus, if he punishes the legally accountable person, he punishes him only for failing to perform the commanded act, not for omitting its necessary requirements or doing its opposite.

This issue is commonly expressed in the maxim: “Whatever is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation is itself obligatory.”

Some people have erred in this matter by dividing such requirements into two categories: those beyond the legally accountable person’s ability, such as soundness of the limbs, the requisite number of participants for Friday prayer, and similar matters that he cannot secure; and those within his ability, such as travelling the distance required for Hajj, washing a portion of the head during ablution, observing the fast for part of the night, and similar matters.

They therefore said: “Whatever is indispensable to fulfilling an unconditional obligation, and lies within the legally accountable person’s ability, is itself obligatory.”

## Page 9984

This division is mistaken, for the matters they mentioned are conditions for an obligation to arise. The obligation cannot be fulfilled without them, and whatever is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation must, by agreement of the Muslims, be undertaken by the servant, whether it is within his ability or not—such as possessing the means for Hajj and acquiring the minimum amount of wealth liable to zakat. When a person possesses the means for Hajj, Hajj becomes obligatory upon him; and when he owns the minimum amount liable to zakat, zakat becomes obligatory upon him. The obligation does not arise without these conditions, but he is not required to acquire the means for Hajj or ownership of that minimum amount.

Hence, those who hold that possessing the means for Hajj means possessing sufficient wealth—as is the position of Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad—do not require a person to earn that wealth. Their disagreement concerns only the case in which the means are offered to him: either an offer to perform Hajj on his behalf or an offer of money from his child. There is a well-known disagreement over this in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. The well-known position in Ahmad’s school is that it is not obligatory. Only a group of his followers held it obligatory, because, according to his underlying principle, a father is entitled to take ownership of his child’s wealth; accepting it would therefore be like taking possession of things freely available for ownership. The well-known position in al-Shāfiʿī’s school is that it becomes obligatory when the son offers to perform the act.

The point here is to distinguish between what is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation and what is indispensable for that obligation to arise. The discussion of the second category concerns only what is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation, such as travelling the necessary distance for Friday prayer, Hajj and the like. The legally accountable person must do this, by agreement of the Muslims. However, someone who neglects Hajj while living far from Mecca, or neglects

---

## Page 9985

Friday prayer while living far from the congregational mosque has omitted more than someone who lives nearby. Yet it is not said that his punishment is greater than that of someone who lives nearby.

An obligatory act is one whose omission is grounds for blame and punishment. If what a person is required to do as a subsidiary matter were itself an intended object of the obligation, the blame and punishment for omitting it would be greater. Thus, someone from India or al-Andalus who neglected Hajj would face greater punishment than someone from Mecca or al-Tā’if who neglected it; and someone from the farthest part of the city who neglected Friday prayer would face greater punishment than someone living beside the congregational mosque who neglected it. Since it is known that the person who lives farther away receives a greater reward, yet does not face greater punishment for omission than someone who lives nearby, the following uncertainty arose: is this obligatory or not?

The precise distinction is that its obligatory character follows by rational necessity, not because it is an intended object of the command. Indeed, someone who commands an act may not intend thereby to demand its prerequisites, even though he knows that they must exist. If the person issuing the command is liable to inattention, those prerequisites may not even occur to him.

Whoever understands this will find al-Ka‘bī’s objections concerning whether the Sharia contains anything merely permissible resolved. Al-Ka‘bī claimed that nothing in the Sharia is merely permissible … etc.

You will never find an innovator who does not love to conceal the scriptural texts that contradict him, hate those texts, and hate their being made known, transmitted, and discussed. He also hates those who do so, as one of the early generations said:

---

## Page 9986

“No one introduces an innovation without the sweetness of hadith being taken from his heart.”

Moreover, the position with which he opposes the scriptural texts inevitably mixes truth with falsehood through the equivocal and ambiguous expressions he uses. Hence Imam Ahmad said, at the beginning of his Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah concerning the Ambiguous Passages of the Quran about Which They Entertained Doubts and Which They Misinterpreted—a work he wrote during his imprisonment. Al-Khallāl mentioned it in his Book of the Sunnah, as did Judge Abū Yaʿlā, Abū al-Fadl al-Tamīmī, Abū al-Wafāʾ ibn ʿAqīl, and several other followers of Ahmad. None of them denied its attribution to him, and all praise belongs to Allah. The statement relevant here is:

“They speak in ambiguous language and deceive ignorant people through the confusion they create for them.”

If they are calling people to their doctrine and requiring them to adhere to it, they may be told:

“No one is obliged to answer any caller except when he calls to what the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, called to. Unless it is established that the Messenger called people to something, people are not obliged to answer anyone who calls to it, nor is he entitled to call people to it—even supposing that the meaning in question is true.”

This approach is more effective when one of their deceivers misleads those in authority and they draw them into their innovations. This is what the Jahmiyyah did to the caliphs whom they misled, drawing them into their innovations, such as the doctrine that the Quran is created and other such doctrines. One of the best ways to debate them was therefore to say:

“Bring us evidence from the Book or the Sunnah, and we will accept what you call us to. Otherwise, we will not accept from you anything for which the Book and the Sunnah provide no evidence.”

## Page 9987

This is because disputes among people can be settled only by a Book sent down from heaven; if they are referred to their own reason, each reasons in his own way. Whatever contradicts the scriptural texts is an innovation by the agreement of the Muslims. Whatever is not known to contradict them, however, may not be called an innovation.

Al-Shāfiʿī—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Al-Bayhaqī related these words, or words to this effect, with an authentic chain of transmission in his Introduction. It is also related from Mālik—may Allah have mercy on him—that he said:

“When knowledge becomes scarce, coarseness appears; and when transmitted reports become scarce, opinions born of desire proliferate.”

Thus, you find many people loving some and hating others because of views born of desire, whose meaning and supporting evidence they do not know. Rather, they base their loyalties and hostilities on the mere profession of these views, although they have not been authentically transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or the early generations of the Muslim community, and although they themselves neither understand their meaning nor know what they imply and entail. The cause of this is the unqualified assertion of statements not set forth in the scriptural texts, making them into doctrines and calling people

---

## Page 9988

to them and making them the basis of loyalty and hostility. It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say in his sermons:

“The truest speech is the speech of Allah,” and so on.

The religion of the Muslims is founded upon following the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Prophet, and the consensus of the Muslim community. These three are foundations protected from error. Whatever the community disputes is to be referred back to Allah and the Messenger.

No one may set up for the community any person other than the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, calling people to follow that person’s way and making it the basis of loyalty and hostility. Nor may anyone set up for them any statement as the basis of loyalty and hostility other than the words of Allah and His Messenger and that upon which the community has reached consensus. Rather, this is the practice of the proponents of religious innovation, who set up a person or a statement by which they divide the community, basing their loyalties and hostilities upon that statement or affiliation.

The Khawārij merely interpreted verses of the Quran according to their beliefs and declared those who disagreed with them to be disbelievers, because they believed that such people had contradicted the Quran. Thus, whoever introduces statements that have no basis in the Quran and declares those who disagree with them to be disbelievers holds a position worse than that of the Khawārij.

It must be understood that objections to matters known to be part of the Muslims’ religion must be answered decisively, leaving no room for doubt, unlike the approach followed by some speculative theologians. For whoever does not debate the heretics and proponents of religious innovation

---

## Page 9989

in a manner that decisively refutes them has not given Islam its due or fulfilled the demands of knowledge and faith. His words have neither brought healing to hearts and reassurance to souls nor yielded knowledge and certainty. Allah has obliged the believers to believe in the Messenger and strive alongside him. Believing in him includes affirming the truth of everything he has conveyed, and striving alongside him includes repelling everyone who opposes what he brought and deviates concerning Allah’s names and signs.

It is well known that every question involving affirmation or denial must have an objectively true answer, or require distinctions to be drawn. But anyone unfamiliar with the reports of the early generations, the true meaning of their statements, the true import of the Book and the Sunnah, and what sound reason truly establishes—which cannot conceivably contradict them—cannot make pronouncements on the strength of the knowledge he possesses. Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.

There is no doubt that errors concerning subtle points of knowledge are forgiven for this community, even when they concern theoretical matters. Were this not so, most of the community’s eminent scholars would have perished. If Allah forgives someone who was unaware that wine is forbidden because he grew up in a land of ignorance, even though he did not seek knowledge, then a person of virtue who diligently seeks knowledge according to what is accessible in his time and place, intending to follow the Messenger to the best of his ability, is all the more deserving of Allah accepting his good deeds, rewarding his earnest efforts, and not holding him accountable for his mistakes, in fulfilment of His words:

---

## Page 9990

“Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make a mistake.”

Ahl al-Sunnah affirm with certainty that everyone who fears Allah Most High will attain salvation, as the Quran explicitly declares. They withhold judgment only concerning a particular individual, because they do not know whether he is among the God-fearing.

Such is also the case of the other proponents of weak views who, when the matter is unclear to them, invoke the apparent wording of the Quran to support positions contrary to the Sunnah—even though nothing in the Quran’s apparent wording contradicts the Sunnah. Examples include those among the Khawārij who say, “One must pray only four units of prayer while travelling”; those who say that praying four is preferable; and those who say, “We do not issue judgments on the basis of one witness and an oath.”

What the apparent wording of the Quran indicates is true. It is not a general expression whose scope has been restricted, for the wording conveys no generality here; rather, it is unrestricted, as in His words:

“Kill the polytheists.”

This is general with respect to individuals and unrestricted with respect to circumstances. Likewise, His words:

“Allah instructs you concerning your children”

are general with respect to children and unrestricted with respect to circumstances.

The term “apparent” may mean what appears to a person, or it may mean what the wording itself indicates. The former depends on people’s understanding, and much in the Quran contradicts faulty understanding.
