Whoever categorically denies any matter of knowledge merely because there is no conclusive evidence for its existence—as is the approach of a group of speculative theologians—is plainly mistaken.

However, if we know that the existence of something necessarily entails the existence of evidence for it, and we know that this evidence is absent, we can categorically conclude that the thing entailing it does not exist. For the absence of a necessary consequence establishes the absence of that which entails it. We know that there are abundant motives for transmitting Allah’s Book and His religion, and that the Muslim community cannot collectively conceal what needs to be transmitted as universally binding proof. Thus, since neither a sixth prayer nor an additional surah has been transmitted on a widespread basis, we know with certainty that neither exists.

---

## Page 10087

Threats of punishment, however, do not fall into this category. Not every threat attached to an act must be conveyed through mass-transmitted reports, just as mass transmission is not required for the ruling concerning that act. Thus, hadiths containing threats must be acted upon according to their import: one must believe that whoever commits the act is threatened with that punishment. Its actual infliction, however, depends upon certain conditions, and there are impediments that may prevent it.

This principle becomes clear through examples. It is authentically reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah has cursed the one who consumes ribā (usury), the one who pays it, its two witnesses, and its scribe.”

It is also authentically reported through several chains that he said to someone who exchanged two sāʿ for one, hand to hand:

“Alas! That is ribā itself!”

He also said:

“Wheat for wheat is ribā unless exchanged on the spot”—and the hadith continues.

This entails that both kinds of ribā—that involving an excess and that involving deferment—are included in the hadith.

Yet some people received the Prophet’s statement, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Ribā is only in deferment,”

and consequently regarded exchanging two sāʿ for one, hand to hand, as permissible. These included Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, and his companions: Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ, ʿAtāʾ, Tāwūs, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, and other eminent Meccans who were among the finest of this community in knowledge and practice. No Muslim may believe that the curse upon those who consume ribā befalls any one of them individually, or anyone who followed their opinion where such following was permissible. For they acted on an interpretation that was, in general, defensible.

---

## Page 10088

The same applies to reports that a group of eminent Medinans engaged in anal intercourse, despite the report narrated by Abū Dāwūd that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever has intercourse with a woman in her anus has disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad.”

Would any Muslim consider it permissible to say that so-and-so and so-and-so disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad?

Likewise, it is authentically reported from him, peace and blessings be upon him, that “he cursed ten people in connection with khamr (intoxicating drink): the one who presses it, the one who has it pressed, and the one who drinks it.”

It is also authentically reported through several chains that he said:

“Every drink that intoxicates is khamr.”

And he said:

“Every intoxicant is khamr.”

ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, addressed the Emigrants and the Helpers from the Prophet’s pulpit, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: “Khamr is whatever clouds the mind.” Allah revealed the prohibition of khamr, and the occasion for that revelation was what they used to drink in Medina. Their only drink was fadīkh, a drink made from crushed unripe dates; they had no grape wine at all.

Yet some Kufans, among the finest of this community in knowledge and practice, believed that only drink made from grapes was khamr, and that, for infused drinks made from anything other than grapes and dates, only the quantity that caused intoxication was forbidden. They would drink what they believed to be lawful.

It is therefore impermissible to say that these men fall under the threat of punishment, because of the excuse underlying their interpretation or because of other impediments. Nor may it be said that the drink they consumed was not among the khamr whose drinker is cursed. For the particular circumstance that occasioned a general statement must necessarily fall within its scope, and there was no grape wine in Medina. Furthermore, “the Prophet

---

## Page 10089

peace and blessings be upon him, cursed the seller of khamr.” One of the Companions sold khamr, and when news of this reached ʿUmar, he said:

“May Allah confound so-and-so! Did he not know that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: ‘Allah cursed the Jews: animal fats were forbidden to them, yet they sold them and consumed the proceeds’?”

That Companion did not know that selling it was forbidden. Yet ʿUmar’s knowledge of his ignorance did not prevent him from explaining the punishment for this sin, so that he and others would refrain from it once they learned of its prohibition.

The Prophet also cursed the one who presses it and the one who has it pressed. Yet many jurists permit a man to press grapes for another person even when he knows that the latter intends to make khamr from them. This is an explicit text cursing the one who presses it, although we know that the ruling does not apply to an excused person because an impediment prevents its application.

Likewise, in several authentic hadiths, he cursed the woman who attaches hair extensions and the woman who has them attached. Yet some jurists merely regard this as disliked.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever drinks from silver vessels is only gulping the fire of Hell into his belly.”

Yet some jurists regard this as disliked rather than forbidden.

Likewise, he said, peace and blessings be upon him:

“When two Muslims confront one another with their swords, both the killer and the one killed are in the Fire.”

This hadith must be applied in establishing the prohibition of fighting believers

---

## Page 10090

without right. Yet we know that those who fought at the Camel and Siffīn are not in the Fire, for both sides had excuses and an interpretive basis for fighting, as well as good deeds that prevented the grounds for punishment from taking effect.

He said, peace and blessings be upon him, in an authentic hadith:

“There are three whom Allah will neither speak to nor look at on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and theirs will be a painful punishment: a man who has surplus water but withholds it from a wayfarer—Allah will say to him, ‘Today I withhold My bounty from you, just as you withheld the surplus of what your hands did not produce’; a man who pledges allegiance to a ruler solely for worldly gain—if he is given something, he is pleased, but if he is not, he is displeased; and a man who, after the afternoon prayer, swears falsely concerning a commodity that he had been offered more for it than he actually had.”

This is a grave warning against anyone who withholds his surplus water, although some scholars permit a man to do so. This disagreement does not prevent us from believing that it is forbidden, citing the hadith as evidence. Nor does the existence of the hadith prevent us from believing that someone who adopts a different interpretation is excused in this matter and is not subject to this warning.

He also said, peace and blessings be upon him:

“May Allah curse the man who marries a woman to make her lawful again for her former husband, and the man for whom this is done.”

This is an authentic hadith transmitted from him through several routes, and also from his Companions. Nevertheless, some scholars have held such a marriage to be valid without qualification. Others have held it to be valid if this purpose is not stipulated in the contract. They have well-known grounds for being excused in this matter. According to the first group, analogy with established principles dictates that a marriage is not invalidated by stipulations, just as it is not invalidated by either of the two considerations being unknown. According to the second group, analogy with established principles dictates that contracts without an accompanying stipulation do not alter

---

## Page 10091

the rulings governing contracts. This hadith had not reached those who held this view. That is what appears to be the case, for their earlier books did not include it. Had it reached them, they would have mentioned it, either accepting it or answering it. Alternatively, it may have reached them and they interpreted it differently, believed it to have been abrogated, or possessed evidence that conflicted with it. We therefore know that someone such as these would not incur this warning if he engaged in such a marriage believing it lawful on these grounds. This does not prevent us from knowing that such a marriage constitutes grounds for this warning, even if the warning does not apply to certain individuals because a condition is absent or an impediment is present.

The same applies to Mu'āwiya’s acknowledgment—may Allah be pleased with him—of Ziyād ibn Abīhi, who was born to the bed of al-Hārith ibn Kilda, as belonging to his paternal lineage, because Abū Sufyān used to say that Ziyād had been conceived from his seed. Yet the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever claims descent from someone other than his father, knowing that he is not his father, is forbidden Paradise.”

He also said:

“Whoever claims descent from someone other than his father, or takes patrons other than his own, incurs the curse of Allah, the angels, and all mankind. Allah will accept neither compensation nor ransom from him.”

This is an authentic hadith.

He also ruled that the child belongs to the man whose bed it is born to. This is among the rulings on which there is consensus. We therefore know that anyone who claims descent from someone other than the father whose bed he was born to falls within the scope of the Messenger’s words, peace and blessings be upon him. Nevertheless, it is not permissible to single out anyone of lesser standing than the Companions—let alone a Companion—and say that this warning applies to him. For it is possible that the Messenger of Allah’s ruling, peace and blessings be upon him, that the child belongs to the man whose bed it is born to had not reached them, and that they believed

---

## Page 10092

that the child belongs to the man who impregnated his mother, and believed that Abū Sufyān was the one who impregnated Sumayya, Ziyād’s mother. This ruling may be unknown to many people, especially before the Sunnah became widely known, particularly since this had been the custom in pre-Islamic times. Or there may have been other impediments preventing the grounds for this warning from taking effect, such as good deeds that erase evil deeds, and other such factors.

This is a broad subject. It encompasses everything prohibited by the Quran or Sunnah when some members of the Muslim community have not received the evidence establishing its prohibition and therefore regard it as lawful, or when they believe that other evidence outweighs the evidence of prohibition, having exercised independent judgment in weighing the evidence according to their understanding and knowledge. Prohibition entails consequences such as being held sinful, censure, punishment, being deemed a transgressor, and other consequences. These, however, have conditions and impediments. Thus, the prohibition may remain established while these consequences do not apply because a condition is absent or an impediment is present. Alternatively, the prohibition may not apply to that particular person, even though it applies to others.

We have expressed the matter in these alternative terms because there are two views on this issue:

The first—which is the view of the overwhelming majority of the early generations and jurists—is that Allah’s ruling is one, and that anyone who departs from it through a legitimate exercise of independent judgment is mistaken, yet excused and rewarded. On this view, the very act committed by someone acting on an interpretation is forbidden, but the consequences of its prohibition do not apply to him because Allah pardons him, for He does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.

---

## Page 10093

The second view is that the act is not forbidden for that person because the evidence of its prohibition has not reached him, even though it is forbidden for others. Thus, that person’s very act is not forbidden. The two positions are close, and their difference resembles a difference in wording.

This, then, is what may be said concerning hadiths containing threats of punishment when they concern a disputed matter. Scholars unanimously agree that these hadiths may be cited as evidence that the act carrying the threat is forbidden, whether its prohibition is agreed upon or disputed. Indeed, it is in disputed matters that they most need to invoke these hadiths as evidence. They have differed, however, over citing them as evidence for the threatened punishment when they are not definitive, as we have explained.

If it is said:

“Why, then, do you not say that hadiths containing threats of punishment do not encompass disputed matters, but only matters of agreement? Any act whose perpetrator is cursed or threatened with wrath or punishment would thus be understood as an act whose prohibition is agreed upon, so that no scholar exercising independent judgment would fall under the threat for doing something he believed lawful. Indeed, the one who believes it lawful is even more implicated than the one who performs it, since he is the one who directs the latter to do it. Thus, by necessary implication, the threat of a curse or wrath would extend to him?”

We reply:

There are several answers. (First: prohibition as such must either apply in a disputed matter

---

## Page 10094

or not. If it never applies in a disputed matter, it follows that nothing is forbidden unless its prohibition is unanimously agreed upon. Everything whose prohibition is disputed would therefore be lawful. This contradicts the consensus of the Muslim community, and its falsity is necessarily known from the religion of Islam. If, however, prohibition does apply, even in a single case, does a scholar exercising independent judgment who considers that forbidden act lawful incur the blame and punishment due to someone who declares the forbidden lawful or commits it, or does he not?

Whether the answer is that he does incur them or that he does not, the same applies to the prohibition which, by agreement, is established by a hadith containing a threat, and to the threat established in a disputed matter, subject to the distinctions we have explained. Indeed, the threat concerns the person who performs the act, whereas, in principle, the punishment for declaring the forbidden lawful is greater than the punishment for committing it without believing it lawful. Thus, if an act may remain forbidden in a disputed case while the scholar exercising independent judgment who considers it lawful escapes punishment for doing so because he is excused, then there is all the more reason for the person performing the act to escape its threatened punishment.

Just as the scholar exercising independent judgment does not necessarily fall under the consequences of this prohibition in terms of blame, punishment, and the like, neither does he necessarily fall under its threatened punishment. A threat of punishment is merely one form of blame and punishment. If he may fall under this general category, whatever answer is given concerning some of its forms also answers the others. Nor does it help to distinguish between lesser and greater blame, or between severe and mild punishment, for the objection that arises from a small measure of blame

---

## Page 10095

and punishment in this context is the same as that arising from a large measure of either. For the scholar exercising independent judgment incurs neither a small nor a large measure of these; rather, he receives their opposite: recompense and reward.

Second:

Whether the ruling on an act is unanimously agreed upon or disputed is extrinsic to the act and its attributes. These are merely relative matters arising from what some scholars happen not to know. If a general expression is intended to have a restricted meaning, evidence must be provided to establish that restriction. According to those who do not permit clarification to be delayed, this evidence must accompany the statement; according to the majority, its presentation may be delayed until it is needed.

There is no doubt that those addressed by these statements during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, needed to know the rulings they conveyed. Thus, if the general wording cursing one who consumes usury, a man who contracts a marriage intended to make a woman lawful again for her former husband, and others like them were intended to cover only cases unanimously deemed forbidden—and that could not be known until after the Prophet’s death, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and after the Muslim community had expressed its views on every instance covered by that general wording—then he would have delayed clarifying his words until the entire community had expressed its views on every such instance. This is impermissible.

(Third:

These words were addressed to the Muslim community so that they might recognize what is forbidden and avoid it, rely on them as the basis for their consensus, and cite them as evidence in their disputes. If their intended scope were limited to cases on which they unanimously agreed, knowing what was intended would depend on consensus. It would then be invalid to cite these words as evidence before consensus was reached, so they could not serve as its basis. For the evidence on which consensus rests must precede it and therefore cannot come after

---

## Page 10096

it, for this leads to invalid circular reasoning. Those forming the consensus would then be unable to cite the hadith as evidence regarding a particular case until they knew that the case fell within its intended scope; yet they could not know that until they reached consensus. Thus, citing the hadith as evidence would depend on a prior consensus, while consensus would depend on previously citing it as evidence, if the hadith were their basis. Something would therefore depend upon itself, making its existence impossible. Nor could the hadith serve as evidence in a disputed case, because that case was not intended. This would strip the hadith of its capacity to establish the ruling in cases of both agreement and disagreement. It would follow that none of the texts condemning an act in severe terms taught us that the act was forbidden. This is categorically false.

Fourth:

This would entail that none of these hadiths could be cited as evidence until it was known that the Muslim community had reached consensus concerning the particular case. The earliest generation would therefore not have been permitted to cite them as evidence. Indeed, even someone hearing them directly from the mouth of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would not have been permitted to do so. If a person heard such a hadith, found that many scholars had acted upon it, and knew of no opposition to it, he would have to refrain from acting upon it until he had investigated whether anyone anywhere in the world disagreed with it—just as he may not invoke consensus as evidence on a question without a thorough investigation.

Thus, the mere disagreement of a single scholar qualified to exercise independent judgment would invalidate citing the hadith of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as evidence. The opinion of one person would thereby invalidate the words of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, while his agreement would establish the validity of the statement of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. If that one person were mistaken, his error would become

---

## Page 10097

a basis for invalidating the words of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. All of this is self-evidently false.

If it is said, “It may only be cited as evidence once consensus is known to exist,” then the texts’ force as evidence becomes dependent upon consensus, which itself contradicts consensus. The texts would then cease to have any force as evidence, since consensus alone would count, while the text would have no effect.

If it is said, “It may be cited as evidence when no disagreement is known,” then the opinion of a single member of the Muslim community would invalidate the text’s force as evidence. This too contradicts consensus, and its falsity is a matter of self-evident knowledge in Islam.

(Fifth:

Either the text’s applicability is conditional upon the entire Muslim community believing the act to be forbidden, or the belief of the scholars is sufficient. If the former is intended, one could not cite hadiths containing threats of punishment as evidence that an act is forbidden until one knew that the entire Muslim community—including those growing up in remote desert regions and those who had only recently embraced Islam—believed it to be forbidden. No Muslim, indeed no rational person, would say this, for it is impossible to ascertain that this condition has been fulfilled.

If it is said, “The belief of all the scholars is sufficient,” the response is: You have only stipulated scholarly consensus to avoid having the threat of punishment encompass any scholar qualified to exercise independent judgment, even if he is mistaken. Yet precisely the same consideration applies to a layperson who has not heard the evidence that the act is forbidden. For

---

## Page 10098

the objection to the curse encompassing the one applies equally to its encompassing the other. Nor can this argument be escaped by saying, “The former is one of the great figures of the Muslim community and among the most virtuous of the truly faithful, whereas the latter is one of its lesser members.” Their difference in this respect does not prevent them from sharing the same ruling. Just as Allah, glorified be He, forgives a scholar qualified to exercise independent judgment when he errs, He also forgives an ignorant person who errs and has no opportunity to learn. Indeed, the harm caused by a layperson committing a forbidden act, without knowing or being able to learn that it is forbidden, is far less than the harm arising when an imam declares lawful something the Lawgiver has forbidden, without knowing or being able to learn that it is forbidden.

For this reason, it has been said, “Beware of a scholar’s slip, for when he slips, a multitude slips with him.” Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said, “Woe to the scholar on account of his followers!”

If the scholar is pardoned despite the great harm arising from his action, then the other person has an even greater claim to pardon, given the lesser harm arising from his action. They do, however, differ in another respect: the scholar has exercised independent judgment and expressed his view on that basis, and his efforts to spread knowledge and revive the Sunnah yield benefits so great that this harm is eclipsed by them. Allah has distinguished between the two in this respect: He rewards the scholar qualified to exercise independent judgment for his efforts, and the learned person for his knowledge, with a reward in which that ignorant person has no share. Thus, both share in pardon, but they differ in reward.

It is impossible for punishment to befall someone who does not deserve it, whether eminent or lowly. This impossible case must therefore be excluded from the hadith in a manner that encompasses both groups.

---

## Page 10099

Sixth: Some hadiths containing warnings explicitly address the very case under dispute, such as the curse upon the man for whose benefit a woman is married to another man to make her lawful again for him. Some scholars maintain that this man incurs no sin whatsoever. He was in no way a party to the first marriage contract, so it cannot be said that he was cursed for believing that the arrangement had to be fulfilled. Whoever holds that the first man’s marriage is valid even though the condition is void, and that the woman therefore becomes lawful for the second man, absolves the second man of sin.

Indeed, the same reasoning applies to the intermediary husband. He is cursed either for making her lawful again for her former husband, solely for believing that the condition attached to the marriage contract must be fulfilled, or for both together. If it is the first or the third, our point is established. If it is the second, then this belief is what incurs the curse, whether or not any such arrangement takes place. In that case, what the hadith mentions would not be the cause of the curse, while the actual cause would go unmentioned. This is untenable.

Furthermore, if the person who believes that the condition must be fulfilled is ignorant, no curse falls upon him. If he knows that fulfilling it is not obligatory, it is impossible for him to believe it obligatory unless he is deliberately defying the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in which case he would be a disbeliever. The hadith would thus amount to a curse upon disbelievers. Yet disbelief is not confined to denying this particular ruling rather than another. This would be equivalent to saying:

“May Allah curse anyone who accuses the Messenger of falsehood in his ruling that a condition requiring divorce in a marriage contract is void.”

Moreover, this statement is general in both wording and meaning; it is general from the outset. General language of this kind cannot be restricted to rare cases, for that would render the statement inarticulate

---

## Page 10100

and incoherent, as when someone interprets his words:

“Any woman who marries without her guardian’s permission”

as referring only to a female slave under a contract to purchase her freedom.

The rarity of such a case is clear: an ignorant Muslim is not included in the hadith, while a Muslim who knows that this condition need not be fulfilled would not stipulate it while believing its fulfilment obligatory unless he were a disbeliever. A disbeliever would not enter into a Muslim marriage unless he were a hypocrite. For such a marriage to occur in this manner would be exceedingly rare. Indeed, anyone who said that such a case would scarcely cross the speaker’s mind would be speaking the truth.

Elsewhere, we have presented abundant evidence that this hadith concerns the intermediary husband who intends to make the woman lawful again for her former husband, even when this is not stipulated. Likewise, specific warnings of a curse, Hellfire, and the like have been explicitly pronounced in various cases despite scholarly disagreement concerning them. One example is the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, reporting that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“May Allah curse women who frequently visit graves and those who establish places of worship over them and place lamps upon them.”

Al-Tirmidhī graded this hadith as good. Some scholars permitted women to visit graves, while others considered it disliked without declaring it forbidden.

Another example is the hadith of ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir, may Allah be pleased with him, reporting that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“May Allah curse those who have intercourse with women in their anuses.”

There is also the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, reporting that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The trader who brings goods to market is granted provision, while the hoarder is cursed.”

---

## Page 10101

And the hadith concerning the three to whom Allah will neither speak, nor look at, nor purify, and who will suffer a painful punishment, has already been cited. Among them is one who withholds his surplus water. He also cursed the seller of wine, although some of the early scholars sold it.

It has been authentically reported from him through several chains of transmission that he said:

“Whoever drags his lower garment out of pride, Allah will not look at him on the Day of Resurrection.”

He also said:

“There are three to whom Allah will neither speak, nor look at on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify, and who will suffer a painful punishment: one who lets his garment trail, one who reminds others of his favors, and one who sells his goods by swearing falsely.”

Yet a group of jurists say that dragging one’s garment and letting it trail out of pride is disliked, not forbidden. Likewise, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“May Allah curse the woman who adds hair extensions and the woman who has them added.”

This is among the most authentic hadiths, yet there is a well-known disagreement over adding hair extensions.

Likewise, he said:

“Whoever drinks from silver vessels is only gulping the fire of Hell into his belly.”

Yet some scholars did not consider this forbidden.

(Seventh: The grounds for general application are present, and the objection mentioned cannot validly counter them. At most, it may be said that applying the wording to both agreed-upon and disputed cases necessarily includes some who do not deserve to be cursed. The response is: if restricting its scope runs counter to the basic presumption, then multiplying such restrictions also runs counter to that presumption. Thus, an exception to this general scope is made for

---

## Page 10102

those who are excused on account of ignorance, independent scholarly reasoning, or reliance on scholarly authority. The ruling still encompasses those without an excuse, just as it encompasses cases on which there is agreement. This entails fewer restrictions on its general scope and is therefore preferable.

Eighth:

If we understand the wording in this way, it identifies the grounds for the curse, while the ruling does not apply to those excepted because an impediment prevents its application. Undoubtedly, promises and warnings need not expressly exclude those for whom they do not take effect because of a countervailing factor. The wording thus remains entirely sound.

If, however, we understand the curse as applying to the commission of an act unanimously held to be forbidden, or take its grounds to be a belief contrary to scholarly consensus, then the grounds for the curse would not be mentioned in the hadith. Moreover, that general wording would still require exceptions. Since exceptions are necessary under either interpretation, accepting them under the first is preferable: it accords with the apparent meaning of the wording and requires no unstated qualification.

Ninth:

The sole reason for this interpretation is to deny that the curse applies to someone who has an excuse. We have already explained that hadiths containing warnings are intended to establish that the act in question is a cause for that curse. Their meaning is therefore: “This act is a cause for being cursed.” Such a statement would not entail that the ruling takes effect in the case of every individual. It would, however, entail that the cause is present even where the ruling does not follow, and there is nothing objectionable in this. We have already established that

---

## Page 10103

blame does not attach to a scholar exercising independent judgment. Indeed, we even say that declaring something forbidden to be lawful is a greater sin than committing it; nevertheless, whoever has an excuse remains excused.

If it is asked: “Who, then, is punished? Whoever commits this forbidden act is either exercising independent scholarly judgment or following the authority of someone who does, and both are exempt from punishment.”

We reply that there are several answers:

First:

The purpose is to explain that this act constitutes grounds for punishment, whether or not anyone actually commits it. If we suppose that everyone who commits it either lacks a condition necessary for punishment or has an impediment preventing it, this does not detract from its being forbidden. Rather, we recognize that it is forbidden so that those to whom its prohibition becomes clear may avoid it. That someone who commits it has an excuse is part of Allah’s mercy towards him.

Similarly, minor sins are forbidden even though they are expiated by avoiding major sins. This is the case with all forbidden acts whose prohibition is disputed. If it becomes clear that they are forbidden—even though someone who commits them may be excused because he is exercising independent scholarly judgment or following scholarly authority—that does not prevent us from believing them to be forbidden.

Second:

Explaining the ruling is a means of removing the uncertainty that prevents punishment from applying. An excuse arising from a belief is not meant to remain; rather, what is sought is its removal as far as possible. Otherwise, there would be no obligation to impart knowledge, and leaving

---

## Page 10104

people in their ignorance would have been better for them, and leaving the evidence concerning uncertain issues unexplained would have been better than explaining it.

Third:

Explaining the ruling and the threatened punishment helps those who refrain from such acts remain steadfast in avoiding them. Were it not for this, the practice would become widespread.

Fourth:

This excuse is valid only when a person is unable to remove it. Whenever someone can ascertain the truth but neglects to do so, he is not excused.

Fifth:

Some people may commit the act without either exercising independent scholarly judgment in a manner that permits them to do so or following scholarly authority in a manner that permits it. In such a person, the grounds for the threatened punishment are present without this particular impediment. He therefore exposes himself to the threatened punishment and incurs it, unless another impediment exists, such as repentance, good deeds that erase sins, or something else.

This, however, may vary: a person may think that his independent judgment or his following scholarly authority permits him to act, sometimes being right in this and sometimes mistaken. Yet whenever he sincerely seeks the truth and is not diverted from it by following his desires, Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.

(Tenth:

If allowing these hadiths to retain their implications necessarily brings some scholars exercising independent judgment within the scope of the threatened punishment, and if this is inevitable on either supposition, then the hadith remains free of any countervailing argument and must therefore be acted upon.

---

## Page 10105

This may be explained as follows:

Many leading scholars have explicitly declared that someone who performs an act in a form whose ruling is disputed is cursed. Among them is ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both. He was asked about a man who married a woman to make her lawful again for her former husband, without either the woman or her former husband knowing of his intention. He replied: “This is fornication, not marriage. ‘Allah has cursed the man who marries a woman to make her lawful again for her former husband, and the former husband for whom he does so.’”

This is reliably reported from him through several chains of transmission, and similar statements are reported from others, including Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who said: “If he intends to make her lawful again for her former husband, then he is marrying for that purpose and is cursed.” Such statements are transmitted from numerous leading scholars concerning many disputed cases involving wine, usury, and other matters.

If the curse pronounced in the revealed texts, and the other threatened punishments reported in them, applied only to cases on which there is agreement, then these scholars would have cursed people whom it is impermissible to curse. They would therefore incur the threatened punishment mentioned in several hadiths, such as the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Cursing a Muslim is like killing him.”

And his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as narrated by Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him:

“Reviling a Muslim is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief.”

Both are reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

Abū al-Dardāʾ, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that he heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say:

“Those who habitually disparage and curse others will be neither intercessors nor witnesses on the Day of Resurrection.”

Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“It does not befit a person of utmost truthfulness to be given to cursing.”

Both are reported by Muslim. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A believer is not one who habitually disparages or curses others, nor is he obscene or foul-mouthed.”

Reported by al-Tirmidhī

---

## Page 10106

and said: “It is a good hadith.” Another report states:

“No man curses something undeserving of it without the curse returning upon him.”

This threatened punishment for cursing—such that whoever curses someone undeserving of it is himself cursed, such cursing is wickedness, and it excludes one from the rank of utmost truthfulness, intercession, and bearing witness—applies to anyone who curses someone undeserving of it. Thus, if someone who performs a disputed act does not fall within the scope of the text, he does not deserve the curse, and whoever curses him becomes liable to this threatened punishment. Those scholars exercising independent judgment who considered the disputed case to fall within the hadith would therefore themselves be liable to this threatened punishment.

If the objectionable consequence follows both on the assumption that the disputed case is excluded and on the assumption that it remains included, then it is clear that this is not an objectionable consequence and does not prevent the hadith from being cited as evidence. If the objectionable consequence does not follow on either assumption, then no objectionable consequence arises at all.

For once this necessary connection is established, and it is known that their coming under the threat on the assumption of inclusion entails their coming under it on the assumption of exclusion, one of two things must hold: either both the antecedent and its consequent obtain, meaning that they all come under the threat, or neither the consequent nor its antecedent obtains, meaning that none of them comes under it. For when the antecedent obtains, its consequent obtains; and when the consequent is absent, its antecedent is absent.

This much suffices to refute the objection. What we believe, however, is that in fact they do not come under the threat on either assumption, as already established. This is because coming under the threat is conditional upon having no excuse for the act, whereas someone who has an excuse recognized by Islamic law is not

---

## Page 10107

subject to the threat under any circumstances. A scholar exercising independent judgment is excused—indeed, rewarded—so the condition for coming under the threat is absent in his case. He therefore does not come under it, whether he believes that the hadith retains its apparent meaning or that the matter admits of disagreement for which one may be excused. This is a conclusive argument from which there is only one possible escape: for the questioner to say:

“I concede that some scholars exercising independent judgment believe that the disputed case falls within the texts containing threats of punishment and, on that basis, invoke the threat against it, cursing, for example, anyone who commits that act. Yet this belief of theirs is mistaken, though their error is one for which they are excused and rewarded. They therefore do not come under the threat against those who curse unjustly, because I understand that threat to apply to cursing that is unanimously agreed to be forbidden. Whoever utters a curse unanimously agreed to be forbidden exposes himself to the punishment threatened for cursing. But when the cursing itself is a matter of disagreement, it does not fall within the hadiths containing threats of punishment, just as an act whose permissibility, and the permissibility of cursing its perpetrator, are disputed does not fall within those hadiths. Thus, just as I exclude the disputed case from the first threat, I exclude it from the second.

“I believe that, on both sides, the hadiths containing threats of punishment do not encompass the disputed case, whether the disagreement concerns the permissibility of the act or the permissibility of cursing its perpetrator, and whether the act is held to be permissible or impermissible. Under either assumption, I do not deem it permissible to curse its perpetrator, nor do I deem it permissible to curse someone who curses its perpetrator. I do not believe that either the perpetrator or the one who curses him falls within a hadith containing a threat of punishment. Nor do I rebuke the one who curses as harshly as someone who considers him exposed to that threat would do; rather,

---

## Page 10108

I regard his cursing someone who commits the disputed act as itself a matter open to independent judgment. I believe him mistaken in this, just as I may believe the one who permits the act mistaken. There are three positions concerning the disputed case:

The first is that it is permissible.

The second is that it is forbidden and that the threat of punishment applies.

The third is that it is forbidden without this severe threat applying.

I may choose this third position because the evidence establishes both that the act is forbidden and that cursing someone who commits the disputed act is forbidden, while believing that the hadith threatening punishment for the perpetrator and for the one who curses does not encompass these two cases.”

The questioner is then told:

“If you allow that cursing this perpetrator is a matter open to independent judgment, then the apparent meaning of the explicit text may be invoked as evidence for it. In that case, there is no assurance that the disputed case is not intended by the hadith containing the threat of punishment. Moreover, the grounds for including it are present, so the text must be acted upon. But if you do not allow this to be a matter open to independent judgment, then cursing him is definitively forbidden. There is no doubt that anyone who curses a scholar exercising independent judgment, when that curse is definitively forbidden, falls within the threat of punishment directed at those who curse—even if he acts on an interpretation, as does someone who curses some of the righteous predecessors.

“Thus, the circularity is unavoidable, whether you hold that cursing someone who commits the disputed act is definitively forbidden or allow legitimate disagreement over it. The belief you have stated does not invalidate the use of the texts containing threats of punishment as evidence under either assumption. This is clear.”

---

## Page 10109

He is also told:

“Our aim in this argument is not to establish that the threat of punishment applies to the disputed case, but to establish the validity of citing the hadith containing that threat as evidence concerning the disputed case. The hadith conveys two rulings: prohibition and the threat of punishment. What you have mentioned only challenges its indication of the threat of punishment, whereas our purpose here is to explain its indication of prohibition. If you maintain that the hadiths threatening those who curse do not encompass cursing whose permissibility is disputed, then no evidence remains for prohibiting such cursing. The cursing under discussion is precisely of this disputed kind, as explained earlier. If it is not forbidden, then it is permissible.”

Or it may be said:

“If there is no evidence establishing its prohibition, it is impermissible to believe it forbidden. Moreover, grounds for permitting it exist: namely, the hadiths cursing those who commit this act. Scholars have differed over whether it is permissible to curse such a person, and on this assumption there is no evidence prohibiting it. It is therefore obligatory to act upon the evidence supporting its permissibility, since no opposing evidence stands against it.”

This refutes the objection. The questioner is thus caught in circularity from another direction. This further circularity arises because most texts prohibiting cursing also contain a threat of punishment. If texts containing threats of punishment cannot be cited as evidence concerning disputed cases, they cannot be cited as evidence against cursing whose permissibility is disputed, as explained earlier.

If he were to say:

“I rely on scholarly consensus as evidence that this cursing is forbidden,”

he would be told:

“Consensus has been established that it is forbidden to curse a specific virtuous individual.

---

## Page 10110

As for cursing those described by a particular characteristic, you are already aware of the disagreement concerning it. It has also been explained that such a curse does not necessarily fall upon every individual fitting that description unless the conditions are fulfilled and the impediments removed; and that is not always the case.”

He is also told:

“All the preceding evidence against restricting these hadiths to cases on which there is agreement applies here. It refutes this objection just as it refuted the original objection. This is not a case of making one proof a premise in another proof, such that someone might say: ‘Despite its length, this amounts to only one proof.’ The purpose here is to show that the unacceptable consequence they imagined follows on either assumption, and thus cannot be regarded as an unacceptable consequence. A single proof therefore establishes both that the texts are intended to encompass disputed cases and that there is nothing objectionable in this. Nor is there anything objectionable about the proof of one proposition serving as a premise in the proof of another, even if the two propositions necessarily entail one another.”

(Eleventh:

The scholars agree that it is obligatory to act upon hadiths containing threats of punishment insofar as they establish prohibition. Some scholars differed only over acting upon solitary reports among them specifically with regard to the threatened punishment. As for prohibition, there is no disagreement worthy of consideration. The scholars among the Companions, the Successors, and the jurists who came after them—may Allah be pleased with them all—have consistently cited these hadiths as evidence in their speech and writings, in disputed matters and otherwise. Indeed, when a hadith contains a threat of punishment, this indicates prohibition all the more emphatically, as is recognized by

## Page 10111

people’s hearts. It has also already been noted that the stronger view is to act upon these hadiths both in establishing the ruling and in affirming the threatened punishment, and that this is the view of the majority. Accordingly, an objection contrary to the position of the scholarly community cannot be accepted.

Twelfth:

The texts containing threats of punishment in the Quran and Sunnah are exceedingly numerous. It is obligatory to affirm what they entail in general and unqualified terms, without singling out any individual and saying, “This person is cursed, is under Allah’s wrath, or deserves the Fire”—especially if that person has virtues and good deeds to his credit. Anyone other than the prophets may commit minor and major sins, while still being a person of consummate truthfulness, a martyr, or a righteous person. As explained earlier, the consequence of a sin may be averted through repentance, seeking forgiveness, good deeds that erase sins, afflictions that expiate them, intercession, or solely through Allah’s will and mercy.

Thus, if we affirm what is entailed by His words, Exalted is He:

“Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will burn in a blazing Fire.”

And His words, Exalted is He:

“And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire in which he will abide forever, and he will have a humiliating punishment.”

And His words, Exalted is He:

“Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly, but only through trade by mutual consent. And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you.”

“And whoever does that in aggression and injustice, We shall cast him into a Fire. And that is easy for Allah.”

And other verses containing threats of punishment—or if we affirm what is entailed by his words

(may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Allah has cursed whoever drinks wine, mistreats his parents, or changes land boundary markers”;

or, “Allah has cursed the thief”;

or, “Allah has cursed the one who consumes usury, the one who pays it, its two witnesses, and its scribe”;

or, “Allah has cursed whoever withholds obligatory charity or transgresses concerning it”;

or, “Whoever commits an offense in Medina or shelters an offender is subject to the curse of Allah, the angels, and all people”;

and, “Whoever cheats us is not one of us”;

and other hadiths containing threats of punishment—we may not single out someone who has committed any of these deeds and say, “This particular person has incurred this threatened punishment.” Repentance and other factors that avert punishment remain possible. Nor may we say, “This entails cursing Muslims, cursing the community of Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), or cursing people of consummate truthfulness or the righteous.”

The answer is that whenever a person of consummate truthfulness or a righteous person commits any of these deeds, there must be an impediment preventing the threatened punishment from reaching him, even though its cause is present. Thus, someone who does these things believing them permissible on the basis of independent scholarly judgment, following another’s scholarly opinion, or the like, would at most fall into a category of people of consummate truthfulness whom the threatened punishment does not reach because of an impediment—just as it does not reach a person because of repentance

---

## Page 10113

or good deeds that erase sins, or other such factors.

Know that this is the path that must be followed, for the alternatives are two pernicious paths:

The first is to assert that the threatened punishment applies to every particular individual, claiming that this gives effect to the texts. This is more reprehensible than the position of the Khawārij, who declare people unbelievers for committing sins, or that of the Mu‘tazilah and others. Its invalidity is self-evident, and the evidence against it is well known from discussions elsewhere.

The second is to refrain from affirming and acting upon the implications of the hadiths of Allah’s Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), supposing that affirming their implications necessarily entails impugning whatever conflicts with them. Such abandonment leads to misguidance and to joining the followers of the two Scriptures,

“who took their rabbis and monks, as well as the Messiah, son of Mary, as lords besides Allah.”

For the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“They did not worship them; rather, when those leaders made the unlawful lawful for them, they followed them, and when they made the lawful unlawful for them, they followed them.”

It also leads to obeying created beings in disobedience to the Creator, and to dire consequences and an evil outcome, as implied by the words of Allah Most High:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and best in outcome.”

---

## Page 10114

Moreover, scholars frequently disagree. If, whenever someone takes a position contrary to a report containing a stern warning, that warning is no longer affirmed or the report is not acted upon at all, the resulting dangers—disbelief and departure from the religion—would be beyond description. Even if the danger of this course were not greater than that of the preceding one, it would be no less.

We must therefore believe in the Scripture and follow everything sent down to us from our Lord. We must not believe in part of the Scripture while disbelieving in another, or let our hearts incline to following some of the Sunnah while recoiling from accepting other parts, according to habit and desire. This is a departure from the straight path onto the path of those who have incurred wrath and those who have gone astray.

May Allah enable us to say and do what He loves and is pleased with, granting us and all Muslims goodness and well-being. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah bestow His blessings and abundant peace upon our master Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets; upon his good and pure family, his chosen Companions, his wives—the Mothers of the Believers—and those who follow them in righteousness until the Day of Judgment.

## Page 10115

He was also asked:

“Is it true that Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qādir is the foremost of the shaykhs and that Imam Ahmad is the foremost of the imams?”

He replied:

As for ranking some imams and shaykhs above others—for example, someone preferring the imam whose legal school he studied, or preferring the shaykh he follows over others, as when someone gives preference to Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qādir, Shaykh Abū Madyan, Ahmad, or others—most people speak on this subject on the basis of conjecture and personal desire.

They do not know the true ranks of the imams and shaykhs, nor do they seek to follow the truth for its own sake. Rather, each person desires to give preference to the one he follows, and does so on the basis of his own suppositions, even without any proof. This may lead them to dispute, fight, and become divided. Such conduct is among the things Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, as Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, fear Allah as He should be feared, and do not die except as Muslims.”

“And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. And remember Allah’s favor upon you when you were

---

## Page 10116

enemies, and He brought your hearts together, so that by His favor you became brothers. You were on the brink of a pit of Fire, and He saved you from it. Thus Allah makes His signs clear to you, so that you may be guided.”

“Let there be among you a group calling to good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. It is they who will be successful.”

“And do not be like those who became divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them. For them there is a tremendous punishment.”

“On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black.”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “The faces of the people of the Sunnah and unity will turn white, while the faces of the people of innovation and division will turn black.”

Whatever falls within this category of partisanship, division, disagreement, and speaking without knowledge that Allah and His Messenger have forbidden must be prohibited. No one may engage in what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden.

As for someone who, on the basis of his own independent judgment, considers one imam superior to another, or one shaykh superior to another, this is comparable to the disagreements among Muslims over which is preferable: repeating the testimonies of faith in the call to prayer or not repeating them; saying the phrases of the call immediately before prayer once or twice; performing the dawn prayer while it is still dark or when it has grown light; offering the qunūt supplication in the dawn prayer or omitting it; reciting “In the name of Allah” aloud, reciting it quietly, or not reciting it; and similar questions.

These are matters of independent scholarly judgment over which the early generations and the imams differed, each allowing the others to follow their own judgment. Whoever reached the correct conclusion receives two rewards; whoever exercised independent judgment but erred receives one reward, and his error is forgiven. Thus, whoever considers following al-Shāfi‘ī preferable does not censure someone who considers following Mālik preferable; and whoever considers following Ahmad preferable

---

## Page 10117

does not censure someone who considers following al-Shāfi‘ī preferable, and so on.

No one in Islam can give all Muslims a blanket answer that one person is superior to another and have that answer accepted by all. For it is well known that every group favors the person it follows and will not accept an answer that contradicts its assessment. Likewise, someone who considers a particular view or practice preferable will not accept a ruling to the contrary. However, if a person follows a scholar’s judgment, let him follow the one he considers more likely to be right. If he is qualified to exercise independent scholarly judgment, let him do so and follow what he considers to be the truth. Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. The Exalted has said:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

He must, however, neither follow his own desires nor speak without knowledge. The Exalted has said:

“Here you are—you have argued about matters of which you have knowledge. Why, then, do you argue about matters of which you have no knowledge?”

The Exalted has also said:

“They argue with you concerning the truth after it has become clear.”

Every imam has certain issues on which his view carries greater weight than that of others. Only someone who has delved into the details of scholarly knowledge can discern these differences in merit. And Allah knows best.

## Page 10118

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about “the soundness of the foundational principles of the school of the people of Medina,” and about Mālik, to whom their school is attributed: his standing in scholarly leadership and religious devotion, and his mastery of the Islamic religious sciences, as assessed by the leading scholars of the various cities and trustworthy experts throughout the ages.

He replied—may Allah be pleased with him:

Praise be to Allah. During the time of the Companions, the Successors, and their followers, the school of the people of Medina, the Prophet’s city, was the soundest of the schools of the Muslim cities, east and west, in both fundamentals and subsidiary matters. Medina is the home of the Sunnah, of emigration, and of support: there Allah prescribed for His Messenger Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, the practices and laws of Islam; to it the Emigrants migrated for the sake of Allah and His Messenger; and there lived the Ansār, who had settled in the city and embraced faith before the Emigrants’ arrival.

These three eras are those of the three favored generations, concerning which

---

## Page 10119

the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said in an authentic hadith transmitted through several chains:

“The best of generations is the generation among whom I was sent, then those who follow them, then those who follow them.”

Ibn Hibbān thus mentioned two generations after the Prophet’s own, without dispute. Some hadiths express uncertainty about a third generation after his own, while other narrations affirm it unequivocally, making four generations in all. Ibn Hibbān al-Bustī and other hadith scholars likewise affirmed this in their accounts of the generations of this community, for this additional wording is established in the Sahīh.

As for the hadiths mentioning three generations, both Sahīh collections relate that Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The best of my community are the generation closest to me, then those who follow them, then those who follow them. Then there will come people whose testimony precedes their oath and whose oath precedes their testimony.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said:

“A man asked the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, ‘Which people are best?’ He replied, ‘The generation among whom I was sent, then the second, then the third.’”

As for the uncertainty concerning the fourth generation, both Sahīh collections relate from Imrān ibn Husayn that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The best of you are my generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them”—Imrān said, “I do not know whether the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, mentioned two or three generations after his own”—“then

---

## Page 10120

there will be people after them who give testimony without being asked, betray trusts and cannot be trusted, make vows but do not fulfil them, and among whom fatness becomes widespread.”

Another version reads:

“The best of this community are the generation among whom I was sent, then those who follow them, then those who follow them.”

The hadith continues, including the words:

“They swear oaths without being asked to do so.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayrah reported that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The best of my community are the generation among whom I was sent, then those who follow them”—and Allah knows best whether he mentioned the third generation—“then they will be succeeded by people who love fatness and give testimony before being asked.”

Some scholars understood his words in these hadiths, “They give testimony before being asked,” to mean giving truthful testimony before the person in whose favour it is given requests it. They took this to apply when that person already knows of the testimony, thereby reconciling it with his saying:

“Shall I tell you who is the best witness? The one who brings forward his testimony before being asked for it.”

They understood the latter to mean that the witness approaches the person in whose favour he can testify and informs him of his testimony.

The correct understanding, however, is that these hadiths condemn those who testify falsely, as stated in one version of the hadith: “Then lying will become so widespread among them that a man will give testimony without being asked.” This is why he coupled it with betrayal of trust and failure to fulfil vows. These three traits are the sign of a hypocrite, as established in the hadith recorded in both Sahīh collections and narrated from him

---

## Page 10121

—peace and blessings be upon him—in which he said:

“The signs of a hypocrite are three: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks his promise; and when he is entrusted with something, he betrays that trust.” In one version recorded by Muslim: “Even if he fasts, prays, and claims to be a Muslim.”

Thus, he, peace and blessings be upon him, condemned them for the traits of hypocrisy that would become widespread among them. He explained that they would rush to lie, to the point that a man would give false testimony before being asked to do so. Such a person is worse than one who does not lie until he is asked to lie.

As for reports mentioning the fourth generation, an example is the hadith in the two Sahīh collections, narrated by Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who said:

“A time will come when groups of people will go into battle and be asked, ‘Is there anyone among you who saw the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him?’ They will say, ‘Yes,’ and victory will be granted to them.

“Then groups of people will go into battle and be asked, ‘Is there anyone among you who saw the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him?’ They will say, ‘Yes,’ and victory will be granted to them.

“Then groups of people will go into battle and be asked, ‘Is there anyone among you who saw the companions of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him?’ They will say, ‘Yes,’ and victory will be granted to them.

“Then groups of people will go into battle, and it will be asked, ‘Is there anyone among you who saw the companions of the companions of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him?’ They will say, ‘Yes,’ and victory will be granted to them.”

Al-Bukhārī’s wording is: “Then a time will come when groups of people will go into battle.” Accordingly, he, peace and blessings be upon him, used this wording in the second and third instances. In all of them, he said “had accompanied,” not “had seen.”

---

## Page 10122

Muslim also records another version:

“A time will come when an expedition will be dispatched, and the people will say, ‘Look and see whether you can find among you any of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him.’ Such a man will be found, and victory will be granted to them on his account.

“Then a second expedition will be dispatched, and they will ask, ‘Is there anyone among you who saw the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him?’ They will say, ‘Yes,’ and victory will be granted to them.

“Then a third expedition will be dispatched, and they will say, ‘Look and see whether there is anyone among you who saw someone who saw the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him.’

“Then there will be a fourth expedition, and it will be said, ‘Look and see whether there is anyone among you who saw someone who saw someone who saw the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him.’ Such a man will be found, and victory will be granted to them on his account.”

This hadith of Abū Saʿīd establishes two points: that a Companion of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is anyone who saw him while believing in him, however brief his companionship. This was explicitly stated by the imams, including Ahmad and others. Mālik said:

“Anyone who accompanied the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, for a year, a month, or a day, or saw him while believing in him, is one of his Companions, with a share in companionship corresponding to that.”

This is because “companionship” is a generic term encompassing various forms. One may say, “He accompanied him for a month,” or “for an hour.” This hadith makes clear that the status of companionship applies to someone who saw him while believing in him, for this is indispensable.

In Muslim’s second version, four generations are mentioned. Those who affirm this

---

## Page 10123

addition say:

“This addition comes from a trustworthy narrator. Its omission from the other hadiths does not negate it, just as uncertainty in Abū Hurayrah’s hadith about whether the third generation was mentioned does not undermine the other authentic hadiths in which the third generation is established.”

Those who reject it say concerning the authentic hadith of Ibn Masʿūd:

“He stated that after the three generations, people would come whose testimony would precede their oaths, and whose oaths would precede their testimony. Thus, those who come after the three generations were mentioned with censure.”

It may be said:

“There is no contradiction between the two reports. Lying may become prevalent in the fourth generation, yet that generation may still include someone on whose account victory is granted, owing to an unbroken succession of people who saw one another.”

During the generations praised by the Messenger of Allah, may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace, the way of the people of Medina was the soundest among those of the various cities. They followed the example of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, more closely than the inhabitants of other cities, who were less knowledgeable about the Prophetic Sunnah and less observant of it. Indeed, they had no need for any form of royal governance, while scholars and the pursuits of devout worshippers stood in greater need than did the people of Medina. They were less dependent than others on all such things because of the Prophetic traditions they possessed, which everyone needs to know and follow.

For this reason, no Muslim scholar held that the consensus of the inhabitants of any city other than Medina constituted binding proof that must be followed, whether in those times or in the times

---

## Page 10124

that followed—neither the consensus of the people of Mecca, nor that of Syria, Iraq, or any other Muslim city. Whoever attributes to Abū Hanīfah or any of his followers the view that the consensus of the people of Kufa constitutes binding proof that every Muslim must follow has misrepresented Abū Hanīfah and his followers.

As for Medina, scholars have discussed the consensus of its inhabitants. Mālik and his followers are well known for holding that their consensus constitutes binding proof, although the other imams dispute this with them. This discussion concerns only their consensus during those favored generations. As for subsequent times, scholars have agreed that the consensus of Medina’s inhabitants does not constitute binding proof, since by then there were scholars elsewhere who were not to be found there. This was especially so after Rāfidism appeared in Medina.

Its inhabitants had remained attached to their longstanding religious way, identifying with the school of Mālik, until the beginning of the sixth century AH, or before or after that. Then some of the Rāfidīs of the East, from Qāshān and elsewhere, came to them and corrupted the beliefs of many of them, particularly those among them who traced their descent to the Prophet’s family. They brought books by adherents of religious innovation that contradicted the Quran and Sunnah, and lavished considerable sums of money upon them. From that time onward, religious innovation became widespread there.

During the three favored generations, however, no religious innovation was openly manifest in the Prophet’s city whatsoever. Nor did any innovation concerning the foundations of religion originate there, as happened in the other cities. For the major cities inhabited by the Companions of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless

---

## Page 10125

him and grant him peace, exalted be He—and from which knowledge and faith spread, were five: the two Sacred Cities, the two Iraqi cities, and Syria. From them spread the Quran, hadith, jurisprudence, worship, and the other related aspects of Islam. Innovations concerning the foundations of religion arose in these centres, except for the Prophet’s city. Shiism and the doctrine of the Murjiʾah arose in Kufa and subsequently spread elsewhere. Qadarism, Muʿtazilism, and corrupt asceticism arose in Basra and subsequently spread elsewhere. In Syria there was hostility toward the Prophet’s family, as well as Qadarism.

As for Jahmism, it emerged only from the region of Khurasan, and it is the worst of innovations. The emergence of innovations corresponded to the distance from the Prophet’s city. When division arose after the killing of ʿUthmān, the innovation of the Harūriyyah appeared. Punitive measures had already been prescribed against the three categories of Shīʿah: the extremists, whom ʿAlī burned with fire; those who accorded him precedence, for whom he prescribed eighty lashes; and the Sabaʾiyyah, whom he threatened, seeking to punish Ibn Sabaʾ with death or otherwise, whereupon Ibn Sabaʾ fled from him. Then, toward the end of the era of the Companions, the Qadariyyah emerged, late in the lifetime of Ibn ʿUmar

---

## Page 10126

and Ibn ʿAbbās, Jābir, and other Companions like them. The Murjiʾah emerged at around the same time.

As for the adherents of Jahmism, they emerged only toward the end of the era of the Successors, after the death of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. It is reported that he warned against them. Jahm appeared in Khurasan during the caliphate of Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. Before that, the Muslims had killed their teacher, al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham. Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī slaughtered him as a sacrifice, saying:

“O people, offer your sacrifices, and may Allah accept them from you. I am sacrificing al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham, for he claimed that Allah did not take Abraham as a close friend and did not speak directly to Moses. Exalted is Allah, far above what al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham says!”

He then descended and slaughtered him. It is reported that news of this reached al-Hasan al-Basrī and other Successors like him, and they commended it.

The Prophet’s city, however, remained free of the open emergence of these innovations. Although some people there secretly harboured such beliefs, they were held in contempt and censured by its inhabitants. There were indeed some Qadarīs and others there, but they were censured and kept in check. This was unlike Shiism and the doctrine of the Murjiʾah in Kufa, Muʿtazilism and the innovations of the ascetics in Basra, and hostility toward the Prophet’s family in Syria, all of which were openly manifest. It is authentically reported “from the Prophet, may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace, that

---

## Page 10127

the Dajjāl will not enter it.”

In the well-known account, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, the leader of the Muʿtazilah, passed a man who was speaking privately with Sufyān al-Thawrī, without realizing that it was Sufyān. ʿAmr asked the man, “Who is this?”

He replied, “This is Sufyān al-Thawrī,” or said, “He is from Kufa.”

ʿAmr said, “Had I known that, I would have invited him to adopt my views. But I thought he was one of those Medinans who come at you from above.”

Knowledge and faith continued to flourish there until the time of Mālik’s students, who belonged to the fourth generation. That generation learned from Mālik and his contemporaries, such as al-Thawrī, al-Awzāʿī, al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Hammād ibn Zayd, Hammād ibn Salamah, Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah, and others like them. These scholars had learned from various groups of Successors, who in turn had learned from the Companions whom they had met.

The discussion concerns the consensus of the people of Medina during those eras.

A precise assessment of “the question of the consensus of the people of Medina” is that some aspects are agreed upon among Muslims, others represent the position of the majority of Muslim imams, and still others are upheld by only some of them. The consensus of the people of Medina falls into four levels.

“The first” is that which amounts to transmission from the Prophet, may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace.

---

## Page 10128

such as their transmission of the volume of the sāʿ and the mudd, and their practice of not levying zakat on vegetables or endowed property. Scholars unanimously agree that this constitutes authoritative evidence. Al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and their followers accept it as authoritative evidence without dispute, just as Mālik does. This is also the position of Abū Hanīfah and his followers.

When Abū Yūsuf—may Allah have mercy on him, the foremost of Abū Hanīfah’s followers and the first to bear the title “Chief Judge”—met Mālik and asked him about these questions, Mālik answered him with the mass-transmitted reports of the people of Medina. Abū Yūsuf then adopted Mālik’s position and said, “Had my teacher seen what I have seen, he would have revised his position as I have.”

Abū Yūsuf thus related that his teacher Abū Hanīfah regarded transmission of this kind as authoritative evidence, just as others did. However, this transmission had not reached Abū Hanīfah, just as many hadiths had not reached him or other imams. They cannot therefore be blamed for not following something of which they had no knowledge.

Abū Yūsuf’s acceptance of this transmission was like his acceptance of many hadiths which he and his colleague Muhammad followed, setting aside their teacher’s opinion. They knew that their teacher used to say, “These hadiths, too, are authoritative evidence if authentic”; they simply had not reached him.

Anyone who supposes that Abū Hanīfah or any other imam of the Muslims deliberately opposed an authentic hadith on the grounds of analogical reasoning or anything else has misjudged them and spoken either from conjecture or personal inclination. Here, for example, is Abū Hanīfah acting upon the hadith concerning ablution with nabīdh (a drink made by steeping fruit in water) during

---

## Page 10129

travel, contrary to analogical reasoning, and upon the hadith concerning laughing aloud during prayer, although it too conflicts with analogical reasoning. He did so because he believed both hadiths to be authentic, even though the leading hadith scholars did not authenticate them.

We have explained this in the treatise *Removing Blame from the Eminent Imams*, showing that none of the imams of Islam departs from an authentic hadith without an excuse. Indeed, they have some twenty grounds for excuse: a hadith may not have reached an imam; it may have reached him through a route he did not trust; he may not have believed that it established the ruling in question; or he may have believed that this evidence was opposed by stronger evidence, such as an abrogating text or evidence indicating abrogation, and so forth.

In some of these cases, the scholar is correct and receives two rewards. In others, he errs after exercising independent judgment; he is rewarded for his effort, and his error is forgiven, for Allah Most High says:

“Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake.”

It is established in an authentic report that Allah answered this supplication, saying, “I have done so.” Moreover, scholars are the heirs of the prophets. Allah relates that David and Solomon both passed judgment in a case, and that He granted one of them understanding of it, without censuring the other. Rather, He praised both, stating that He had given each judgment and knowledge. He said:

“And remember David and Solomon, when they passed judgment concerning the field into which some people’s sheep had strayed by night. We were witnesses to their judgment.”

“So We gave Solomon understanding of the case, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge.”

---

## Page 10130

This judgment involves two issues on which scholars have differed. The first concerns livestock straying into cultivated fields at night. Most scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad, hold that compensation is due for the damage, whereas Abū Hanīfa did not. The second concerns compensation in kind and compensation based on value. There is disagreement over this within the schools of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad, and among others. Reports from most of the early generations concerning such cases indicate that equivalent compensation should be provided whenever possible, as Solomon ruled.
