Many jurists, however, require compensation only on the basis of value, as is the well-known position in the schools of Abū Hanīfa, al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad.

The point here is that the practice of the people of Medina that amounts to transmitted evidence constitutes authoritative proof by the agreement of the Muslims. Thus, when Abū Yūsuf asked Mālik about the sā' and mudd measures, Mālik instructed the people of Medina to bring their sā' measures. They explained that these had been transmitted to them from their forebears. Mālik then asked, “Do you think these people are lying, Abū Yūsuf?”

He replied, “No, by Allah, they are not lying.” Mālik said, “I have carefully checked these sā' measures and found them to equal five and one-third ratls (units of weight) by your standard, people of Iraq.”

He then said, “I have adopted your view, Abū 'Abd Allāh. Had my companion seen what I have seen, he would have changed his view as I have.”

He also asked him about zakāh on vegetables. He replied, “These are the vegetable plots of the people of Medina. No zakāh was collected from them during the time of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor during the times of Abū Bakr or 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.” He meant that vegetables grow in these plots.

He also asked him about endowments. He replied, “This is the endowment of so-and-so, and this is the endowment of so-and-so,” citing these to illustrate the Companions’ practice. Abū Yūsuf said concerning each of these two matters:

---

## Page 10131

“I have adopted your view, Abū 'Abd Allāh. Had my companion seen what I have seen, he would have changed his view as I have.” Abū Yūsuf and Muhammad agreed with the other jurists that no zakāh is due on vegetables, as held by Mālik, al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad, and that no zakāh is due on less than five wasqs, as these scholars also held. They also agreed concerning endowments, which he considered legally binding, in accordance with these scholars’ position.

Mālik said, “Your ratls, people of Iraq,” because the Umayyad dynasty had come to an end and the dynasty of the descendants of al-'Abbās had only recently come to power. His brother Abū Ja'far, known as al-Mansūr, then assumed power, built Baghdad and made it his seat of rule. Abū Ja'far knew that the people of the Hijaz at that time were more concerned with the religion of Islam than the people of Iraq. It is related that he said this to Mālik or another of the scholars of Medina:

“I examined this matter and found the people of Iraq given to lying and misrepresentation”—or words to that effect—“and found the people of Syria devoted to military campaigns and jihad, while I found this matter among you.”

It is also said that he told Mālik, “You are the most learned person in the Hijaz,” or words to that effect. Abū Ja'far therefore asked the scholars of the Hijaz to go to Iraq and spread knowledge there. Those who came to them included Hishām ibn 'Urwa, Muhammad ibn Ishāq, and Yahyā ibn

---

## Page 10132

Sa'īd al-Ansārī; Rabī'a ibn Abī 'Abd al-Rahmān; Hanzala ibn Abī Sufyān al-Jumahī; 'Abd al-'Azīz ibn Abī Salama al-Mājishūn; and others. Abū Yūsuf used to attend their gatherings and learn hadith from them, acquiring much from those who came from the Hijaz.

Thus, it is said of Abū Hanīfa’s companions that Abū Yūsuf was the most knowledgeable in hadith; Zufar was the most consistent in applying analogical reasoning; al-Hasan ibn Ziyād al-Lu'lu'ī was the most prolific in elaborating subsidiary rulings; and Muhammad was the most knowledgeable in Arabic and arithmetic. Sometimes Muhammad was also described as the most prolific in elaborating subsidiary rulings.

When Iraq became the seat of government, and it became necessary to acquaint its inhabitants with the Sunnah and the revealed Law, the legally prescribed measure was recalibrated using the Iraqi ratl. Their ratl, measured in dense wheat and lentils, was then ninety mithqāls: 128 dirhams and four-sevenths of a dirham. This, then, is the first level of the consensus of the people of Medina, and it constitutes authoritative evidence by agreement of the Muslims.

The Second Level

The early practice in Medina before the killing of 'Uthmān ibn 'Affān constitutes authoritative evidence in Mālik’s school. This is also al-Shāfi'ī’s expressly stated position. As reported by Yūnus ibn 'Abd al-A'lā, he said:

“If you find the early generations of the people of Medina agreed upon something, entertain no doubt in your heart that it is the truth.”

Likewise, the apparent position of Ahmad’s school is that whatever the Rightly Guided Caliphs instituted constitutes authoritative evidence that must be followed. Ahmad said:

“Every pledge of allegiance given in Medina established a caliphate on the prophetic model.”

It is well known that the pledges of allegiance to Abū Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthmān were given in Medina. Likewise, the pledge of allegiance to 'Alī was given in Medina; he subsequently left it, and thereafter no pledge of allegiance was concluded in Medina.

---

## Page 10133

It is established in the authentic hadith of al-'Irbād ibn Sāriya that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Adhere to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after me. Hold firmly to it and cling to it with your molar teeth. Beware of newly introduced matters, for every religious innovation is misguidance.”

In the Sunan collections, Safīna relates that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The caliphate upon the prophetic model will last thirty years; then it will become oppressive kingship.”

What is reported from Abū Hanīfa thus implies that the statements of the Rightly Guided Caliphs constitute authoritative evidence. No early practice of the people of Medina during the time of the Rightly Guided Caliphs is known to have contradicted the Sunnah of the Messenger, may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace.

The Third Level

When two proofs concerning an issue conflict—such as two hadiths or two analogical arguments—and it is unclear which carries greater weight, while the people of Medina act upon one of them, there is disagreement over this. Mālik and al-Shāfi'ī hold that the practice of the people of Medina gives that proof precedence. Abū Hanīfa holds that their practice does not give it precedence.

Ahmad’s followers have two views. The first, held by al-Qādī Abū Ya'lā and Ibn 'Aqīl, is that it does not give it precedence. The second, held by Abū al-Khattāb and others, is that it does. It has been said that this is Ahmad’s explicitly stated position. Among his statements is the following:

“When the people of Medina accept a hadith and act upon it, that is the ultimate.”

He used to issue fatwas according to the school of the people of

---

## Page 10134

Medina and frequently affirmed its precedence over the school of the people of Iraq. He would direct those seeking fatwas to the schools of the scholars of hadith and the school of the people of Medina. He would refer them to Ishāq, Abū 'Ubayd, Abū Thawr, and other jurists among the scholars of hadith, and direct them to the Medinan study circle—the circle of Abū Mus'ab al-Zuhrī and others like him.

Abū Mus'ab was the last surviving transmitter of al-Muwatta' from Mālik. He died one year after Ahmad, in 242 AH. Ahmad was reluctant to refute the people of Medina as he refuted the proponents of independent juristic reasoning, saying, “They followed the transmitted reports.” Thus, the positions of the majority of the imams agree with Mālik’s position in giving preference to the views of the people of Medina.

“The Fourth Level”

This concerns the later practice of Medina. Does it constitute binding evidence in Islamic law that must be followed, or not? The leading imams hold that it does not constitute such evidence. This is the position of al-Shāfi'ī, Ahmad, Abū Hanīfa, and others. It is also the position of the discerning scholars among Mālik’s followers, as noted by the distinguished scholar 'Abd al-Wahhāb in his book Usūl al-fiqh (Principles of Jurisprudence), and by others. He stated that this constitutes neither consensus nor authoritative evidence according to the discerning scholars among Mālik’s followers. Some of his followers in the Maghreb have sometimes treated it as authoritative evidence, but they have neither an explicit statement from the imams nor any proof to support this; rather, they merely follow others’ authority.

I say:

I have seen nothing in Mālik’s words that would require treating this as authoritative evidence. In al-Muwatta', he merely mentions the principle upon which they agree, thereby reporting their position, and at times

---

## Page 10135

he says, “What the scholars of our city have always followed,” referring back to the early consensus; at other times he does not mention it. Had Mālik believed that the later practice constituted authoritative evidence which the entire Muslim community was obliged to follow, even when it contradicted the scriptural texts, he would have been obliged to require people to follow it as far as possible, just as he was obliged to require them to follow hadith, the established Sunnah in which there is no contradiction, and consensus. Yet when al-Rashīd, or someone else, offered to compel people to follow his Muwatta’, he declined, saying, “The Companions of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace—dispersed throughout the lands, whereas I have only compiled the knowledge of the people of my city,” or words to that effect.

Once it is clear that the majority of the imams differed in their assessment of the consensus of the people of Medina, it becomes apparent that the views of the people of Medina are the soundest among those of the people of the various cities, both in transmitted reports and in reasoned opinion. Their position sometimes constitutes conclusive evidence, sometimes strong evidence, and sometimes a factor that gives one piece of evidence precedence over another. No other Muslim city possesses this distinction.

It is well known that the Companions who were in Medina were the finest of the Companions, for no one left it before the civil strife without someone superior to him remaining there. When Syria, Iraq, and other lands were conquered, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—sent people to the various cities to teach their inhabitants the Book and the Sunnah. Thus, among those who went to Iraq was ‘Abd Allāh

---

## Page 10136

ibn Mas‘ūd, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yamān, ‘Ammār ibn Yāsir, ‘Imrān ibn Husayn, Salmān al-Fārisī, and others. Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal, ‘Ubādah ibn al-Sāmit, Abū al-Dardā’, Bilāl ibn Rabāh, and others like them went to Syria. Those who remained with ‘Umar included ‘Uthmān, ‘Alī, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf, Ubayy ibn Ka‘b, Muhammad ibn Maslamah, Zayd ibn Thābit, and others.

Ibn Mas‘ūd—who was then the most knowledgeable of the Companions in Iraq—would issue a fatwa, then come to Medina and consult its scholars. They would persuade him to abandon his opinion, and he would adopt theirs. This happened, for example, concerning the mothers of one’s wives. Ibn Mas‘ūd thought that the condition of consummation applied both to them and to stepdaughters: if a man divorced his wife before consummating the marriage, he could marry her mother, just as he could marry her daughter. When he came to Medina and asked about this, the scholars among the Companions informed him that the condition applied to stepdaughters, not to mothers. He therefore adopted their opinion and instructed the man to separate from his wife, although she had already become pregnant.

The practice of the people of Medina was based either on a Sunnah transmitted from the Messenger of Allah—may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace—or on the judgments of ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb. It is said that Mālik received most of the Muwatta’ from Rabī‘ah, Rabī‘ah from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, and Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib from ‘Umar; and ‘Umar was a man granted inspiration.

In al-Tirmidhī’s collection, it is reported that the Messenger of Allah—may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Had I not been sent among you, ‘Umar would have been sent among you.”

And in the two Sahīh collections, it is reported from him—may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace—that he

---

## Page 10137

said:

“Among the nations before you were men who were inspired. If there is any such man in my nation, it is ‘Umar.”

In the Sunan collections, the Prophet—may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace—is reported to have said:

“Follow the example of the two who come after me: Abū Bakr and ‘Umar.”

‘Umar would consult the leading Companions, such as ‘Uthmān, ‘Alī, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa‘d, and ‘Abd al-Rahmān, who were the members of the consultative council. Hence al-Sha‘bī said: “Consider the judgments delivered by ‘Umar, for he used to be consulted.” It is well known that the judgments and fatwas ‘Umar issued in consultation with these men carry greater weight than those issued by Ibn Mas‘ūd or others like him—may Allah be pleased with them all.

In matters of religion, both fundamental and subsidiary, ‘Umar followed only what the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had ruled. He would consult ‘Alī and other members of the consultative council, as when he consulted him about a woman observing her waiting period following a revocable divorce during illness: would she inherit if her husband died? He consulted him on similar matters as well.

When ‘Uthmān was killed, turmoil and division arose, and ‘Alī, Talhah, and al-Zubayr moved to Iraq, no one equal to these men remained in Medina. Nevertheless, there were Companions there such as Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās, Abū Ayyūb, Muhammad ibn Maslamah, and others like them, who were more eminent than the Companions accompanying ‘Alī. The most knowledgeable Companions who had been in Kufa were ‘Alī and Ibn Mas‘ūd, and ‘Alī had been

---

## Page 10138

in Medina when ‘Umar and ‘Uthmān were there, while Ibn Mas‘ūd served as their deputy. It is well known that ‘Alī, together with these men, surpassed all his Iraqi companions in knowledge and merit. Thus, when al-Shāfi‘ī debated certain Iraqi scholars on jurisprudence, he cited the opinions of ‘Alī and Ibn Mas‘ūd against his opponent. Al-Shāfi‘ī accordingly wrote The Book of the Disagreements of ‘Alī and ‘Abd Allāh, explaining which of their opinions his opponent and other scholars had set aside.

After him, Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazī wrote more extensively on this subject than al-Shāfi‘ī had. He said:

“You and the rest of the Muslims set aside their opinions in favor of what carries greater weight than those opinions. Likewise, others set them aside in favor of what carries greater weight.”

What further clarifies this matter is that the people of all Muslim cities other than Kufa deferred to the knowledge of the scholars of Medina and did not regard themselves as their equals in learning. This was true of the scholars of Syria and Egypt, such as al-Awzā‘ī and the Syrian scholars before and after him, and al-Layth ibn Sa‘d and the Egyptian scholars before and after him. Their great regard for the practice of the people of Medina and their adherence to the earlier Medinan positions are clear and evident. The same applies to the scholars of Basra, such as Ayyūb, Hammād ibn Zayd, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī, and others like them.

This is why the school of the people of Medina gained prominence in these cities. The Egyptians became supporters of the Medinan position, including Mālik’s eminent Egyptian disciples, such as Ibn Wahb, Ibn al-Qāsim, Ashhab, and ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Hakam. And the Syrians

---

## Page 10139

such as al-Walīd ibn Muslim, Marwān ibn Muhammad, and others like them, have well-known transmissions from Mālik. As for the Iraqis, such as ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī, Hammād ibn Zayd, Judge Ismā‘īl ibn Ishāq, and others like them, they followed Mālik’s school and served as chief judges. Ismā‘īl and his peers were among the most eminent scholars of Islam.

The Kufans claimed equality with the people of Medina after the turmoil and division. Before that, however, they followed the people of Medina and deferred to them. Before ‘Uthmān’s killing, no one from Kufa or any other city is known to have claimed that the people of his city were more learned than the people of Medina. When ‘Uthmān was killed, the Muslim community divided into factions, and some Kufans began to place the scholars of Kufa on an equal footing with the scholars of Medina.

What gave rise to this misconception was that Medina’s standing weakened when the prophetic caliphate moved away from it, while the standing of the Iraqis grew stronger through ‘Alī’s presence among them. Yet the questions of fundamental principles and subsidiary matters under discussion had already been settled during ‘Umar’s caliphate. It is well known that the position of the Kufans, together with that of the other cities, before the division deserves greater weight than their opinions and reports after it. ‘Ubayda al-Salmānī, ‘Alī’s judge—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

“We prefer the view you held with ‘Umar when the community was united to the view you hold alone amid division.”

---

## Page 10140

It is well known that the turmoil and division in Kufa are attested by scriptural evidence and scholarly consensus, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Turmoil comes from here; turmoil comes from here; turmoil comes from here—from where Satan’s horn rises.”

This hadith is authentically established from him through several chains of transmission in the authentic hadith collections.

What further clarifies this matter is that knowledge consists of either transmitted reports or scholarly judgment. Of all the cities, Medina’s people are the soundest in both transmission and judgment. Their hadiths are the most authentic. Hadith scholars agree that the most authentic hadiths are those transmitted by the people of Medina, followed by those transmitted by the people of Basra. The hadiths transmitted by the people of Syria rank below these, for they did not possess the same continuity of transmission chains or precision in preserving the wording. Among these people—meaning the people of Medina, Mecca, Basra, and Syria—there were none known for lying, though some were precise in transmission and others were not.

As for the people of Kufa, lying was more prevalent among them than among the inhabitants of any other city. During the generation of the Successors, there were many people there who were known for lying, especially the Shia, who, as the scholars agree, were the most given to lying of all the sects. For this reason, it is reported that Mālik and other scholars of Medina would not use the bulk of the hadiths transmitted by the people of Iraq as evidence: they knew that there were liars among them, but could not distinguish the truthful from the liars. When, however, they knew a hadith to be true, they would use it as evidence. Thus Mālik narrated from Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī, who was an Iraqi, and he was asked

---

## Page 10141

about this, and he replied:

“There is no one from whom I have narrated to you whom Ayyūb does not surpass,” or words to that effect.

This was also al-Shāfiʿī’s earlier position. Indeed, it is reported that he was asked: “If Sufyān narrates a hadith from Mansūr, from ʿAlqama, from ʿAbd Allāh, is it not to be used as evidence?” He replied: “If it has no basis in the Hijaz; otherwise, no.”

Al-Shāfiʿī later retracted this position and said to Ahmad ibn Hanbal: “You are more knowledgeable about hadith than we are. When a hadith is authentic, inform me of it so that I may follow it, whether it comes from Syria, Basra, or Kufa.” He did not mention Mecca or Medina because he already accepted their reports as evidence.

As for the hadith scholars, such as Shuʿba, Yahyā ibn Saʿīd, and the compilers of the Sahīh and Sunan collections, they distinguished reliable narrators with precise retention from others. They therefore knew which narrators in Kufa and Basra were unquestionably reliable, and that some of them surpassed many of the people of the Hijaz. No scholar doubts the likes of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd’s companions—ʿAlqama, al-Aswad, ʿUbayda al-Salmānī, al-Hārith al-Taymī, and Shurayh the judge—or those who followed them, such as Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, al-Hakam ibn ʿUtayba, and their peers. They were among the most reliable narrators and the most precise in their retention.

For this reason, Muslim scholars came to agree on accepting as evidence whatever the hadith specialists judged authentic, regardless of the city from which it originated. Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī compiled Mafārīd Ahl al-Amsār (Reports Unique to the Scholars of Each City), in which he records the reports transmitted exclusively by the Muslim scholars of the Sunnah in each city.

---

## Page 10142

As for jurisprudence and juristic opinion, it is well known that none of the people of Medina introduced an innovation into the fundamentals of religion. When discussion of juristic opinion arose in the early Abbasid period, Rabīʿa ibn Hurmuz formulated detailed rulings for them, just as ʿUthmān al-Battī and his peers did in Basra, and Abū Hanīfa and his peers in Kufa. Some people accepted this, while others rejected it. Among those who rejected it were Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, Abū al-Zinād, al-Zuhrī, Ibn ʿUyayna, and their peers. If they rejected those newly introduced opinions in Medina, they rejected the newly introduced opinions in Iraq all the more strongly. Thus, the people of Medina were no more involved than the people of Iraq in what was blameworthy, while surpassing them in the very things they praised. This demonstrates their superiority.

As for Hishām ibn ʿUrwa’s statement:

“The affairs of the Children of Israel remained sound until those of mixed descent—the sons of women taken captive from other nations—became widespread among them. They then spoke among them on the basis of opinion, going astray themselves and leading others astray.”

Ibn ʿUyayna said:

“We examined this and found that the newly introduced opinions came only from those of mixed descent, the sons of women taken captive from other nations.”

He mentioned some of those who were in Medina, Basra, and Kufa. In this regard, those in Medina were more praiseworthy than the Medinans who were in Iraq.

When Mālik—may Allah be pleased with him—said of one of the two dynasties that its rulers adhered more closely to the Sunnah than those of the other dynasty, he said this because of the innovations that appeared around the latter’s time, for those men had a stronger claim to the caliphate by virtue of their lineage and generation.

---

## Page 10143

Indeed, al-Mansūr, al-Mahdī, and al-Rashīd—the foremost Abbasid caliphs—used to favor the scholars of the Hijaz and their opinions over the scholars of Iraq, just as the Umayyad caliphs favored the scholars of the Hijaz over those of Syria. When some of them departed from this course and turned instead to Eastern opinions, innovations multiplied among them and the caliphate weakened.

Baghdad attained its standing in knowledge and faith, and its preeminence over other cities, only after the death of Mālik and his peers among the scholars of the Hijaz. It became home to men who spread the Sunnah there and made the truths of Islam manifest, such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abū Ubayd, and other jurists among the scholars of hadith. From that time onward, the Sunnah flourished there in both doctrinal foundations and practical rulings, becoming widespread and spreading from Baghdad to other cities. From that time, it also spread throughout the East and the West. Thus, the East had such scholars as Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Rāhawayh and his companions, as well as the companions of Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak. The knowledge of the scholars of Medina also reached the West through what the scholars of hadith transmitted to its people. Consequently, Baghdad, Khurasan, and the West came to possess knowledge whose like was not then found in the Hijaz or Basra.

As for the state of the Hijaz, after the age of Mālik and his companions, none of its scholars surpassed the scholars of the East, Iraq, and the West.

---

## Page 10144

This subject would take a long time to trace in detail. Were we to exhaustively discuss the merits of the scholars of Medina and the soundness of their principles, the discussion would be lengthy.

With this established, no one doubts that Mālik—may Allah be pleased with him—was the foremost exponent of the school of the scholars of Medina, both in transmitted knowledge and juristic judgment. Neither in his lifetime nor afterward was anyone more accomplished in this than he. His standing among Muslims, scholars and laypeople alike, is evident to anyone with even the slightest acquaintance with knowledge.

The hadith master Abū Bakr al-Khatīb compiled accounts of those who narrated from Mālik, and they numbered some 1,700. These were only those whose narrations reached al-Khatīb nearly three hundred years later. What, then, of those whose accounts had been lost or whose reports had not reached him? Al-Khatīb died in 462 AH; he was a contemporary of Ibn Abd al-Barr, al-Bayhaqī, Judge Abū Ya‘lā, and others like them. Mālik died in 179 AH, Abū Hanīfa in 150 AH, al-Shāfi‘ī in 204 AH, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal in 241 AH.

For this reason, al-Shāfi‘ī—may Allah have mercy on him—said: “Beneath the sky, there is no book, after the Book of Allah, more correct than Mālik’s al-Muwatta’.” It is indeed as al-Shāfi‘ī—may Allah be pleased with him—said.

This does not contradict the position of the imams of Islam that, after the Quran, no book is more authentic than the Sahīh collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim, although the imams agree that al-Bukhārī’s

---

## Page 10145

is more authentic than Muslim’s. Those who prefer Muslim’s collection do so because he gathers the various wordings of a hadith in one place, making it easier for anyone wishing to collect them. But anyone who claims that the hadith found only in Muslim’s collection are more authentic than those found only in al-Bukhārī’s, or that the narrators included only by Muslim are more reliable than those included only by al-Bukhārī, is mistaken beyond any scholar’s doubt. Likewise, no one doubts that al-Bukhārī was more knowledgeable than Muslim about hadith, hidden defects in transmission, and biographical history, and that he possessed a deeper understanding of jurisprudence. Indeed, al-Bukhārī and Abū Dāwūd were the most accomplished jurists among the compilers of the well-known Sahīh and Sunan collections. Although some material found only in Muslim’s collection may surpass some found only in al-Bukhārī’s, such cases are few; the reverse is generally true. The scholars agree that, after the Quran, no book is more authentic than the collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

These two books attained this standing because their compilers specifically assembled sound hadith with connected chains of transmission. Their purpose was not to include reports from the Companions and Successors, nor other kinds of hadith, such as fair hadith, reports with incomplete chains, and the like. Undoubtedly, works devoted to sound hadith transmitted through connected chains from the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—are the most authentic books, for among compiled works they contain the most reliably transmitted reports from the infallible Prophet.

As for al-Muwatta’ and similar works, they were compiled according to the method followed by scholars writing at that time. During the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—people used to write down the Quran, and the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had forbidden them to write down anything from him other than

---

## Page 10146

the Quran, saying:

“Whoever has written down anything from me other than the Quran should erase it.”

According to the majority of scholars, this prohibition was later abrogated: he permitted 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Amr to write and said, “Write it down for Abū Shāh.” He also had a document written for 'Amr ibn Hazm. They explained that the initial prohibition arose from fear that the Quran might become confused with other material. Once that danger had passed, he permitted writing. People would thus write down portions of the hadith of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and they also wrote down other material.

They did not, however, arrange this material into organized books until the generation following the Successors, when scholarly knowledge began to be compiled. The first to compile was Ibn Jurayj, who collected some material on Quranic exegesis and some on the dead. Sa'īd ibn Abī 'Arūbah, Hammād ibn Salamah, Ma'mar and others like them also compiled works, gathering under each subject reports from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—the Companions and the Successors. After the Quran, these were their books of jurisprudence and religious knowledge, covering foundational principles and subsidiary matters. Mālik compiled al-Muwatta’ according to this method.

Thereafter, 'Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, 'Abd Allāh ibn Wahb, Wakī' ibn al-Jarrāh, 'Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī, 'Abd al-Razzāq, Sa'īd ibn Mansūr and others compiled works. It was these books, recognized at that time, to which al-Shāfi'ī—may Allah have mercy on him—referred when he said:

“After the Quran, no book is more accurate than Mālik’s al-Muwatta’.”

For Mālik’s hadith are more authentic than those of his peers. Likewise, when Imām Ahmad was asked about Mālik’s hadith and his legal opinions

---

## Page 10147

and the hadith and legal opinions of others, he preferred Mālik’s hadith and legal opinions to theirs.

This corroborates the hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhī and others from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who said:

“Soon people will drive their camels hard in pursuit of knowledge, yet find no scholar more learned than the scholar of Medina.”

It has been reported from several scholars, including Ibn Jurayj, Ibn 'Uyaynah and others, that they said, “He is Mālik.”

Those who disputed this did so on two grounds. The first was to question the hadith: some claimed that its chain of transmission contained a break. The second was that the Prophet meant someone other than Mālik, such as al-'Umarī the ascetic or someone like him.

The response is that what the hadith describes, and the fact that Mālik is the one intended, were established for those who were present and are known through mass transmission to those who were absent. There is no doubt that, in Mālik’s time, no one attracted more people who drove their camels hard to reach him than Mālik.

This can be established in two ways. The first is by seeking to establish his superiority over such scholars as al-Thawrī, al-Awzā'ī, al-Layth and Abū Hanīfah. This, however, is disputed, and there is no need to pursue it here.

The second is to say that Mālik outlived all of them, for he

---

## Page 10148

died in 179 AH, whereas all these scholars had died before then. It is therefore well known that, after their deaths, no one in the Muslim community at that time was more learned than Mālik. No Muslim disputes this. Nor did people ever travel to any scholar of Medina, before or after him, as they travelled to Mālik. They came to him from the East and the West, from every walk of life: scholars, ascetics, kings and ordinary people. His Muwatta’ spread throughout the lands, so much so that no book other than the Quran is known to have circulated more widely at that time. People from the Hijaz, Syria and Iraq learned the Muwatta’ directly from him. Among his younger students were al-Shāfi'ī, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan and others like them. When Muhammad ibn al-Hasan narrated in Iraq from Mālik and the scholars of the Hijaz, his house would fill with people. When he narrated from the scholars of Iraq, fewer people attended, knowing that the learning of Mālik and the scholars of Medina was sounder and more firmly established.

The two most eminent scholars under whom al-Shāfi'ī studied were Mālik and Ibn 'Uyaynah. Everyone knows that Mālik was more eminent than Ibn 'Uyaynah; indeed, the latter used to say:

“Mālik and I are as the poet said:
‘A young camel, tethered alongside the others,
Cannot match the charge of mighty, full-grown camels.’”

As for anyone who claims that the man to whom people drove their camels hard in pursuit of knowledge was al-'Umarī the ascetic—although he was a righteous man, an ascetic who enjoined what is right

---

## Page 10149

and forbade what is wrong—it is not known that people needed any of his knowledge or travelled to him to acquire it.

Whenever he intended to undertake something, he would consult Mālik and seek his ruling. It is reported, for example, that he consulted him after receiving a letter from Iraq urging him to assume the caliphate. He said, “Not until I consult Mālik.” When he consulted him, Mālik advised him not to become involved, explaining that the descendants of al-'Abbās would not relinquish it until much blood had been shed over it. He also related to him what 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Azīz had said when urged, “Appoint al-Qāsim ibn Muhammad”: that the Umayyads would not relinquish power until much blood had been shed over it.

As for Quranic exegesis, hadith, the issuing of fatwas and the other disciplines, people are not known to have acquired any noteworthy knowledge of them from al-'Umarī the ascetic. How, then, can he be compared with Mālik in learning or in the journeys people undertook to study with him?

Then consider the collections of authentic hadith, foremost among which is al-Bukhārī’s book. He opens a chapter with a hadith narrated by Mālik; whenever a chapter contains a hadith narrated by Mālik, he places no other hadith before it. We know that people drove their camels hard in pursuit of knowledge, yet found no scholar more learned than Mālik in his time.

Everyone either agrees or disagrees with Mālik and the scholars of Medina. Those who agree with them support and assist them, while those who disagree with them hold them in high esteem and show them great reverence

---

## Page 10150

and recognize their true standing. You will find no one who belittles their views and schools of thought except someone who is not counted among the leading scholars. This is because they know that Mālik is the upholder of the school of Medina—a fact even more evident to scholars and laypeople than the superiority of the Medinan school over those of other cities.

His Muwatta’ is filled with hadiths transmitted by the people of Medina; matters on which they agreed, whether in earlier or later times; and questions disputed among the people of Medina and others, concerning which he selects a view and says, “This is the best view I have heard.” There are also reports well known to the scholars of Medina. Even supposing that, in earlier times, someone adhered more closely than Mālik to the school of Medina, that is no longer the case.

We do not deny that some people initially criticized Mālik for departing from their hadiths on certain questions. For example, it is related that ‘Abd al-‘Azīz al-Darāwardī said to him, concerning the determination of the minimum bridal gift by reference to the threshold for the prescribed punishment for theft: “You have turned Iraqi, Abū ‘Abd Allāh!” That is, on this question he had adopted the position of the scholars of Iraq, who set the minimum bridal gift at the threshold for the prescribed punishment for theft. However, according to Abū Hanīfa and his companions, that threshold is ten dirhams, whereas according to Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad, it is three dirhams or a quarter of a dinar, as established in authentic hadiths.

The response is, first: an account such as this indicates that the scholars of Medina considered the positions of the scholars of Iraq weak, and that they disliked anyone agreeing with them.

---

## Page 10151

and this was well known among them: they would reproach a man for it, as Ibn ‘Umar did when asked for a ruling about mosquito blood, and as Ibn al-Musayyib did when Rabī‘a asked him about the compensation due for a woman’s fingers.

Second, such instances are exceedingly rare in Mālik’s views, and every scholar has some views that warrant rejection. How aptly Ibn Khuwayz Mindād spoke concerning the sale and rental of books of juristic opinion: “In this ruling, we make no distinction between the opinions of our imam Mālik and those of anyone else; he is, however, less prone to error than others.”

As for hadiths, we find that Mālik upheld most of them according to one of the two reports of his position. Rather, it was a group of his followers who abandoned them, as in the question of raising the hands when bowing and when rising from bowing. The scholars of Medina transmitted from Mālik that the hands should be raised, in agreement with the authentic hadith he himself narrated. Yet Ibn al-Qāsim and others among the Basrans adopted the first reported position.

It is well known that Ibn al-Qāsim’s Mudawwana was based on the questions of Asad ibn al-Furāt, which the scholars of Iraq had developed through their detailed legal reasoning. Asad then put these questions to Ibn al-Qāsim, who answered him by transmitting Mālik’s views and, at times, by drawing analogies from them. Its source material, in turn, is in Sahnūn’s transmission. For this reason, Ibn al-Qāsim’s statements contain some inclination toward the views of the scholars of Iraq, even where these were not among the principles of the scholars of Medina.

Then, as it happened, when Mālik’s school spread in al-Andalus and Yahyā ibn Yahyā was

---

## Page 10152

governor of al-Andalus and the governors consulted him, they would instruct the judges to rule only according to his transmission from Mālik, and then according to that of others. Thus Ibn al-Qāsim’s transmission from Mālik became widespread because of those who acted upon it, even though it might be less well-supported when judged against the school’s positions, the practice of the people of Medina, and the Sunnah. They even came to abandon the account in al-Muwatta’, which was transmitted from Mālik through numerous independent channels and which he continued to teach until his death, in favour of Ibn al-Qāsim’s transmission. A group of leading Mālikī scholars, however, objected to this. If there is any fault in such a case, it lies only with those who transmitted this, not with Mālik. A follower of his school can follow the Sunnah in most matters, for scarcely any Sunnah lacks a corresponding position from him. This contrasts with much of the doctrine of the scholars of Kufa, who frequently depart from the Sunnah, even if they do not do so deliberately.

Moreover, anyone who reflects upon the foundations of Islam and the principles of the Sharia will find the foundations and principles of Mālik and the people of Medina to be the soundest. Al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others stated this. Indeed, when al-Shāfi‘ī debated Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and Muhammad favoured his own teacher over al-Shāfi‘ī’s teacher, al-Shāfi‘ī asked him:

“Are you speaking fairly, or merely being obstinate?”

“Fairly,” he replied.

Al-Shāfi‘ī said, “I adjure you by Allah: is our teacher more knowledgeable about the Book of Allah, or yours?”

“Yours,” he replied.

He asked, “Is our teacher more knowledgeable about the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace, or yours?”

“Yours,” he replied.

He asked, “Is our teacher more knowledgeable about the statements of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace, or

---

## Page 10153

yours?”

“Yours,” he replied.

Al-Shāfi‘ī said, “Then nothing remains between us and you except analogical reasoning. We too accept analogical reasoning, but whoever knows the foundational sources better will reason more soundly by analogy.”

Imam Ahmad was asked, “Who is more knowledgeable about the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace: Mālik or Sufyān?”

He replied, “Mālik.”

He was asked, “Who is more knowledgeable about the reports from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: Mālik or Sufyān?”

He replied, “Mālik.”

He was asked, “Who is more ascetic: Mālik or Sufyān?”

He replied, “On that point, I concede to you.”

It is well known that Sufyān al-Thawrī was the most knowledgeable scholar in Iraq at that time in jurisprudence and hadith. Abū Hanīfah, al-Thawrī, Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Abī Laylā, al-Hasan ibn Sālih ibn Hayy, and Sharīk ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Nakha‘ī, the judge, were roughly contemporaries and were the leading jurists of Kufa in that period.

Abū Yūsuf initially studied jurisprudence under Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Abī Laylā, the judge. He then met Abū Hanīfah and, finding him more knowledgeable in jurisprudence, became his devoted student. He compiled the book “The Differences between Abū Hanīfah and Ibn Abī Laylā.” Muhammad ibn al-Hasan received it from him, and al-Shāfi‘ī transmitted it from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, recording his own preferred views in it. This is the work known as “The Differences between the Iraqi Scholars.”

---

## Page 10154

It is well known that Sufyān al-Thawrī was the most knowledgeable of this generation in hadith, besides his preeminence in jurisprudence and asceticism. Those scholars from Iraq and elsewhere who criticized the newly introduced opinion-based reasoning in Kufa did not direct that criticism at Sufyān al-Thawrī. Rather, they regarded Sufyān as the leading scholar of Iraq. Thus, Ahmad’s preference for Mālik’s school over Sufyān’s amounted to preferring it over the school of the Iraqi scholars. Imam Ahmad’s assessment of their respective knowledge of the Book, the Sunnah, and transmitted reports has already been mentioned, even though Ahmad ranked Sufyān al-Thawrī above all the other scholars of this generation and held him in the highest esteem. Nevertheless, he knew that the school of the scholars of Medina was closer to the Book and the Sunnah than that of the scholars of Kufa.

Ahmad was balanced and well informed, giving everyone their due. Thus, he loved al-Shāfi‘ī, praised him, prayed for him, and defended him against those who disparaged him or accused him of religious innovation. He would speak of al-Shāfi‘ī’s reverence for the Sunnah, his adherence to it, and his knowledge of the principles of jurisprudence, such as abrogating and abrogated texts, and texts requiring clarification and those whose meaning has been explained. He affirmed the authority of singly transmitted reports and recounted al-Shāfi‘ī’s debates in defense of the school of the hadith scholars against those who opposed it through opinion-based reasoning or other means.

Al-Shāfi‘ī used to say:

“In Baghdad, they called me the champion of hadith.”

Al-Shāfi‘ī’s virtues were many, as were his efforts to follow the Book and the Sunnah and to refute those who opposed them. He followed the school of the scholars of the Hijaz and had studied jurisprudence according to the approach of the Meccan scholars, the disciples of Ibn Jurayj

---

## Page 10155

such as Muslim ibn Khālid al-Zinjī and Sa‘īd ibn Sālim al-Qaddāh. He then travelled to Mālik, studied al-Muwatta’ under him, and completed his grounding in the principles of the scholars of Medina. From the time of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, until the time of Mālik, they surpassed the scholars of Mecca in knowledge, jurisprudence, and standing.

He then underwent an ordeal that took him to Iraq, where he met Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, copied his books, debated with him, and became acquainted with the principles of Abū Hanīfah and his companions. He also studied hadith under the scholars of Iraq before returning to the Hijaz.

He subsequently came to Iraq a second time, during which he composed his earlier work, known as al-Hujjah (The Proof). Ahmad ibn Hanbal met him during this visit to Iraq and also met him in Mecca. Ahmad brought him together with Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, and the two debated in Ahmad’s presence. May Allah be pleased with them all.

He did not meet Abū Yūsuf, al-Awzā‘ī, or the others in question. Whoever claims otherwise in the travel account attributed to him is lying. That account contains lies about him, Mālik, Abū Yūsuf, Muhammad, and other scholars that would be obvious to anyone knowledgeable. It belongs to the same category as the fabrications of storytellers. Abū Yūsuf and Muhammad never sought to harm al-Shāfi‘ī, nor was Mālik’s relationship with him as described in that fabricated travel account.

Al-Shāfi‘ī then returned to Egypt and composed his later work. In his speech and writings, he associated himself with the school of the scholars of the Hijaz. Thus, he would say, “Some of our companions said,” meaning the scholars of Medina, or some of their scholars, such as Mālik. He also says in

---

## Page 10156

the course of his discussion: “We differed with some of the scholars of the East.”

Mālik’s companions regarded al-Shāfi‘ī as one of their own, and he was counted among their associates. He chose to settle in Egypt at that time because its scholars followed the school of the scholars of Medina and like-minded Egyptian scholars, such as al-Layth ibn Sa‘d and others. Some scholars of the western lands followed their school, while others followed that of al-Awzā‘ī and the scholars of Syria. The schools of Syria, Egypt, and Medina were closely aligned, but everyone held the scholars of Medina in the highest esteem.

Then, since al-Shāfi‘ī—may Allah be pleased with him—exercised independent scholarly judgment and encountered authentic hadiths and other evidence that he was obliged to follow, even when these contradicted the views of the followers of the Medinan scholars, he acted upon what he considered his duty. He composed al-Imlā’ ‘alā Masā’il Ibn al-Qāsim (Dictation on Ibn al-Qāsim’s Legal Questions) and openly expressed his disagreement with Mālik on the issues where he differed with him. Al-Shāfi‘ī did well in this and fulfilled his duty, even though some resented it and harmed him, and a well-known ordeal took place in Egypt. May Allah forgive all believing men and women, living and dead.

Abū Yūsuf and Muhammad were the two companions of Abū Hanīfah, closely associated with him just as al-Shāfi‘ī was with Mālik. Their disagreements with him may have been comparable to al-Shāfi‘ī’s disagreements with Mālik. All of this was in adherence to the evidence and in fulfillment of duty.

Al-Shāfi‘ī—may Allah be pleased with him—affirmed the principles of his companions, as well as the Book

---

## Page 10157

and the Sunnah, and he diligently followed the hadiths he considered authentic. For this reason, ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Hakam used to tell his son Muhammad:

“My son, remain close to this man, for he is a man of proofs. You need only leave Egypt to find yourself laughed at for saying, ‘Ibn al-Qāsim said.’”

Muhammad said:

“When I reached Iraq, I joined a study circle that included Ibn Abī Dāwūd. I said, ‘Ibn al-Qāsim said,’ and he asked, ‘Who is Ibn al-Qāsim?’ I replied, ‘A mufti whose pronouncements reach from Egypt to the farthest West.’”

I believe he also said: “I said, ‘May Allah have mercy on my father.’”

His father’s intention was: seek evidence for the positions of your companions, rather than merely following them. Appeals to authority are accepted only where that authority is held in esteem, whereas evidence is accepted everywhere. Allah has obliged every scholar qualified to exercise independent judgment to speak in accordance with the knowledge he possesses. Allah grants one person knowledge and understanding that He does not grant another. One may be distinguished by greater knowledge and understanding in a particular field, chapter, or question, while another is similarly distinguished in a different field.

Nevertheless, taken as a whole, the positions of the scholars of the Prophet’s Medina generally carry greater weight than those of the scholars of the western and eastern lands. This becomes clear through several comprehensive principles.

Among them is the principle governing what is lawful and unlawful concerning impurities in water. It is well known that Allah says in His Book:

“My mercy encompasses all things, so I shall ordain it

---

## Page 10158

for those who fear Me and give zakah, and those who believe in Our signs.”

“Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find described in the Torah and the Gospel they possess. He enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong, makes good things lawful for them and forbids them foul things, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them.”

Allah Most High has thus made good things lawful for us and forbidden us foul things. Foul things are of two kinds: those that are inherently foul because of some quality within them, such as blood, carrion, and pork; and those whose foulness arises from how they are acquired, such as property taken unjustly or through an unlawful transaction involving usury or gambling.

Regarding the first kind, anything with which contact is forbidden, such as ritually impure substances, is forbidden to consume. Yet not everything forbidden to consume is forbidden to come into contact with, as in the case of poisons. Allah has forbidden us certain foods and drinks, and certain kinds of clothing.

It is well known that the position of the scholars of Medina concerning drinks is stricter than that of the Kufans. The scholars of Medina, those of the other cities, and the jurists versed in hadith prohibit every intoxicant. They hold that every intoxicant is wine and is forbidden, and that whatever intoxicates in large quantities is forbidden even in small quantities. None of the scholars of Medina, early or late, disputed this, whether the drink is made from fruit, grain, honey, mares’ milk, or anything else.

The Kufans, however, recognize as wine only grape juice that has fermented to an intoxicating strength. If it is cooked before reaching that stage until two-thirds of it has evaporated, it is lawful. Drinks made from dates or raisins are forbidden if they are intoxicating and uncooked; but if cooked even slightly, they are lawful even if they intoxicate. As for all other such drinks,

---

## Page 10159

they are lawful even if intoxicating, but they prohibit an amount that causes intoxication.

As for foods, the Kufans are stricter than the scholars of Medina. Besides prohibiting every fanged predator and every bird with talons, their restrictions on meat extend even to the spiny-tailed lizard and the hyena. According to one of their two positions, horse meat is also forbidden. Mālik categorically prohibits what is prohibited in the Quran. As for fanged predators, his well-known position is either to prohibit them with a lesser degree of prohibition or to regard them as disliked. It is also reported that he regarded taloned creatures as disliked. As for birds, he neither prohibits nor dislikes any of them, although prohibition admits of degrees. He regards horse meat as disliked, though both permissibility and prohibition have also been reported from him.

Anyone who carefully considers the authentic hadiths on this subject will recognize that the scholars of Medina follow the Sunnah more closely. Concerning drinks, so many hadiths have been authentically transmitted from the Prophet—may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace—that anyone familiar with them knows they are among the clearest instances of mass transmission. Indeed, authentic reports of his prohibition of infusing two ingredients together and of using certain vessels are well known to anyone versed in the Sunnah.

As for foods, although it may be said that Mālik contradicted authentic hadiths establishing prohibition, that is disputed. The authentic hadiths contradicted by those who prohibit the spiny-tailed lizard and other animals are comparable to those reports, or outweigh them. Moreover, these hadiths are very few compared with the hadiths concerning drinks.

---

## Page 10160

Moreover, Mālik’s position is supported by reports from the early generations, including Ibn ‘Abbās, ‘Ā’ishah, ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar, and others, alongside his interpretation of the Quran’s apparent meaning. Those who permit such drinks, however, have neither textual evidence nor analogy to support them; rather, their position contradicts both. Furthermore, the prohibition of wine as a category is more stringent than the prohibition of unwholesome meats: wine must be avoided altogether, anyone who drinks it is subject to the prescribed punishment, and keeping it is impermissible.

Moreover, Mālik permitted destroying the wine itself, following the Sunnah reported on this matter, and prohibited turning it into vinegar. All of this reflects an adherence to the Sunnah absent from the position of his Kufan opponents. Since the Lawgiver’s prohibition of intoxicating drinks is more stringent than His prohibition of foods, the position that accords with the Lawgiver is sounder.

This is further illustrated by the fact that a group of the scholars of Medina deemed singing lawful, to the point that this view came to be attributed to the scholars of Medina generally. Yet ‘Īsā ibn Ishāq al-Tabbā‘ reported that Mālik was asked about the singing in which some people of Medina allowed themselves latitude. He replied, “Only the sinful among us do that.”

It is well known that this is less serious than what was deemed lawful by those who permitted such drinks. The widely transmitted texts from the Prophet—may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace—prohibiting singing are not comparable to those prohibiting intoxicating drinks. It is therefore clear that the scholars of Medina follow the Sunnah more closely.

---

## Page 10161

Another issue of great importance is the mixing of something lawful with something inherently unlawful, such as impurities mixing with water or other liquids. The scholars of Kufa prohibit any water or liquid into which an impurity falls, whether its quantity is small or large. They then judge that impurity cannot reach beyond the point to which movement in the water extends, setting the measure at ten cubits by ten cubits.

Some of them say that if an impurity falls into a well, it cannot be purified; rather, it must be filled in. Some of their jurists say that either a specified number of bucketfuls must be drawn from it, or all its water must be drawn out, according to their well-known rules. This follows from their view that water and other liquids become impure when an impurity falls into them.

The scholars of Medina take the opposite position: according to them, water does not become impure unless it undergoes a change. They do, however, hold two views on whether a small quantity of water becomes impure through a small amount of impurity. Ahmad’s position is close to this, as is al-Shāfi‘ī’s, although these two, unlike Mālik, define a small quantity as less than two qullahs (large jarfuls). Conflicting views are reported from Mālik concerning foods; likewise, within Ahmad’s school there is disagreement concerning liquids other than water.

It is clear that this position accords more closely with the Book and the Sunnah. The designation “water” still applies, and the designation on account of which it was lawful before the impurity fell into it remains unchanged. The Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—concerning the well of Budā‘ah and other cases indicates that it does not become impure. Nor is this contradicted by the hadith prohibiting urination in stagnant water, for it does not explicitly address the point at issue: the ruling may apply specifically to urine.

---

## Page 10162

Some of them restricted the prohibition to urinating directly into it, rather than urine flowing into it. It may also be restricted to a small quantity of water.

It may also be argued that the prohibition on urinating does not necessarily mean that the water becomes impure. Rather, it may be prohibited because it leads to impurity if the amount of urine becomes large. This is reinforced by the fact that Muslims do not dispute that the prohibition on urinating in stagnant water does not encompass all bodies of water. Seawater is excluded by explicit textual evidence and consensus. Likewise, by agreement, urine does not render impure the water in large reservoirs that cannot be drained and in which movement at one end does not cause movement at the other. An authentic, explicit hadith cannot be countered by a hadith so lacking in specificity and open to different interpretations.

Likewise, concerning whether used water and the like become impure, the position of the scholars of Medina and those who agree with them—that it remains pure—is established by authentic hadiths from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—such as the hadith about his ablution water being poured over Jābir, and his saying:

“The believer does not become impure.”

There are other similar reports. Likewise, concerning the urine of a boy who has not yet been fed food, some of the scholars of Medina and those who agree with them have authentic hadiths from the Prophet—may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace—supporting their position, with nothing to contradict them.

---

## Page 10163

Likewise, the position of Mālik and the scholars of Medina concerning physical impurities in acts of worship accords most closely with authentic hadiths and the practice of the Companions. Moreover, they do not regard the urine and dung of animals whose meat is lawful to eat as impure. This is supported by over a dozen arguments drawn from revealed texts, early consensus, and reasoned inference, which we have discussed elsewhere. Those who regard them as impure have nothing but wording presumed to be general when it is not, or an analogy in which the case under consideration is presumed to be equivalent to the original case when it is not.

Since impurities are among the foul things prohibited in themselves, and their position on this matter was taken from that of the scholars of Kufa, as in the case of foods, the range of things the latter declared impure was broader. If it is objected that Mālik contravened the hadith concerning a dog lapping from a vessel and similar reports concerning impurities, this is like saying that he contravened the hadith concerning birds of prey and similar reports. Undoubtedly, this involves less contradiction of the revealed texts than the position of those who regard the dung and urine of animals whose meat is lawful to eat—or either of these—as impure, or consider it disliked to use water from which a cat has drunk.

Some have held that all animal dung and urine are pure, except human urine and excrement. In terms of supporting evidence, this view is no less tenable than the position of those scholars of Kufa and their followers who declare impure what the scholars of Medina regard as pure. Anyone who reflects on the position of the scholars of Medina and is knowledgeable about the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah

---

## Page 10164

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—will recognize with certainty that the position of the scholars of Medina, which embodies ease in this matter, accords more closely with the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, than the position that entails hardship. In an authentic hadith, when the Bedouin urinated in the mosque and the Prophet instructed them to pour water over his urine, he said:

“You were sent to make things easy, not to make them difficult.”

This is the position of the scholars of Medina and the scholars of hadith. Those who disagree with them maintain that the area must be washed and that pouring water over it does not suffice. They cite in support of this a disconnected hadith that is not authentic.

Section

As for the second category of prohibited things—those prohibited because of how they are acquired—this includes whatever is taken wrongfully through various forms of appropriation, such as theft, breach of trust, and forcible seizure; whatever is acquired through usury or gambling; and whatever is received in exchange for a forbidden item or benefit, such as the price paid for wine, blood, swine, or idols, a prostitute’s earnings, a soothsayer’s fee, and the like.

The position of the scholars of Medina on this matter is among the most balanced. The prohibition of wrongdoing and whatever necessarily entails it is more emphatic than the prohibition of the first category. Allah prohibited foul foods because they provide foul nourishment that leads a person to wrongdoing, as when someone feeds on swine, blood, or predatory beasts. For the consumer resembles what he consumes, and oppression and aggression develop within him in keeping with what he has consumed.

---

## Page 10165

These foods are permitted to someone compelled by necessity because preserving life takes precedence over averting this harm. Moreover, such consumption is temporary and, in a state of dire need, does not have a harmful effect on him. Wrongdoing, however, is forbidden in both small and large amounts. Allah, Most High, has forbidden it to Himself and made it forbidden for His servants. He prohibited usury because it entails wrongdoing: taking an additional amount without giving anything in exchange for it. The prohibition of usury is more emphatic than that of gambling, because the usurer takes a guaranteed gain from someone in need. A gambler, by contrast, may or may not gain: one may win against the other, or the reverse may happen.

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited sales involving uncertainty; sales by touch (mulāmasah) or by tossing (munābadhah); selling fruit before it shows signs of ripeness; and habal al-habalah sales.”

He likewise prohibited similar transactions involving an element of gambling. He granted concessions in such matters where need calls for them and they are incidental to something else. Thus, he permitted purchasing fruit once it shows signs of ripeness and leaving it until it fully ripens, even though some of its parts have not yet formed. He also permitted purchasing pollinated date palms together with their new crop if the buyer stipulates its inclusion, even though the fruit has not yet shown signs of ripeness. This is permissible by the consensus of the Muslims. The same applies to all other trees bearing visible fruit.

He assigned the fruit of pollinated date palms to the seller unless the buyer stipulates its inclusion. The tree thus belongs to the buyer, while the seller benefits from it by leaving his fruit on it until harvest.

---

## Page 10166

It is also established in the Sahīh that he ordered payment to be remitted for crops struck by calamities, saying:

“If you sell fruit to your brother and a calamity strikes it, it is not lawful for you to take any of your brother’s money. On what grounds would any of you take his brother’s money without right?”

The position of Mālik and the scholars of Medina on this matter is more consistent with the Sunnah and justice than that of their opponents among the scholars of Kufa and others. Their opponents held that a sale is valid whenever its subject matter exists, whether or not the fruit has begun to show signs of ripeness. They also held that every contract requires possession of the item sold immediately upon its conclusion, and did not permit possession to be deferred. Thus, they said that purchasing fruit is valid whether or not it shows signs of ripeness, but the contract requires it to be picked immediately: the buyer may neither leave it until it fully ripens nor stipulate that he may do so.

They regarded such taking possession as transferring the risk of loss from the seller to the buyer. Applying this principle consistently, they said that selling an item already under lease is invalid because its delivery is deferred. They also said that a sale is impermissible if the seller reserves the use of the item sold, such as riding a camel or living in a house. All these rulings derive from that analogical reasoning.

The scholars of Medina and the scholars of hadith disagreed with them on all these points and followed the authentic texts. Their position also accords with sound and equitable analogical reasoning. To someone who says that a contract requires possession immediately upon its conclusion, the response is: the effect of a contract must derive either from the Lawgiver or from the intention of the contracting party. There is nothing in the Lawgiver’s words to imply that this

---

## Page 10167

necessarily entails that contractual effect. The contracting parties, however, are bound by what they mutually agree upon and make the basis of their contract. Sometimes they agree to exchange possession immediately afterward, and sometimes they agree to defer possession, as with fruit. A contract without a specified term calls for immediate performance, but they may defer it when doing so serves their interests. The same applies to tangible property. If the property sold carries a benefit belonging to the seller or someone else—as with trees bearing visible fruit, property under lease, or property whose use the seller has reserved for a period—the contract does not entitle the buyer to demand what is not his and what he has not acquired. Just as the seller may sell one part of a property without another, he may sell it without its usufruct.

Whether one says that the buyer takes possession of the property or that he does not take possession of it at all makes no difference here. Taking possession is not a requirement for completing a sale contract as it is for a pledge. Rather, the buyer acquires ownership as a consequence of the sale before taking possession, and any increase or yield of the property belongs to him, without dispute, even while it remains in the seller’s hands. The effect of taking possession concerns either liability for loss or the right to dispose of the property. It is authentically reported that Ibn ʿUmar said:

“The established Sunnah is that whatever is alive and intact when the sale is concluded is at the buyer’s risk.”

This is therefore the position adopted by the scholars of Medina and the scholars of hadith. Making liability depend on having the opportunity to take possession is sounder than making it depend on actually taking possession, and this is what the Sunnah establishes. In the case of fruit struck by a calamity, the buyer had not had the opportunity to harvest it

---

## Page 10168

and was not at fault; thus, if it perished, the seller bore the loss. For this reason, fruit that perishes after the buyer has neglected to take possession is at his risk. Likewise, a slave or riding animal that he has had the opportunity to take possession of is at his risk, according to the reports of Alī and Ibn Umar.

Whoever makes the right to dispose of property dependent on liability for its loss is mistaken. Scholars agree that if the benefits conferred by a lease are lost before the lessee has the opportunity to enjoy them, the lessor bears the loss. Nevertheless, the lessee may sublet at the same rent. They disagree only over subletting at a higher rent, lest this constitute profit from something for which one bears no liability. The correct view is that this is permissible, because the lessee does bear liability for those benefits: if they are lost when he has had the opportunity to enjoy them, he bears the loss; but if they are lost before he has had that opportunity, he does not.

This is also the underlying principle. It is authentically reported that Ibn Umar said:

“We used to buy food in unmeasured quantities during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He forbade us to sell it until we had moved it to our dwellings.”

It was also Ibn Umar who said:

“The established Sunnah is that whatever is alive and intact when the sale is concluded is at the buyer’s risk.”

It is therefore clear that food of this kind is at the buyer’s risk, yet he may not sell it until he has moved it. As for fruit yields and usufructs, he may dispose of them; yet if they are lost before he has had the opportunity to take possession of them, the lessor or seller bears the loss. Usufructs cannot be disposed of until after

---

## Page 10169

they have been enjoyed. Likewise, fruit cannot be sold on the trees after it has been picked, unlike food that has been moved. In this matter, the Sunnah distinguishes between those able to take possession and those unable to do so, both regarding liability for loss and the right to dispose of the property. The scholars of Medina therefore follow the Sunnah more closely in this entire ruling, and their position is more balanced than that of those who oppose the Sunnah.

There are many comparable examples, such as the sale of property not present for inspection. Some jurists permit its sale unconditionally, even without a description, while others prohibit its sale even with a description. Mālik permits its sale with a description, but not without one. This is the more balanced position.

Regarding contracts, some require verbal declarations, offer and acceptance in succession, and similar conditions. The scholars of Medina, however, make people’s customs and established practices the reference point for contracts. Whatever people regard as a sale is a sale; whatever they regard as a lease is a lease; and whatever they regard as a gift is a gift. This accords more closely with the Quran and Sunnah and is more balanced.

Some terms have definitions established by language, such as the sun and moon. Others have definitions established by Islamic law, such as prayer and pilgrimage. Still others have no fixed definition in either language or Islamic law, but are instead determined by custom, such as taking possession. It is well known that the Lawgiver has not defined the terms sale, lease, and gift in this regard, nor do they have fixed linguistic definitions. Rather, their application varies

---

## Page 10170

according to people’s customs and established practices. Whatever they regard as a sale is a sale; whatever they regard as a gift is a gift; and whatever they regard as a lease is a lease.

Another example is Mālik’s permission to sell produce concealed underground, such as carrots and turnips, and to sell cucumber crops in bulk, just as he and the majority of scholars permit the sale of broad beans and similar produce in their pods. Undoubtedly, this has been the practice of Muslims from the time of their Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, until the present day. People’s needs cannot be met without it. Whatever uncertainty may be thought to exist in such transactions is likewise permitted in other sales, since it is slight and there is a need for it. Either consideration alone makes this permissible; how much more so when both are present?

Similarly, Mālik’s permission to include the benefit of trees as incidental to a lease of land—for example, leasing land or a house containing one or two trees—is more consistent with the established legal principles than the view prohibiting this. Some followers of Ahmad ibn Hanbal also permit this without restriction. They allow the leasing of an orchard comprising both land and trees, as ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb did when he arranged the lease of Usayd ibn al-Hudayr’s orchard for a third and used the payment received in advance to settle a debt Usayd owed. I have discussed this issue at length elsewhere.

This becomes clearer through a discussion of usury. Its prohibition is more stringent than that of gambling, because it constitutes an unequivocal injustice. For when Allah, glorified and exalted be He, made His creation of two kinds—the rich and the poor

---

## Page 10171

—He enjoined zakat upon the rich as a right belonging to the poor, and forbade the rich from engaging in usury, which harms the poor. He, Most High, said:

“Allah destroys usury and gives increase to charities.”

And He, Most High, said:

“Whatever you give in usury so that it may increase through people’s wealth does not increase with Allah. But whatever you give in zakat, seeking the countenance of Allah—it is those givers whose reward will be multiplied.”

Thus, wrongdoers withhold zakat and consume usury. In gambling, however, either gambler may win the other’s money, and the loser may be the wealthy one, or both may be equally rich or poor. Gambling therefore constitutes consuming wealth unlawfully, so Allah has forbidden it. Yet it does not involve the same injustice and harm to the needy as usury does. It is well known that wronging someone in need is graver than wronging someone who is not in need.

It is also well known that the scholars of Medina prohibited usury, forbade legal stratagems intended to make it lawful, and blocked the means leading to it. How can this be compared with the conduct of those who permit stratagems for taking usury—indeed, who even show people how to do so? This becomes clear by considering, for example, usury through unequal exchange and usury through deferment.

As for usury through unequal exchange, authentic hadith establish—and the majority of the Companions and Successors, together with the four imams, agree—that gold, silver, wheat, barley, dates and raisins may be sold for their own kind only in equal quantities. Any excess over an equal quantity constitutes consuming wealth unlawfully and committing injustice. Thus, if a debtor wishes to sell a hundred broken dinars

---

## Page 10172

weighing a hundred and twenty dinars, and someone who permits legal stratagems allows him to add a loaf of bread or a cloth in which a hundred dinars are placed, or something similar that any usurer can easily provide, then the prohibition of usury would serve no purpose and embody no wisdom. Whenever a usurer wished to exchange any of these commodities for a larger quantity of the same kind, he could simply add something of negligible value to the smaller quantity. Likewise, if the two parties are allowed to agree beforehand that one will sell it to the other in exchange for merchandise in which the buyer has no interest, and then buy it from him for the higher price, anyone seeking usury could do so.

It is well known that if even someone of lesser standing than the Messenger were to prohibit something because of the harm it entails, yet permit it through a procedure that serves no useful purpose, this would be blameworthy and foolish. The harm remains, but he has made them more deceitful. If the procedure entails a burden, he has burdened them with something of no benefit. How, then, could this be thought of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace?

Indeed, it is well known that if kings prohibited what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited, and someone evaded their prohibition through such a stratagem, they would regard him as toying with their commands and mocking them. Allah punished the owners of the garden who devised a scheme to avoid giving charity. Allah also punished the people of the town by the sea when they used a stratagem to treat what was forbidden as lawful, turning them into apes and swine. It is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not commit what the Jews committed, treating what Allah has forbidden as lawful through the most trivial of stratagems.”

---

## Page 10173

We have discussed at length “the principle of invalidating legal stratagems and blocking the means to unlawful ends” in a substantial, separate work. There we established the position of the people of Medina on the basis of the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the earliest forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers.

The same applies to usury involving deferment. Among the people of Thaqīf, concerning whom the Quran was revealed, a creditor would approach his debtor when payment fell due and say, “Will you repay, or increase the debt?” If he did not repay, the debtor would increase the amount owed, and the creditor would extend the term. Thus the debt would multiply over time because of the deferment. This is unquestionably usury, by the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community, and it was concerning this that the Quran was revealed. Its injustice and harm are plain.

Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has permitted sales and trade and forbidden usury. A buyer purchases something from which he can benefit, such as food, clothing, a dwelling, a mount, or other things. A merchant purchases something he intends to sell at a profit. The usurer, however, seeks only to receive money in exchange for money, with repayment deferred. The other party thus becomes liable for more than he received, without gaining any benefit; he has neither sold anything nor engaged in trade. Through his injustice, the usurer consumes wealth wrongfully and benefits people neither through trade nor otherwise. Rather, he puts out his money for an increase, without any benefit accruing to him or to others.

If this is the aim of both parties, then whatever means they use to achieve it, corruption and injustice result. An example is their agreeing beforehand that one will sell something to the other and then buy it back. This constitutes two sales in a single transaction, and in

---

## Page 10174

the Sunan collections it is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever combines two sales in one transaction is entitled to the lower of the two prices; otherwise, it is usury.”

An example is their bringing in an intermediary to give the transaction a semblance of lawfulness. One of them buys from him something he has no interest in, so that the recipient of usury can sell it to the payer of usury; the payer then sells it back to the intermediary for a lower price. It is established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, cursed the recipient of usury, its payer, its witness, and its recorder. He also “cursed the man who marries a divorced woman to make her lawful for her former husband, and the man for whose benefit this is done.”

Another example is their combining usury with a form of loan. It is established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“It is not lawful to combine a loan with a sale, stipulate two conditions in a sale, profit from something for which one has not assumed liability, or sell what one does not have.”

Furthermore, “the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited muzābanah and muhāqalah”—purchasing fruit and grain on the basis of estimated quantities. Likewise, he prohibited selling a heap of food whose volume is unknown in exchange for a specified quantity of food. This is because, where equality is required, not knowing that the quantities are equal is equivalent to knowing that they are unequal. Estimation does not establish the actual quantity by measure; it is merely approximation and conjecture. The imams agree on this.
