Yet it is established that he granted a concession for ‘arāyā sales, allowing those concerned to purchase the fresh dates for their estimated equivalent in dried dates. Thus, in this instance, a commodity subject to the rules of usury may be purchased on the basis of its estimated quantity. Where there was a need, he allowed estimation to take the place of measurement. This is part of the perfection of the Sharia’s merits. Likewise, he allowed estimation to take the place of measurement when determining the zakat due and dividing crops. He would estimate people’s fruit crops to calculate their zakat, and ‘Abd Allāh ibn Rawāhah would divide the crops with the people of Khaybar by estimation, at the command of the Prophet

---

## Page 10175

, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It is well known that whenever quantities can be determined by measurement, this is done. When that is not possible, estimation takes its place because of the need, like other substitutes in matters of knowledge and indication. Thus, analogy takes the place of an explicit text when none is available, and valuation takes the place of an equivalent or an unavailable stipulated price when these cannot be supplied.

Another example is determining lineage through physical resemblance when other circumstantial evidence is unavailable, since a child resembles his father. Estimation, determining lineage through resemblance, and valuation thus provide substitute means of knowledge, just as analogy does in relation to an explicit text. The same applies to justice in practice, for the Sharia is founded upon justice, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, We sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance, so that people might uphold justice.”

“Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.”

Allah has prescribed retaliation for violations of life, property, and honour, insofar as this is possible. Allah Most High says:

“Retaliation is prescribed for you in cases of killing”—and the rest of the verse.

And He Most High says:

“We prescribed for them therein: a life for a life”—and the rest of the verse.

And He Most High says:

“The recompense for an evil is an evil like it”—and the rest of the verse.

And He Most High says:

“So whoever transgresses against you”—and the rest of the verse.

And He Most High says:

“If you retaliate, then retaliate with the like of that which was inflicted upon you”—and the rest of the verse.

If a man deliberately and wrongfully kills someone of equal legal standing, he is liable to execution in retaliation. He may then be subjected to the same treatment that he inflicted, insofar as possible. This is the position of the scholars of Medina and those who agree with them, such as al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad, according to one of the two reports from the latter, provided that the act is not prohibited on account of Allah’s right

---

## Page 10176

as when he has crushed his victim’s head. Thus, “the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, crushed the head of the Jew who had crushed the girl’s head.” This more fully achieves justice than killing him with a sword-blow to the neck. When retaliation is not possible, recourse is made to blood money, which serves as a substitute because equivalent retaliation is impossible.

If someone destroys another person’s property—as when a borrowed item perishes while in his possession—he must provide its equivalent if one exists. If an equivalent cannot be obtained, its monetary value—in dirhams and dinars—serves as a substitute. Hence, requiring an equivalent for everything, insofar as possible and with due regard for its value, comes closer to justice than requiring monetary compensation rather than an equivalent. The story of David and Solomon concerned this matter.

We have discussed all these subjects at length elsewhere; the purpose here is merely to draw attention to them. Accordingly, permitting ‘arāyā sales on the basis of estimated quantities, because of need when sale by measured volume is not possible, accords with the principles of the Sharia. Moreover, it is established by the authentic Sunnah. This is the position of the scholars of Medina and the scholars of hadith. Mālik also permitted estimation in comparable circumstances because of need. This is sound understanding of the law in its truest sense.

The position of the scholars of Medina and those who agree with them, such as al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad, concerning compensation for hunted game is that an animal equivalent in physical form must be provided, as established by the Sunnah and the judgments of the Companions. The Sunan collections report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ruled that a ram was due for a hyena

---

## Page 10177

and the Companions ruled that a camel was due for an ostrich, a sheep for a gazelle, and similarly in other cases. Those scholars of Kufa who disagree with them hold that compensation for hunted game is assessed only by its monetary value, and that this amount is used to purchase livestock. Monetary value, however, varies over time.

Section

Things may be forbidden either in themselves or because of how they are acquired. Acquisition through dealings with others takes two forms: exchange and partnership. Buying, selling, hiring, leasing, and similar transactions constitute exchange. Partnership includes capital partnerships and other forms of partnership.

Mālik’s position on partnerships is among the soundest and most equitable. He permits capital partnerships, labor partnerships, and other forms, as well as profit-sharing investment partnerships, crop-sharing arrangements, and musāqāh (orchard-tending partnerships). Al-Shāfiʿī, however, permits partnerships only when they are subsidiary to joint ownership.

There are two kinds of partnership: joint ownership of property and contractual partnership. Joint ownership, such as heirs sharing an inheritance, requires no contract. But if

---

## Page 10178

two people enter into a partnership by contract, al-Shāfiʿī’s position is that neither partnership nor division of the assets is effected by contract. Ahmad, however, holds that both are effected by contract. He therefore permits capital partnerships even when the two capital contributions differ and are not mixed together. In his view, if the partners settle their accounts without physically separating their shares, this constitutes a division, so that any subsequent loss of capital is not made good from the earlier profit.

Al-Shāfiʿī does not permit labor partnerships, credit-based partnerships, or partnerships in which the two capital contributions are not mixed together. Nor does he permit a stipulation granting one partner a higher rate of profit on his capital than the other, since, in his view, the contract has no effect in this respect. He permits profit-sharing investment partnerships, certain forms of orchard-tending partnership, and crop-sharing as a subsidiary arrangement, on grounds of need rather than conformity with analogical reasoning.

Abū Hanīfah himself permits neither orchard-tending partnerships nor crop-sharing arrangements, because he regards them as contracts of hire, in which the remuneration must be known.

Mālik is more accommodating than either of them in this area: he permits orchard-tending partnerships for all kinds of fruit, alongside such forms of partnership as capital and labor partnerships. He does not, however, permit crop-sharing on bare land, agreeing in this with the scholars of Kufa.

As for the early authorities of Medina and other Companions and Successors, they would

---

## Page 10179

permit all of this. This is also the position of al-Layth, Ibn Abī Laylā, Abū Yūsuf, Muhammad, and hadith scholars such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others.

The misconception that led those scholars to prohibit these transactions was that they regarded them as contracts of hire, in which the amount of remuneration must be known. They then made an exception for profit-sharing investment partnerships on grounds of need, since money cannot be leased. The correct view, however, is that these transactions belong to the category of partnerships, not contracts of exchange. Someone who hires another seeks to obtain that person’s work, as when hiring a tailor, baker, cook, or the like. In these arrangements, however, the work itself is not the intended object. Rather, one party contributes his labor and the other the use of his property, so that they may share whatever profit Allah provides: either both gain or both sustain a loss. It was on this basis that:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, contracted with the people of Khaybar to cultivate it at their own expense in return for half the fruit and crops it yielded.”

The prohibition of the form of agricultural leasing that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade in the hadith of Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj and others is agreed upon, as al-Layth and others explained. For:

“He forbade leasing land in return for what grew along the irrigation channels and watercourses, together with some straw.”

One area might yield a crop while another did not. He therefore forbade the owner to reserve for himself the crop of a particular plot, just as, in a profit-sharing investment partnership, he forbade the working partner to stipulate a fixed amount of profit and the profit from a particular garment

---

## Page 10180

because that undermines fairness in the partnership. The principle adopted by the scholars of Medina in this matter is sounder than that of others, which requires remuneration at the customary rate. The former is correct, for the contract was not for the labor itself; hence, the work did not have to be specified. Moreover, remuneration at the customary rate might exceed the capital and its profit combined.

Under an invalid contract, one is entitled only to the counterpart of what one would receive under a valid contract. Thus, if what is payable under a valid sale and lease is a price and rent, a share of the profit becomes payable under an invalid contract; what is payable under an invalid contract is a share of the profit. The same applies to orchard-tending partnerships, sharecropping, and other such arrangements.

Where the position of the later Medinan scholars on this subject is weak, that of the Kufan scholars is weaker still. It seems that all this belongs to the newly introduced reasoning known to those of the early generations who criticized it. What the Sunnah and established practice prescribe, however, is justice.

Anyone who reflects on the underlying principles will recognize that orchard-tending partnerships, sharecropping, and profit-sharing investment partnerships are closer to justice than leasing. Leasing involves risk: the lessee may or may not benefit. By contrast, in orchard-tending partnerships and sharecropping, both parties share in gains and losses. These arrangements therefore do not expose either party to the same degree of risk as leasing.

---

## Page 10181

Section

As for acts of worship, a fundamental principle of religion is that nothing is unlawful except what Allah has forbidden, and nothing is part of religion except what Allah has prescribed.

In Surahs al-An‘ām and al-A‘rāf, Allah, glorified be He, reproached the polytheists for forbidding what He had not forbidden and instituting religious practices for which He had given no permission. As Ibn ‘Abbās said: “If you wish to understand the ignorance of the Arabs, read from His words, ‘They assign to Allah a share of the crops and livestock He has created,’ and the rest of the verse.”

Allah condemned the polytheists for their innovations in forbidding crops and livestock, and for the forms of polytheism they had introduced. He also condemned them for invoking divine decree to justify their innovations. He, the Exalted, said:

“Those who associate partners with Allah will say, ‘Had Allah willed, we would not have associated partners with Him’”—and the rest of the verse.

It is related in al-Sahīh from ‘Iyād ibn Himār that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “Allah, the Exalted, says: ‘I created My servants as upright monotheists, but the devils led them astray, forbade them what I had made lawful for them, and commanded them to associate with Me that for which I had sent down no authority.’”

In Surah al-A‘rāf, He mentioned what they had forbidden and what they had instituted as religion. He, the Exalted, said:

“Say, ‘My Lord has only forbidden shameful deeds’”—and the rest of the verse. And He said:

---

## Page 10182

“Say, ‘My Lord has commanded justice’”—and the rest of the verse.

Thus He explained to them what He had commanded and what He Himself had forbidden. He also said, condemning them:

“Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them a religion”—and the rest of the verse.

This is discussed at length elsewhere. The point is that no one may declare anything forbidden unless the Sharia has forbidden it; otherwise, the default is that it is not forbidden. This applies equally to things and actions. Nor may anyone institute a religious practice as obligatory or recommended without evidence from the Sharia establishing its obligatory or recommended status.

With this understood, the people of Medina adhere to this principle more firmly than anyone else. Of all the inhabitants of Muslim cities, they are the most averse to religious innovations. We have already noted things and transactions that others prohibit but they do not. As for religious practice, they adhere more closely than the inhabitants of other cities to prescribed acts of worship and keep furthest from innovated acts of worship.

There are many examples of this. Some scholars of Kufa and elsewhere, for instance, recommended that those performing ablution, the ritual bath, prayer, and similar acts of worship should state their intention verbally. They said that expressing the intention verbally gives it greater force than merely forming it inwardly, although none of the imams considered its verbal expression obligatory. The people of Medina, however, did not recommend any of

---

## Page 10183

that, and this is the correct view. Ahmad’s followers hold two views on the matter. This is an innovation that neither the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor his Companions practised. Rather, he would begin the prayer with the takbīr (proclamation of Allah’s greatness), without uttering any of these expressions beforehand. Likewise, when teaching his Companions, he taught them only to begin with the takbīr. Thus, this is an innovation in religious practice and also reflects a misunderstanding of intention itself. The intention to perform an action necessarily arises within the mind, so stating it aloud is pointless—like someone eating announcing his intention to eat, someone drinking announcing his intention to drink, someone marrying announcing his intention to marry, or a traveller announcing his intention to travel, and so forth.

Another example concerns “the forms of acts of worship.” Mālik and the people of Medina do not permit altering the prescribed form of an act of worship. Thus, prayer may not begin with anything other than the prescribed takbīr, namely, “Allah is the Greatest.” This same takbīr is prescribed for the call to prayer and the Eid festivals. They do not permit reciting the Quran in a language other than Arabic, nor do they permit replacing the specifically prescribed item due as zakat with other property of equivalent value chosen by its owner.

Regarding prayer times, they follow the Sunnah more closely than the people of Kufa: they recommend offering the dawn and afternoon prayers early. They hold that the time for the afternoon prayer begins when the shadow of an object equals its height, which marks the end of the time for the noon prayer. They regard the times of the night and sunset prayers as shared for someone with a valid excuse, such as a menstruating woman whose period has ended or an insane person who has regained his sanity.

---

## Page 10184

and they permit combining prayers for a traveller pressing on with his journey, for someone who is ill, and during rain. Their position on prayer during travel is moderate. Some jurists consider performing the prayers in full preferable to shortening them; others prefer shortening them but do not regard performing them in full as disliked—indeed, they regard it as the more evident ruling—and hold that a person may shorten them only if he intends to do so. Other jurists regard performing them in full as impermissible. They, however, hold that shortening the prayers is the Sunnah and that performing four rak‘ahs (units of prayer) is disliked. They regard shortening as an established Sunnah and combining as a concession for particular circumstances. Undoubtedly, this position accords most closely with the Sunnah.

Likewise, concerning “regular Sunnah prayers,” they hold that witr consists of a single rak‘ah, even if preceded by an even number of rak‘ahs. This is sounder than the position of the Kufans, who say: “Witr must be like the sunset prayer.” Although permitting both forms is sounder, separating the final rak‘ah from those preceding it is preferable to joining them. Their position is therefore stronger than that of the Kufans in all cases.

They do not recognize a regular Sunnah prayer before the Friday prayer, unlike those Kufans who disagree with them. Mālik does not lay down fixed prescriptions for prayers accompanying the obligatory prayers, whereas some Iraqi scholars have specified particular practices on the basis of weak hadiths. Mālik’s position is therefore closer to the Sunnah.

The people of Medina hold that pilgrims may combine and shorten prayers at ‘Arafah and Muzdalifah, and shorten them

---

## Page 10185

at Minā, whether they are from Mecca or elsewhere. Undoubtedly, this is the established Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is also one of the positions within the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad.

Those who maintain that only pilgrims who have travelled the distance required for shortening prayers may shorten them hold a position contrary to the Sunnah. Weaker still is the position of those who permit combining prayers only for those who have travelled that distance, for it is well known that there are grounds for combining prayers other than a long journey.

Thus, the position that combining prayers is permissible on a short journey, just as it is on a long one, is stronger than the position that permits it only on a long journey, not a short one. Those Iraqis and others who held these views supposed that “the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed at Minā and then said: ‘People of Mecca, complete your prayers, for we are travellers.’”

This report is falsely attributed to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, according to the agreement of hadith scholars. What is actually reported in the Sunan collections is that he said this when he prayed in Mecca during the campaign of the Conquest. They have likewise transmitted this statement from ʿUmar.

It is related that when al-Rashīd performed Hajj, he instructed Abū Yūsuf to lead the people in prayer. After pronouncing the concluding salutation, Abū Yūsuf said: “People of Mecca, complete your prayers, for we are travellers.” One of the Meccans said to him: “Do you say this to us, when the Sunnah originated among us?”

Abū Yūsuf said: “Such is your understanding of jurisprudence! You spoke while you were still in prayer.”

---

## Page 10186

This Meccan agreed with Abū Yūsuf’s assumption that they should not shorten their prayers, but spoke out of his limited understanding of jurisprudence. Speaking out of forgetfulness or ignorance of the prohibition on speaking does not invalidate one’s prayer according to Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad in one of the two reports from him, whereas it does invalidate it according to Abū Hanīfah.

Had this Meccan known the Sunnah, he would have said: “This is not the Sunnah. Rather, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed two rak‘ahs at Minā, as did Abū Bakr and ‘Umar. Likewise, they prayed two rak‘ahs at ‘Arafah and Muzdalifah, without instructing the Meccans praying behind them to complete their prayers there.” This accords with the position of the people of Medina.

Another example is the eclipse prayer. Mass-transmitted reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, establish that he performed it with two bowings in each rak‘ah. The people of Medina followed this Sunnah, whereas it remained unknown to the people of Kufa, who did not permit this.

The same applies to the prayer for rain. It is established in an authentic hadith “that the Prophet performed the prayer for rain.” The people of Medina hold that prayer should be offered to seek rain, whereas this Sunnah remained unknown to those among the people of Iraq who rejected the prayer for rain.

Another example is the additional takbīrs in the Eid prayer. Most Prophetic reports and reports from the early generations accord with the position of the people of Medina: seven in the first rak‘ah, including the opening takbīr by which one enters the prayer, and five in the second.

---

## Page 10187

Another example is the question of whether a prayer is caught by catching one rak‘ah or less than a rak‘ah. Mālik’s position is that it is caught only by catching one rak‘ah. This is what is authentically established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“Whoever catches one rak‘ah of the prayer has caught the prayer.”

He also said:

“Whoever catches one rak‘ah of the dawn prayer before the sun rises has caught it, and whoever catches one rak‘ah of the afternoon prayer before the sun sets has caught it.”

Thus, Mālik holds that the Friday prayer and congregational prayer are caught only by catching one rak‘ah. The same applies to catching a prayer at the end of its allotted time, and likewise to being in time for the prayer, as when a menstruating woman becomes pure or a person suffering from insanity regains sanity before the time expires.

Abū Hanīfah makes catching the prayer in all these cases dependent on the time needed to say a single takbīr. Even concerning the Friday prayer, he says that anyone who catches enough of it to say a takbīr has caught it. Al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad agree with Mālik concerning the Friday prayer, while their reported positions vary in the other cases. Most scholars of their respective schools agree with Abū Hanīfah in the remaining cases. It is evident that the position of those who agree with Mālik in all these cases is sounder in terms of both textual evidence and analogy.

Some have argued against Mālik by citing the wording in the authentic hadith:

“Whoever catches one prostration of the prayer…”

This, however, provides no evidence against him, because “prostration” here means a rak‘ah. Likewise, Ibn ‘Umar said:

“I learned from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to offer two prostrations before the noon prayer and two after it.”

There are numerous similar examples.

---

## Page 10188

Another example is the position of the people of Medina that if an imam leads the prayer, forgetting that he is in a state of major or minor ritual impurity, and then realizes this, he must repeat the prayer, but those who prayed behind him need not. This is what is reported from the Rightly Guided Caliphs, such as ‘Umar and ‘Uthmān. According to Abū Hanīfah, everyone must repeat the prayer. This has also been mentioned as a reported position of Ahmad, but his well-known, explicit position agrees with Mālik’s. This is also the position of al-Shāfi‘ī and others.

Further support for this is an incident involving Abū Yūsuf. The caliph appointed him to lead the Friday prayer in his place, and he led the people, then remembered that he had been in a state of ritual impurity. He repeated his prayer but did not instruct the people to repeat theirs. When questioned about this, he said: “Sometimes a matter becomes difficult for us, so we adopt the position of our brothers from Medina.” Yet there is considerable disagreement concerning the Friday prayer, since having an imam is a condition of it.

Mālik also applied this principle consistently to other errors on the imam’s part. If the imam prays according to his own independent legal judgment and omits something that a person praying behind him considers obligatory—for example, the imam does not consider it obligatory to recite “In the name of Allah…” or does not consider bleeding, loud laughter, or touching women to necessitate ablution, whereas the person praying behind him considers this obligatory—then Mālik’s position is that the follower’s prayer is valid. This is also one of the two positions reported from Ahmad and al-Shāfi‘ī. Their other position is that it is invalid, in agreement with Abū Hanīfah. As for the position of the people of Medina, there is no doubt about

---

## Page 10189

its correctness. It is established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“They lead you in prayer. If they perform it correctly, both you and they receive the reward; if they err, you receive the reward, while they bear responsibility.”

This explicitly addresses the issue. Moreover, since the imam has prayed according to his independent legal judgment, his prayer cannot be deemed invalid. Do you not see that when he issues a judicial ruling according to his independent legal judgment, his ruling is enforced? Following him in prayer is therefore all the more warranted. Those who disagree base their position on the claim that the follower believes the imam’s prayer to be invalid. This is mistaken, for the imam has prayed according to his independent legal judgment or the scholarly opinion he follows. If he is correct, he receives two rewards; if he is mistaken, he receives one reward, and his error is forgiven. How, then, can it be said that the follower believes his prayer to be invalid?

Furthermore, it is established through mass transmission from the early generations of this community that they continued to pray behind one another despite such differences. Al-Shāfi‘ī and others like him regularly prayed behind the people of Medina, although the latter recited “In the name of Allah…” neither silently nor aloud.

It is also reported that al-Rashīd underwent cupping and asked Mālik for a ruling. Mālik ruled that he did not need to renew his ablution, and Abū Yūsuf then prayed behind him. The position of Abū Hanīfah and Ahmad is that the discharge of impure matter from anywhere other than the urinary and anal passages invalidates ablution, whereas Mālik and al-Shāfi‘ī hold that it does not. Abū Yūsuf was asked, “Do you pray behind him?” He replied, “Glory be to Allah! He is the Commander of the Faithful!” Refusing to pray behind the imams on such grounds is one of the distinguishing practices of the people of innovation, such as the Rāfidah and the Mu‘tazilah. Thus, when Imam Ahmad was asked about this matter,

---

## Page 10190

he ruled that renewing ablution was obligatory. The questioner then asked him, “If the imam does not renew his ablution, should I pray behind him?” He replied, “Glory be to Allah! Would you not pray behind Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib and Mālik ibn Anas?”

Mālik holds that speaking during prayer out of forgetfulness or ignorance does not invalidate it, on the basis of the hadith concerning Dhū al-Yadayn; the hadith concerning Mu‘āwiyah ibn al-Hakam, when he invoked Allah’s mercy upon someone who had sneezed; and the hadith concerning the Bedouin who said during prayer, “O Allah, have mercy on me and Muhammad, and do not have mercy on anyone else along with us.”

This is also the position of al-Shāfi‘ī and of Ahmad according to one of the two reports from him. According to the other report, Ahmad’s position agrees with that of Abū Hanīfah. They argued, “The incident of Dhū al-Yadayn occurred before speaking during prayer was prohibited.” But that is not so. Rather, the incident of Dhū al-Yadayn occurred after Khaybar, since Abū Hurayrah witnessed it, and he only embraced Islam in the year of Khaybar. Speaking during prayer was prohibited before Ibn Mas‘ūd returned from Abyssinia, and Ibn Mas‘ūd was present at Badr.

The school of the people of Medina allows latitude consistent with the Sunnah in supplication during prayer, drawing attention by reciting the Quran or glorifying Allah, and similar matters. The Kufans, by contrast, imposed very severe restrictions in this area, classifying all of this as prohibited speech.

---

## Page 10191

Another example concerns ritual purification. Mālik held that ablution is required after touching the penis or touching women with desire, but not after laughing aloud during prayer, touching women without desire, an unusual discharge from either of the two private passages, or an impure discharge from elsewhere in the body. Abū Hanīfah held that it is required after laughing aloud during prayer and after any impure discharge from either of the two private passages, but not after touching the penis.

It is well known that the hadiths establishing that touching the penis invalidates ablution are more firmly established and better known than those concerning laughter. No one transmitted any of the latter in the Sunan collections; hadith scholars regard them as weak reports in which a Successor narrates directly from the Prophet. Thus, no hadith scholar held that laughing aloud requires ablution, knowing that no authentic report establishes this.

There are two approaches to ablution after touching the penis. Some regard it as a purely devotional requirement whose rationale is not understood; thus, it would not be far removed from established principles, like ablution after laughing aloud during prayer. Others do not regard it as purely devotional; on that understanding, its basis is clearer and stronger.

As for touching women, there are three well-known positions: Abū Hanīfah’s position is that it never requires ablution; and the position of Mālik and the people of Medina—which is also the well-known position reported from

---

## Page 10192

Ahmad—is that touching invalidates ablution if accompanied by desire, but not otherwise. Al-Shāfi'ī’s position is that it requires ablution in all cases.

There is no doubt that the positions of Abū Hanīfah and Mālik are the two well-known positions among the early generations. As for requiring ablution after touching women without desire, this is an anomalous position with no basis in the Quran, the Sunnah, or any report from the early generations of this community. Nor does it accord with the fundamental principles of Islamic law. Touching without desire has no effect on pilgrimage consecration or devotional retreat in the mosque, whereas touching with desire does. It is not disliked for someone who is fasting, does not establish a relationship of marital affinity, and has no effect on any act of worship or other legal ruling. Whoever makes it invalidate ritual purity has therefore departed from the established principles.

As for the Most High’s words:

“Or have touched women,”

if they mean sexual intercourse alone, as stated by ‘Umar and others, then it is clear that His words “or have touched women” concerning ablution are like His words concerning devotional retreat:

“And do not have relations with them while you are staying for worship in the mosques.”

Physical contact without desire has no effect there; likewise, it has no effect here. The same applies to His words:

“Then divorce them before you have touched them.”

Moreover, we know that men have always touched women without desire. Had ablution been obligatory because of this, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have commanded the Muslims to perform it, and this would have been transmitted and reported.

---

## Page 10193

This is comparable to the argument advanced against Mālik concerning semen: people continually experience wet dreams, and semen gets onto their bodies and clothes. If washing it off were obligatory, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have commanded it. Yet he never commanded any Muslim to wash semen from either his body or his clothes, whereas he commanded a menstruating woman to wash menstrual blood from her garment. It is well known that semen gets onto people’s clothes more frequently than menstrual blood gets onto women’s clothes. How, then, could he explain this to a menstruating woman while leaving that general ruling unexplained, when delaying clarification beyond the time it is needed is impermissible?

The authentic report that ‘Ā’ishah used to wash semen from his garment does not establish that doing so is obligatory. It is also authentically reported from her that she would rub it off. This is all the more telling given that rubbing it off is established, and that washing may simply be prompted by its unpleasantness. As Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās and Ibn ‘Abbās said:

“Remove it from yourself, even with a stalk of idhkhir grass, for it is no different from mucus and spittle.”

If this argument is sound, the same may be said concerning ablution after touching women without desire. As for touching them with desire, whether this requires ablution has long been a matter of juristic interpretation and disagreement. As for touching them without desire, the matter is as you see.

The same applies to bathing to remove major ritual impurity. Mālik’s position, and one of the two positions in Ahmad’s school—indeed, the position transmitted from Ahmad himself—is to follow the Sunnah in this matter. Those who described the Prophet’s ritual bath, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, such as ‘Ā’ishah and Maymūnah, did not report that he washed his body

---

## Page 10194

in its entirety three times. Rather, they reported that, after performing ablution and working water through the roots of his hair, he poured a handful of water over one side of his head, then poured water over the rest of his body. Those who recommended washing three times did so only by analogy with ablution, whereas the Sunnah distinguishes between the two. It is also established that:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to perform ablution with one mudd of water and bathe with one sā‘, which is four mudds.”

Clearly, had washing three times been the Sunnah when bathing, that amount would not have sufficed, since the parts of the body other than those washed in ablution are more than four times as extensive.

Another example concerns dry ablution. Some maintain that it need not be renewed for every prayer, as Abū Hanīfah held. Others maintain that it must be renewed for every prayer, as al-Shāfi‘ī held. Mālik’s position is that it should be renewed for each prayer time. This is the most balanced opinion and accords with the reports transmitted from the Companions and those concerning women with non-menstrual bleeding. Hence this is the well-known position on both matters among the jurists versed in hadith.

Another example is that the people of Medina require zakat on the combined property of two owners as though it belonged to a single owner. When the number of camels exceeds one hundred and twenty, they prescribe one two-year-old she-camel for every forty and one three-year-old she-camel for every fifty. This accords with the Prophet’s letter

---

## Page 10195

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—concerning zakat, which al-Bukhārī transmitted on the authority of Abū Bakr al-Siddīq. Most of the Prophet’s letters, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, including those preserved by the families of ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb and ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, agree with this.

Those Kufans who disagree with them restart the schedule of prescribed dues after that point and give no effect to the combining of livestock belonging to different owners. They have reports supporting this restarting of the assessment, but these cannot stand against the evidence just mentioned. Even if authentic, they have been abrogated, just as the reported practice of paying zakat on cattle in sheep was abrogated.

The people of Medina hold that amounts between successive zakat thresholds are exempt only in the case of livestock. For gold and silver, zakat is therefore due proportionately on any amount above the minimum threshold, as transmitted in the reports. Abū Hanīfah, however, links these exempt increments to the existence of a minimum threshold. Thus, in his view, increments of gold and silver between successive thresholds are exempt from zakat, just as they are for livestock. As for agricultural produce subject to the tithe, he recognizes neither exempt increments nor a minimum threshold; rather, a tenth is due on vegetables, whether the amount is small or large. His two leading disciples, however, agreed with the people of Medina, because it is established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No zakat is due on less than five wasqs, and no zakat is due on fewer than five camels.”

They also relied on the established fact that he refrained from collecting zakat on vegetables, together with the report that he said:

“No zakat is due on vegetables.”

The people of Medina hold that buried treasure, concerning which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A fifth is due on buried treasure,”

does not include mineral deposits; rather, mineral deposits are subject to zakat

---

## Page 10196

just as it was collected from the mines of Bilāl ibn al-Hārith, as Mālik mentioned in his Muwatta’. Anyone who carefully studies the Muwatta’, its chapter headings, its reports, and its arrangement will recognize the views of the Iraqis who disagreed with these teachings. Through that arrangement and those reports, Mālik intended to explain the Sunnah and refute those who opposed it. The better acquainted one is with the doctrines of the people of Medina and Iraq, the better one appreciates the worth of the Muwatta’.

For this reason, he used to say:

“I spent so many years compiling this book, yet you receive it in so many days! How can you understand what it contains?”

Or he said something to that effect. Those Iraqis who disagree regard the term rikāz (buried treasure) as encompassing both mineral deposits and treasure buried in pre-Islamic times.

The same applies to the pilgrimage rites. The people of Medina hold that someone combining Hajj and ‘umrah in a single state of consecration should perform only one tawāf (circumambulation of the Ka‘bah) and one sa‘y (walking between Safā and Marwah). It is well known that all the authentic hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, agree with this position. Those Kufans who maintain that such a pilgrim should first perform tawāf and then sa‘y for ‘umrah, followed by a second tawāf and sa‘y for Hajj, rely on reports transmitted from ‘Alī and Ibn Mas‘ūd. Even if authentic, these reports cannot stand against the authentic Sunnah.

If it is said:

“Abū Hanīfah considers combining Hajj and ‘umrah preferable, whereas Mālik considers performing Hajj alone

---

## Page 10197

preferable; yet hadith scholars have no doubt that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, combined Hajj and ‘umrah in a single state of consecration, as explained in detail elsewhere.”

The reply is:

These questions have been much disputed, and people have been confused by the reports transmitted concerning them. Every group has adopted a less sound position on some aspect of these questions. The conclusion established by authentic hadiths is as follows:

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed Hajj with his Companions, he instructed them to leave their state of consecration and make their pilgrimage an ‘umrah, except those who had brought sacrificial animals. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had brought sacrificial animals, so when he did not leave his state of consecration, they hesitated. He therefore said: ‘Had I known at the outset what I know now, I would not have brought the sacrificial animals, and I would have made it an ‘umrah.’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had combined ‘umrah and Hajj. The Sunnah thus indicates that, for someone who has not brought sacrificial animals, performing ‘umrah followed by Hajj, with release from consecration between them, is preferable. For someone who has brought sacrificial animals, combining them in a single state of consecration is preferable. This applies when both are performed on one journey. If, however, someone makes one journey for Hajj and another for ‘umrah, performing Hajj alone is preferable for him. The four imams agree on this: performing Hajj alone is preferable when a separate journey is made for each.

When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, combined Hajj and ‘umrah, he performed only one tawāf and one sa‘y. He did not combine them with two tawāfs and two sa‘ys, as some followers of Abū Hanīfah suppose. Nor did he perform Hajj alone, as some followers of al-Shāfi‘ī and Mālik suppose. Neither he nor any of his Companions performed ‘umrah after Hajj, except ‘Ā’ishah, on account of the ‘umrah during which she had menstruated, although it has already

---

## Page 10198

been authentically established that he performed four ‘umrahs, one of them during the Farewell Hajj. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not leave his state of consecration, contrary to what some followers of Ahmad supposed.

Their position is that someone prevented from completing the pilgrimage is not required to make it up. This is sounder than the position of the Kufan scholars. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions were prevented from performing ‘umrah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. The following year, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed ‘umrah, but some of those who had been with him did not. Those present at al-Hudaybiyah numbered more than fourteen hundred; they were the ones who pledged allegiance beneath the tree. Some of them died before the ‘umrah of al-Qadiyyah.

Their position is also that it is not recommended for anyone—indeed, it is disliked—to enter the state of consecration before reaching the designated geographical boundary. The Kufan scholars, however, recommend entering it before that boundary. The position of the scholars of Medina accords with the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the practice of his rightly guided caliphs.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed three ‘umrahs before the Farewell Hajj: the ‘umrah of al-Hudaybiyah and the ‘umrah of al-Qadiyyah, for both of which he entered consecration at Dhū al-Hulayfah; and the ‘umrah in the year of Hunayn, for which he entered consecration at al-Ji‘rānah. Then came the Farewell Hajj, for which he entered consecration at Dhū al-Hulayfah. He never entered consecration from Medina. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would not have consistently neglected what was preferable. And his caliphs

---

## Page 10199

such as ʿUmar and ʿUthmān, prohibited entering consecration before reaching the designated geographical boundary. Mālik was asked about a man who had entered consecration before that boundary. He replied, “I fear that he may be put to trial,” and cited the words of Allah Most High:

“So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial afflict them.”

The questioner said, “What trial could there be in that? It is merely an additional act of obedience to Allah Most High.”

He replied, “What trial could be greater than thinking that you have been singled out to perform an act that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not perform?”—or words to that effect.

He also used to say, “Nothing will set right the later generations of this community except what set right its first generations.” And: “Whenever someone comes to us who is more skilled in argument than another, are we to abandon what Gabriel brought to Muhammad because of this man’s arguments?”

The position of the scholars of Medina is that if a pilgrim has intercourse after standing at ʿArafāt but before leaving consecration, his Hajj is invalidated. Whoever has intercourse after the first stage of release from consecration must perform an ʿumrah. This is what has been transmitted from the Companions, rather than the view that intercourse after standing at ʿArafāt does not invalidate Hajj, or the view that intercourse after the first stage of release does not require entering consecration again.

In this, Mālik followed the opinion of Ibn ʿAbbās and mentioned it in his Muwattaʾ. However, he did not name the person who transmitted it from Ibn ʿAbbās, since its transmitter was ʿIkrimah, because of what had reached him concerning ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿUmar and Saʿd—although his final assessment was that ʿIkrimah was reliable. For this reason, al-Bukhārī included narrations from him.

If it is said, “He went against the hadith of Dubāʿah bint al-Zubayr concerning her stipulation

---

## Page 10200

that she could leave consecration if something prevented her from continuing; {and the hadith of ʿĀ’ishah about her applying perfume to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, before he entered consecration and before he circumambulated the House}; {and the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās stating that he continued reciting the talbiyah until he stoned Jamrat al-ʿAqabah}; and other reports?”

The reply is: If these instances are compared with those in which others among the Kufans and the like went against hadiths, the latter are more numerous. Moreover, in such matters he followed reports from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, Ibn ʿUmar, and others. Although the correct course when the Companions disagree is to refer the matter back to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, someone who had not received certain Sunnah reports and therefore followed ʿUmar, Ibn ʿUmar, and others like them held a stronger position than someone who was unaware of more of the Sunnah than the people of the Prophet’s city and lacked predecessors comparable to theirs.

Another example is the sanctuary of the Prophet’s city. Hadiths establishing its sanctuary status have been mass-transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through numerous channels. Indeed, it is also authentically reported from him that he prescribed, as the penalty for someone cutting down a tree there, that his belongings should go to whoever found him doing so. The position of the scholars of Medina and those who agree with them, such as al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, is that Medina too is a sanctuary, although they disagree about the penalty for hunting there. Those Kufans who differed on this had not received these Sunnah reports. Some of their followers, however, began countering them with reports such as the hadith of Abū ʿUmayr and the hadith about the wild animal. Even if these reports were comparable in authenticity, they could not legitimately be used to oppose those reports; yet those reports are mass-transmitted. The hadith of Abū ʿUmayr is understood to mean that

---

## Page 10201

the game was caught outside Medina and then brought into it. The same applies to the hadith about the wild animal, if it is authentic. Even assuming that the two conflict, the case would be comparable to that of declaring Medina a sanctuary, for the hadiths concerning its sanctuary status were narrated by Abū Hurayrah and others who became Companions relatively late, whereas the Prophet’s visit to Abū Talha took place in the early period after the Hijrah. Alternatively, when two texts conflict, one establishing a departure from the original ruling and the other negating that departure and maintaining the original ruling, the former takes precedence. Giving it precedence requires the ruling to be determined only once, whereas giving precedence to the text that maintains the original ruling entails two changes in the ruling.

Thus, if it were said that the incident reported in the hadith of Abū ʿUmayr occurred after the hadiths declaring Medina a sanctuary, this would mean that he had prohibited it and then permitted it. If, however, the incident is assumed to have occurred earlier, this would entail only that he prohibited it after it had been permissible. There is no doubt about this. And Allah knows best.

Section

As for marriage, there is no doubt that the position of the scholars of Medina—that marriages arranged to make a woman lawful again for her former husband, and reciprocal exchange marriages, are invalid—conforms more closely to the Sunnah than the position of those scholars of Iraq who do not invalidate them. For it is authentically established {that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, cursed the man who marries a woman to make her lawful again for her former husband, and the man for whom this is done},

---

## Page 10202

and it is established that his Companions—including ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās—prohibited such marriages. None of them is known to have permitted them. This accords with the principles of the scholars of Medina. Among their principles is that intentions count in contracts: they treat a prior stipulation like one made when the contract is concluded, and a customary stipulation like an expressly stated one.

On these principles, they invalidated marriages intended to make a woman lawful again for her former husband, as well as khulʿ (marital dissolution for compensation) employed as a device to perform the act covered by an oath. They also invalidated legal devices used to render usury permissible, and similar practices. Their opponents among the Kūfan scholars, and those who agreed with them, disregarded intentions in these acts, treated good intentions and bad intentions alike, and permitted the outward performance of acts that had neither substance nor genuine intent behind them. Rather, these are a form of hypocrisy and deceit. As Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī said: “They try to deceive Allah as they deceive children. Had they done it outright, it would have been less grave for them.”

Al-Bukhārī included in his Sahīh a book refuting those who resort to legal devices. The early generations of this community and its leading scholars have consistently denounced those who do so, as we have explained at length in a separate work.

As for reciprocal exchange marriages, it is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through more than one

---

## Page 10203

chain of transmission that he prohibited it. However, those Kūfan scholars who considered it valid held that its only defect was the failure to specify the dower, whereas a marriage is valid without a specified dower. Those who deemed it invalid therefore advanced two grounds:

The first is that it makes each woman’s conjugal rights the dower of the other, thereby entailing shared entitlement to those rights. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and many of Ahmad’s followers. Some of these scholars consider it invalid unless a dower is specified, since specifying one eliminates that shared entitlement.

Others consider it invalid only if it is expressly stated: “Each woman’s conjugal rights constitute the other’s dower.” Without that statement, the conjugal rights are not necessarily designated as the dower. Still others consider it invalid in all cases, as explicitly stated in a hadith reported from the Prophet in the Sunan collections. These three views are found within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere.

The second ground is that it is invalid because it stipulates that there shall be no dower. There is a difference between leaving the dower unspecified and stipulating a dower, for this kind of marriage is among the exclusive prerogatives of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Accordingly, if something both parties know to be forbidden—such as wine or a pig—is specified as the dower, the marriage is invalid. This is the view of some of Mālik’s followers and one of the two positions within Ahmad’s school. It accords more closely with the apparent meaning of the Quran and with analogical reasoning based on established legal principles.

Likewise, marriage to a woman who is pregnant or observing a waiting period as a result of fornication is invalid according to Mālik’s school.

---

## Page 10204

and this accords more closely with the transmitted reports and legal analogy, so that semen from lawful intercourse is not mixed with semen from unlawful intercourse. Abū Hanīfa disagreed with Mālik, permitting the marriage contract but not intercourse, while al-Shāfiʿī permitted both. Ahmad agreed with Mālik and went further: he did not permit marriage to a woman who had committed fornication until she repented, because the Quran and hadiths indicate that marrying such a woman is forbidden. As for those who claim that this has been abrogated and that what is meant here is intercourse, the unsoundness of their position is evident on several grounds.

Likewise, there is the question of whether two waiting periods arising from relations with two different men may run concurrently—for example, when a woman marries during her waiting period or has intercourse under a mistaken presumption of lawfulness. Mālik’s position is that the two waiting periods do not run concurrently; rather, she must observe a separate waiting period for each man. This is what is reported from ʿUmar and ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them both, and it is also the position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. Abū Hanīfa, however, held that they run concurrently.

Likewise, there is the question of intercourse with a second husband: does it cancel the effect of fewer than three prior divorces? This concerns a man who divorces his wife once or twice, after which she marries another man who consummates the marriage, and then returns to her first husband. According to Mālik, she returns with only the remaining number of divorces available to her first husband. This is the view of the leading Companions, such as ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb and others like him. It is also the position of al-Shāfiʿī and, according to the well-known report from him, Ahmad. Only Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās held that she does not return subject to the remaining number of divorces; this is also Abū Hanīfa’s position.

---

## Page 10205

Likewise, regarding an oath to abstain from marital intercourse, the position of the scholars of Medina, the jurists versed in hadith, and others is that, once four months have elapsed, the husband must either resume marital relations or divorce his wife. This is what is transmitted from more than ten Companions, and both the Quran and established legal principles support it in several ways. The Kufan scholars, however, hold that the resolve to divorce is established by the expiry of the waiting period: if it expires without his resuming marital relations, she is divorced. At most, this is reported from Ibn Masʿūd—if the report from him is authentic.

There is also the question of taking a wife back through an action: if a man divorces his wife, does intercourse constitute taking her back? There are three positions. The first is that it does, as Abū Hanīfa holds. The second is that it does not, as al-Shāfiʿī holds. The third is that it does if accompanied by the intention to take her back. This is the well-known position of Mālik, and it is the most balanced of the three positions within Ahmad’s school.

Section

As for punishments and judicial rulings, the school of the scholars of Medina is stronger than that of the Kufan scholars in several respects.

First, they require execution in retaliation for killing with a heavy object, as established by the Sunnah and supported by legal principles. Indeed, Mālik went further still, denying the category of accidental killing resembling

---

## Page 10206

intentional killing. Others disagreed with him on this because the resemblance was disregarded. In reality, however, it is a type of accidental killing distinguished by an additional ruling; it is therefore not a subdivision of the accidental killing mentioned in the Quran.

Another example is the question of executing a Muslim for killing an unbeliever or a non-Muslim under Muslim protection, and a free person for killing a slave. There are three positions on this:

The first is that he is executed in retaliation in all circumstances. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa and his followers.

The second is that he is never executed in retaliation. This is the position of al-Shāfi‘ī and one of the two positions reported from Ahmad.

The third is that he is executed only in cases of brigandage. Execution in such cases is a prescribed punishment serving the public interest, so equivalence between the perpetrator and the victim is not required: a free person is executed even if the victim was a slave, and a Muslim even if the victim was a non-Muslim under Muslim protection. This is the position of the scholars of Medina and the other position reported from Ahmad. It is the most balanced position, and it also reconciles the reports transmitted on this subject. Mālik’s position concerning brigands and others is that the same ruling applies to the supporting accomplice and the direct perpetrator, just as scholars agree on the corresponding principle in jihad.

Those who dispute this with him nevertheless concede that people who jointly commit a killing are liable to execution in retaliation. This is agreed upon in the schools of the leading imams, as ‘Umar said: “Had all the people of Sana’a conspired in his killing, I would have executed them all for him.” If all were direct perpetrators, there is no disagreement. If some were not direct perpetrators, but brought about the killing through a cause that would ordinarily lead to death—such as a person acting under coercion, a false witness who subsequently retracts his testimony, or an unjust judge who subsequently retracts his judgment—the majority concede Mālik’s position that these people are liable to execution in retaliation. This is illustrated by what ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, said concerning the two men who testified that a man had stolen

---

## Page 10207

whereupon he had the man’s hand cut off. The two then retracted their testimony and said, “We made a mistake.” He said:

“If I knew that you had done this deliberately, I would cut off your hands.”

This indicates that several hands may be cut off in retaliation for a single hand, and that a false witness must be subjected to retaliation. The Kufan scholars disagree on both points. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, held brigands jointly liable to execution. It is well known that the position which holds those who cooperate in sin and aggression jointly liable to punishment accords more closely with the wording and meaning of the Quran and Sunnah than the position which imposes punishment only on the direct perpetrator.

Another example is that the scholars of Medina follow what ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb proclaimed from the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he said:

“Stoning is a punishment established in the Book of Allah for any man or woman who commits unlawful sexual intercourse after having consummated a valid marriage, when there is testimony establishing the offence, pregnancy, or a confession.”

Likewise, they impose the prescribed punishment for drinking wine when someone is found intoxicated, vomits wine, or has its smell on his breath, provided there are no grounds for doubt. This is what has been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Rightly Guided Caliphs, such as ‘Umar, ‘Uthmān, and ‘Alī. Abū Hanīfa and al-Shāfi‘ī hold that the prescribed punishment may be imposed only on the basis of a confession or testimony establishing the act itself. They maintain that such indications leave grounds for doubt. Two positions are reported from Ahmad. It is well known that the first position accords more closely with the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace

---

## Page 10208

and the Sunnah of his Rightly Guided Caliphs. It also safeguards the limits set by Allah Most High, which He has commanded be safeguarded. The grounds for doubt here are like those attending testimony and a confession that may be false or mistaken.

Another example is that the scholars of Medina regard “financial penalties” as lawful wherever they are established by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and that of his Rightly Guided Caliphs, just as bodily punishments are lawful wherever they are established by the Sunnah. Some Kufan scholars and their followers rejected financial penalties, claiming that they had been abrogated. But where is their evidence for that abrogation? They frequently do this when they encounter an authentic hadith that contradicts their position.

The scholars of Medina and the scholars of hadith, however, found that Prophetic traditions and transmitted reports established financial penalties just as they established bodily punishments. Examples include breaking wine jars, slitting wineskins, and burning down a wine merchant’s shop, as Moses did with the calf and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did with the idols. Likewise, he, peace be upon him, ordered ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Amr to burn the two garments dyed with safflower, and ordered his Companions to break the cooking pots containing donkey meat, before permitting them to wash the pots instead. Similarly, retaliatory punishment was doubled for someone who stole property not kept in secure custody. The hadith of ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb also mentions liability for a lost animal that has been concealed, and payment of twice the amount of blood money for a non-Muslim under Muslim protection who is killed deliberately.

Likewise, their position on “contracts and blood money” is among the soundest positions. Among

---

## Page 10209

these is the blood money payable for a non-Muslim under Muslim protection. Some hold that it equals the blood money for a Muslim, as Abū Hanīfa maintains. Others hold that it is one-third of the blood money for a Muslim, because that is the lowest amount proposed, as al-Shāfi‘ī maintains. The third view is that it is half the blood money for a Muslim. This is Mālik’s position, and it is the soundest view, because this is what is reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by the compilers of the Sunan collections, including Abū Dāwūd and others.

Another example concerns whether those collectively liable for blood money bear all such compensation, as al-Shāfi‘ī holds; or bear the prescribed amounts, such as compensation for a wound exposing the bone or for fingers, and anything greater, as Abū Hanīfa holds; or bear amounts exceeding one-third, which is Mālik’s position. This third view is the one supported by transmitted reports, and it is also Ahmad’s position. As for an amount of exactly one-third, there are two opinions within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad.

It is related that a Medinan and a Kufan debated. The Medinan said to the Kufan: “You have certainly been blessed with one-quarter! You say that one-quarter of the head is to be wiped, that lesser impurity covering a quarter of the affected area is excused, and you make similar statements in other matters.”

The Kufan replied: “And you have been blessed with one-third! You say that if someone vows to give his wealth in charity, giving one-third suffices. You also say that those collectively liable for blood money bear amounts exceeding one-third, and that compensation for a woman’s injuries equals that for a man’s up to one-third, but once it exceeds that, hers is half his—and other such rulings.”

This is true. Yet the Kufan may be told: “There is no basis for the one-quarter rule, either

---

## Page 10210

in the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Messenger. They merely argue that a person has four sides, and that one says, ‘I saw the person,’ upon seeing just one of those four sides; thus, one-quarter is treated as equivalent to the whole. One-third, however, has a basis in several passages of the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The authentic Sunnah and the agreement of the Muslims establish that a sick person may bequeath one-third of his wealth, but no more, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās when he visited him during the Farewell Pilgrimage. Likewise, an authentic hadith relates that a man freed six slaves belonging to him at the time of his death. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, divided them into three groups, freed two, and kept four enslaved. It is also reported that he told Abū Lubāba, ‘One-third suffices for you.’ There are other such examples. How, then, can the two be compared?”

The people of Medina accept the ruling contained in this hadith. Drawing lots is supported by a verse in the Book of Allah and six hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, including this hadith.

Another is his saying:

“If people knew what reward there is in the call to prayer and the first row, and could find no way other than drawing lots for it.”

Another relates:

“When he intended to travel, he would draw lots among his wives, and whichever wife’s lot was drawn, he would take her along with him.”

Another relates that the Ansār would draw lots over the Emigrants when they migrated to them. Another concerns the two rival claimants whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered to draw lots to determine who should take the oath, whether they wished to or not. Another concerns “the two who

---

## Page 10211

disputed over inheritances whose details had been lost. He said to them, ‘Seek what is right, draw lots, and let each of you release the other from any claim.’”

Drawing lots is accepted by the people of Medina and those who agree with them, such as al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others. Those among the Kufans who disagree with them do not accept it. Indeed, some of them are reported to have said, “Drawing lots is gambling,” classifying it as a game of chance. Yet the distinction between drawing lots as prescribed by the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the gambling he prohibited is clear and evident.

Lots are drawn only when rights are equal and no particular person or share can otherwise be selected. This is of two kinds:

The first is where no particular entitlement has already been determined, as with joint owners when there is no allotted share, so that each person’s share is determined by drawing lots. Other examples are the slaves whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, divided into three groups, and the wives, one of whom a man wishes to take on a journey. Those who accept drawing lots agree that it is used in such cases.

The second is where the rightful selection is already determined in reality, as in the story of Jonah and the case of the two rival claimants. Other examples include drawing lots when a man frees a particular slave and then forgets which one, or divorces one of his wives and then forgets which one, or dies, and similar cases. This kind of drawing lots is disputed: Ahmad permits it, whereas al-Shāfi‘ī does not.

---

## Page 10212

Section

Their position in judicial rulings is to give precedence to the litigant whose case is stronger and assign the oath to that party. Thus, in disputes over rights, they rule on the basis of one witness together with the claimant’s oath. In qasāma (the oath procedure in homicide cases), they begin by having the claimants swear; if they swear fifty oaths, they become entitled to claim redress for the blood shed.

The Kufans, however, hold that only the defendant takes an oath. They therefore do not require the claimant to swear, whether in qasāma or otherwise, nor do they rule on the basis of one witness and an oath. They do not consider an oath incumbent upon the claimant.

It is well known that the authentic Sunnah of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, accords with the position of the Medinans. The hadith concerning qasāma is authentic and firmly established on this matter. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to the Ansār:

“You swear fifty oaths and thereby establish your right to redress for your companion’s blood.”

When al-Shāfi‘ī and others like him among the scholars of Iraq debated Medinan scholars, such as Abū al-Zinād and others, concerning qasāma, the Medinans would argue against them on the basis of the Sunnah, which no one can avoid accepting. They would tell them: “The Sunnah and the various aspects of truth may indeed run counter to personal opinion, yet Muslims have no choice but to accept them.” These words form part of a lengthy account transmitted with a chain of narration.

---

## Page 10213

Likewise, the question of “ruling on the basis of one witness and an oath” is supported by hadiths in the Sahīh and Sunan collections, such as the hadith of Ibn ‘Abbās narrated by Muslim, and the hadith of Abū Hurayra and others narrated by Abū Dāwūd. When some scholars said, “We hold that a judgment based on one witness and an oath should be overturned,” scholars such as Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abū ‘Ubayd and others rose to defend this Sunnah. Mālik discussed it in his Muwatta’ at a length unparalleled elsewhere in that work. Al-Shāfi‘ī devoted approximately ten leaves to it in al-Umm, as did Abū ‘Ubayd in his Book of Judicial Rulings.

The Kufans have nothing to support their position except the saying they transmit:

“The burden of proof rests upon the claimant, and the oath upon the one who denies the claim.”

This wording is not found in the Sunan collections, although some compilers of hadith have narrated it. The Sahīh does, however, contain the hadith of Ibn ‘Abbās reporting that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Were people to be granted what they claim, some would lay claim to the lives and property of others. Rather, the oath rests upon the defendant.”

This wording may be understood as not being general in scope. Rather, the definite article refers to the particular defendant envisaged: one against whom the claimant has nothing but a bare allegation, as indicated by the words, “Were people to be granted what they claim.” Those who require the claimant to swear do not do so on the basis of a bare allegation. They require his oath only when evidence has been established that lends greater weight to his side, such as a witness in disputes over rights, or inheritance in qasāma proceedings. If, however, the wording is held to be general, then the specific evidence qualifies the general.

As for their appeal to the Quran’s mention of two witnesses, and of one man and two women,

---

## Page 10214

it is very weak indeed. For this is mentioned only in connection with witnessing a transaction, not adjudicating on the basis of testimony. Even if it concerned adjudication, judgment based on testimony alone would not require this. When an oath is sworn alongside a witness, the judgment is not based on testimony other than that mentioned in the Quran. Moreover, the imams agree that judgment may be given without any testimony at all, merely on the basis of refusing to swear an oath or referring the oath back to the claimant. They also agree that, in certain cases, judgment may be based on the testimony of women alone. How, then, are such judgments given without this being contrary to the Quran? What, then, of an oath alongside a witness?

Mālik requires retaliatory execution on the basis of qasāma and imposes the prescribed punishment on a woman if her husband takes the oaths of imprecation but she does not. Al-Shāfi‘ī imposes the prescribed punishment but does not authorize execution on the basis of qasāma. Abū Hanīfa disagrees on both issues. Ahmad agrees regarding retaliatory execution on the basis of qasāma, but not regarding the prescribed punishment for the woman; rather, he detains her if she does not take the oaths of imprecation, and releases her. The apparent meaning of the Quran and Sunnah supports Mālik’s position.

Another example is that the scholars of Medina hold that both the active and passive participants in sodomy are to be executed, whether muhsan or otherwise. This is what the Sunnah and the agreement of the Companions indicate, and it is one of the two positions within the schools of al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad. Those Kufans who hold that no execution is due have neither Sunnah nor any report from the Companions to support them. Rabī‘a said to the Kufan who debated him: “Can what is never lawful be treated like what is permissible in some circumstances

---

## Page 10215

but not in others?” Al-Zuhrī mentioned that established Sunnah practice was to this effect.

Another example is that, in accusations involving such offences as theft and murder, they take the accused’s character into account: is he a person of suspicious reputation or not? They hold that punishment may be imposed on someone against whom grounds for suspicion have become apparent. Those among the followers of al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad who wrote on the ordinances of government discussed this. They mentioned two views concerning the punishment of such a person: may both the governor and the judge punish him, or only the governor?

It must also be understood that the command of Allah Most High and His Messenger applies to everyone who judges between people, whether a governor, a judge, or anyone else. Whoever distinguishes between them regarding the command of Allah and His Messenger is mistaken. But distinguishing between them on the basis of their jurisdiction—because one has authority over such matters while the other does not—is reasonable.

An example of this occurs frequently in the statements and writings of some followers of the Kufans. When someone argues against them by citing people whom the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, executed or ordered to be executed—such as his execution of the Jewish man who crushed the girl’s head, his withdrawal of protection from the life of the woman who reviled him despite her being under treaty protection, or his order to execute a man who commits sodomy, and similar cases—they say: “He does this as a matter of governance.”

They should be told: “If you say that this form of governance is prescribed for us, then it is right, and it is governance in accordance with Islamic law. But if you say that it is not prescribed for us, that contradicts the Sunnah.”

Furthermore, when someone then says, “This is a matter of governance,” he must mean either that people

---

## Page 10216

are governed by Islamic law, or that this governance lies outside Islamic law. If the former is meant, then it is part of the religion; if the latter, that is an error. The source of this error, however, is that the Kufan school falls short in its knowledge of the governance of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and of his rightly guided caliphs.

It is authentically reported that he said:

“The Children of Israel were governed by the prophets. Whenever a prophet died, another prophet succeeded him. There will be no prophet after me, but there will be caliphs, and they will be numerous.”

They asked, “What do you command us to do?”

He replied, “Honour your pledge of allegiance to the first, then the next, and give them their due rights, for Allah will question them about those He entrusted to their care.”

When the caliphate passed to the descendants of al-‘Abbās, they needed to govern the people. Those jurists of Iraq who assumed judicial office under them did not possess sufficient knowledge to ensure just governance. They therefore found it necessary to establish a jurisdiction for the redress of grievances, and they made military authority separate from religious judicial authority. This division grew more pronounced in many Muslim cities, until people began speaking of ‘religious law’ and ‘governance’: one litigant would summon his opponent to religious law, while the other would appeal to governance. It became permissible for one judge to rule according to religious law and another according to governance.

The reason for this was that those who identified themselves with religious law fell short in their knowledge of the Sunnah. Consequently, in many matters their judgments neglected rights and left the prescribed punishments unenforced, to the point that blood was shed, wealth seized, and forbidden acts freely committed. Meanwhile, those who identified themselves with governance came to govern by a kind of personal judgment, without holding fast

---

## Page 10217

to the Book and the Sunnah. The best among them are those who judge without personal bias and strive for justice. Many of them, however, judge according to their own desires, favouring the powerful, those who bribe them, and the like.

Likewise, cities in which the Medinan school prevailed enjoyed a degree of just governance not found elsewhere: military authority was made subordinate to the authority of those versed in the Book. This was not the case in cities where the school of the people of Iraq and their followers prevailed, where the military governor did not follow the guidance of the scholar. Allah Most High says in His Book:

“We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them…”—to the end of the verse.

Thus, religion is sustained by a Book that guides and a sword that lends support:

“And sufficient is your Lord as a guide and a helper.”

Islam requires that the sword be subordinate to the Book. When knowledge of the Book and the Sunnah prevails and the sword follows that knowledge, Islam stands firm. The people of Medina exemplify this more than the people of any other city. This was indeed the situation during the time of the rightly guided caliphs; after their time, the people of Medina remained superior to others in this respect.

But when knowledge of the Book is deficient, and the sword sometimes accords with the Book and sometimes opposes it, the religious condition of those concerned reflects that. Whoever is guided to understand these matters and others like them will clearly see that the foundational principles of the people of Medina are sounder than those of the people of the East, to a degree that admits no comparison.

---

## Page 10218

Another example concerns the fighting during the great civil strife. The Companions were divided into three groups: one fought on one side, another fought on the other, and a third abstained. The jurists today hold two views: some favour fighting on ʿAlī’s side—as do most authors who write on fighting rebels—while others favour abstaining. The latter is the well-known position of the people of Medina and the scholars of hadith.
