The firmly established, authentic hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning this strife support the latter view. Hence, those who compile statements of the creed of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah mention abstaining from fighting during civil strife and refraining from discussing the disputes that arose between the Companions.

The people of Medina nevertheless hold that those who depart from the Sharia, such as the Harūriyyah and others, should be fought. They distinguish this from fighting during civil strife. This is also the position of the jurists versed in hadith, and it accords with the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and that of his rightly guided caliphs. The hadith concerning the Khawārij is authentically reported from him through ten routes of transmission, which Muslim included in his Sahīh; al-Bukhārī also included some of them.

In it, he said:

“One of you would consider his own prayer insignificant compared with theirs, his fasting compared with theirs, and his recitation compared with theirs. They recite the Quran, but it does not go beyond their throats. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will have a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection.”

It is also established that the Companions agreed on

---

## Page 10219

fighting them. The Commander of the Faithful, Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, fought them and cited the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which called for fighting them. He rejoiced at their being killed and prostrated to Allah in gratitude when he saw their father, Dhū al-Thudayyah, lying dead. This was unlike what happened at the Battle of the Camel and at Siffīn: Alī did not rejoice at that; rather, his pain and regret were plain to see. Nor did he cite any Sunnah from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning that fighting. Instead, he stated that he had fought on the basis of his own independent judgment.

Thus, the people of Medina followed the Sunnah in fighting those who departed from the Sharia and in refraining from fighting during civil strife. This is also the position of the leading scholars of hadith, unlike those who equated fighting the former with fighting the latter. Indeed, they also equated this with al-Siddīq’s fighting those who withheld zakat, placing all these groups in the category of rebels, as some authors writing on fighting rebels have done. This conflates matters that Allah has distinguished. The people of Medina and the Sunnah, however, distinguished between what Allah has distinguished and followed authentic texts and sound, just analogical reasoning.

Sound analogical reasoning is a form of justice: it means treating like cases alike and distinguishing between unlike cases. The people of Medina have the strongest claim to following authentic texts and just analogical reasoning. An exhaustive treatment of this subject would be lengthy; we have discussed as much of it as Allah has willed

---

## Page 10220

concerning the major principles, in our discussions of legal maxims and elsewhere. This, however, is only a response to a request for a fatwa, in which we have briefly highlighted general points that convey some of the merits of the people of the Prophet’s city, Medina. Knowing this is part of religion, especially when people are unaware of the extent of their knowledge and religious devotion. Explaining this is akin to explaining the knowledge and religious devotion of the Companions to those unaware of it.

Just as explaining the Sunnah, the virtues of the Companions, and their giving precedence to al-Siddīq and al-Fārūq is among the most important matters of religion when the innovations of the Rāfidah and others like them emerge, so too explaining the Sunnah and the positions of the people of Medina, and giving these precedence over the positions of the people of other cities, is of the greatest religious importance when the innovations of the ignorant emerge—those who follow conjecture and their own desires.

Allah knows best. May Allah Most High guide us and all our fellow believers to what He loves and is pleased with. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. May Allah bless our master Muhammad, his family, and his Companions, and grant them peace.

## Page 10221

He also said:

Section

As for “the abrogation of the Quran by the Sunnah,” al-Shāfi‘ī does not permit it, nor does Ahmad according to the best-known position reported from him, though he permits it according to another report. This is also the position of the followers of Abū Hanīfah and others. They have argued for it on the grounds that the injunction to make a bequest to parents and close relatives was abrogated by the statement:

“Allah has given everyone entitled to a share their due, so no bequest may be made to an heir.”

This is mistaken. Rather, it was abrogated by the verse concerning inheritance, as the early generations agreed. For, after mentioning the prescribed shares, Allah says:

“These are the limits set by Allah. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit them into Gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein forever. That is the great triumph.”

“But whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him into a Fire, to abide therein forever, and he will have a humiliating punishment.”

By declaring the prescribed shares to be His limits and forbidding their transgression, He made it clear that no one may be given more than Allah has allotted them. This is the meaning of the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah has given everyone entitled to a share their due, so no bequest may be made to an heir.”

Taken on its own, however, this hadith was narrated only by Abū Dāwūd and other compilers of Sunan collections; it is not

---

## Page 10222

in the two Sahīh collections. Were it a solitary report, it would not be permissible to regard a mere report whose authenticity is not known as abrogating the Quran. In short, it has not been established that anything in the Quran was abrogated by the Sunnah without a Quranic text. Among the examples they have cited is Allah’s saying:

“Confine them to their homes until death takes them or Allah makes a way for them.”

It is authentically reported in Sahīh Muslim that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Take this from me! Take this from me! Allah has now made a way for them: for a virgin with a virgin, one hundred lashes and banishment for a year; for a previously married person with another previously married person, one hundred lashes and stoning.”

This argument is weak for two reasons.

First, this is not the kind of abrogation under dispute. Allah established the ruling until a particular endpoint, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, clarified that endpoint. Here, however, the endpoint was unknown, so this came to be called abrogation, unlike an endpoint made clear in the wording of the address itself, as in His saying:

“Then complete the fast until nightfall.”

This is undoubtedly not called abrogation.

Second, flogging a person who commits unlawful sexual intercourse is established by the explicit text of the Quran. Likewise, a Quranic passage concerning stoning had been revealed and recited; its wording was then abrogated while its ruling remained, namely,

---

## Page 10223

His saying:

“The elderly man and the elderly woman, if they commit unlawful sexual intercourse, stone them without fail as a punishment from Allah. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”

Stoning has been established by the mass-transmitted Sunnah and the consensus of the Companions.

This answers the claim that His saying,

“Those of your women who commit unlawful sexual intercourse,”

and the remainder of the verse have been abrogated. For even if this is assumed to have been abrogated, it was abrogated by a Quranic passage revealed afterward. Its wording was subsequently abrogated, while its ruling remained, conveyed through mass transmission. This is not a point of dispute.

Al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and the other imams require adherence to the firmly established, mass-transmitted Sunnah, even when it entails the abrogation of some Quranic verses. They maintain, however, that the Quran was abrogated only by the Quran, not by the Sunnah alone. They cite as evidence His saying, Exalted is He:

“Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or like it.”

They regard Allah’s abrogating the Quran only through Quranic revelation as part of the full reverence accorded to it.

---

## Page 10224

And Shaykh al-Islām Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

Section

Abū al-Hasan al-Āmidī said in his Ahkām:

“The second issue”: Scholars of legal theory have disagreed over whether language includes figurative designations. The scholar Abū Ishāq and his followers denied this—meaning Abū Ishāq al-Isfarāyīnī—while the remaining scholars affirmed it, and this is the correct view.

I say: The discussion concerns two matters: first, scrutinizing this report; and second, examining the evidence for the two views.

Regarding the first, we say:

If by “the remaining scholars of legal theory” he means everyone who has spoken about

---

## Page 10225

the principles of jurisprudence, whether from the early or later generations, then that is not the case. For discussion of the foundations of jurisprudence and their division into the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, and the exercise of independent judgment, as well as discussion of how legal proofs indicate rulings, has been known since the time of Muhammad’s Companions—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and those who followed them in righteousness, and the Muslim imams who came after them. They were more firmly grounded in this discipline and the other religious sciences than those who came later. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—wrote to Shurayh:

“Judge according to what is in Allah’s Book. If nothing is found there, then according to what is in the Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. If nothing is found there, then according to what the people have agreed upon—or, in another wording, ‘according to what the righteous have ruled.’ If you find nothing, then, if you wish, exercise your own judgment.”

Ibn Mas‘ūd and Ibn ‘Abbās likewise said this, and the hadith of Mu‘ādh is among the best-known hadiths among scholars of legal theory.

If, however, by a legal theorist he means someone who knows “the principles of jurisprudence”—namely, the proofs of the rulings of Islamic law considered in general terms—such that he distinguishes a legal proof from what is not, knows the relative ranks of proofs, and gives precedence to the stronger among them—this being the subject matter of the principles of jurisprudence: knowledge of legal proofs and their relative ranks—then every scholar exercising independent legal judgment in Islam is a legal theorist. For knowledge of legal proofs and their relative ranks is part of what such a scholar knows. Merely knowing the general categories of proofs does not suffice to qualify him to exercise independent legal judgment; he must also know the specific proofs. Whoever knows these specific proofs and distinguishes between the particular instances of

---

## Page 10226

legal proofs and things that are not such proofs is even better acquainted with their general category. Likewise, someone who can distinguish individual human beings from other beings must necessarily be able to distinguish their species, for individuals cannot be distinguished without distinguishing species.

Moreover, in discussing questions of legal theory, legal theorists cite the views of scholars qualified to exercise independent legal judgment, such as Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, al-Awzā‘ī, Abū Hanīfah, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Dāwūd, as well as the views of their followers. Indeed, these scholars and others like them have the strongest claim to knowledge of the principles of jurisprudence, since they knew their particular instances and employed these principles in establishing legal rulings. This contrasts with those who discuss hypothetical principles in the abstract—some of which exist and others do not—without knowing their particular instances. Even if what these people say were true, it would be of little or no benefit, since it amounts to discussing proofs conceived in the mind that have no concrete existence. They resemble someone who discusses jurisprudence in relation to hypothetical human actions while not knowing the rulings on actions that actually occur. How much more so when most of what they say about these hypothetical matters is false!

Thus, if the designation “legal theorists” includes the renowned scholars whose independent legal judgments are followed, such as the four imams, al-Thawrī, al-Awzā‘ī, al-Layth ibn Sa‘d, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, and others; and if by “legal theorists” is meant those who discuss the principles of jurisprudence separately from particular proofs, as al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and those after them did, as did ‘Īsā ibn Abān and others like him, and as did the authors who wrote on the principles of

---

## Page 10227

jurisprudence, among both jurists and speculative theologians—then it is well known that the first person known to have treated the principles of jurisprudence separately was al-Shāfi‘ī. Yet he did not divide speech into literal and figurative usage. Indeed, despite his frequent and extensive use of evidence and his knowledge of legal proofs, he is not known to have described any speech as figurative, nor did he mention this in any of his books, whether al-Risālah or elsewhere.

Thus, anyone who believes that the renowned scholars qualified to exercise independent legal judgment, along with other imams of Islam and scholars of the early generations, divided speech into literal and figurative usage, as some later scholars did, holds this belief out of ignorance and limited familiarity with the writings of the religious imams and the early Muslims. Likewise, another group may suppose that this distinction was learned through direct transmission from Arab speech, and that the Arabs themselves said, “This is literal, and this is figurative.” Some writers on the principles of jurisprudence have supposed this, owing to their ignorance of Arab speech, as will be discussed later, Allah Most High willing. Similarly, some suppose that what appears in the writings of certain later scholars, such as al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and Ibn al-Hājib, represents the position of the renowned imams and their followers. Yet they are unfamiliar with the principles of jurisprudence set out by the followers of al-Shāfi‘ī, Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, Ahmad, and others in accordance with their imams’ methods. This, too, stems from ignorance and limited knowledge.

If the person attributing this view to many legal theorists says:

“By this I mean most authors on the principles of jurisprudence from among the proponents of speculative theology and reasoned opinion, such as the Mu‘tazilah, the Ash‘ariyyah, and the followers of

---

## Page 10228

the four imams, most of whom divided speech into literal and figurative usage.”

He is told:

There is no doubt that this division appears in the books of the Mu‘tazilah and those who learned from them or resembled them, and that most of these scholars mentioned it. But the same is not true of those who did not belong to these groups.

He is then told:

Among these men there is no imam of the Muslims who devoted himself to deriving rulings from the evidence of revelation. Accordingly, those who compiled works recording the differing opinions of scholars qualified to exercise independent legal judgment and engaged in deriving rulings from scriptural evidence do not mention any of these men among them. Those scholars possess the fullest knowledge of the principles of jurisprudence and are most deserving of the title “legal theorist” in its praiseworthy sense. Yet none of them divided speech into literal and figurative usage.

If, however, he means the later scholars known for this division—the Mu‘tazilah and other speculative theologians, together with the jurists who followed their approach in this matter—he is told:

There is no doubt that most of these men adopted this division. But among them there is no imam in any of the Islamic disciplines: neither Quranic exegesis, hadith, jurisprudence, Arabic language, nor grammar. Indeed, the leading grammarians and scholars of Arabic, such as al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, al-Kisā’ī, al-Farrā’ and their peers, Abū ‘Amr ibn al-‘Alā’, and Abū

---

## Page 10229

Zayd al-Ansārī, al-Asma‘ī, Abū ‘Amr al-Shaybānī and others, did not divide speech as these men did.

Section

As for “the second point of discussion,” it concerns the evidence for the two positions.

Al-Āmidī said:

“The argument of those who affirm figurative usage is that speakers of Arabic demonstrably apply the word ‘lion’ to a courageous person and ‘donkey’ to a dull-witted person. They also use such expressions as ‘the back and spine of the road,’ ‘so-and-so is on the wing of a journey,’ ‘the night’s locks have turned grey,’ ‘war has risen upon its leg,’ and ‘the liver of the sky,’ among others. Only obstinacy could lead anyone to deny these linguistic usages.

“Given this, these terms must be said to be either literal or figurative in these instances, since linguistic terms cannot fall outside these two categories, except at their initial coinage, as has already been established. They cannot be said to be literal in these instances, because they are agreed to be literal in other senses: ‘lion’ literally denotes the predatory beast, and ‘donkey’ the animal; ‘back,’ ‘spine,’ ‘leg’ and ‘liver’ literally denote the corresponding bodily organs of animals; and ‘locks’ denotes hair extending beyond the ears. Thus, if these terms were literal in the instances mentioned

---

## Page 10230

then each expression would have multiple literal meanings. If that were so, none of those meanings would come to mind before the others when these expressions were used without qualification, since the evidence for their literal senses would necessarily be equal. Yet there is no doubt that what first comes to mind when ‘lion’ is used without qualification is the predatory beast, and when ‘donkey’ is so used, the animal. The same applies to the remaining examples. Moreover, throughout the ages, people have continually transmitted in their speech and writings, from those who established linguistic usage, the designation of one usage as literal and the other as figurative.

If it is objected:

‘If Arabic contains a figurative expression, its meaning must either be specified by an accompanying indication or not. In the first case, the expression, together with that indication, admits no meaning other than the one intended; thus, together with the indication, it is literal in that meaning. In the second case, it is likewise literal, since literal usage means nothing other than an expression used to convey a meaning without an accompanying indication. Furthermore, there is no instance that cannot be expressed by the literal expression specific to it. Using a figurative expression instead, despite its need for an accompanying indication and without any necessity, is therefore far removed from the wisdom and eloquence of those who established linguistic usage.’

We reply:

The answer to the first objection is that, when a figurative usage is not widely familiar, it conveys its meaning only with an accompanying indication. Figurative usage means nothing other than this kind of use of the expression concerned. Moreover, figurative and literal are attributes of expressions, not of nonverbal indications; hence, literalness cannot be an attribute of the combination.

---

## Page 10231

A second answer:

The benefit of using a figurative rather than a literal expression may lie in its being easier to pronounce; its suitability for the rhythm of speech, in verse or prose; rhetorical correspondence, wordplay, or rhymed prose; the intention to magnify something, or departure from the literal expression to belittle it; and other purposes sought in speech. These are the words of Abū al-Hasan al-Āmidī in his major work, the most distinguished of the works by later scholars defending this distinction.

This argument can be answered in several ways.

First:

The usages you mention are not disputed. However, your statement that these terms must be either literal or figurative is valid only if the division of speech into literal and figurative has been established. Otherwise, someone may dispute your position and say:

“You have not given an intelligible dividing line between literal and figurative usage by which one can be distinguished from the other. I ask you to state this distinction between the two categories.”

Or he may say:

“There is, in fact, no definite distinction between them.”

Or he may say:

“I do not affirm the division of speech into literal and figurative, whether because of a rational or scriptural objection, or for some other reason.”

Or he may say:

“It has not been established to my satisfaction that speech is divided into these two categories, or that such a division is admissible in language, revealed law, or reason.”

If he makes any of these or similar statements, you cannot argue against him by saying, “They must be either literal or figurative,” since placing these expressions in either category presupposes the establishment of

---

## Page 10232

this division. To establish the division on this basis would therefore be circular. For one cannot say that these expressions belong to one category rather than the other unless one has established that there are exactly two categories, with no third, and that neither includes anything belonging to the other. Yet this is precisely the point in dispute. How, then, can you make the disputed point a premise in establishing itself, thereby begging the question? The former establishes something by means of itself, so you have supplied no evidence; the latter establishes the underlying principle through a consequence that can only be established by that principle. All this elaboration thus amounts to the height of begging the question.

The second argument:

Among those who affirm literal and figurative usage, some regard certain speech as both literal and figurative, describing a single expression as having both qualities. An example is general expressions whose scope has been restricted. Many have said that these are literal insofar as they signify what remains within their scope, and figurative insofar as they do not signify what has been excluded. According to these scholars, speech is either literal, figurative, or both literal and figurative.

The third argument:

You and a group of scholars, such as al-Rāzī and his followers, including Ibn al-Hājib, say that expressions, before being used but after being assigned meanings, are neither literal nor figurative; or that a figurative expression is one used in a sense other than that for which it was assigned. Accordingly, unless they establish that expressions such as “the back of the road,” “the wing of travel,” and the like were assigned one meaning and then used in another, they have not established that these expressions are figurative—and there is no way

---

## Page 10233

for anyone to do so, since no one can report on the authority of the Arabs that they assigned these expressions to meanings other than those in which they are used.

If they say:

“They did say ‘the bird’s wing’ and ‘the human back,’ and used the words ‘back’ and ‘wing’ to mean the human back and the bird’s wing.”

They may be answered:

This does not imply that they assigned meanings to “the wing of travel” and “the back of the road.” Rather, these expressions were used in a genitive construction with something different from that used in the other expressions—if those other expressions were indeed in a genitive construction. If they were not, an expression in a genitive construction is not the same as a definite expression outside such a construction.

Thus, a definite expression, or one annexed to a particular thing, is not the same as an expression annexed to something else. If someone says “the wing” and “the back,” or says “the bird’s wing” and “the human back,” neither form is the same as “the wing of travel,” “the back of the road,” or “the wing of humility.”

Likewise, when one speaks of the road’s head, back, middle, upper part, and lower part, each has a meaning specific to the road, even if it is not like a human being’s head, back, middle, upper part, and lower part. Similarly, the lower and upper parts of a mountain have meanings specific to it. The same applies to all other nouns in genitive constructions: their meanings are distinguished by what they are annexed to. It is well known that, in their language, an expression formed through fusion, predication, or a genitive construction is not equivalent to an expression without such a construction, whether in grammatical inflection or in meaning. Rather, they distinguish

---

## Page 10234

between the two in vocative constructions and negation. Thus they say yā Zaydu and yā ʿAmru (“O Zayd” and “O ʿAmr”), with a final u-vowel, as in His words, “O Adam” and “O Noah.” With nouns in genitive constructions and similar forms, they say yā ʿAbda Allāhi (“O servant of Allah”) and yā ghulāma Zaydin (“O Zayd’s servant”), as in His words: “O children of Adam,” “O children of Israel,” “O People of the Scripture,” “O people of Yathrib,” and “O our people, respond to Allah’s caller.” These and similar examples have the first noun of the genitive construction in the accusative. The same applies to compounds formed by fusion: khamsa (“five”) is not the same as khamsata ʿashara (“fifteen”); rather, combining the words changes the meaning.

That being so, anyone who said, “‘Five’ is literal when it means five, but figurative in ‘fifteen,’” would be ignorant. For the latter expression is not the former, even though the word “five” occurs in both places: it has entered into a different construction. This type of construction is established by linguistic convention, just as the genitive construction itself is.

Likewise, the expressions “the wing of travel,” “the wing of humility,” and “the back of the road” constitute a different construction, in which the noun is annexed to something other than that to which it was annexed in the other instance. This is neither like the word standing alone, such as “five,” nor like its being joined to another word, as in “twenty-five.”

This same point may be made in the fourth argument: whether an assignment of meaning prior to usage is established, or whether “assignment” means what is known from usage, on either assumption this expression in a genitive construction was assigned and used only for this meaning. Nothing else is understood from it; indeed, it admits no other meaning. Understanding what is intended by it requires only a contextual indication of meaning other than what has been mentioned

---

## Page 10235

in the genitive construction. Rather, the genitive construction conveys its meaning just as all other genitive constructions do. Whenever one word is annexed to another, it conveys a meaning specific to that to which it is annexed. Thus, when one says, “Zayd’s hand and head; his knowledge and religion; his statement, judgment, and report,” these expressions denote what is particular to him, even when Zayd’s religion differs from Amr’s—one being unbelief and the other Islam—and his judgment differs from the other’s—one being unjust and the other just—and his report differs from the other’s—one being true and the other false.

Likewise, when one says, “the colour of this and the colour of that,” each has its own particular colour, even if one is black and the other white. The word used in the genitive construction may thus be the same, while the realities in the two instances differ, as with blackness and whiteness. The word “colour” distinguishes one from the other only by being annexed to something that distinguishes it.

If it is said: “The words ‘being,’ ‘religion,’ ‘report,’ and the like, when used without qualification, encompass these various kinds. They are therefore general terms, termed univocal, unlike ‘head,’ ‘back,’ and ‘wing,’ which, when used without qualification, refer only to the body parts of living creatures.”

The reply is: “Grant that this is so. Is it not through the genitive construction that their scope becomes restricted? They were general and unqualified, then became restricted through annexation or being made definite. They therefore fall under the case of a general expression whose scope is restricted through annexation or definiteness. Restricting it in this way is like restricting it through an adjective, an exception, an apposition, or a stated limit, as when one says: ‘the red colour’ and ‘the true report’

---

## Page 10236

or when one says, ‘a thousand less fifty.’ Their meaning thus changes according to whether they are used without qualification or with qualification.

Moreover, in neither case has the particular expression been used in a sense other than that in which it was originally used. When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is prayer, and the summit of its hump is jihad in the cause of Allah,”

and said:

“Is it anything but what their tongues reap that casts people into the Fire on their noses?”

he annexed ‘head’ to ‘the matter’; this expression was not used to refer to the head of a living creature. Likewise, when people speak of ‘the head of wealth,’ meaning capital, and say that the two partners divide whatever remains beyond the capital, and that the investment manager is entitled to his share of the profit after the capital has been accounted for, the expression ‘the head of wealth’ has not been used to refer to the head of a living creature. The same applies to ‘the head of the spring,’ whether it is a common noun or a proper name established through predominant usage.

Furthermore, there are two answers to their statement that these words, when used without qualification, refer to the bodily organs of living creatures. The first is that an expression is never used entirely without qualification; it is always qualified. For it becomes qualified only after it has been linked and combined with other words, whether in a nominal or verbal sentence, uttered by a known speaker whose customary manner of speaking is familiar. These are qualifications through which the intended meaning becomes clear.

---

## Page 10237

Second: leaving an expression free of particular qualifications is itself a qualification. Hence it is said that commands have a linguistically designated form which, on its own, indicates a command, and that generality has a linguistically designated form which, on its own, indicates general scope. The very act of uttering an expression without qualification is therefore a qualification. For this reason, its signification is conditional upon withholding particular qualifications; withholding those qualifications is itself a qualification.

Similarly, a noun uttered with the intention of predicating something of it, while leaving it free of explicit grammatical governors, is the subject of a nominal sentence and takes the nominative case. The underlying reason is its freedom from explicit grammatical governors: this absence is a condition of its taking the nominative case, just as qualifying it with an expression such as “kāna” (was), “inna” (indeed), or “zanantu” (I thought) entails a different grammatical ruling.

Thus, a speaker may proceed in either of two ways. Sometimes he falls silent and ends his utterance, intending a particular meaning. At other times he joins that utterance to further speech, conveying a meaning different from what the initial expression would indicate on its own. The initial expression therefore occurs in either of two circumstances: the speaker accompanies it with silence, withholding further speech and leaving it unconnected to anything else; or he accompanies it with an additional expression. In the speaker’s customary usage, withholding further speech conveys one meaning, while continuing conveys another. In both circumstances, his intention has become clear, and he has accompanied his expression with something that clarifies what he intends.

It is well known that an expression signifies a meaning. Signification may depend on either presence or absence. This applies equally to evidence that signifies intrinsically, which may

---

## Page 10238

be called rational evidence, and to evidence that signifies through the intention and will of the one providing it—the latter being called transmitted, conventional, or intentional evidence. In both categories, one thing often entails another: its existence indicates the existence of its necessary concomitant, while the absence of that concomitant does not indicate its absence. Thus, the absence of an entity indicates the absence of the attributes subsisting in it, and the absence of any substantive condition indicates the absence of that which depends upon it. For example, the absence of life indicates the absence of knowledge, and the absence of disorder indicates the absence of divinity in anyone other than Allah, and so forth.

As for the second category, which signifies through intention and choice, consider how people write the letters of the alphabet: they distinguish some by a dot and others by the absence of a dot. Thus, among jīm, hā, and khā, jīm is marked by a dot below, khā by a dot above, and hā by the absence of a dot. The same applies to rā and zāy, sīn and shīn, sād and dād, and tā and zā.

Likewise, grammatical particles are said to be distinguished by the absence of the identifying features of nouns and verbs. The same applies to expressions. If someone says to another, “I owe a thousand dirhams,” and then falls silent, this indicates that he means a thousand dirhams of full weight. But if he says, “A thousand debased or underweight dirhams,” or, “Except fifty,” his addition of the qualification or exception provides an indication contrary to the first.

Here, “a thousand” is connected to another expression; there, “a thousand” is left unconnected to any continuation. Its being unconnected is distinct from its signification. Thus, what signifies is not the expression alone, but the expression together with

---

## Page 10239

leaving it as it stands, with nothing added to it.

This holds whether the speaker’s refraining from adding anything is regarded as something positive or as a mere absence. Most people maintain that refraining is something positive that subsists in the person who refrains, whereas Abū Hāshim and a group of others hold that it is a mere absence. They are called the Dhimmiyya because they maintain that a person is blameworthy for what he has not done. On either view, the speaker intends to convey meaning through the expression alone, not through the expression together with the meaning. Its standing alone is a condition of its signification, and this condition is absent when another expression accompanies it.

The usual pattern in language is that adding qualifying expressions restricts the scope of the expression standing alone. Hence the saying, “An addition to the definition restricts what is defined.” The more qualifications a general expression receives, the narrower its meaning becomes. Thus, “human being” and “animal” have broader meanings than “Arab human being” and “rational animal,” respectively.

The fifth argument: These expressions cannot be said to be literal in these applications, because they are unanimously acknowledged to be literal in other applications. The word “lion” is literal when applied to the beast of prey, and “donkey” when applied to the animal; “back,” “loins,” “shin,” and “chest” are literal when applied to the corresponding bodily parts of animals. If these expressions were literal in the applications mentioned, each expression would be equivocal. Were it equivocal, one of its meanings rather than another would not immediately come to mind when it was used without qualification, since the meanings would necessarily be equal in their literal signification.

---

## Page 10240

He may be answered as follows:

When you say, “If the expression were literal in the applications mentioned, it would be equivocal,” what do you mean by “equivocal”? If you mean equivocation in the strict sense—that an expression signifies two meanings without signifying any meaning common to them—some people dispute that this exists within a single language based on a single assignment of meanings. They say that it occurs only in two separate settings, as when one man gives his son a name and another gives his son that same name.

They do not say that giving heavenly bodies such names as Suhayl, al-Mushtarī, the Lion’s Heart, the Eagle, and the like involves a second assignment, whereby the Arabs and others who named them gave them transferred names, like transferred proper names—as when a man names his son Kalb (“dog”), Asad (“lion”), Namir (“leopard”), Bahr (“sea”), and so forth.

No reasonable person disputes equivocation in this sense. Yet it is clear that this is a second assignment. This is not altered by the way assigned proper names signify their referents, or by the distinguishing mark in figurative usage. In giving a name, one may intend the bearer to possess the quality it signifies: one may take its meaning as a good omen, seek to ward off the evil eye, name him after someone dear to oneself—a father, a teacher, or someone distinguished—or choose a name with a praiseworthy meaning, such as ‘Abd Allāh, ‘Abd al-Rahmān, Muhammad, or Ahmad.

In any event, this is a second assignment of the name to this bearer, and in this respect the expression becomes equivocal. Hence, with proper names, it is necessary to distinguish a person by his father’s name, or by his grandfather’s name together with his father’s if his own name and his father’s do not suffice to distinguish him. When these suffice, one confines oneself to them, as the Prophet did

---

## Page 10241

—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—when drawing up the peace treaty between himself and Quraysh, in which he wrote:

“This is what Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allāh has agreed upon with Suhayl ibn ‘Amr.”

This was after the polytheists had refused to write “Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah.” He—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is distinguished before Allah by his status as Messenger and Prophet. When he changed from being identified by the description that requires people to accept his truthfulness and believe in him, he agreed to their identifying him by his father’s name.

The point is that some people say that whenever an expression has two meanings within a single language, those meanings necessarily share something in common. Indeed, they maintain this even regarding letters, holding that there is a correspondence between them and their meanings which motivates the speaker to assign a particular expression to a particular meaning.

No reasonable person has ever said that an expression signifies its meaning by itself, without anyone intending it to do so, and that this signification is an inseparable attribute of the expression. There is therefore no basis for the objection: “If an expression bore a correspondence to its meaning, it would not differ from one nation to another.” For matters involving choice, such as expressions and customary actions, do possess correspondences that motivate an agent acting by choice, even though they vary according to place, time, and circumstances.

Natural phenomena that do not result from a creature’s choice also vary. Heat and cold, blackness and whiteness, and similar natural phenomena vary according to the natural characteristics of different lands. Matters involving choice—food, drink, clothing, housing, mounts, marriage, and so forth—vary according to people’s customs

---

## Page 10242

, even though these are matters of choice and have their own correspondences. Thus, some of these things suit people in one place and time but do not suit people in another time. People choose things in winter and in cold countries that they do not choose in summer and in hot countries, yet in each case there is a correspondence motivating their choice. In hot weather, they choose light foods and fruit that are easy to digest, because their insides are cold and their digestive faculties weak. In winter and in cold countries, they choose heavier foods instead, because the digestive heat within them is strong; or because winter is a time when the interiors of inanimate things, animals, trees, and other things grow warm while their exteriors grow cold. This is because the air grows cold in winter, and like is drawn to like: cold is drawn towards the air, leaving the interiors warm. In hot weather, the air grows warm, drawing heat towards it and leaving the interiors cold. Springs are therefore cold in summer because the earth’s interior is cold, and grow warm in winter because the earth’s interior is warm.

The point here is that it is not ‘Abbād ibn Sulaymān alone, but many people—indeed, most discerning scholars of Arabic and rhetoric—who affirm a correspondence between expressions and meanings. They divide derivation into three types:

Minor derivation: two words share the same root letters in the same order, as in ‘ilm (knowledge), ‘ālim (one who knows), and ‘alīm (very knowledgeable).

The second is intermediate derivation: the two words share the same root letters, but not in the same order

---

## Page 10243

, as in summiya (was named) and wusima (was marked).

The Kufans’ statement that ism (name) is derived from sima (mark) is correct if this kind of derivation is intended. If, however, what is intended is correspondence in both the letters and their order, then the Basrans’ view—that it is derived from sumuww (elevation)—is correct. For the verb is sammāhu (he named him), not wasamahu (he marked him); its diminutive is sumayy, not wusaym; and its plural is asmā’, not awsām.

The third kind of derivation involves correspondence in some letters but not others. More specifically, the remaining letters may belong to the same class—for example, they may be letters articulated in the throat, as in hazara, ‘azara, and azara. The root material conveys strength, while hā’, ‘ayn, and hamza belong to the same class insofar as they are throat letters.

This also includes alternation between a weak radical and a doubled consonant, as in taqaddā al-bāzī (the hawk swooped) and taqaddada. Another example is the statement that surriyya (concubine) is derived from sirr, meaning sexual intercourse. Likewise, Abū Ja‘far al-Bāqir said: “Al-‘āmma (the common people) is derived from al-‘amā (blindness).” Another example is their statement that damān (guarantee) is derived from damm (joining), meaning joining one party’s legal liability to another’s.

When it is said that one expression is derived from another, this can mean two things. The first is that there is a correspondence between them in wording and meaning, without considering

---

## Page 10244

whether one is the original and the other its derivative. In this case, derivation denotes a different kind of relationship between the two expressions. Derivation may also mean that one precedes the other and is its source, just as a father is the source of his child.

According to the first meaning, whether one says that the verb is derived from the verbal noun or that the verbal noun is derived from the verb, both positions—that of the Basrans and that of the Kufans—are correct. According to the second meaning, however, if logical order is intended, the Basrans’ position is more correct, since the verbal noun denotes only the action, whereas the verb denotes both the action and time. If the order of actual existence is intended—meaning that one came into existence before the other—there is no fixed rule: speakers may have used the verb before the verbal noun, or the verbal noun before the verb. They have also used verbs without verbal nouns, such as budd, and verbal nouns without verbs, such as “wayh” (alas) and “wayl” (woe).

They may also predominantly use a verb together with the verbal noun belonging to another verb, as in the case of hubb (love). Its usual verb is the four-letter form: ahabba, yuhibbu (he loved, he loves), while its usual verbal noun is hubb rather than ihbāb. For the active participle, they say muhibb (one who loves), not hābb. For the passive participle, they say mahbūb (beloved), and they use muhibb only as the active participle. By morphological analogy, one would expect ahabbahu ihbāban (he loved him), just as one says a‘lamahu i‘lāman (he informed him).

---

## Page 10245

And this too has causes known to grammarians and morphologists: frequent usage, the transfer of certain word forms, or other factors. As specialists in grammar and morphology know, the strongest vowel is damma (u), the lightest is fatha (a), and kasra (i) lies between them.

The language follows this pattern in both inflected and uninflected words. An inflected word that constitutes an indispensable core element of the sentence takes the nominative, as with the subject and predicate of a nominal sentence, the subject of a verb, and the object that takes its place in a passive construction. A supplementary element takes the accusative, as with the object, the circumstantial qualifier, and the accusative of specification. What occupies an intermediate position—because either a core element or a supplementary element may be annexed to it—takes the genitive: this is the second term of a possessive construction.

The same applies to uninflected words. Thus, they say of ayna (where) and kayfa (how) that their endings are fixed with fatha to ease pronunciation because of the yā’. Likewise, in the vocalization of fixed forms, the stronger takes damma and the weaker takes fatha. They say kariha al-shay’a (he disliked the thing), and for dislike they use karhan, with fatha, as Allah Most High says:

“To Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly.”

And He says:

“Come, willingly or unwillingly.”

The same applies to the contrast between kasra and fatha. For something slaughtered or taken as booty, they say dibh and nihb, with kasra, as Allah Most High says:

“And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.”

And as it occurs in the hadith:

“Camels taken as booty were brought to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

And in the familiar proverb:

“I hear the millstones clattering, but see no flour.”

Here tihn is pronounced with kasra; that is: I see no

---

## Page 10246

flour. Whoever pronounces it with fatha means the act of grinding, just as dhabh (slaughtering) and nahb (plundering) denote actions. Some consider the person who uses this pronunciation mistaken.

These and similar features of Arabic are familiar to those acquainted with the language. They are known sometimes through induction and experience, and at other times through analogy, just as physicians investigate the natural properties of bodies, and as ordinary phenomena are known through experience combining sensory perception and reason. As has been said:

“Through analogy you know what you have not experienced.”

It is well known that, according to the vast majority of rational people, Muslims and others alike, these things have causes and fitting connections. As for any speculative thinker who denies this, there is no point discussing these particular connections with him, for he holds that created things possess no power through which an action occurs, nor any cause that singles out one of two like things. Rather, his fundamental principle is that the Creator’s sheer will singles out one of two like things without any cause or wise purpose.

Such a person therefore says: if a word’s signifying a meaning comes about through Allah’s speech, this is merely a matter of customary association. In his view, the Lord does not single anything out for a cause or a wise purpose; rather, will itself singles out one of two like things without wisdom or cause. If, however, it comes about through a servant’s choice, the cause may be that this particular word, rather than another, occurred to the person assigning it its meaning.

A detailed treatment of these matters belongs elsewhere. The point here is that the argument which

---

## Page 10247

he adduced to establish figurative usage—namely, his statement, “If these expressions are literal, they must be homonymous”—rests on two premises: first, that homonymy necessarily follows; and second, that it is invalid. This argument is weak, for the first premise may be challenged, the second may be challenged, or both may be challenged together.

His assertion that “homonymy necessarily follows” holds only if he is granted that, within a single language and under a single linguistic convention, there are expressions denoting disparate meanings with no shared element. This is a matter of well-known dispute. Even if it is conceded, those who accept homonymy agree that language contains expressions whose meanings have both a shared element and a distinguishing element. This occurs sometimes with identical word forms and sometimes with different ones. Just as a single expression may have multiple meanings, multiple expressions may have a single meaning, as in the case of synonyms.

Although some people deny absolute synonymy, the point is that two expressions may agree in denoting a meaning, while one conveys something additional. For example, a sword may be called sayf (sword), sārim (cutter), and muhannad (Indian blade). The word sayf denotes it without qualification; sārim originally denotes its quality of cutting; and muhannad denotes its association with India. Nevertheless, usage is known to shift terms from adjectival to nominal status, so that this term comes to be applied to

---

## Page 10248

the object itself, without regard to this association. When this association is taken into account, however, some say that these names are not synonymous, because some convey an additional meaning.

Others regard them as synonymous because they all denote the same entity. The former say, “They are disparate terms, like ‘man’ and ‘lion’,” while the latter reply, “They are not like disparate terms.”

The fair assessment is that they agree in denoting the same entity but differ in the attributes they denote. They therefore constitute another category, which may be called “equivalent terms.” Allah’s most beautiful names, and the names of His Messenger and His Book, belong to this category.

For when you say that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise, All-Forgiving, Most Merciful, All-Knowing and All-Powerful, all these names denote the One possessed of these attributes—glorified and exalted is He. Each name also denotes an attribute particular to it: one denotes might, another wisdom, another forgiveness, another mercy, another knowledge, and another power.

Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have five names: I am Muhammad; I am Ahmad; I am al-Māhī, through whom Allah effaces disbelief; I am al-Hāshir, in whose wake people will be gathered; and I am al-Āqib, after whom there is no prophet.”

---

## Page 10249

The names for which Allah rebuked the polytheists when they applied them to their idols also belong to this category. He said:

“They are nothing but names you and your forefathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority.”

They called them gods, thereby attributing to them the divinity that would entitle them to be worshipped. This meaning cannot be affirmed without authority—that is, proof. To say that something is an object of worship may mean that Allah has commanded its worship; this can only be established through a revealed scripture. Or it may mean that it possesses lordship and the power of creation, which would entitle it to worship; whether it possesses these attributes or not can be established through reason.

For this reason, the Exalted said:

“Say, ‘Have you considered those you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created of the earth. Or do they have a share in the heavens? Bring me a scripture predating this, or some remnant of knowledge, if you are truthful.’”

And He said in Sūrah Fātir:

“Say, ‘Have you considered those partners of yours whom you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created of the earth. Or do they have a share in the heavens? Or have We given them a scripture, so that they stand on clear evidence from it?’ Rather, the wrongdoers promise one another nothing but delusion.”

Thus, He demanded of them proof grounded in reason and direct observation, as well as proof grounded in revelation and divine law. He said:

“Show me what they have created of the earth. Or do they have a share in the heavens?”

Then He said:

“Or have We given them a scripture, so that they stand on clear evidence from it?”

Likewise, He said in the other passage:

“Show me what they have created of the earth. Or do they have a share in the heavens?”

Then He said: “Bring me a scripture

---

## Page 10250

predating this, or some remnant of knowledge.” Here, “scripture” means a revealed scripture, while “remnant” means what is transmitted from the prophets through narration and chains of transmission. This may also be recorded in books; hence it has been interpreted as both narration and writing. This is a demand for evidence from revelation that Allah has prescribed worshipping another besides Him, taking that being as an intercessor or seeking nearness to Allah through worshipping it. It also makes clear that no worship is legitimate without a command from Allah.

For this reason, the Exalted said:

“Whoever invokes another god alongside Allah, for whom he has no proof, his reckoning rests only with his Lord.”

As He said elsewhere:

“So direct your face toward the religion, inclining to truth—the natural disposition with which Allah created mankind. There is no altering Allah’s creation. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know. Turn to Him in repentance, fear Him, establish prayer, and do not be among the polytheists—those who divided their religion and became sects, each faction rejoicing in what it has. When hardship touches people, they call upon their Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then, when He lets them taste mercy from Him, some of them associate partners with their Lord, showing ingratitude for what We have given them. So enjoy yourselves; you will soon know. Or have We sent down to them an authority that speaks in support of the partners they associate with Him?”

The authority that speaks in support of this would be a revealed scripture, as He said:

“Or do you have a clear authority? Then bring your scripture, if you are truthful.”

And He said:

“Those who dispute concerning Allah’s signs without any authority having come to them have nothing in their hearts but an ambition for greatness that they will never attain.”

---

## Page 10251

And the point here is that expressions with different wordings may have the same meaning, such as julūs and quʿūd (both meaning “sitting”); these are synonyms. Others have distinct meanings, such as “heaven” and “earth.” Still others agree in one respect and differ in another, such as sārim (“a sharp sword”) and muhannad (“a sword made of Indian iron”). This is a third category: the meaning of one is neither distinct from that of the other as heaven is distinct from earth, nor identical to it as the meaning of julūs is identical to that of quʿūd.

Likewise, expressions identical in wording may have the same meaning; these are univocal terms. Or they may have distinct meanings; these are lexically equivocal terms, such as “Suhayl,” used for both the star and a man. Or their meanings may agree in one respect and differ in another. This is a third category, unlike either lexical equivocation or univocal agreement. They thus share an element of meaning in one respect and differ in meaning in another. This, however, occurs only when each expression is qualified by something indicating its particular meaning.

Such expressions are frequent in connected discourse; indeed, they constitute most of the expressions found in the connected discourse of any speaker. For expressions described as univocal—generic nouns such as “messenger,” “governor,” “judge,” “man,” “woman,” “leader,” “house,” and the like—may convey their general meaning, or they may convey a more specific meaning when made definite by a genitive construction or the definite article, as in His words:

“Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger

---

## Page 10252

as a witness over you, just as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger.”

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger.”

He says elsewhere:

“Do not treat the Messenger’s call among you like your calls to one another.”

The expression “the messenger” is identical in both passages and includes the definite article. In each passage, however, it refers to the messenger known to those being addressed in that context. Thus, when He says here:

“Just as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger.”

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger.”

the definite article identifies the messenger sent to Pharaoh: Moses, son of ʿImrān, peace be upon him.

When He says to the community of Muhammad:

“Do not treat the Messenger’s call among you like your calls to one another,”

the definite article identifies the Messenger known to those addressed by the Quran, who are commanded to obey his commands and refrain from what he forbids: the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

It is well known, by common agreement, that an expression of this kind cannot be said to be figurative in either instance. Nor can it be described as purely lexically equivocal, like al-mushtarī, which denotes both a buyer and the planet Jupiter, or Suhayl, which denotes both a star and a man.

Nor can it be described as a univocal term indicating only the shared meaning in both passages. For it is known that in one passage it refers to Muhammad and in the other to Moses, although the expression “the messenger” is identical. Rather, this expression was uttered within a context whose import is conveyed by the definite article. The same applies to all definite nouns, for nouns are of two kinds: definite and indefinite.

---

## Page 10253

And definite nouns include pronouns and demonstratives, such as “I,” “you,” and “he,” and “this” and “that”; relative pronouns, as in:

“Those who establish prayer and give zakah”;

nouns made definite by the definite article, such as “the messenger”; and proper names, such as Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, as well as the month of Ramadan.

They also include nouns made definite through their attachment to a definite noun, as in His words:

“And purify My House,”

and His words:

“Wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows,”

and:

“Allah’s she-camel and her right to drink,”

and His words:

“It has been made lawful for you on the night of fasting.”

They also include a vocative referring to a particular person, as in Joseph’s words:

“O my father, I saw eleven stars,”

and the words of the daughter of the man of Midian:

“O my father, hire him.”

The word “father” in the former passage refers to Jacob, while in the latter it refers to the man of Midian whose daughter Moses married. He was not Shuayb, as some mistakenly suppose. Rather, Muslim scholars of the early generations and the People of the Book know that he was not Shuayb, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

The point here is that these definite nouns fall into several categories, and each

---

## Page 10254

category has a single verbal form, as with “I” and “you,” or “this” and “that.” Yet in each instance it denotes a particular speaker, addressee, or person spoken of. These expressions cannot be called equivocal, like the name “Suhayl,” nor univocal, like the word “human.” Rather, they have both a shared element and a distinguishing element. In respect of the shared element, they resemble univocal terms; in respect of the distinguishing element, they resemble terms that share only their wording. They are never used without accompanying indications that identify the referent of the pronoun, the object pointed to, and so forth. Their meaning thus derives jointly from their wording and an accompanying contextual indication that identifies the referent. Everyone agrees that this is literal usage. No rational person calls it figurative, even though these expressions never convey their meaning without a contextual indication specifying the intended referent.

If one asks about the expression “I,” the answer is that it denotes the speaker in general. Yet no one has ever uttered it in the abstract, for there is no abstract, universal speaker common to many individuals. Rather, every speaker is a particular individual distinct from others. Thus, when one seeks to understand what these expressions denote and mean, one asks: Who is speaking these words? Who is being addressed by “you,” whether as subject or object, and by similar expressions?

If the one speaking is Allah, as in His words to Moses:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me,”

and similar passages, then this expression in this context is a designation for Allah Most High and can refer to no other. No created being can say:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.”

---

## Page 10255

He, glorified be He, also relates that the man who disputed with Abraham about his Lord said:

“I give life and cause death.”

He relates that Joseph’s companion said:

“I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me.”

He tells us that a mighty one among the jinn said:

“I will bring it to you before you rise from your place,”

and that the one who had knowledge of the Scripture said:

“I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you.”

Thus, in each particular context, the expression “I” denotes someone different from the one it denotes in another context, although the expression itself is identical in both. No rational person has ever called this expression equivocal or figurative, even though it conveys its meaning only with a contextual indication that makes the intended referent clear.

Section

If this is understood, he may be told:

These nouns you have mentioned—such as zahr (back), matn (back), sāq (leg), and kabid (liver)—can only be used in the language with an accompanying indication of the thing to which they are attributed. This makes the intended meaning clear.

Thus, saying “the zahr and matn of a road” is not like saying “the zahr and matn of a person,” nor even “the zahr and matn of a horse,” nor “the zahr of a mountain.”

---

## Page 10256

Likewise, the expression “the kabid (centre) of the sky” is not like “the kabid (middle) of a bow,” and neither is like “the kabid (liver) of a human being.”

Similarly, the word “sword” in the Prophet’s statement, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Indeed, Khālid is a sword that Allah has drawn against the polytheists,”

is not like the word “sword” in his statement:

“If anyone comes to you while you are united under one man, seeking to divide your community, strike his neck with the sword, whoever he may be.”

In each instance, the word “sword” is accompanied by something that clarifies its meaning.

Admittedly, one might say: “The meanings of ‘messenger’ in its two uses resemble each other more closely than do those of ‘kabid’ or ‘sword’ in their respective uses.”

The reply is that this distinguishing element is indicated by the particular wording, as in His words:

“Indeed, the frailest of houses is the spider’s house,”

and His words:

“And purify My House for those who circle it,”

and His words:

“Do not enter the Prophet’s houses,”

and the Prophet’s statement, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Whoever builds a mosque for Allah, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise.”

It is well known that the spider’s house is not identical in its actual nature to His House, the Prophet’s house, peace and blessings be upon him, or a house in Paradise. Yet the word “house” is indisputably used literally in every instance, since it is the possessive construction that specifies the meaning. In “the spider’s house” and “the Prophet’s house,” it indicates that the house’s occupant lives there. “Allah’s House,” however, does not indicate that Allah dwells there. Rather, each attribution is understood according to what is being attributed. His House is the one He has designated for remembering Him, worshipping Him, and calling upon Him. This is like knowing Him in the heart and mentioning Him with the tongue.

Every existing thing has an existence in external reality, in knowledge, in speech, and in writing. The name “Allah” is used to refer to each of these four in the speech of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and in Allah’s speech.

the reference is to Allah Himself. And when He says:

and when He says:

what is in the hearts of believers is faith in Allah, knowledge of Him, and love for Him. This may be expressed as “the highest likeness” or “the mental representation.” One also says, “You are in my heart,” as in the verse:

## Page 10258

“Allah Most High says: ‘I am with My servant as long as he remembers Me and his lips move in remembrance of Me.’”

By “in remembrance of Me,” He meant that his lips move in uttering His name, not His very Essence. Nor is what is in the heart here His Essence. In the Sahīh, it is related from Anas:

“The inscription on the Prophet’s ring, peace and blessings be upon him, consisted of three lines: ‘Allah’ on one line, ‘Messenger’ on one line, and ‘Muhammad’ on one line.”

It is well known that by the word “Allah” he meant the inscription engraved on the ring, corresponding to the spoken word that signifies the meaning known to the heart, which in turn corresponds to what actually exists. The same applies to the expression “His house.”

We have said: Mosques are the houses of Allah. Within them is what has been established for hearts and tongues: knowledge of Him, faith in Him, remembrance of Him, supplication to Him, and the lights He places in the hearts of believers. Thus, He says:

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth.”

Then He says:

continuing to His words:

“In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised.”

He thus made clear that this light is in these hearts and these houses, as stated in the report:

“The mosques shine for the inhabitants of the heavens just as the stars shine for the inhabitants of the earth.”

Since this is so, the statement of one who says, “If these names were used in their literal sense

---

## Page 10259

in the cases he mentioned, the term would be equivocal,” is answered as follows:

“What do you mean by an equivocal term? Do you mean lexical equivocity, as discussed in your book?” There, in your classification of terms, you said:

“A name is either one or multiple. If it is one, its concept can be classified in several ways.

“The first division: either its concept can be shared or it cannot. If the former, it is talabī.”

He completed this discussion with statements, some true and others false, in which he followed the logicians. He then said:

“If, however, its concept cannot be shared by many, it is a particular.”

He stated that this applies specifically to the proper name, and classified it according to the grammarians’ classification. He then said:

“If the name is one but its referents differ, either it was originally assigned to all of them in a literal sense, or it is used metaphorically for some of them. In the former case, it is equivocal, whether the referents are mutually distinct—as with al-jawn, meaning both blackness and whiteness—or not mutually distinct, as when we apply the name al-Aswad to someone both as a proper name and as a descriptive term derived from blackness. In the latter case, it is figurative.”

If this is what you mean, then an equivocal term is a single name whose referents differ and which was originally assigned to all of them in a literal sense. The classification here is that the referent is one, and the name is universal or particular, as you stated.

You are then answered:

“We do not concede that, if these names are literal in the cases mentioned, the term must be equivocal. For this classification only

---

## Page 10260

holds for a single term whose meaning is either one or multiple. We do not concede that the point in dispute falls within what you have described. This classification is valid only when the expression is the same in both instances, whereas that is not the case here. The expressions at issue are ‘the back of the road,’ ‘its ridge,’ ‘the wing of a journey,’ and the like. Each such expression has only one meaning, not several different meanings. Wherever it occurs, its meaning is one, as with other names.

If you say, ‘But the words “back,” “ridge,” and “wing” have meanings other than these,’ the reply is:

‘The expression “the back of the road” or “its wing” is not the expression “the back of a human being,” “the wing of a bird,” or “the wings of the angels.” The words “the back” and “the road” are made definite by the definite article, which indicates a known referent denoted by the expression—the human back, for example. This is not like the expression “the back of the road”; rather, the two expressions differ.’

Thus one cannot say, ‘The expression occurs in a single context.’ More telling still, it is unanimously agreed that the word ‘back’ is used literally of all animals. Nevertheless, for many people, only the human back may immediately come to mind. They do not think of the back of a dog, a fox, a wolf, a weasel, an ant, or a louse. This is because the human back is what they picture and frequently refer to in their ordinary speech. When used with the definite article, the word refers to the familiar back.

---

## Page 10261

For this reason, jurists interpret oaths according to what the person addressed understands in his own language, even if the expression is also used literally of other things. Thus, if someone swears not to eat heads, this may mean the heads of livestock, the heads of sheep and goats, or the kinds of heads customarily eaten. Likewise, the word “eggs” means the eggs familiar to them. The heads of ants, fleas, and the like do not fall within the expression, nor do fish eggs fall within the oath, even though “ants’ eggs” and “fish eggs” are literal expressions when used in these possessive constructions.

Similarly, if someone says, “I have sold it to you for ten dirhams or dinars,” the unqualified wording refers to what people understand that expression to denote in such a transaction in that locality. Indeed, even within a single locality, “dinar” may mean pure gold when pricing certain goods, debased gold when pricing others, and a particular sum of dirhams when pricing still others. By the unanimous agreement of the jurists, an unqualified contract is therefore interpreted according to the shared understanding of buyer and seller, even though the expression is used in other senses only with something that clarifies its meaning.

How much more so, then, when the expressions themselves differ, as with “the back of a human being” and “the back of the road”; “the head of a human being,” “the head of a lane,” “the head of wealth” (capital), or “the head of a spring” (its source)? Or when one expression is qualified by the definite article, as in “the back,” while the other is qualified by a possessive construction? The definite article indicates what is familiar to the person addressed, whereas the possessive construction specifies the referent through its relation to the noun that follows. Thus, an expression made definite by the definite article is not the same as one made definite by a possessive construction, either in wording or in meaning.

---

## Page 10262

The definite article may be used in both instances, yet the meaning may still differ, as with the expression “the messenger.” This is because the addressee’s knowledge forms part of what determines the meaning, while the expression is literal in both instances. How much more, then, when definiteness through a possessive construction is compared with definiteness through the definite article?

It is thus clear that the expression denoting a human being’s back is not the same expression as that denoting the back of a road. Accordingly, the difference in meaning between the two expressions does not entail homonymy, because homonymy does not occur in a single expression whose meaning differs; and that is not the case here.

If it is objected, “This would entail that there are no homonymous expressions in the language, since a homonymous expression is used only alongside something that clarifies which of its two meanings is intended,” the reply is: Either this conclusion necessarily follows or it does not. If it does not, the objection falls away. If it does, we accept the position of those who deny homonymy, provided that this is indeed the case, just as one accepts the position of those who deny figurative usage.

If it is asked, “How can you deny the existence of homonymy when evidence has established it?” the reply is: We do not concede that evidence has established its existence in the manner they claim. The author of the book, Abū al-Hasan al-Āmidī, himself acknowledges the weakness of the arguments advanced by those who affirm it. He has offered an argument of his own that is weaker still than those advanced by others. For, in his discussion of these questions, he says:

---

## Page 10263

“The First Question”: People have differed over whether homonymous expressions exist in the language. Some affirm their existence, while others deny it.

He says:

“The preferred position is that their occurrence is possible. As for rational discourse, nothing precludes a single person from assigning an expression more than one meaning. Nor is it impossible for one tribe to assign a name to one meaning and another tribe to assign it to a different meaning, neither knowing what the other has assigned it to. Both usages then become widespread, while their origin remains obscure.”

He says: “This is the more likely explanation.”

He says:

“As for establishing their actual occurrence, the argument is that, if homonymous expressions did not occur in the language, most things named would lack names denoting them, despite the need for such names. This is because effects are infinite, whereas names are finite, since they are necessarily composed of a finite set of letters. Such a lack is impossible.”

He says:

“This argument is unsound. Although names are composed of a finite set of letters, it does not follow that the names themselves are finite unless the combinations produced by repeated compounding are also finite. Nor do we concede that mutually opposed and distinct things named—those in relation to which an expression would be homonymous—are infinite.

“Even if they are infinite, assigning names to their referents requires each referent to be individually intended in the act of naming, which is impossible with an infinite number of things. Even if we concede that this is not impossible, it still does not follow that such names have actually been assigned. Thus, many meanings arise for which the Arabs have assigned no expressions to denote them, whether through homonymy or preference, such as kinds of smells and many qualities.”

---

## Page 10264

He says:

“Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī said: ‘Speakers of the language apply the term qur’ to both menstruation and purity, which are opposites. This demonstrates that homonymous expressions occur in the language.’”

He says:

“One may object: Those who originally assigned the term have not been reported as declaring it homonymous. All that is established is that a single term has multiple referents. Perhaps it was applied to both on account of a single meaning common to them, rather than their differing realities. Alternatively, it may be literal in one case and figurative in the other, even though we do not know which usage is literal and which is figurative. These explanations are preferable: the first avoids both figurative usage and homonymy, while the second rests on the principle that figurative usage is preferable to homonymy, as will be explained in its proper place.”

He says:

Were its application figurative in either case, it could validly be denied, since this is a sign of figurative usage; yet such denial is impossible. Accordingly, the term ‘existence’ must denote either the Lord’s essence or a reality additional to His essence.

“If the former, it is evident that the Lord’s essence is intrinsically different from all other, temporally originated beings. Otherwise, it and whatever shared its meaning would necessarily share necessary existence, since they would be equal in what is meant by ‘essence’; but this is impossible. If, however, the term ‘existence’ denotes an attribute additional to the essence of the Lord—exalted is He—

---

## Page 10265

then either the meaning of this attribute is the same as what the term ‘existence’ means in temporally originated beings, or it is different. The former entails that what ‘existence’ denotes is intrinsically necessary in reality, since the Creator’s existence is intrinsically necessary; or else that the Lord’s existence is contingent, since the existence of everything other than Allah is contingent. This is impossible. If the latter is the case, homonymy necessarily follows, which is what was to be proved.”

This, then, is his argument, and it is extremely weak, for it rests on two premises: that the term ‘existence’ applies literally to both the necessary and the contingent, and that this entails homonymy. The second premise is unquestionably false. The first is disputed, contrary to his claim of consensus.

Some have said:

“Every name used to designate a created being can be applied to the Creator only figuratively—even the word ‘thing.’”

This is the position of Jahm and those among the Bātiniyyah (esotericists) who agree with him. These people do not call Him ‘existent’ or ‘a thing,’ nor do they apply any other names to Him.

Others have taken the opposite position, saying:

“Rather, every name applied to the Lord is literal when applied to Him and figurative when applied to anyone else.”

This is the position of Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Nāshī of the Muʿtazilah.

---

## Page 10266

The majority held that the term applies literally to both. Most of them, however, considered it univocal in the broad sense—or graded in its application, if graded terms are treated as a separate category. This differs from strict univocity, in which a term’s meanings are identical across its applications. Only a small handful of later thinkers considered it homonymous; this view is not known to have been held by any major school or prominent speculative thinkers.
