Whoever attributes it to al-Ashʿarī, as al-Rāzī did, is mistaken.

For his position, and that of most of his followers, is that ‘existence’ is a general term divided into eternal and temporally originated existence. His position, however, is that the existence of each thing is identical with its quiddity. This is the position of the vast majority of rational thinkers, Muslims and others alike. Some supposed that this necessarily makes the term homonymous, as al-Āmidī argued. This is mistaken, as we have explained at length elsewhere, and as will become clear through our discussion of his argument.

As for his statement:

“The term ‘existence’ must denote either the essence or an attribute additional to the essence.”

He should be asked: Do you mean the general term ‘existence,’ which is divided into necessary and contingent existence, or existence in a particular sense, as when one says ‘the existence of the necessary’ and ‘the existence of the contingent’? For it is well known that names used to designate the Lord and others—indeed, any

---

## Page 10267

two entities—are sometimes understood in an unrestricted, general sense encompassing both kinds, and sometimes as restricted to a particular entity. When terms such as ‘living,’ ‘knowing,’ ‘powerful,’ ‘hearing,’ ‘seeing,’ ‘existent,’ ‘thing,’ and ‘essence’ are used generally, they encompass the necessary existent. But when it is said:

“And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die,”

“Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence,”

“And He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise,”

or similar expressions referring specifically to the Lord, these do not encompass the creature. Likewise, when it is said:

“He brings the living out of the dead,”

the Creator is not included in the designation ‘the living’ here.

Similarly, terms such as knowledge, power, speech, rising, and descent are sometimes used in an unrestricted, general sense. At other times, one speaks of Allah’s knowledge, power, speech, descent, and rising. These are specific to the Creator; the creature has no share in them. Likewise, when one speaks of the creature’s knowledge, power, speech, descent, and rising, these are specific to the creature; the Creator has no share in them. Thus, a possessive construction or definite designation specifies and distinguishes the referent, eliminating the shared application between Creator and creature.

Likewise, when the term ‘existence’ is used without qualification, and when one speaks of ‘the existence of the necessary’ and ‘the existence of the contingent,’ these are three meanings.

When one speaks of the servant’s existence, essence, quiddity, and reality, these expressions refer specifically to him, denoting his own particular essence, characterized by its attributes.

---

## Page 10268

Likewise, when one speaks of the Lord’s existence, His self, His essence, His quiddity, and His reality, these expressions denote what is specific to the Lord: His very self, characterized by His attributes.

As for his statement, “The term ‘existence’ denotes either the Lord’s essence or an additional attribute,” he is told: If you mean the unrestricted, general term ‘existence,’ which encompasses both the necessary and the contingent, it denotes neither what is specific to the necessary nor what is specific to the contingent. Rather, it denotes the shared universal. Yet the shared universal is shared and universal only in the mind and in language; nothing that exists in external reality is itself a universal.

This is like using the terms ‘essence’ and ‘self’ in a sense encompassing both the necessary and the contingent: they denote only the general, universal meaning, not what is specific to either one. Examples include saying, “Existence is divided into necessary and contingent,” or “Essence is divided into necessary and contingent,” and similar expressions.

If, however, ‘existence’ is intended to encompass both together—as when one says, “All existence, both necessary and contingent,” or “Necessary and contingent existence”—then it denotes what is specific to each, just as when one says, “The existence of the necessary and the existence of the contingent.”

In sum, a term may denote only what is shared, as with existence considered as divisible into categories, or only what is distinctive, as in the expressions ‘the existence of the necessary’ and ‘the existence of the contingent’

---

## Page 10269

or both, as when you say, “All existence, both necessary and contingent,” or “Necessary and contingent existence.” In every case, equivocation does not necessarily follow.

As for his statement, “If it denotes the Lord’s essence, then His essence differs from all other existent things,” the response is: The unrestricted term ‘existence,’ considered as divisible into categories, does not denote what is specific to the Lord. But when ‘existence’ is used specifically for the Lord’s existence, or inclusively, as when we say, “Necessary and contingent existence,” and similar expressions, it does denote what is specific to the Lord’s essence, even though His essence differs from that of others. Likewise, the expressions ‘the Lord’s essence’ and ‘the servant’s essence’ denote what is specific to the Lord and to the servant, even though the reality of the one differs from that of the other. Similarly, the term ‘existence’ denotes both, despite the difference between the realities of the two existent beings.

If it is said, “If the reality of this existence differs from the reality of that existence, then the term is equivocal,” the response is:

This is a mistake from which the error of this man and others like him has arisen. All differing realities share general names that encompass them through univocal and graded predication. For example, the term ‘color’ encompasses blackness, whiteness, and redness, despite the differences between the realities of these colors. Likewise, the terms ‘attribute,’ ‘accident,’ and ‘meaning’ encompass knowledge, power, life, taste, color, and smell, despite the differences between the realities of colors.

---

## Page 10270

Likewise, the term ‘animal’ encompasses both humans and beasts, despite the difference between their realities. This applies all the more to the term ‘existence’. These differing realities may share a general meaning that encompasses them, with the term denoting that meaning, as with the term ‘color’. Then, when qualified, it encompasses what is specific to each, as when one says, ‘the color of a black thing’ and ‘the color of a white thing’, or ‘the Lord’s existence’ and ‘the servant’s existence’.

If one uses a general term encompassing its individual instances, such as ‘color’, ‘colors’, ‘animal’, ‘accident’, or ‘existence’, it encompasses everything falling within its scope, even if these have differing realities. This is because the term encompasses them, just like other general terms, even though their individual instances differ in a respect other than that denoted by the general term.

Furthermore, regarding his statement, ‘If what the term “existence” denotes is an attribute, then, if the concept is the same for the necessary and the contingent, it follows that the necessary is contingent and the contingent necessary; otherwise, equivocation follows,’ the response is:

Do you mean that the term denotes unrestricted existence, or existence qualified by attribution, as when one says, ‘the existence of the necessary’ and ‘the existence of the contingent’? If you mean the former, then the concept is one and the same, but this does not entail that the two instances are alike. Even if the meaning of existence in the mind is alike in both cases, it does not follow that its instances in external reality are alike.

---

## Page 10271

and it need only apply to both and encompass them, like other univocal terms that admit differences of degree. Thus, “blackness” applies to the blackness of pitch and ink, although the two are not alike. Likewise, “white,” “red,” and similar terms encompass both perfect and imperfect instances. The term “living” likewise encompasses the life of angels, the inhabitants of Paradise, flies, and mosquitoes, although their lives are not alike. How, then, could the Lord’s existence, knowledge, or power be considered like the creature’s existence, knowledge, or power merely because they fall under the unrestricted terms “existence,” “knowledge,” or “power”?

If he says, “Rather, I mean qualified existence, as when we say ‘the existence of the necessary’ and ‘the existence of the contingent,’” the reply is:

Here the concepts differ, because each has a distinct expression qualifying “existence,” namely, the attribution. This qualifying attribution precludes their being alike, but it does not entail equivocation. For the difference here arises in the very term “existence”—rather, in the attribution added to the term, and in attribution or definiteness, as when we say “the Lord’s existence” or “necessary existence,” and “the creature’s existence” or “contingent existence,” and the like.

Thus, the argument he uses to establish equivocation in terms applied to both the Lord and the servant would entail equivocation in all other general terms. It is of the same kind as the argument that

---

## Page 10272

he used to argue for figurative usage when he said:

“If the word is used literally in both instances, equivocation necessarily follows.”

This is mistaken. For what indicates the specific meaning in one instance is not what indicates the specific meaning in the other; rather, it is what is added to the word.

Thus, saying “the Lord’s existence” and “the servant’s existence” is comparable to saying “a man’s back” and “a horse’s back,” just as one speaks of a man’s back and the surface of a road. In all these instances, what indicates the distinction between one and another is the wording specific to each instance, not merely the shared word. Rather, the shared wording indicates what is shared, and the distinctive wording indicates what is distinctive. This entails that the two backs have an aspect in common and an aspect in which they differ. Likewise, the two instances of existence have an aspect in common and an aspect in which they differ. This is what is meant by commonality and distinction.

Some people, however, imagine that what the two have in common exists in external reality as something shared between them. This is mistaken. Rather, each is distinct in external reality, while the mind abstracts from them a common universal element. Thus, one says, “They share in existence, animal nature, and human nature.” As Allah Most High says:

“Since you did wrong, it will not benefit you today that you share in the punishment.”

And He says:

“Indeed, on that Day they will share in the punishment.”

Thus, the punishment that befalls one corresponds to that which befalls the other and is of the same kind: they share in the kind of punishment. There is no single, particular thing in external reality that they both share. Rather, they share in the particular punishment in the sense that each has a portion of it, like those who share ownership of a property and the like.

---

## Page 10273

The sixth response:

One may contest the second premise, namely his statement:

“If the term were equivocal, one meaning rather than another would not come first to mind when these words are used without qualification, since they necessarily signify their literal meanings equally. Yet there is no doubt that what first comes to mind when ‘lion’ is used without qualification is the beast of prey, and when ‘donkey’ is used without qualification, it is the animal. The same is necessarily true in similar cases.”

The reply is:

When ‘lion’ and ‘donkey’ are used with the definite article al-, they refer to what is known to the speaker or the addressee. If the identified referent is the animal, the word refers to it. This is indeed the familiar referent for most people most of the time. But it does not follow that, when the definite form directs the reference to a dullard or a brave man, the usage cannot also be literal. An example is Abū Bakr’s statement:

“No, by Allah! He would not single out one of Allah’s lions, who fights for Allah and His Messenger, and give you his spoils.”

Likewise, someone may point to a person and say, “This lion,” or to a dullard and say, “This donkey.” Here, definiteness identifies the referent and rules out any other intended meaning. Similarly, when words such as ‘heads,’ ‘eggs,’ and ‘houses’ are used without qualification, ‘heads’ and ‘eggs’ refer to those customarily eaten, while ‘houses’ refers to people’s dwellings. Yet when one says ‘a spider’s house,’ ‘ants’ eggs,’ or ‘locusts’ heads,’ these usages are also literal, by common agreement.

The seventh response:

One may say: You have made the criterion of literal usage that its meaning should come first to mind when the word is used without qualification. Thus, on the listener’s side, you have taken into account what first comes to his mind;

---

## Page 10274

and, on the speaker’s side, his use of the expression without qualification. Yet there is no fixed criterion for this: in each instance, what first comes to the listener’s mind is whatever the evidence in that context indicates. If someone speaks of “the back of the road” or “its spine,” the back of an animal never comes to the listener’s mind; indeed, he considers it impossible that this could be intended.

The eighth response:

Your phrase, “from the unqualified use of the entire expression,” is ambiguous. If you mean that the expression is free of all qualifications, this never occurs.

For the inquiry concerns nouns as they occur in the speech of any speaker: Allah, His angels, His prophets, the jinn, and all other human beings and nations. An expression occurs only in conjunction with other words, within either a nominal or a verbal sentence. It necessarily comes from a speaker, and it can serve as evidence only when that speaker’s customary use of such an expression is known. Thus, we have a qualified expression conjoined with other words, a speaker whose customary usage is known, and a listener who knows the speaker’s customary use of that expression. These qualifications are indispensable to speech whose meaning can be understood; the expression cannot, therefore, be free of them. If he means that it is free of one qualification but not another, what he has said does not establish that.

It is thus clear that his statement comes down to what is understood when the expression is used without qualification.

The ninth response:

One may say to him: Mention whatever qualification you wish, and distinguish between a qualifier and what it qualifies. Whatever he mentions will be open to refutation. I shall show you, from the definitions you cite to distinguish literal from figurative usage, that what you classify as literal you also classify as figurative, and what

---

## Page 10275

you classify as figurative you also classify as literal, and that anyone who distinguishes between the two on the basis of unqualified and qualified usage speaks like someone who has no clear conception of what he is saying, much less the ability to express it. Expression depends upon conception; whoever has no conception of what he is saying says nothing that is not mistaken.

Section

As for his second argument, he says:

“How can that be, when people throughout the ages have continually transmitted, in their speech and writings, from those who established linguistic conventions, the designation of this as literal and that as figurative?”

The response is that this is known with certainty to be false. No one has ever transmitted from those who established linguistic conventions that they said, “This is literal and that is figurative.” It is self-evident that they never did this, nor did anyone who transmitted their language report it from them. Indeed, no one has even reported this from the Companions who explained the Quran, clarified its meanings, and explained what it indicates in each passage. None of them said, “This expression is literal and that is figurative,” or anything resembling it: neither Ibn Mas'ūd and his companions, nor Ibn 'Abbās and his companions, nor Zayd ibn Thābit and his companions, nor those who came after them; neither Mujāhid, Sa'īd ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhāk, Tāwūs, al-Suddī, Qatādah, nor anyone else among them; nor any of the imams of jurisprudence, such as the imams

---

## Page 10276

of the four schools and others, nor al-Thawrī, al-Awzā'ī, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, or anyone else. The term does occur in the words of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, but with a different meaning, just as it occurs in the words of Abū 'Ubaydah Ma'mar ibn al-Muthannā with a different meaning. Nor is the division of speech into literal and figurative found in the writings of the leading authorities on grammar and language, such as Abū 'Amr ibn al-'Alā', Abū 'Amr al-Shaybānī, Abū Zayd, al-Asma'ī, al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, al-Kisā'ī, and al-Farrā'. None of them knew of this distinction as something received from the Arabs.

Anyone who investigates this matter knows it with certainty, just as it is known with certainty that the Arabs did not speak using the terminology of the grammarians, who classified one expression as a subject, another as an object, and a third as a verbal noun, and classified some words as declinable and others as indeclinable. This is known to be the grammarians’ terminology, but it is terminology whose meaning is sound, unlike the terminology adopted by those who use the terms “literal” and “figurative.”

The latter is a later convention, and its meaning is unsound in this respect: there is no actual distinction between the two that would warrant assigning one term to this and another to that. Rather, whatever meaning they assign exclusively to the term “literal” is also found in what they call figurative, and whatever meaning they assign exclusively to the term “figurative” is also found in what they call literal. They cannot provide anything that distinguishes the two categories.

Nor are they being required to supply what is said to constitute a real definition, composed of genus

---

## Page 10277

and differentia; for even if this were true, they would not be required to provide it—how much less so when it is false? Rather, what is required is a distinction between what the two terms denote. This is what a nominal definition amounts to, just as one distinguishes between what is denoted by “declinable noun,” “indeclinable noun,” “subject,” and “object,” and between the things denoted by all other terms. They are therefore required to provide a means of distinguishing what they call literal from what they call figurative. Yet no such distinction actually exists, for there are not, in reality, two distinct categories such that one may be called literal and the other figurative.

This is a rational inquiry, distinct from the terminological inquiry, for they acknowledge that the dispute over this question is terminological. They have supposed that this terminology and distinction were transmitted from the Arabs, and in this they are mistaken. Equally mistaken is anyone who supposes that this terminology and distinction occur in the words of the Companions, the Successors, and the leading scholars; that al-Shāfi‘ī or another scholar mentioned them; or that any of these authorities spoke in these terms. This error resembles that of someone brought up with terminology devised by a particular group, who then supposes that the earlier scholars used the same terminology.

Still more plainly mistaken is anyone who supposes that the Arabs themselves made this classification, or that it was received from them through direct transmission, as is found in the writings of some authors on the principles of jurisprudence. Such a claim occurs in the writings of a number of authors, including Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī, al-Qādī Abū al-Tayyib, al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā, and others.

---

## Page 10278

More astonishing still is the claim that this has been transmitted on a mass scale from the original coiners of the language and from successive generations, who have continually passed down in their statements and writings, on the authority of those original coiners, the designation of one usage as literal and another as figurative. Yet neither the claimant nor anyone else can produce even a single report establishing this, let alone the mass transmission he alleges.

Section

As for the argument he mentioned of those who deny figurative usage, he said:

“If it is objected: ‘Were there a figurative expression in the Arabic language, its meaning would either be delimited by a contextual indication or not. In the first case, the expression, together with the indication, would admit of no other meaning; thus, together with that indication, it would be literal in that meaning. In the second case, it would likewise be literal, since a literal expression means nothing other than one that conveys its meaning independently, without a contextual indication.’”

He then said:

“We reply: Our answer to the first case is that, unless a figurative usage is widely familiar, it conveys its meaning only through a contextual indication. This is all that is meant by figurative usage, and the dispute over this is terminological. Moreover, are not figurativeness and literalness attributes of expressions rather than of nonverbal contextual indications? Literalness therefore cannot be an attribute of the combination.”

The response is:

He has conceded that the dispute is terminological. We therefore say: If the dispute is terminological, and this distinction is a newly introduced convention which neither the Arabs nor any other nation employed, nor the Companions, the Successors, or the early generations, then speaking with the established expressions which they used, and in which the Quran was revealed, would be preferable to speaking using terminology

---

## Page 10279

that is newly introduced, even if it involved no harm. If it entails harmful consequences, it ought to be abandoned even if the distinction were intelligible. How much more so when the distinction is unintelligible, entails religious harms, and introduces an innovation into the language! It is therefore invalid rationally, religiously, and linguistically. As for reason, the two cannot be distinguished on rational grounds. As for religion, it entails harms that the Sharia requires us to eliminate. As for language, changing established linguistic conventions brings no overriding benefit; rather, it entails harm.

If it is asked, “What are these harms?” the answer is:

Among these harms is that the term “figurative,” as opposed to “literal”—whether considered an attribute of expressions or of usage—conveys and suggests that figurative usage is inferior to literal usage, especially since one of the signs of figurative usage is that it can validly be negated. Thus, when someone says, “Allah Most High is neither Merciful nor Most Merciful in a literal sense, but only figuratively”—among other such statements they make about many of His names and attributes—and says that “There is no god except Allah” is figurative rather than literal, as this al-Āmidī maintained in stating that a general expression whose scope has been restricted is figurative, and then presented the following objection on behalf of his opponent:

“If it is objected: ‘If someone were to say, “There is no god,” as a complete, unqualified statement, it would be disbelief. But if it were accompanied by the exception, namely, “except Allah,” it would be faith. Likewise, if a man said to his wife, “You are divorced,” she would be divorced with immediate effect. But if this were accompanied by a condition, namely, “if you enter the house,” it would be

---

## Page 10280

conditional, even though the exception and the condition each have meaning. Were it not for signification and linguistic convention, this would not be so.’

We reply: ‘We do not concede any change in linguistic convention. At most, a contextual indicator diverts the expression from what it would signify when unqualified to another meaning.’”

Thus, if “There is no god except Allah” falls within the matter under dispute, he has passed judgment on it: he claims that every general expression whose scope is restricted, even by an exception, is figurative. Accordingly, “There is no god except Allah” would, in his view, be figurative. It is well known that this statement is among the gravest enormities in the Sharia. Its proponent is more deserving of being called upon to repent—if he repents, so be it; otherwise, he is to be executed—than of being counted among Muslim scholars.

Moreover, the person making this claim misrepresents language, the Sharia, and reason. The Arabs did not use the expression “There is no god” on its own, nor did they deny the Creator such that they would say, “There is no god.” Rather, they set up other gods alongside Allah. Allah Most High says:

“Do you truly testify that there are other gods besides Allah? Say, ‘I do not so testify.’”

This is why they said:

“Has he made the gods into one God? This is truly an astonishing thing!”

The entire Quran affirms that Allah alone is worthy of worship and censures them for associating partners with Him. Mass-transmitted reports establish that the first thing he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—called people to was the testimony that there is no god except Allah. He said:

“I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.”

The polytheists did not dispute with him concerning

---

## Page 10281

affirmation, but rather concerning negation. The Messenger and the polytheists agreed in affirming Allah’s divinity. The Messenger denied the divinity of anything besides Allah, whereas they affirmed it. No one, whether Muslim or polytheist, uttered this statement except to affirm Allah’s divinity and deny the divinity of anything besides Him. The polytheists, however, affirmed the divinity of others alongside Him. As for gods without qualification in this sense, this was not something they believed in such that they would give expression to it. How, then, can anyone say that this is the meaning for which they originally coined this expression in their language?

As for the assertion:

“We do not concede any change in signification. At most, a contextual indicator diverts the expression from what it would signify when unqualified to another meaning.”

The reply is: This is a fallacy. When qualified, the expression is not unrestricted. It does not entail universal negation when it is unrestricted and unqualified. With qualification, however, the statement is: “There is no god except Allah.” As for the expression without qualification, how can it be said that it has been diverted from what it would have entailed had it been unrestricted? Had it been unrestricted, it would have entailed universal negation. Qualification therefore removes the unrestrictedness that would entail this. This is what a change in signification means: if the expression had a particular signification when unrestricted, that signification would cease, and it would acquire another when qualified and accompanied by an exception.

According to the majority, who affirm general applicability, the exception excludes from the expression something that would otherwise have fallen within its scope. According to those who suspend judgment, it excludes something that could otherwise have fallen within its scope. On either view, the expression does not exclude something that has already fallen within its scope, but rather something that would have fallen within it but for the exception. The exception

---

## Page 10282

prevents that entailment. With the exception, therefore, the expression no longer entails negating the excepted term at all, just as it no longer carries that entailment. His statement, “Diverting it from what it entails by virtue of being unrestricted,” is unsound. For if it were unrestricted in its entailment, there would be no exception and nothing would be diverted. If, however, it is not unrestricted but qualified by an exception, there is no unrestrictedness carrying such an entailment, no expression entailing the negation of the excepted term, and no excepted term that is negated.

Another harmful consequence of this is that most of the Quran is classified as figurative. Some have even written works on figurative usages in the Quranic readings, and they frequently describe Quranic verses as figurative. This conveys false meanings and creates misleading impressions. That is so even if the meanings they mention are correct. How much worse, then, when most of these people classify as figurative what is not figurative, deny the established meanings that Allah has affirmed, and deviate from the truth concerning Allah’s names and signs—as is found among the heretical proponents of religious innovation who make extensive use of figurative interpretation.

As for his statement:

“How can that be, when the figurative and the literal are attributes of expressions, not of contextual indicators relating to meaning?”

The reply is:

First, that is not how you yourselves proceed. Rather, you frequently use ‘literal’ and ‘figurative’ as designations for meanings, saying, “The literal meaning of this expression is such-and-such, and its figurative meaning is such-and-such.” You also say, “The literal meaning of this expression.” You thus treat it as a property of expressions at one time, and of

---

## Page 10283

meanings at another. You may also treat it as a property of usage, saying: “Using this expression in this sense is literal, whereas using it in that sense is figurative.”

It may then be said: These people have no consistent criterion. Some regard using an expression for part of its meaning as literal; others regard it as figurative; and still others regard it as both literal and figurative, as he has mentioned in discussing generality and a command intended to convey recommendation. This demonstrates the inconsistency of this principle.

It may further be said: Granted that this is a property of expressions, it is nevertheless a property of an expression as actually used to convey its intended meaning. Your statement, “It is an attribute of expressions, not of contextual indicators relating to meaning, so being literal cannot be an attribute of the combination,” is therefore false for several reasons.

First, an expression has never conveyed meaning without contextual indicators relating to meaning: the speaker is rational, habitually uses that expression in that sense, and is speaking in accordance with his customary usage, while the listener knows this. All these are contextual indicators relating to meaning, apprehended through reason, and the expression conveys meaning only in conjunction with them. The claim that an expression conveys meaning while stripped of all rational contextual indicators is therefore mistaken.

Second, it may be said: You have not distinguished between contextual indicators relating to meaning and verbal contextual indicators; for

---

## Page 10284

the governing expression restricted by an exception, a condition, a qualifying description, or an appositive is accompanied only by verbal contextual indicators; yet you have classified it as figurative. Likewise, consider the Prophet’s statement, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Indeed, Khālid is a sword Allah has drawn against the polytheists.”

And Abū Bakr’s statement, may Allah be pleased with him:

“He would not move against one of Allah’s lions who fights for Allah and His Messenger.”

These and similar examples, including those you cited—“the back of the road” and “its spine”—contain verbal contextual indicators through which the meaning is understood; yet you regard this as figurative.

Third, we may say: Give us a criterion distinguishing the contextual indicators that make an expression literal from those that make it figurative. This is impossible: you have no way of doing so, because the distinction has no basis in reality.

Fourth, it may be said: Granted that it requires a contextual indicator relating to meaning. Suppose you were told that “literal” designates the expression itself, with the requirement that it be accompanied by something clarifying its meaning, whether the contextual indicator is verbal or relates to meaning, and that in both cases the term “literal” designates the expression in relation to what accompanies it: you would have nothing with which to refute this.

Fifth, if someone said to you, “I shall use the term ‘literal’ to designate the expression and whatever accompanies it, without qualification,” your only answer would be to say, “I use it to designate the expression together with its verbal contextual indicator, but not a contextual indicator relating to meaning.” Even if this conception were sound, you would have done no more than counter one arbitrary stipulation with another, and your arbitrary stipulation has no greater claim to acceptance

---

## Page 10285

so how can you make that a substantive argument for invalidating your opponent’s position?

This is clarified by the sixth point: Your claim, “How could that be, when ‘figurative’ and ‘literal’ are attributes of expressions, not of contextual indicators relating to meaning, so that ‘literal’ cannot be an attribute of the combination?” merely restates the terminology you have devised. If your opponent replies, “Rather, ‘literal’ designates the whole that conveys meaning—the expression together with the contextual indicator relating to meaning,” he has countered your terminology with his own. His terminology is better than yours, since he calls all the forms of expression Allah has taught His servants literal, whereas you classify much or most of them as figurative.

If you say, “Then this dispute is merely verbal,” you will be told: That is your first answer—your statement that the dispute over this is merely verbal.

The statement, “I have another answer beyond this”—namely, your claim, “How could that be, when ‘figurative’ and ‘literal’ are attributes of expressions, not of contextual indicators relating to meaning, so that ‘literal’ cannot be an attribute of the combination?”—implies that you have offered a second answer distinct from the first. Yet it merely restates what that terminology means: we have agreed to call the expression ‘literal,’ excluding the contextual indicators relating to meaning.

It is therefore clear that you have nothing beyond your acknowledgment that the dispute is merely verbal. Thus, even if this terminology were sound, those who deny figurative usage and call all speech literal, provided that it makes the intended meaning clear, would not have been any worse

---

## Page 10286

off than those who call some of the finest, most beautiful, and most fully expressive speech figurative, treating it as derivative rather than foundational in language, as a later assignment of meaning that altered an earlier one, and as dependent on other usage rather than something other usage follows.

Section

Those who deny figurative usage have advanced a weak argument, saying:

“Furthermore, there is no situation that cannot be expressed by a literal expression specific to it. Using a figurative expression instead, when it requires a contextual indicator and serves no need, is far removed from the practice of wise and eloquent people in establishing linguistic conventions.”

He answered this by saying:

“The answer to the second argument is that using a figurative expression rather than a literal one may offer the advantage of being easier on the tongue; fitting the cadence of speech, in wording and prose; achieving correspondence, similarity of sound, or rhymed prose; conveying magnification; or departing from the literal expression for emphasis—among other purposes sought through speech.”

The response is:

This argument is weak. Whoever advances it must concede the division of speech into literal and figurative usage, but then insists that literal rather than figurative expressions must be used. This contradicts his statement, “There is no figurative usage in language.” Rather, the instances they have called

---

## Page 10287

figurative—if their use in the language is established—are all literal according to this view. Some literal expressions are finer and more eloquent than others, and clarity and eloquence vary in degree. All these meanings are conveyed literally by the wording, and wording conveys meaning only alongside a contextual indicator. Whoever thinks that the literal meaning of His words,

“And ask the town,”

is to question the walls is ignorant.

This line of argument resembles that of these people: they all deny that a word can be used in one situation with one meaning and in another situation with another meaning, as the word “town” is sometimes used for the inhabitants and sometimes for the dwellings. They claim that it means only the dwellings. In this error they agree with the other group, but that group says, “Something has been omitted here; the full wording is: ‘And ask the people of the town.’” The former group, however, says, “Rather, what is meant is: ‘And ask the walls.’”

The correct view is that “town” refers to the people themselves who live together in that place. Here, the word “town” is intended to refer to these people, as in the words of Allah Most High:

“How many a town, mightier than your town which drove you out, We destroyed! They had none to help them.”

Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“Such is your Lord’s seizure when He seizes towns while they are doing wrong.”

And He says:

“How many a town rebelled against the command of its Lord and His messengers! So We called it to a severe account and punished it with a terrible punishment.”

There are many similar examples.

---

## Page 10288

Section

To complete this discussion, we must address what he mentioned concerning figurative language in the Quran. He said: “An explanation must be offered for His words,

‘Beneath which rivers flow,’

although rivers themselves do not flow.”

The answer is that “river,” like “town,” “waterspout,” and similar terms, may refer either to what occupies a place or to the place itself. Thus, when one says, “He dug the river,” the place is meant; when one says, “The river flowed,” what occupies it is meant.

As for His words,

“And my head has blazed with grey hair,”

the claim that the head does not blaze as fire blazes is conceded. But the answer is that the word “blazing” is not used here in that sense. Rather, it is used for the whiteness that emerged and spread from the blackness, as a flame spreads from fire. This is a comparison and a metaphor. Yet in His words,

“And my head has blazed,”

the word “blazed” is qualified by its reference to the head, so the wording does not admit the meaning of firewood burning. This expression—namely, His words,

“And my head has blazed with grey hair”—

has never been used outside its proper setting; indeed, it has only ever been used with this meaning. Even if this usage brings a change after the establishment of “the fire blazed,” that poses no difficulty. Nor does it pose any difficulty if the intention is to liken that meaning to this one. Rather, this is the nature of general terms: it is necessary that

---

## Page 10289

the two meanings have something in common by virtue of which their individual instances resemble one another. As for calling it a metaphor, it is well known that they did not borrow the word itself. Rather, they combined the word “blazed” with “head” in a construction they have never used, or intended, in any other sense.

For this reason, one cannot say in such a case, “The head has not blazed with grey hair.” Rather, one says, “The blazing of the head is not like the blazing of firewood, even though it resembles it in certain respects.”

He said: “And what of His words,

‘And lower to them the wing of humility,’

when humility has no wing?”

The answer is: There is no doubt that humility has no wing like a bird’s wing, just as a bird has no wing like the wings of the angels. Nor is the wing of humility like the wing of travel. Yet a person’s wing is his side, just as a bird’s wing is its side. A child is commanded to lower his side before his parents, doing so in humble submission to them, not merely lowering it without humility. He also said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“And lower your wing to those of the believers who follow you.”

He did not say, “the wing of humility.” Thus, the Messenger was commanded to lower his wing, which is his side, whereas the child was commanded to lower his wing in humility. Along with lowering his wing, he must therefore humble himself before his parents, unlike the Messenger, who was not commanded to humble himself. Thus, the way the words of the Quran are combined indicates how their meanings are combined, with each meaning given its due.

---

## Page 10290

Then He, glorified is He, completed this with His words:

“Out of mercy.”

Thus, it is a wing of humility born of mercy, not a wing of humility born of helplessness and weakness: the former is praiseworthy, whereas the latter is blameworthy.

He said: “And what of His words, ‘well-known months,’ when the months are not Hajj itself?”

The answer is: It is understood that the times for Hajj are well-known months. The meaning is not that the acts themselves are a period of time, nor does anyone understand this from the wording. One may, however, say that something has been omitted, and that the full expression is: “The time for Hajj is well-known months.” It is an admirable feature of Arab discourse that, for brevity, they omit what the stated words indicate, just as they sometimes add words to reinforce and emphasize the meaning.

An example of the former is His saying:

“Strike the sea with your staff, and it split apart.”

It is understood that the meaning is: “He struck it, and it split apart.” Yet there was no need to state this explicitly, since the wording, “We said, ‘Strike,’” followed by “and it split apart,” indicates that he struck it and it split apart.

Likewise, His words, “whoever believes,” are understood as “the righteousness of whoever believes,” or “befriend whoever believes.”

Similarly, His words, “Hajj is months,” mean: “The times for Hajj are months.” The meaning is therefore agreed upon; the dispute concerns calling this a metaphor. The objection, “Hajj itself is not months,” would be pertinent only if that were what the statement signified. But it is not. Rather, what it signifies to both its speaker and its hearer is that the times for Hajj are well-known months.

---

## Page 10291

He said: “And what of His words, ‘Monasteries, churches, salawāt (prayers), and mosques would have been demolished’—when prayers cannot be demolished?”

The answer is: It has been said that salawāt is a name for Jewish houses of worship. They call them salawāt after what is performed in them, as in similar instances. He used the word salawāt to designate places only in conjunction with His words, “would have been demolished.” Demolition applies only to places, so it is in conjunction with this wording that He used it to designate places.

He said: “And what of His words, ‘or one of you comes from al-ghā’it (the low ground)’?”

We answer: In the Quran, the word al-ghā’it is used in its linguistic sense: a low-lying piece of ground. People used to frequent low-lying places for that purpose; this is al-ghā’it. Likewise, a privy is called khalā’ (an empty place) because someone relieving himself seeks out an unoccupied spot, and mirhād (a place for washing) because of rahd (washing) with water, and so forth. Coming from the low ground is an expression for relieving oneself, since a person ordinarily comes from such a place only after relieving himself. The expression thus acquired a literal meaning through customary usage and, when used without qualification, is understood to mean defecation. They may also call what comes out of a person ghā’it, naming what occupies a place after the place itself, as in the expression, “The gutter ran.” Another example is the statement of Ā’ishah: “Tell your spouses to wash the traces of excrement off themselves.”

His words, “or one of you comes from the low ground,” do not use the expression in a sense other than its own. Rather, coming from the low ground implies defecation, so He alluded to that meaning through an expression denoting the act

---

## Page 10292

that is outwardly apparent and entails the concealed matter; both are intended. This is common in speech: something is mentioned so that what it necessarily entails may be understood from it. Both are indicated by the wording, but one serves as a means to the other. An example is what one of the women said in the account of Umm Zarʿ:

“My husband has a great heap of ashes, a long sword-belt, and a house near the gathering place.”

A great heap of ashes implies much cooking, which, according to their custom, implies many guests, which in turn implies generosity. A long sword-belt implies tall stature, while the nearness of his house to the gathering place implies that people seek him out at home on account of the gathering. The word nād denotes both those present and the place itself.

Examples include His words:

“Then let him summon his assembly,”

and His words:

“And you commit evil in your gatherings.”

Here it denotes the place, whereas in the former verse it denotes those present—the people who assemble. The name Dār al-Nadwah (Assembly House) derives from the same usage.

Its root sense is that of people calling out to one another, in contrast to private conversation, in which people speak confidentially to one another. Al-Shaʿbī said: “When a gathering grows large, there is either calling aloud or private conversation.” Allah Most High said:

“We called to him from the right side of the Mount and brought him near for intimate conversation.”

Thus, He both called to him and spoke privately with him.

He said: “And what of His words, ‘Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth’?”

The answer is: It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say in his supplication: “O Allah, to You belongs all praise. You are the Sustainer of the heavens and the earth

---

## Page 10293

and all who are in them. To You belongs all praise. You are the Light of the heavens and the earth and all who are in them.” The wording does not mean that He is the radiance of the sun and fire, for that is not the light of the heavens and the earth, as some have mistakenly supposed the wording to mean.

The term “light” denotes One who is luminous and illuminates others through His guidance. This includes the meaning: “You are the Guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth.” Ibn Masʿūd said: “With your Lord there is neither night nor day; the light of the heavens comes from the light of His Face.”

His being the Lord and Sustainer of the heavens and the earth does not contradict His having some of His servants nurture others in certain respects and impart understanding to them. Likewise, the fact that “Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth”—the One who illuminates them—does not contradict His making some of His creatures illuminate others.

When the name “Light” encompasses His attribute and His action, both fall within what that name denotes. When He made the moon a light, it possessed light and illuminated other things, yet it is merely one of His creatures. The Creator is more worthy than anything besides Him of the attribute of perfection that is free of all deficiency.

He said: “And His words:

‘Then transgress against him in the same way that he has transgressed against you.’”

He said: “But just retribution is not aggression?”

The answer is: Aggression means overstepping a limit. If done unjustly, it is forbidden; if done as retribution, it is just and permissible. Thus, the term “aggression” in

---

## Page 10294

such a case means crossing the boundary separating the two parties. Yet once one party has transgressed, it becomes permissible to transgress against him. The first transgression is unjust, whereas the second is permissible. The term “just” is permissible.

Here, “transgression” is qualified by wording that makes clear that it is an act of retribution, unlike initiating aggression, which is unjust. When the term is not qualified as retribution, it is understood to mean initiating aggression, since the default assumption is that no corresponding act preceded it.

He said: “And what of His words, ‘The recompense of an evil is an evil like it,’ and His words, ‘Allah mocks them,’ and ‘They plot, and Allah plots’?”

The answer is: An evil is a name for something that precedes the person concerned. If it is inflicted upon him justly, as retribution, then he deserves the evil inflicted upon him. It is not meant that it precedes the doer, such that he should be forbidden to do it; rather, it precedes the person being requited with it. The terms “evil” and “good” can refer to disobedience and obedience, or to misfortune and blessing, as in His words:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

And His words:

“If good touches you, it distresses them; but if evil befalls you, they rejoice at it.”

His words, “The recompense of an evil,” do not refer to everyone who commits a sin. Rather, they refer to requiting someone who has wrongfully harmed another. That harm is among the misfortunes suffered by the injured party, and its recompense is for the wrongdoer to suffer a similar misfortune. It is as though He said: The recompense of someone who harms you is that you harm him just as he harmed you. This is an evil in the literal sense.

---

## Page 10295

As for mockery and plotting—whereby a person outwardly displays good while intending evil—if this involves denying the truth and wronging others, it is a forbidden sin. If, however, it requites someone who has acted in this way with the like of his own deed, it is good and just. Allah Most High says:

“When they meet those who believe, they say, ‘We believe.’ But when alone with their devils, they say, ‘We are with you; we were only mocking.’”

“Allah mocks them.”

For recompense corresponds to the deed. He Most High also says:

“They plotted, and We too plotted.”

Likewise, He says:

“They are surely plotting,”

“And I too am plotting.”

And He says:

“Thus did We plan for Joseph.”

The same applies to requiting an aggressor with the like of his own deed: recompense corresponds to the deed, and this is good and just. It constitutes plotting and scheming when one outwardly shows him something contrary to what one conceals.

He said:

“Whenever they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it.”

This expression originally refers to combatants kindling a fire around which their supporters gather to help their ally against their enemy. Their war effort cannot be fully mounted without it; when it is extinguished, they cannot unite their forces. The expression then came to be used proverbially of any combatant whose scheme is thwarted. It is like the saying, “Your own hands tied the skin, and your own mouth inflated it,” meaning: you brought this upon yourself.

Likewise, people say, “In summer you squandered the milk,” meaning: you neglected the opportunity when it was available. These expressions originally had a specific meaning, but customary usage transferred them to a meaning

---

## Page 10296

broader than that. Through predominant usage, this broader meaning came to be understood whenever these expressions were used without qualification, rather than their original, specific meaning. This is like other expressions that customary usage has extended beyond their original scope, such as “neck” and “head,” as in His saying:

“Then the freeing of a slave.”

It may be said that this is a case of implication, since freeing the neck necessarily entails freeing the rest of the body. Hence the jurists disagreed concerning someone who says, “Your hand is free if you enter the house,” whereupon the slave’s hand is cut off and he subsequently enters the house: is he emancipated? There are two views, depending on whether this is a case of emancipation extending from a part to the whole or a case of 'ibāda (worship). The correct view is that it is a case of 'ibāda, meaning: “You are free if you do such-and-such.” Letter-based and Sharīʿah-defined literal usage are recognized in the language.

He said: “And so on, to countless instances of figurative usage?”

They replied: “In the examples cited under this heading, either the meaning is disputed, or the meaning is agreed upon and the dispute concerns calling it figurative. In either case, it provides no evidence for your position.”

An example is His saying:

“O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold! And the water subsided.”

It has been said that “sky” here means rain—that is, “O rain, cease!” But that is not so. Rather, ceasing means withholding: “O sky, withhold your rain.” Those making such claims frequently take expressions with well-known meanings and claim that they are used

---

## Page 10297

in senses other than these, without evidence, and say: “This is figurative.” Such a claim is unacceptable. Those who divide speech into literal and figurative usage agree that the presumption in speech is literal usage. This has two meanings. First, when an expression’s meaning is known and someone says, “This usage is figurative,” the reply is: “Rather, the presumption is literal usage.” Second, when an expression is known to have two senses, one literal and the other figurative, the presumption is that it bears its literal meaning. Thus, sometimes the known meaning is used to establish that the expression denotes it, and sometimes an expression whose signification is known is used to establish the meaning it denotes.

If someone says, concerning the words of the Most High,

“So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear,”

that tasting is originally done with the mouth, the reply is: that is tasting food. Tasting may apply to food, but it may also apply to punishment generally, as He says:

“And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment before the greater punishment, so that they may return.”

And His words:

“Taste! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble!”

And His words:

“Taste the touch of Hell!”

His words, “Taste the touch of Hell!” explicitly refer to tasting the touch of punishment and cannot mean tasting food. Moreover, when hunger and fear clothe the body, the pain is greater, unlike a slight degree of either. Thus, when He said:

“So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear,”

it did not indicate that it clothed and encompassed the sufferer. These meanings are conveyed by these expressions, unlike saying, “It became hungry and afraid,” which indicates the general experience, but not its severity or extent. This is an instance of perfect clarity of expression. In all these instances, each expression is used only in its familiar linguistic meaning. For His expression, “tasting the garment of hunger and fear,” is not

---

## Page 10298

tasting food, and tasting hunger is not the same as tasting the garment of hunger. Thus, a precise understanding of this subject belongs to the science of rhetoric, through which a person appreciates something of the Quran’s greatness. No expression in the Quran occurs without something accompanying it that clarifies its intended meaning. Whoever misunderstands the Quran does so because of his own limitations or negligence.

If someone claims that the preposition bā’ in “drink of it” is redundant, that reflects his own understanding. A person may drink without having his thirst quenched. Saying “He drinks from it” does not indicate that his thirst is quenched. But when the meaning of quenching thirst is incorporated into the expression “drink of it,” it indicates drinking that quenches thirst. This is a particular kind of drinking, indicated by the preposition bā’.

Likewise, the preposition bā’ in His words,

“Wipe over your faces and hands,”

indicates bringing the substance used for wiping into contact with the bodily part; what is intended is not simply wiping the face. Whoever says that the bā’ is redundant makes the meaning “Wipe your faces.” Yet simply wiping the face does not entail applying the water or earth used for wiping.

As for the reading “and your feet” with the accusative ending, it refers back to the face and hands, as shown by His words, “up to the ankles.” If it were coordinated according to the underlying syntactic position, the meaning would be spoiled: it would amount to saying, “Wipe your heads.”

Moreover, all the reciters read His words concerning dry ablution:

“Wipe over your faces and hands with it.”

The wording of the two verses follows the same pattern. If the expression coordinated with a noun in the genitive were coordinated according to its underlying syntactic position, they would have read “your hands” in the accusative. Since they do not read it that way, it becomes clear that His words:

---

## Page 10299

“Wipe over your heads, and [wash] your feet up to the ankles”

has “your feet” coordinated with the faces and hands.

Ibn Aqīl said:

Section: Their Questions

They have gone to the utmost lengths of strained reasoning and forced interpretation to demonstrate that the wording is literal.

Among their statements is the following:

Qaryah (“village”) means a gathering of people. It is derived from qaraytu al-mā’a fī al-hawd (“I collected water in the basin”), and from mā qara’at al-nāqatu fī rahimihā (“the she-camel has carried nothing in her womb”). Likewise, the hospitality-related terms muqri’ and muqrin refer to guests gathering with their hosts. The Quran and qirā’ah (“recitation”) are so named for the same reason, since they comprise words gathered together. Similarly, gathering properly applies to people, not walls. Thus, He intended only the gathering of people, which is itself the literal meaning of qaryah. This is clarified by His words, Most High:

“And those towns—We destroyed them when they did wrong,”

and His words, Most High:

“And how many a town rebelled against the command of its Lord and His messengers!”

This refers to the gathering—to the people, not the walls. And ‘īr means a caravan.

They said:

If Allah wills buildings and donkeys to speak, He makes them speak. The age of prophethood is a time of extraordinary occurrences. Had he questioned them, they would have answered him about his situation, as a miracle and an honor granted to him.

---

## Page 10300

As for His words, Most High:

“That is Jesus, son of Mary—the word of truth,”

by “the word of truth,” He referred only to his name and his attribution to his mother, and that is literally Allah’s speech. Your own imam, Ahmad, said: “Allah is Allah,” meaning that the name is the one named.

As for His words, Most High:

“And, because of their disbelief, they were made to drink the calf into their hearts,”

when the calf was scattered into the sea after being filed down, and they drank from the water, what they drank was that very calf. Thus, everything you have mentioned is literal.

Ibn Aqīl said:

The reply is that qaryah denotes that which gathers people and in which they gather, not the gathered people themselves. Similarly, qur’ and its plural aqrā’ designate the time of menstruation or the time of purity. Likewise, tasriyah (retaining milk), musarrāh (an animal whose milk is retained), and sarāh designate where milk and water collect, not the collected milk and water themselves. A qārī is one who gathers provisions for hospitality, and a muqrī is one who gathers guests—not the guests themselves.

Nor is a caravan called an ‘īr unless it includes particular beasts of burden. Pedestrians and men on foot are not called an ‘īr. If the word merely meant a caravan, it would apply to men on foot just as it applies to those with riding animals. Their claim is therefore disproved.

As for their statement, “Had he asked, the wall would have answered,” such a thing does not happen at one’s choosing, nor can one rely on its occurrence except when presenting it as a miraculous challenge. It does not happen merely because the thought occurs to someone, or at any and every time.

---

## Page 10301

As for His words,

“That is Jesus,”

referring to the name: if they interpret them in this way, they are figurative, because the utterance—which is the name—is not ascribed to him. For this reason we say:

“It is not for Allah to take a son. Glory be to Him!”

The name, which is an utterance, is not the son of Mary. Rather, the son of Mary is the very body and spirit to which the name applies—the one at whose hands miraculous signs appeared, and whom they made a god because those signs appeared.

As for their statement that what is meant is the very substance of the calf when he scattered it: once scattered, it ceased to be a calf. Rather, “the calf” properly denotes the particular form that lowed. Otherwise, gold filings reach only the hearts, and the furthest they reach is the bodily cavities. As for the natural faculty preceding them and transforming them until they reach the heart, that is not the case. Rather, when gold filings enter the stomach, they settle there, unable to rise beyond that location, let alone reach the heart.

Furthermore, the Arabic expression “they were made to imbibe” does not refer to drinking itself, but to its causes—namely, making something be swallowed. This pertains to love, not to entities that are physical bodies. Hence one does not say, “They were made to imbibe water into their hearts,” even though water is something drunk. How, then, could this be said of the calf, especially when its very association with the heart associates it with the seat of love?

It is related in a report that, when they consumed its filings, they would say, “This is dearer to us than Moses and the God of Moses,” because of the love for it that had taken hold of their hearts.

---

## Page 10302

I say:

As for their discussion of the settlement: “settlement,” “river,” and similar terms designate both a place and what occupies it. Thus, “settlement” encompasses both the dwellings and their inhabitants. A statement about it may concern the inhabitants, the dwellings, or both. This is like the term “human being,” which designates both soul and body, although a statement may concern only one of them. Likewise, “speech” designates both wording and meaning, although a statement may concern only one of them.

As for the derivation of these words, some scholars have erred here by failing to distinguish between qaraʾa, with a hamza, and qarā–yaqrī, with a yā. The verb meaning “to gather” is qarā–yaqrī, without a hamza. From it come qarya (settlement), qirāʾa (reading), and similar words. Another example is qaraytu al-dayfa, aqrīhi: that is, “I brought the guest in and drew him close.” Qaraytu al-māʾa fī al-hawd means “I gathered the water in the basin”; taqarraytu al-miyāh means “I sought out the watering places.” Qarawtu al-bilāda, qaraytuhā, and istaqraytuhā are used when you explore lands, travelling from one to another. From this comes istiqrāʾ: examining something in its entirety. This differs from istaqraʾtuhu al-Qurʾāna, “I asked him to recite the Quran,” for that derives from the root containing a hamza. Thus, a settlement is the place where people gather, and a statement about it sometimes concerns the place and sometimes the people.

As for qaraʾa with a hamza, its meaning is to make manifest and clear. Qurʾ and qirāʾa (recitation) belong to this root. An example is their saying:

“The she-camel—a slaughter camel—has never brought forth a fetal membrane.”

That is, she has not made it manifest and expelled it from her womb. The reciter is the one who brings forth the Quran and makes it manifest. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation.”

Thus, He distinguishes between collecting and reciting.

---

## Page 10303

And qurʾ denotes blood because it becomes manifest and emerges. It likewise denotes a time, since times are determined by something observable. The interval of purity is then included in the term qurʾ by extension, just as the night is included in the term “day.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding:

“Refrain from prayer during the days of your menstrual periods.”

An interval of purity followed by menstruation constitutes a qurʾ; thus, the term encompasses the whole. An interval of purity alone, however, is not called a qurʾ. Hence, if a woman is divorced during a menstrual period, she does not count that as a qurʾ, because she must observe a waiting period of three qurūʾ. If she is divorced during an interval of purity, the qurʾ consists of the menstrual period together with the preceding interval of purity. This is why the senior Companions—including ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Abū Mūsā, and others—held that the qurūʾ are menstrual periods: she is commanded to wait for three qurūʾ. If a qurʾ meant an interval of purity, her waiting period would consist of two qurūʾ and part of a third.

The disagreement between the two groups concerns the third menstrual period. The senior Companions and those who agreed with them say that her husband has the prior right to take her back as long as she has not bathed after her third menstrual period. The younger Companions say that once she enters her third menstrual period, she is free to remarry.

It is established by both scriptural evidence and consensus that the sunnah is to divorce her during an interval of purity in which he has not had intercourse with her. By then, part of that interval of purity has already elapsed. Yet Allah commanded that divorce take place with the waiting period still ahead, not when it is already under way. His words “three qurūʾ” specify a number, unlike the word “months,” which is a plural form, not a number. There must therefore be three qurūʾ, as Allah commanded; part of the third is not sufficient.

---

## Page 10304

As for the words you cite:

“That is Jesus, son of Mary—the word of truth.”

There are two well-known readings: the nominative and the accusative. Under either reading, it has been said that “the word of truth” refers to Jesus, just as he is called the Word of Allah.

It has also been said that the meaning is: “What We have mentioned is the word of truth.” In that case, it is the predicate of an omitted subject. This has parallels, such as His words:

“They will say, ‘Three, their fourth being their dog’”—and the rest of the verse;

and:

“Say, ‘The truth is from your Lord.’”

That is: “This truth is from your Lord.” If Jesus is intended, calling him “the word of truth” is like calling him the Word of Allah. On this interpretation, it functions as a predicate and as an appositive. Either interpretation has parallels, so the question of calling it figurative is the same as with those parallels. The more apparent meaning is that this account We have given of Jesus, son of Mary, is the word of truth—although his being the son of a servant of Allah is included in this.

Some say that “the Truth” means Allah, and that the intended meaning is “the word of Allah.” Although this is a sound meaning, the Quran’s usual practice, when attributing speech to Allah, is to say “the word of Allah.” It does not say “the word of truth” unless a true statement is intended, as in His words:

“His word is the truth”;

“Allah speaks the truth”;

and:

“The truth—and the truth I speak.”

Furthermore, constructions like this, in which a noun is joined to its adjective in a genitive construction—as in His words, “grain of the harvested crop,” and the expressions “the prayer of the first” and “the abode of the Hereafter”—are, according to many of

---

## Page 10305

the grammarians of Kufa and others, instances of a noun being joined to its adjective in a genitive construction without any ellipsis. Many grammarians of Basra, however, maintain that the noun governed by the genitive construction has been omitted, the underlying wording being “the prayer of the first hour.” The first view is more correct: nothing in the wording indicates the supposedly omitted noun, nor does it come to mind. The adjectival construction also occurs in several places, as in His words:

“The final abode”;

and:

“His word is the truth.”

In short, parallels to this are numerous in the Quran and in Arabic speech. This provides no argument for those who call it figurative beyond whatever argument they have concerning its parallels. The matter must therefore be referred back to the underlying principle.

Ibn ʿAqīl said:

“Among our proofs are the words of the Most High:

‘In a clear Arabic tongue.’

Since it is established that the Quran is Arabic, and the Arabic language includes metaphor and figurative expression among its means of clarity and eloquence, were the Quran to omit these, it would not fully encompass the forms of speech or attain complete eloquence. The Arabs’ inability to match it becomes apparent only when the discourse is lengthy and brings together their metaphors, comparisons, and descriptions. Nor is there any text authorizing such wording unless it is lengthy.

“For this reason, the challenge cannot be issued through something like a single line of poetry, or through one or two verses. Likewise, a short portion of the Quran was not accorded the same inviolability as a long passage, so the revealed Law permitted a person in a state of major ritual impurity and a menstruating woman to recite it. All this is because such a portion does not possess inimitability.

“Thus, if He employs figurative and literal expression, together with all the other forms and categories of speech, and His speech surpasses discourse encompassing all those categories, its inimitability is established and their inability to match it becomes evident. This requires that the Quran contain figurative expression.”

---

## Page 10306

I say:

Most scholars dispute his statement that a short surah possesses no inimitability. They maintain that even a short surah is inimitable. Indeed, some of our fellow scholars disputed his claim even regarding one or two verses. Abū Bakr Ibn al-‘Imād—the teacher of my grandfather Abū al-Barakāt—said:

“I do not consider his statement correct that a person in a state of major ritual impurity may recite a small portion of the Quran only because it possesses no inimitability. The whole of it is inviolable. Such a person was permitted to recite part of a verse only to afford ease to the legally accountable person, with consideration for attaining reward and for hardship, while its inviolability remains intact. Likewise, he was permitted to pray with a small amount of blood present, despite its impurity.”

I say:

As for his statement that the Quran was revealed in the language of the Arabs, that is true. More specifically, it was revealed in the tongue of Quraysh, as the Most High says:

“We never sent a messenger except in the language of his people.”

‘Umar and ‘Uthmān said: “This Quran was revealed in the language of this tribe, Quraysh.” Thus, anyone who says that the expressions it contains are not figurative, while their counterparts in Arabic speech are figurative, contradicts himself. However, our fellow scholars who said that the Quran contains no figurative expression are not known to have acknowledged that the Arabic language contains figurative expression. They therefore need not be guilty of contradiction.

Moreover, one may say that Arabic contains figurative expression of a kind whose counterpart is not found in the Quran. The speech of created beings contains exaggeration and reckless overstatement—in praise, satire, al-murā’ī, and other forms—from which the speech of a wise person should be kept free, let alone the speech of Allah. If someone applies the designation “figurative” only to speech of this kind, he is not obliged to apply that designation to

---

## Page 10307

what occurs in the Quran. This is because classifying some speech as figurative is merely a matter of convention, not something determined by religious law, linguistic usage, or reason. Thus, some call an expression figurative when it is used for something distinct from what it denotes, but not when it is used for part of what it denotes. They therefore do not regard a general expression used for only part of its scope as figurative, nor a command intended to convey recommendation. This is the convention followed by most jurists.

They may not describe this as using an expression for something other than what it was assigned to denote, on the grounds that part of a whole is not, without qualification, called something other than that whole. Thus, one out of ten is not said to be something other than those ten, nor a person’s hand something other than that person. Moreover, in their view, figurative usage requires a contextual indicator to establish the intended meaning, except where the indicator serves to exclude an unintended meaning. In the case of a command, the contextual indicator excludes part of what the wording signifies while leaving the remainder signified by the wording itself. By contrast, the contextual indicator accompanying “lion” makes clear that the intended referent does not fall within what the word “lion” denotes when used without qualification.

While most jurists conventionally distinguish between literal and figurative usage in this way, others adopt the convention that whenever an expression is not intended to convey its entire meaning, it is figurative. Most of the latter, however, distinguish between a contextual indicator that is separate or independent and one rooted in the wording, forming part of it, or lacking independent standing. They do not regard the latter cases as figurative, lest they be obliged to consider most speech figurative—even the statement:

“There is no god but Allah.”

This would be so despite its being known that the polytheists did not dispute

---

## Page 10308

that Allah is a true God; rather, they set up other gods alongside Him. Thus, the dispute between the Messenger and them concerned denying divinity to anything other than Allah, in the literal sense, since the expression was not used for anything other than what it was assigned to denote. As for the claim that its original assigned meaning is negation—namely, the absolute denial of any deity—no Arab ever held such a belief. Indeed, they had no intention of expressing it, nor did they originally assign any expression to convey it. Expression conveys meanings conceived in the mind, and they conceived of this meaning only to deny it, not to affirm it. Negating a negation is affirmation.

Anyone who claims that the meaning they intended by this expression in their language was that the Messenger should be sent to deny every deity; that this was the meaning for which they originally assigned the expression; and that their statement, “There is no god but Allah,” uses that expression in a sense other than its assigned meaning—such a person plainly misrepresents them even in their state of polytheism, let alone their state of faith.

Undoubtedly, all restrictions of scope contained within the wording itself—such as an adjectival qualification, a condition, a limiting endpoint, apposition, or an exception—stand on the same footing. However, they used most expressions sometimes without these restrictions and sometimes accompanied by them. This is unlike the statement, “There is no god but Allah,” which they have never been known to use without the exception, since they regarded the resulting meaning as false. Whoever regards that as the literal meaning in their language plainly misrepresents them. If he distinguishes one exception from another, he contradicts himself and departs from consensus. This is so

---

## Page 10309

because it is founded on a false, self-contradictory premise. When the proponent of a contradictory position follows it through consistently and is held to its implications, its falsity and objectionable character become apparent in ways that were not evident before. If he does not follow it through, he contradicts himself, and its falsity becomes apparent. Thus, its falsity follows either way.

For this reason, proponents of figurative usage have no coherent position whatsoever. Rather, all their positions are contradictory, and their definitions and the distinguishing signs they mention are unsound. Since the foundation of their position is false, they have invented a division and terminology within the language that have no basis in reality. Indeed, this division is false, so it cannot be accurately conceived or expressed in sound terms. A sound meaning, by contrast, can be expressed in sound words, as Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, fear Allah and speak words that are right.”

Sound speech is apt and correct, corresponding to the truth without addition or omission; it is just and truthful. This is unlike the speech of someone who seeks to distinguish between two equivalent things and treat them as different—indeed, as opposites. Such speech is not sound. This is discussed at length in its proper place.

The point here is that those who say, “There is no figurative language in the Quran”—if they mean by this that His words,

“Ask the town,”

mean “Ask the walls,” and that “the caravan” means the beasts, and other such things reported from them, then they are mistaken. If they classify an expression used in a particular sense outside the Quran as figurative, but do not classify it as figurative when used in that sense in the Quran, they are also mistaken. If, however, they mean that writings other than the Quran contain exaggerations, reckless assertions, unnecessary expressions, and similar things from which the Quran is free, then they are correct in this.

And if they say:

---

## Page 10310

“We call those things figurative, unlike the expressions used in the Quran and similar Arabic speech,” then their terminology is closer to being correct than that of those who classify most Arabic speech as figurative. Thus, Ibn Jinnī is reported to have said: “The statement ‘Zayd went out’ is figurative, because the verb denotes the verbal noun, and the verbal noun made definite by the definite article encompasses every instance of going out. This would entail that Zayd performed every kind of going out. This is the literal meaning of the expression; if a single instance of going out is intended, it is figurative.”

No one who properly conceives what he is saying would say this. Ibn Jinnī possessed learning and intelligence, and probed subtle meanings in *Sirr al-Sināʿa*, *al-Khasāʾis*, *Iʿrāb al-Qurʾān*, and elsewhere. If he did not say this, that would be more in keeping with his scholarly merit. If he did say it, even a learned man may say something that otherwise only the most ignorant would say.

The verb denotes only what the verbal noun names: the action as such, without any qualification of universality or, indeed, any other qualification.
