Thus, when one says, “Zayd went out,” “Bakr stood up,” or something similar, the verb indicates that an act of going out or standing up occurred on his part, without the wording indicating its kind or extent. Rather, it can apply to these as alternatives, not collectively, as in His words:

“Then the freeing of a slave.”

He has required the freeing of one slave, not every slave; and the expression encompasses all

---

## Page 10311

slaves as alternatives, so whichever slave he frees suffices. Likewise, saying “He went out” indicates that an act of going out occurred. It may have been brief or prolonged, and he may have been riding or walking. Even so, the alternatives encompassed are only instances of going out possible for Zayd. But to claim that this expression entails the universal inclusion of everything in existence called “going out,” though not collectively—no one would say this unless his understanding were corrupted and he were closer to a beast. We should presume that Ibn Jinnī would not say this.

Moreover, this meaning exists in all other languages. Would any rational person say that the speakers of every language who use verbal sentences—which every nation must use—originally assigned those sentences to encompass every kind of that action existing in the world, and that using them for particular instances departs from the meaning for which the expression was originally assigned?

Rather, this demonstrates the unsoundness of the very basis of the doctrine of figurative usage, if it leads to such nonsense being uttered at all and then made into a disputed question included in works on the principles of jurisprudence.

Thus, whoever among those who deny figurative usage in the Quran says: “We do not call anything in the Quran, or in comparable Arabic speech, figurative. We call figurative only what exceeds the bounds of moderation, such as the exaggeration found in poets’ praise and invective

Whoever regards all this as figurative, holding that in all these and similar expressions the Arabs use words in senses other than those for which they were originally coined, advances a claim whose falsity is self-evident. His position also entails that most speech is figurative, since the same consequence follows for every unrestricted expression to which a qualification is added.

Sentences are of two kinds: nominal and verbal. A nominal sentence is fundamentally composed of a subject and predicate. It would therefore follow that whenever its subject and predicate are modified, an exception is introduced, or a circumstantial qualifier is added, the sentence becomes figurative.

His position also entails that when kāna (“was”) and its related verbs, inna (“indeed”) and its related particles, or zanantu (“I thought”) and its related verbs are introduced into the sentence, changing its meaning and grammatical inflection, it becomes figurative. For a qualification may occur at the beginning of a sentence, in its middle, or at its end

, especially in constructions with zanantu (“I thought”). For they say: Zaydun muntaliqun (“Zayd is setting out”) and Zaydan muntaliqan zanantu (“Zayd was setting out, I thought”). Thus, when the verb comes first, it must govern the case of its objects; when it comes in the middle, its grammatical government may be suspended; and when it comes last, suspension is preferable, although government remains permissible. For when the object precedes the verb, the verb’s grammatical government is weakened. They therefore strengthen it by introducing a preposition, just as they strengthen the government of the active participle because it is weaker than the verb, as in His words:

He has thus treated this expression as univocal, denoting a shared meaning like other univocal terms. In each instance, however, it has a distinctive element determined by its particular context, as in his example of blackness. Yet this very point refutes his argument for figurative language.

and His words,

In Arabic, salawāt means either supplications or the prescribed acts of prayer. Neither can be described as being demolished, and an inanimate object cannot possess will.

If it is said:

‘It was part of Arabic usage to call a place of prayer a prayer. Indeed, the words, “And the places of prostration belong to Allah,” have been explained as referring to the bodily parts used in prostration. As for his statement that “the Word of Allah” refers to Jesus himself, there is no doubt that, in Arabic, a verbal noun may denote its object, as when they say, “This is a dirham minted by the ruler.” Another example is His saying:

“This is Allah’s creation.”

Similarly, what is commanded is called a “command”; what is brought about by power is called “power”; that through which mercy is shown is called “mercy”; and what is created through the word is called a “word.” Such wording, however, is used only with accompanying indications that clarify the intended meaning, as in His saying:

“O Mary, Allah gives you good news of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, honoured in this world and the Hereafter, and among those brought near to Him.”

He thus made clear that the word is the Messiah. Yet it is well known that the Messiah himself is not speech.

“She said, ‘My Lord, how can I have a child when no man has touched me?’ He said, ‘Thus Allah creates whatever He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, “Be,” and it is.’”

When she expressed astonishment at having a child, He explained that He—glory be to Him—creates whatever He wills: when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, “Be,” and it is. This indicates that this child is among the things Allah creates by His saying:

“Be,” and it is.

Hence Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: “Jesus was created through ‘Be’; he is not ‘Be’ itself.”

---

## Page 10318

Hence He says in another verse:

“Indeed, the likeness of Jesus before Allah is that of Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him, ‘Be,’ and he was.”

He thus clarified His meaning: Jesus was created through “Be”; he is not himself the word “Be” or any other such speech.

Likewise, He says:

“Hajj is [during] well-known months.”

It is understood that He did not mean that acts are periods of time; rather, He intended to state the time of Hajj. Hence He says immediately afterwards:

“So whoever undertakes Hajj during them…”

The Hajj undertaken during those months is not the months themselves. It is therefore clear that, by saying “months,” He did not mean the act itself. Rather, He clarified His intent through His words, making clear that the expression does not indicate that acts are periods of time.

Likewise, He says:

“Rather, righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah.”

When He said:

“Righteousness is not that you enter houses from the back; rather, righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah,”

the wording indicated that His meaning was: rather, righteousness is fear of Allah. Such usage therefore occurs only alongside something that clarifies the intended meaning. In that case, the expression is used with a qualification that clarifies what is intended here, just as it is used elsewhere with a qualification that clarifies what is intended there.

The two meanings have something in common, yet also differ. This is comparable to names that are synonymous yet distinct, such as al-sārim (the keen-edged sword), al-muhannad (the sword of Indian steel), and al-sayf (the sword). They share a reference to the same entity and, in this respect, resemble univocal terms. Yet each is distinguished by indicating a particular meaning, so they resemble terms with distinct meanings. The names of Allah, His Messenger, and His Book belong to this category.

---

## Page 10319

Likewise, an expression made definite by the definite article referring to something already known denotes, in each instance, what the addressee recognizes, either through prior familiarity or through the preceding wording. Although what is intended in one instance is not what is intended in another, the two have both a shared element and a distinguishing element. Thus Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, We have sent to you a Messenger as a witness over you, just as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger.”

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Do not make the Messenger’s calling among you like your calling one another.”

Both passages contain the word “messenger” with the definite article. However, the familiar, known referent in the former is the messenger sent to Pharaoh, namely Moses, peace be upon him. In the latter, the familiar, known referent for those addressed by His words, “Do not make the Messenger’s calling among you,” is Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Both usages are literal, and the term is univocal. It is made definite by the article in both passages, but the understood reference in one passage differs from that in the other. This is one of the factors through which an expression conveys meaning: the definite article conveys its meaning only when the addressee knows the familiar referent.

The same applies to demonstratives, such as “this,” “these,” and “those.” In each instance, a demonstrative denotes only what is being indicated there. There must therefore be a situational or verbal indication clarifying that what is being indicated is something other than the demonstrative expression itself. The intended meaning is conveyed only through that indication together with the demonstrative expression, just as, with the definite article, the intended meaning is conveyed only through the article itself

---

## Page 10320

and the familiar referent. This manner of conveying meaning cannot be called figurative; otherwise, the signification of demonstratives, indeed of pronouns, the definite article referring to something already known, and other such expressions would also have to be figurative. No rational person would say this. If an ignorant person does say it, this shows that he has not understood how expressions convey meaning. He imagines that literal expressions convey meaning without these factors, which are indispensable to their signification.

Indeed, no expression conveys meaning except in conjunction with other expressions and the circumstances of the speaker, whose customary use of such speech must be known. Merely hearing an expression without knowing the speaker and his customary usage conveys nothing, for expressions signify intentionally and deliberately: they convey what the speaker intends them to convey, rather than signifying by themselves. One must therefore know what the speaker must intend by them. Hence, this cannot be known through hearing alone, but through reason together with hearing.

Understanding what expressions signify thus involves both hearing and reason. This is called fiqh (understanding). Accordingly, someone who grasps their meaning is said to understand, while someone who does not grasp it is said not to understand. Allah Most High says:

“What is the matter with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?”

And Allah Most High says:

“He found, on the near side of the two mountains, a people who could hardly understand speech.”

And He says:

“There is nothing that does not glorify Him with praise, but you do not understand their glorification.”

If you agree with someone in everything, you are loyal to him in everything. If you agree with him in most matters, you are loyal to him in most matters. In the matter under dispute, however, you have not shown him loyalty, even if you have not shown him enmity.

## Page 10328

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about a statement frequently made by jurists: “This is contrary to analogy,” referring to rulings established by a scriptural text, by the statements of the Companions or some of them, or even, at times, by consensus. Examples include their statements that purifying water into which an impurity has fallen is contrary to analogy; (*) indeed, that even purifying impure matter is contrary to analogy; that performing ablution after eating camel meat is contrary to analogy; that breaking the fast through cupping is contrary to analogy; and that advance-payment sales are contrary to analogy. They likewise describe leasing, transfers of debt, contractual manumission, profit-sharing investment partnerships, sharecropping, tending orchards for a share of their yield, loans, the validity of the fast of someone who breaks it forgetfully, and continuing an invalidated Hajj—all these and other rulings—as contrary to analogy. Is this claim correct or not? And can sound analogy conflict with a scriptural text?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The fundamental point to understand here is that “analogy” is an ambiguous term encompassing both sound and unsound analogy. Sound analogy is that which the Sharia has prescribed, and it consists in placing on an equal footing

It should be noted that Ibn al-Qayyim—may Allah have mercy on him—interspersed the treatise with additions of his own and appended a supplementary discussion after its conclusion: 2:38 ff.

---

## Page 10329

like cases and distinguishing between unlike cases. The former is direct analogy, and the latter inverse analogy. This is part of the justice with which Allah sent His Messenger. An example of sound analogy is when the legal cause on which the ruling in the original case depends is present in the new case, without any countervailing factor in the latter preventing that ruling from applying. The Sharia never prescribes anything contrary to such analogy.

The same applies to analogy based on the absence of a relevant distinction: that is, when there is no difference between the two cases that carries weight in the Sharia. The Sharia does not prescribe anything contrary to such analogy. Wherever the Sharia singles out a particular category for a ruling that distinguishes it from comparable categories, that category must possess a characteristic that warrants its distinctive ruling and precludes treating it on an equal footing with others. Yet this distinguishing characteristic may be apparent to some people and not to others. It is not a condition of sound, balanced analogy that everyone should recognize its validity. Thus, when someone regards something in the Sharia as contrary to analogy, it is contrary only to the analogy he has formed in his own mind, not to sound analogy as it actually stands.

Whenever we know that a scriptural text runs contrary to an analogy, we know with certainty that the analogy is unsound. This means that the case addressed in the text differs from those cases thought to resemble it by a characteristic that warranted the Lawgiver’s singling it out for that ruling. There is therefore nothing in the Sharia that contradicts sound analogy, though it does contain rulings contrary to unsound analogy, even if some people do not recognize its unsoundness.

---

## Page 10330

We shall now illustrate this with examples mentioned in the question. Those who said that profit-sharing investment partnerships, orchard-tending partnerships, and sharecropping agreements run contrary to analogy assumed that these contracts belong to the category of hire contracts, since they involve work in return for compensation. Hire contracts require both the compensation and the work provided in return to be known. When they saw that the work involved in these contracts was unspecified and the profit unknown, they said that they ran contrary to analogy. This was their mistake: these contracts belong to the category of partnerships, not exchange contracts in the strict sense, which require both countervalues to be known. Partnerships constitute a different category from exchange contracts, even if they are said to contain an element of exchange.

Likewise, partition constitutes a different category from exchange contracts in the strict sense, although it contains an element of exchange—so much so that some jurists have considered it a sale subject to the conditions governing sales in the strict sense.

To clarify this: work undertaken for financial gain falls into three types.

The first is where the work itself is the object of the contract, is clearly specified, and can be performed as agreed. This is a binding hire contract.

The second is where the work itself is the object of the contract, but is unspecified or uncertain. This is a reward contract, which is revocable, not binding. If someone says, “Whoever brings back my runaway slave shall have a hundred,” the person undertaking the task may or may not be able to bring him back. He may bring him back from somewhere nearby, or he may

---

## Page 10331

bring him back from somewhere far away. For this reason, the contract is not binding but revocable. If he performs the stipulated work, he is entitled to the reward; otherwise, he is not. The reward may be an undivided share of what the work yields, and its amount may be unknown, provided that this uncertainty does not prevent its delivery. For example, the military commander may say, “Whoever points out a fortress shall have one-third of what it contains,” or tell a raiding party he dispatches, “You shall have one-fifth or one-quarter of the spoils you take.”

The scholars differed concerning a slain enemy’s personal effects: is the slayer entitled to them by virtue of the revealed law, as al-Shāfiʿī held, or only through an express stipulation, as Abū Hanīfa and Mālik held? These are two views, both reported from Ahmad. Those who make this entitlement conditional upon a stipulation place it in this category.

Another instance of this category is offering a physician a reward for curing a patient, which is permissible. Likewise, the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, accepted a flock that had been offered to them for curing a clan’s chief. One of them recited over him for healing until he recovered, and they took the flock. The reward was for the recovery, not for the recitation. By contrast, hiring a physician under a binding contract to bring about recovery would not be permissible, because recovery is beyond his control: Allah may cure the patient, or He may not. This and similar cases permit a reward contract, but not a binding hire contract.

The third type is where the work itself is not the objective; rather, the objective is the financial return. This is the profit-sharing investment partnership. The owner of the capital has no interest in the worker’s work in itself, unlike someone offering a reward or hiring a worker, whose objective is the work itself. Thus, if the worker were to work

---

## Page 10332

however much he might, without making any profit, he would be entitled to nothing. If this is called a reward contract granting a share of what the work yields, the disagreement is merely terminological. Rather, this is a partnership: one contributes the benefit of his labor, and the other the benefit of his capital. Whatever profit Allah allots is shared between them in undivided proportions. Neither may therefore be assigned a fixed amount of profit, because this would depart from the justice required in a partnership. This is the form of sharecropping that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited. They used to stipulate that the owner should receive the crop from a particular plot—namely, what grew alongside the large watercourses, at the heads of the smaller irrigation channels, and similar places. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited this.

For this reason, al-Layth ibn Saʿd and others said:

“What he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited is something that anyone with discernment concerning the lawful and unlawful would, upon examining it, recognize as impermissible”—or words to that effect.

He thus explained that this prohibition follows from sound legal analogy. If a similar condition were stipulated in a profit-sharing investment partnership, it would not be permissible, because partnerships are founded upon justice between the two partners. If one is assigned profit to the exclusion of the other, this is not just. By contrast, when each has an undivided share, they share in both gain and loss. If there is a profit, they share in the gain; if there is no profit, they share in being deprived of it: the benefit of one party’s labor is lost just as the benefit of the other’s capital is lost. For this reason, financial loss is borne by the capital, since this corresponds to the loss of the benefit of the worker’s labor.

---

## Page 10333

For this reason, the correct view is that an invalid profit-sharing investment partnership requires payment of the customary share of profit, not the customary wage. The worker is therefore given the share of profit customarily given to someone like him: one half, one third, or two thirds. As for awarding him a fixed sum for which the owner is liable, as in employment and reward contracts, those who advocate this are mistaken. Their error arises from assuming that this is an employment contract, and so awarding him customary remuneration when it is invalid, just as they award him the stipulated payment when it is valid. What demonstrates the error of this view is that the worker might work for ten years: if he were awarded the customary wage, he would receive several times the original capital. Yet under a valid partnership, he is entitled only to a share of the profit, if there is any profit. How, then, could he be entitled under an invalid partnership to several times what he would receive under a valid one?

Likewise, those who deemed sharecropping and orchard-tending partnerships invalid assumed that they were employment contracts with unknown remuneration, and therefore invalidated them. Some of them upheld those arrangements for which there was a need, such as orchard-tending partnerships involving trees, since trees cannot be leased, whereas land can. They permitted sharecropping when ancillary to orchard-tending, either without further restriction or only when the open land constituted one third. All this rests on the assumption that the evidence requires sharecropping to be invalid, and that it was permitted only because of need.

Anyone who gives the matter due consideration will recognize that sharecropping is farther removed from injustice and gambling than leasing land for a specified rent payable as a binding liability. For the tenant seeks only to benefit from the crop growing on the land. If he becomes liable for the rent, while what he seeks from

---

## Page 10334

the crop may or may not be obtained, one party to the exchange thereby obtains what he seeks while the other does not. In sharecropping, however, if there is a crop, both share in it; if nothing is produced, both share in the deprivation. Neither obtains what he seeks to the exclusion of the other. This is closer to justice and farther removed from injustice than leasing. The governing principle in all contracts is justice, for it was with justice that the messengers were sent and the Scriptures revealed. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, We sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance, so that people may uphold justice.”

The Lawgiver prohibited usury because of the injustice it involves, and gambling because of the injustice it involves. The Quran prohibits both, and both constitute consuming wealth wrongfully. The transactions prohibited by the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him—such as sales involving excessive uncertainty, selling fruit before it begins to ripen, selling the yields of future years, and the sales known as habal al-habala, muzābana, and muhāqala, and similar transactions—fall under either usury or gambling.

Leasing for an unknown rent—for example, renting someone a house in return for whatever money the tenant earns in his shop—is a form of gambling and is therefore impermissible. Profit-sharing investment partnerships, orchard-tending partnerships, and sharecropping, however, involve no gambling whatsoever; rather, they are among the most equitable arrangements. This makes clear to you that sharecropping in which the seed is provided by the worker

---

## Page 10335

is more deserving of being deemed permissible than sharecropping in which the seed is provided by the landowner. This is why the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, practised sharecropping in this manner. Likewise, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, contracted with the people of Khaybar for half of the fruit and crops produced there, on condition that they cultivate the land at their own expense.

Those who stipulated that the seed must come from the landowner drew an analogy with profit-sharing investment partnerships. They said: In such partnerships, the capital comes from one party and the labour from another; sharecropping should follow the same pattern. They therefore required the owner to provide the seed, just as he provides the land.

Besides contradicting the Sunnah and the statements of the Companions, this analogy is among the most unsound. In a profit-sharing investment partnership, the capital returns to its owner, and the two parties divide the profit. It therefore corresponds to the land in sharecropping. As for the seed, no equivalent of it is returned to its owner; rather, it is consumed, just as the benefit derived from the land is consumed. It is therefore more appropriate to liken it to the benefit that is consumed than to the underlying asset that remains.

When the contracting party supplies the seed, his labour and seed are expended, while the landowner’s contribution—the benefit derived from his land—is likewise expended. The seed supplied by the former thus corresponds to the land supplied by the latter. Anyone who treats the seed as analogous to capital should therefore require an equivalent amount of seed to be returned to its owner, just as he requires the capital to be returned in a profit-sharing investment partnership. Yet how can this analogy stand when, if the owner of the seed stipulated that an equivalent of his seed be returned to him, they would not permit it?

---

## Page 10336

This is not the place to discuss these issues at length. The purpose is simply to draw attention to the nature of the claim: “This contradicts analogical reasoning.”

Section

As for debt transfer, those who say that it contradicts analogical reasoning argue that it constitutes selling one debt for another, which is impermissible. This is mistaken for two reasons.

First, there is neither a generally applicable scriptural text nor a consensus prohibiting the sale of one debt for another. What has been prohibited is selling one deferred countervalue for another: something deferred and not yet received in exchange for something else deferred and not yet received. An example is a forward sale in which both the payment and the goods owed are deferred. This is impermissible by agreement and constitutes exchanging one deferred countervalue for another. Selling one debt for another, however, includes exchanging one newly incurred obligation for another, as we have described. It also includes extinguishing one debt in exchange for extinguishing another, or extinguishing one debt in exchange for incurring another. These latter forms are disputed.

The second reason is that debt transfer belongs to the category of settling an obligation, not that of sale. When a creditor receives what is owed to him from the debtor, this constitutes collection of his due. If the debtor instead refers him to another person for payment, the creditor has thereby received that debt in settlement of the debt owed to him by the transferor. For this reason, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, mentioned

---

## Page 10337

debt transfer in the context of settling an obligation, saying in an authentic hadith:

“Delaying payment when one can afford to pay is injustice. If any of you is referred to a solvent person for payment, let him accept the referral.”

He thus commanded the debtor to pay, forbade him to delay payment, and explained that he acts unjustly if he delays. He also commanded the creditor to accept settlement when referred to a solvent person. This resembles the words of Allah Most High:

“Then let the claim be pursued fairly, and payment be made to him graciously.”

He commanded the person entitled to payment to pursue his claim fairly, and commanded the debtor to pay graciously.

Settling a debt is not a sale in the strict sense, although it contains an element of exchange. Some jurists have supposed that settlement occurs only through the collection of a debt: when the creditor receives payment, they hold, he becomes liable to the debtor for its equivalent, so that what he owes is set off against what he is owed. This is a contrived explanation rejected by the majority of jurists, who said: Rather, settlement is effected by the very property he receives; there is no need to posit a debt owed by the recipient.

Those jurists sought to make the settlement of a debt a settlement through another debt, but there is no need for this. Rather, a debt belongs to the category of the general and unspecified, whereas an identified asset belongs to that of the particular. When a general, unspecified debt is established as a person’s liability, what is intended is actual, existing assets. Whichever particular asset is received in settlement fulfils the purpose of that unspecified debt.

---

## Page 10338

Section

Those who say that lending is contrary to legal analogy argue that it is the sale of a commodity subject to the rules governing usury for another of the same kind, without taking possession. This is mistaken. Lending belongs to the category of gratuitously granting the use of property, like lending an item for use. This is why the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) called it a grant for use, saying:

“Or a grant of gold for use, or a grant of silver for use.”

The basic principle of lending an item for use is to give someone the underlying asset so that he may benefit from what it continually provides, and then return it to its owner. Sometimes he benefits from its use, as when real estate is lent. Sometimes someone grants him livestock so that he may drink their milk and then return them. Sometimes he lends him a tree so that he may eat its fruit and then return it. Milk and fruit are continually replenished, much like the benefits derived from using an asset. This is why, in endowments, they are treated in the same way as those benefits.

Likewise, a lender advances property to someone so that he may benefit from it and then return its equivalent, for returning an equivalent takes the place of returning the very same asset. This is why the lender is forbidden to stipulate anything beyond its equivalent, just as he would be forbidden, when lending an item for use, to stipulate that something else be returned along with the original asset.

This does not belong to the category of sale. No rational person would sell a dirham for another identical to it in every respect, with payment deferred. An item is sold for another of the same kind with deferred payment only when they differ in quality or quantity, as when one kind of coin is sold for another, or intact coins for broken ones, and the like.

---

## Page 10339

But a loan may benefit the lender, as when a loan is made in one town and repaid in another. This is why some scholars disliked it. The correct view, however, is that it is not disliked, because the borrower also benefits from it: when the lender advances the loan, both parties benefit.

Section

As for the claim that removing impurity is contrary to legal analogy, that marriage is contrary to legal analogy, and similar claims, these are among the most unsound views. Their specious argument is that human beings possess dignity, whereas marriage involves abasement of the woman, and human dignity is incompatible with abasement.

This is mistaken. Marriage serves the interests of the individual woman and of humankind. To the extent that it places the male over the female, this is part of the wisdom through which the welfare of animals generally is secured, let alone that of humankind. Such abasement is not incompatible with being human, any more than defecating when necessary, or eating and drinking, is incompatible with it—even though having no need of these things would be more perfect. Rather, people must not be denied what they need and what serves their welfare. A woman needs marriage, and it contributes to the fullness of her welfare. How, then, can it be said that legal analogy requires preventing her from marrying?

The same applies to removing impurity. The specious argument of those who say that it is contrary to legal analogy is that

---

## Page 10340

water becomes impure when it comes into contact with impurity; then, when more water is poured on, it comes into contact with the first, and so on. They say: “Legal analogy would therefore require the impurity to render each successive quantity of water impure, and what is impure cannot remove impurity.”

This is mistaken. They may be asked: “Why do you say that legal analogy requires water to become impure upon contact with impurity?” If they answer, “Because this is so in certain cases,” the response is that those who hold that water becomes impure only when its properties change dispute the ruling in the original case. Those who accept that ruling say: “There is no stronger reason to regard the removal of impurity as contrary to legal analogy than to regard water’s becoming impure as contrary to it. One could instead say that legal analogy requires water not to become impure upon contact with impurity, just as it does not become impure when it comes into contact with it in the course of removing it.”

This analogy is sounder than the former, because scriptural texts and scholarly consensus establish that water removes impurity, whereas whether water becomes impure merely through contact is disputed. How, then, can disputed cases be made evidence against cases on which there is consensus? Proper analogy requires disputed cases to be judged by analogy with cases on which there is consensus.

Furthermore, reason dictates that water does not become impure if the impurity has not altered it. It retains its original created state and is wholesome, falling within the words of the Most High:

“He makes good things lawful for them and forbids them foul things.”

The same legal analogy applies to all liquids when an impurity falls into them and undergoes transformation until its taste is no longer discernible

---

## Page 10341

nor its colour or smell: such liquids do not become impure. The jurists have differed on this question: does legal analogy require water to become impure upon contact with impurity, except where evidence establishes an exception, or does it require that water remain pure unless its properties change? There are two views: the first is that of the scholars of Iraq, and the second that of the scholars of the Hijaz. Among hadith jurists, some favour the former, while others favour the latter; these latter are the scholars of the Hijaz. This is the correct view, supported by foundational principles, scriptural texts, and reason. Allah has permitted wholesome things and forbidden foul things. Wholesomeness and foulness depend on qualities inherent in a thing; as long as it remains unchanged, it remains wholesome, and there is no basis for prohibiting it. Thus, if a drop of wine fell into a container, someone who drank from it would not be flogged.

Those who concede that legal analogy requires water to become impure upon contact with impurity draw several distinctions between contact occurring in the course of removing impurity and contact in other circumstances.

Some say: “Here, the water is applied to the impurity, whereas there, the impurity enters the water.” This is a weak argument, for if water were poured into an impure container, they would regard it as becoming impure.

Others say: “When water is being applied for purification, whether to remove physical impurity or a state of ritual impurity, it is not deemed impure or classified as used water until it separates from what is being purified. Before that separation, it is neither used nor impure.” This merely states a legal position; it provides no proof.

---

## Page 10342

Others say: “Water is flowing while it removes impurity, and flowing water does not become impure unless its properties change.” This is the position of Abū Hanīfa and Mālik, the more explicit of the two positions reported from Ahmad, and al-Shāfiʿī’s earlier view. Yet impurity is sometimes removed by flowing water and sometimes without it flowing, as when water is poured onto a garment in a basin.

The correct view, therefore, is that legal analogy requires that water not become impure unless its properties change. Impurity cannot be removed with it unless it is free of such change. While its properties remain altered, the water is impure, though it can reduce the impurity. Its removal, however, is achieved only with water whose properties are unaltered.

The same reasoning that applies to water applies to all liquids: they do not become impure if the impurity has undergone transformation within them and no trace of it remains, for they are then wholesome things, not foul things. This reasoning applies equally to small and large quantities of water, and to small and large quantities of other liquids. If evidence from the revealed law establishes that any such liquid is impure, we do not say that this contradicts legal analogy. Rather, we say that this indicates that the impurity has not undergone transformation.

For this reason, the strongest view concerning water is that of the scholars of Medina and Basra: it does not become impure unless its properties change. This is one of the positions reported from Imam Ahmad, supported by a group of his followers, including Imam Abū al-Wafā’ ibn ʿAqīl and Abū Muhammad ibn al-Manī.

---

## Page 10343

Likewise, water used to remove ritual impurity retains its purifying capacity. It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Water does not become impure.”

Water therefore does not itself enter a state of major ritual impurity, nor does the ruling associated with that state pass to it. His prohibition—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—against urinating or bathing in standing water does not indicate that the water becomes impure as a result. Rather, he prohibited it because repeated urination eventually spoils the water, or because it leads to obsessive doubts. Similarly, he forbade a man to urinate where he bathes, saying:

“Most obsessive doubts arise from that.”

As for his prohibition against bathing, one report states that he prohibited bathing in the water after urinating in it. This resembles his prohibition against urinating where one bathes.

It is also established in an authentic hadith that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter. He replied:

“Throw it away, along with what surrounds it, and eat your clarified butter.”

The distinction reported in the wording, “If it is solid, throw it away along with what surrounds it; but if it is liquid, do not go near it,” is an error, as al-Bukhārī, al-Tirmidhī and others have explained. It is an error made by Maʿmar in narrating this hadith.

Ibn ʿAbbās, who narrated it, ruled that if the mouse died, it and the surrounding butter should be discarded, and the rest could be eaten. It was said to them, “But it moved around in it.” He replied, “That was only while it was alive. Once it died, it stayed in one place.” Ahmad reported this in the Masāʾil (Legal Questions) of his son Sālih.

Likewise, al-Zuhrī, another narrator of the hadith, ruled that whether the substance was solid or liquid, small or large in quantity, and whether it was clarified butter, oil or something else, the mouse and whatever was close to it should be discarded, and the remainder could be eaten;

---

## Page 10344

and he cited the hadith as evidence. How, then, could he have narrated a version of it making that distinction?

The hadith concerning two qullahs, if authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also supports this. His statement,

“When water reaches two qullahs (large water jars), it does not carry impurity”—or, in another wording, “nothing renders it impure”—

indicates that what renders water impure is its carrying impurity. Whenever the impurity is completely absorbed into the water, it is no longer carried by it. Thus neither the explicit wording of the hadith nor its underlying rationale indicates that.

As for the specific mention of two qullahs, they had asked him about water in the wilderness frequented by wild beasts and other animals. Such water is ordinarily abundant. He therefore explained, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that water of this kind does not ordinarily contain impurity, unlike a small quantity, which may or may not carry impurity. An abundance of water helps transform the impurity into the water’s own nature. An inferred implication need not apply universally: the fact that two qullahs do not carry impurity does not mean that anything less must invariably carry it. Moreover, this quantity was specified in response to people asking about particular bodies of water. It may have been specified because those waters were abundant and did not carry impurity. Two qullahs constitute a large quantity, but it does not follow that only two qullahs can constitute a large quantity.

Otherwise, if this were a dividing line between the lawful and the unlawful, he would have stated it without waiting to be asked. Furthermore, thresholds established by Islamic law are known quantities, such as the zakat thresholds for gold and crops subject to the tithe, and the like. Yet the volume of water into which impurity falls can be known only by estimation; ordinarily, it cannot be measured. How, then, could a distinction be drawn between

---

## Page 10345

the lawful and the unlawful on the basis of something that most people cannot determine most of the time? In more than one hadith, he stated without qualification:

“Water is purifying; nothing renders it impure,”

and:

“Water does not acquire major ritual impurity.”

He specified no quantity, even though clarification may not be delayed beyond the time when it is needed. The explicit wording of this hadith agrees with those reports. Its implied meaning is authoritative—even according to those who accept such implications—only when there is no reason for singling something out for mention without restricting the ruling to it. The absence of such a reason has not been established here.

As for the hadith commanding that a vessel’s contents be poured away after a dog has lapped from it, this is because the vessels from which dogs ordinarily lap are small. A dog’s saliva is viscous: it remains in the water and clings to the vessel. The water is therefore poured away, and the vessel is washed to remove the saliva, which has not yet been transformed into another substance. This differs from a dog lapping from a large vessel. Harb reported from Ahmad, concerning a dog that had lapped from a large receptacle containing oil, that he instructed the owner to eat it. A detailed discussion of these questions belongs elsewhere. The purpose here is simply to draw attention to what contradicts analogical reasoning and what accords with it.

Section

The claim that purifying water is contrary to analogical reasoning rests on this unsound principle. Otherwise, for someone whose foundational principle is that analogical reasoning entails that water does not

---

## Page 10346

become impure unless its properties change, its purification accords with analogical reasoning. For when a ruling is established on account of an effective cause, it ceases when that cause disappears. If the effective cause is the change in the water’s properties, then once that change disappears, its impurity also disappears. Likewise, since the effective cause in wine is its intoxicating potency, it becomes pure when that potency disappears. This is all the more so because impurity is introduced into water from outside, just as it is into the ground.

One might, however, say that this rests on “the question of transformation,” over which there is a well-known disagreement. There are two positions within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad. The position of Abū Hanīfah and the literalists is that impure substances become pure through transformation, whereas al-Shāfiʿī’s position is that they do not.

The view that they become pure through transformation is more correct. When an impure substance becomes salt or ash, its essential nature has changed, as have its name and properties. The texts prohibiting carrion, blood, and pork do not apply to salt, ash, or earth, either in wording or in meaning. The quality that made those substances foul is absent from these substances, so there is no basis for declaring them foul and impure.

Those who distinguish between this and wine say: “Wine became impure through transformation, so it becomes pure through transformation.” They may be answered: “Likewise, urine, blood, and excrement became impure only through transformation, so they should become pure through transformation.”

Section

As for the claim that performing ablution after eating camel meat is contrary to analogical reasoning, the person making it says this only because camel meat is meat, and eating meat does not require ablution. Yet the Lawgiver has

---

## Page 10347

distinguished between sheep meat and camel meat, just as he distinguished between sheepfolds and the places where camels rest: he commanded prayer in the former and forbade it in the latter. To claim that analogical reasoning requires treating them alike is akin to the words of those who said:

“Trade is only like usury. But Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury.”

The distinction between them is real, just as he distinguished between camel owners and sheep owners, saying:

“Pride and arrogance are found among the loud-voiced camel owners, and tranquility among those who tend sheep.”

It is reported concerning camels that “they are jinn, created from jinn,” and it is also reported: “There is a devil atop every camel.” Camels thus possess a satanic force, and there is a resemblance between food and those who consume it.

This is why every fanged beast of prey and every bird with talons is forbidden: they are aggressive creatures, and eating them imparts aggression to a person’s character that harms his religious life. Allah therefore prohibited this, for the aim is that people uphold justice. When someone eats camel meat, it leaves a satanic force within him.

In the hadith recorded in the Sunan collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Anger comes from Satan, and Satan was created from fire. Fire is extinguished only with water.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “So when one of you becomes angry, let him perform ablution.”

When a servant performs ablution after eating camel meat, this extinguishes the satanic force sufficiently to remove its harmful effect. This is unlike someone who does not perform ablution after eating it, for the harmful effect remains with him. Thus it is said that the Bedouins, through eating camel meat without

---

## Page 10348

performing ablution afterward, have come to harbor the rancor they do. For this reason, “he commanded ablution after eating food touched by fire.” This is an authentic hadith. Yet authentic hadiths also establish that he ate food touched by fire without performing ablution afterward. It has therefore been said that the former ruling was abrogated. However, it has not been established that the former preceded the latter. Indeed, it was narrated by Abū Hurayrah, whose acceptance of Islam came after the events related in some of those hadiths, such as the report concerning parched-grain meal at Khaybar, which preceded his acceptance of Islam.

Another view is that the command to perform ablution after eating food touched by fire indicates recommendation, like the command to perform ablution when angry. This is the stronger of the two views, both of which are positions within Ahmad’s school. Abrogation should only be invoked when there is an irreconcilable conflict and an established chronology; neither is present here. By contrast, interpreting a command as indicating recommendation has many precedents.

Likewise, ablution after touching the penis or touching women belongs to this category, because such contact arouses desire. Performing ablution after something that arouses desire is like performing it because of anger or after eating food touched by fire: all belong to this category, for anger comes from Satan, and Satan was created from fire.

As for camel meat, it has been said that performing ablution after eating it is recommended. However, the Prophet’s distinction—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—between it and sheep meat, even though the latter has been touched by fire and ablution after eating it is recommended, indicates a distinct ruling. Nothing ranks above recommendation except obligation. Moreover, the satanic influence in camels is inherent, whereas in food touched by fire it is incidental. This is why he forbade prayer in their regular resting enclosures: Satan constantly accompanies them there. By contrast, prayer where they rest during travel is permissible, because this is only temporary. And latrines

---

## Page 10349

are frequented by jinn and devils, so there is even stronger reason to prohibit prayer there than in camel enclosures. Likewise, the bathhouse is the abode of Satan. Two positions are reported from Ahmad concerning ablution after eating unwholesome meats, depending on whether the ruling has an intelligible rationale and can therefore be extended to other cases, or not. Unwholesome foods permitted out of necessity, such as the meat of predatory animals, have a greater satanic influence than camel meat, so there is all the more reason to perform ablution after eating them.

Scholars have differed over ablution following the discharge of impurities from somewhere other than the two private passages, as in bloodletting, cupping, wounds, and vomiting; after touching women, with or without desire; after touching the penis; and after laughing aloud. Some Companions, such as Sa‘d and Ibn ‘Umar, would perform ablution after touching the penis, while many of them would not. Is ablution after this obligatory or recommended? Two positions are reported from both Mālik and Ahmad. Al-Shāfi‘ī held it to be obligatory, whereas Abū Hanīfah’s position is that it is not obligatory.

Likewise, regarding touching women with desire, the view that ablution is recommended is tenable. As for its being obligatory, however, the evidence supports only the contrary. No one can ever produce a report from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—that he used to command his Companions to perform ablution after touching women or after the discharge of impurities, despite how commonly these matters arise.

As for the words of Allah Most High,

“or you have touched women,”

they refer to sexual intercourse, as Ibn ‘Abbās and others explained

---

## Page 10350

for several reasons.

The Prophet’s statement—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—to the woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding,

“That is only bleeding from a vein, not menstruation,”

explains why a full ritual bath is not obligatory, not why ablution is obligatory. For the obligation to perform ablution is not specific to blood from veins. Rather, she had thought that this was menstrual blood, which necessitates a full ritual bath. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—therefore explained to her that this was not the menstrual blood that necessitates a full ritual bath: menstrual blood seeps from the womb like sweat, whereas this was blood from a vein that had burst in the womb. Bleeding from veins does not necessitate a full ritual bath. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere.

The purpose here is to point out the error of those who claim that the meanings or wording of the Sharia contain contradictions and allege that the Lawgiver treats like cases differently. Rather, our Prophet Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was sent with guidance and the religion of truth, with wisdom, justice, and mercy. He therefore distinguishes between two things in his rulings only when their attributes differ in a way that warrants that distinction, and treats two things alike only when their attributes are alike in a way that warrants equal treatment.

The stronger view is that ablution is not obligatory after touching the penis or women, the discharge of impurities from anywhere other than the two private passages, laughing aloud, or washing a deceased person. Those who consider it obligatory have no sound evidence; rather, the weightier evidence indicates that it is not obligatory. Nevertheless, there are clear grounds for considering it recommended. It is therefore recommended to perform ablution

---

## Page 10351

after touching women with desire. It is also recommended to perform ablution after cupping, vomiting, and similar occurrences, as reported in the Sunan collections:

“The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—vomited and then performed ablution.”

This action indicates only that doing so is recommended. It is not established that he commanded ablution after cupping, nor that he commanded his Companions to perform ablution when wounded, despite the frequency of their wounds. What is reported from the Companions is that they performed ablution, not that they considered it obligatory.

Likewise, laughing aloud during prayer is a sin, and anyone who commits a sin is encouraged to perform ablution. There are two views within the school of Ahmad and other schools concerning whether ablution after laughing aloud is recommended.

As for performing ablution for each prayer in cases of persistent ritual impurity, there are several hadiths from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—some of which have been authenticated by more than one scholar. Thus, the majority’s view that ablution is obligatory for each prayer is better supported. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad. And Allah knows best.

Section

As for cupping, only those who believe that the fast is broken by what leaves the body, not by what enters it, have considered its being broken by cupping contrary to analogy. Such people have found vomiting, wet dreams, menstrual bleeding, and postnatal bleeding problematic.

---

## Page 10352

But whoever reflects on the foundations and purposes of Islamic law will see that, when the Lawgiver commanded fasting, he also prescribed moderation in it: he discouraged continuing a fast into the next day without breaking it, commanded hastening to break the fast and delaying the predawn meal, and made David’s fast the most balanced and excellent form of fasting. Part of this balance is that a person should not expel what sustains his strength. Vomiting expels nourishment, deliberately inducing ejaculation expels semen, and menstruation expels blood; these substances sustain the body.

However, the Lawgiver distinguished between what can be avoided and what cannot. Wet dreams cannot be avoided, nor can vomiting that overcomes a person. The same applies to non-menstrual bleeding, since it has no fixed time, unlike menstrual bleeding, which does. A person undergoing cupping has his blood drawn, as does someone undergoing bloodletting. This differs from someone whose blood flows involuntarily, such as a wounded person, for this cannot be avoided. Thus, cupping belongs to the same category as vomiting, deliberately inducing ejaculation, and menstruation, while bleeding from a wound belongs to the same category as non-menstrual bleeding, wet dreams, and involuntary vomiting. The rulings of Islamic law are therefore consistent and harmonious, and do not depart from analogy.

The stronger view is that the fast is not broken by applying kohl, instilling drops into the urethra, or swallowing something non-nourishing, such as a pebble. It is, however, broken by using nasal preparations, because the Prophet said:

“Draw water thoroughly into the nose, unless you are fasting.”

---

## Page 10353

Section

As for their claim that salam (a sale against advance payment) is contrary to analogy, this resembles their report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not sell what you do not have,”

and granted a concession for salam. This latter statement is not transmitted in the hadith; rather, it is the wording of some jurists. They reasoned that salam involves selling what one does not have and is therefore contrary to analogy.

The Prophet’s prohibition to Hakīm ibn Hizām against selling what he did not have may refer to selling a specifically identified item, in which case he would be selling someone else’s property before purchasing it—though this interpretation is open to question. Alternatively, it may refer to selling something one cannot deliver, even if it is owed as a contractual obligation. This interpretation is more plausible: he would be undertaking to supply something without knowing whether he could obtain it. This applies to salam with immediate delivery when the seller does not have what he needs to fulfil his obligation, and the rationale here is evident.

As for salam with deferred delivery, it is simply a debt, like other debts, and resembles a purchase with deferred payment. What difference is there between one consideration being owed as a deferred obligation and the other being owed in the same way?

Allah Most High says:

“When you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down.”

Ibn 'Abbās said: “I testify that a guaranteed sale against advance payment

---

## Page 10354

owed as a contractual obligation is lawful according to the Book of Allah.” He then recited this verse. Permitting this therefore accords with analogy rather than contradicting it.

Section

As for kitāba (contractual emancipation), those who say that it is contrary to analogy argue that it amounts to selling one’s own property in exchange for one’s own property.

This is not so. Rather, the master sells the slave to himself for a sum that becomes his contractual liability. The master has no claim upon the slave’s capacity to incur obligations; his claim pertains only to his person. The master’s right concerns the slave’s proprietary value as a human being. Insofar as he is subject to commands and prohibitions, however, the slave is a morally accountable human being. Faith, prayer and fasting are therefore obligatory upon him because he is human. Dhimma means a binding covenant. The slave is only required to discharge the obligations he has incurred after his emancipation, when the master no longer owns him.

Contractual emancipation thus consists of selling the slave to himself for a sum he undertakes to pay. Once he has purchased himself, his earnings and the benefit of his labour belong to him. These accrue under the ownership to which the emancipation contract has entitled him. Nevertheless, he is not emancipated under this contract except with permission, because the master has only agreed to relinquish ownership of him on condition that the slave deliver the payment. Whenever the master does not receive that payment and the slave is unable to make it, the master is entitled to reclaim what he sold. This accords with analogy in exchange contracts.

For this reason, he says: If the purchaser cannot pay the price because of insolvency, the seller is entitled to reclaim what he sold. A slave under an emancipation contract is purchasing himself, so his inability to make the payment is like that of any purchaser. This analogy applies to all exchange contracts: whenever

---

## Page 10355

a party to an exchange cannot provide the consideration he owes, the other party is entitled to reclaim what he provided. This includes a man’s inability to pay the dower and a husband’s inability to have intercourse. Extending the same principle also covers a man’s inability to provide the consideration in khulʿ (divorce in exchange for compensation) or in a settlement in lieu of legal retaliation.

Section

As for contracts of hire, those who regard them as contrary to analogy argue that they constitute the sale of something nonexistent: the benefits do not exist when the contract is concluded, and selling something nonexistent is impermissible. Yet the Quran expressly mentions hiring a wet nurse to breastfeed, in the words of the Most High:

“If they breastfeed for you, then give them their payment.”

Many jurists therefore say that hiring a wet nurse to breastfeed runs contrary to the analogy governing contracts of hire. Such contracts concern benefits, whereas hiring a wet nurse is a contract for milk, and milk belongs to the category of tangible property, not benefits. Remarkably, this is the only permissible contract of hire mentioned in the Quran, yet they say that it is contrary to analogy! Something can only be contrary to analogy when a revealed text establishes a ruling in one case and another text establishes the opposite ruling in a similar case. One may then say: “This runs contrary to the analogy drawn from that text.”

The Quran mentions no invalid contract of hire that would warrant saying: “Analogy requires that this contract of hire be invalid.” Rather, it mentions the permissibility of this contract, without mentioning the invalidity of any similar contract of hire. Nor does the Sunnah identify any invalid contract of hire resembling this one. Rather, the basis of their position is

---

## Page 10356

their assumption that a legally valid contract of hire concerns only benefits, which are accidents, and not tangible things, which are bodies. We shall, Allah willing, explain how this misconception is dispelled.

Since these jurists believed that hiring a wet nurse was contrary to analogy, some sought contrived ways to bring it into conformity with the analogy they accepted. They said: “The subject of the contract is placing the breast in the infant’s mouth, putting the infant in her lap, or similar benefits that are preliminaries to breastfeeding.” Yet it is well known that these acts are merely means to the intended purpose of the contract of hire. In themselves, they are neither sought nor contracted for; indeed, they have no value at all on their own. They are merely like opening the door for someone who has rented a house or shop, or mounting an animal for someone who has hired it. The purpose in the former case is occupancy, and in the latter, riding. These acts are merely preliminaries and means to the purpose intended by the contract.

Those who regarded hiring a wet nurse as contrary to analogy then extended this reasoning to such things as water from wells and springs that flow from the ground. They said: “These are included in the contract implicitly and as ancillary matters.” Even when the contract concerns the water itself—as when someone contracts for a flowing spring to irrigate his orchard or channel its water to his premises to drink from it and benefit from its water—they say: “The subject of the contract is conveying the water through the land,” or offer similar contrived explanations. Thus they exclude the water, the very thing intended by these contracts, from being the subject of the contract.

---

## Page 10357

We shall now address these two underlying claims: that contracts of hire are contrary to analogy, and that hiring a wet nurse and similar arrangements are contrary to analogy.

As for the first, we say: Their assertion, “A contract of hire is the sale of something nonexistent, and selling something nonexistent is contrary to analogy,” consists of two ambiguous premises involving equivocation.

When they say that a contract of hire is a sale, if they mean sale in the specific sense of a contract concerning tangible things, this is false. If they mean sale in the general sense of an exchange for consideration, whether involving a tangible thing or a benefit, then their second premise—that selling something nonexistent is impermissible—can be conceded, if at all, only with respect to tangible things, not benefits. Since the word “sale” admits both meanings, jurists have differed over whether a contract of hire may be concluded using the word “sale,” holding two views on the matter.

The correct position is that if the contracting parties understand what is intended, the contract is concluded. Whatever wording enables both parties to understand their intended agreement suffices to conclude the contract. This applies to all contracts, for the Lawgiver has imposed no fixed limits on their wording, but has mentioned them without qualification. Just as contracts may be concluded through Persian, Greek, or other non-Arabic expressions that signify them, they may also be concluded through Arabic expressions that signify them. Accordingly, divorce and manumission take effect through any wording that signifies them; the same applies to sale and other transactions. This principle also extends to marriage, for the sounder of the two scholarly views is that it may be concluded through any wording

---

## Page 10358

that signifies it; it is not restricted to the terms inkāh and tazwīj (giving in marriage). This is the position of the majority of scholars, including Abū Hanīfah and Mālik, and one of the two views within Ahmad’s school. Indeed, his explicit statements support only this position. The other view—that marriage may be concluded only through the terms inkāh and tazwīj—is that of Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Hāmid and his followers, such as Judge Abū Ya‘lā and those who followed him.

The early scholars of Ahmad’s school, and the majority of its adherents, did not hold this latter view. Ahmad explicitly stated on several occasions that if a man says, “I have freed my slave woman and made her emancipation her dower,” the marriage is concluded, although neither inkāh nor tazwīj appears in this wording. Hence Ibn ‘Aqīl and others observed that this indicates that marriage is not restricted to a particular expression.

Ibn Hāmid, however, consistently applied his own position, saying that the man must also say, “And I have married her.” Judge Abū Ya‘lā treated this as an exception to analogy, allowing marriage in this instance without the terms inkāh and tazwīj. Yet Imam Ahmad’s principles and explicit statements contradict this approach. One of his principles is that contracts are concluded through any words or actions that indicate their intended purpose; he does not regard them as restricted to prescribed formulas. Another of his principles is that indirect wording, when accompanied by contextual indications, is equivalent to explicit wording and requires no declaration of intent. He therefore applied this principle to divorce, accusations of unchastity, and other matters.

Those followers of al-Shāfi‘ī who held that marriage may be concluded only through the terms inkāh and tazwīj argued: “This is because anything other than these two expressions is indirect wording, and indirect wording does not establish

---

## Page 10359

its legal effect except through intent. Intent is inward, whereas marriage requires witnesses, and testimony concerns only what is heard.” This is the basis adopted by those followers of al-Shāfi‘ī who restrict the marriage contract to these two expressions. Ibn Hāmid and his followers agreed with them. However, Ahmad’s principles and explicit statements contradict this, for these premises are invalid according to his principles.

As for the assertion that anything other than these two expressions is indirect wording, this would hold only if the classification of expressions as explicit or indirect were determined by scriptural usage. This is the position of al-Shāfi‘ī and those followers of Ahmad who agreed with him, such as al-Khiraqī, Judge Abū Ya‘lā, and others: they maintain that the explicit expressions of divorce are talāq (divorce), firāq (separation), and sarāh (release), because these occur in the Quran.

The majority of scholars, however—including Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, and others—and the majority of Ahmad’s followers, including Abū Bakr, Ibn Hāmid, Abū al-Khattāb, and others, do not accept this principle. Some maintain that the only explicit expression is talāq, including Abū Hanīfah, Ibn Hāmid, Abū al-Khattāb, other followers of Ahmad, and some followers of al-Shāfi‘ī. Others maintain that explicit wording extends beyond these expressions, as is reported from Mālik. This is also the position of Abū Bakr and other followers of Ahmad. The majority say: “Both of the aforementioned premises—that explicit divorce wording is followed by an invalid premise.”

As for their claim that these expressions are explicit in the Lawgiver’s speech, that is not

---

## Page 10360

the case. Rather, the expressions “release” and “separation” are used in the Quran for something other than divorce. Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, you have no waiting period to count for them. So provide for them and release them graciously.”

He thus commands that they be released after being divorced before consummation. Such a divorce is irrevocable, with no right to take them back. By the consensus of the Muslims, “release” here does not mean pronouncing divorce. Allah Most High also says:

“When you divorce women and they approach the end of their waiting period, retain them honourably.”

And in the other verse:

“Or part with them honourably.”

The expressions “separation” and “release” here do not mean divorce. In the case of a revocably divorced woman, the husband may either take her back or let her go her way; no second divorce is required.

As for the second premise, an expression’s being explicit in the Lawgiver’s speech does not entail that it is explicit in the speech of everyone who uses it.

A fuller discussion belongs elsewhere. The point here is that if someone says, “Leasing is a type of sale,” and means sale in its specific sense—which is what the unqualified word “sale” ordinarily conveys—then this is not so. Such a sale concerns only specified assets or assets owed as a liability. If, however, he means that leasing is a form of exchange in the broad sense, encompassing contracts concerning both assets and usufructs, then this is correct. But his assertion that exchange in this broad sense cannot concern something nonexistent is an unsupported claim—indeed, a false one—for the Lawgiver has permitted exchange in this broad sense involving what does not yet exist. And if he compares the sale of usufructs

---

## Page 10361

to the sale of assets and argues, “Just as assets can be sold only when they exist, so too can usufructs”—which is what his argument really amounts to—then this analogy is utterly unsound. A condition of valid analogy is that the ruling governing the original case must be applicable to the new case. Here, however, that is impossible, because usufructs cannot be made the subject of a contract while they exist. It is therefore inconceivable that usufructs should be sold while they exist in the same way that assets are sold while they exist.

The Lawgiver has instructed people to postpone contracts concerning assets not yet created until they have been created. Thus, He prohibited sales of future years’ crops, the sale known as habal al-habalah, sales of fruit before its ripeness becomes apparent, and sales of grain before it hardens. He also prohibited sales of al-madāmīn and al-malāqīh, and al-majr, meaning what is carried in the womb. All these are prohibitions against selling animals before they have been created, or grain and fruit before they have been created; He commanded that their sale be postponed until they have been created.

This distinction—prohibiting its sale in one circumstance and leasing it in another—cannot apply to usufructs, since they can be sold only in this manner. Thus, the ruling governing the original case no longer matches that governing the new case. The only remaining argument would be to say, “Then I draw an analogy between it and the sale of nonexistent assets.”

The reply is: “There are two things here. One can be sold both when it exists and when it does not, but the Lawgiver has prohibited its sale unless it exists. The other can be sold only while it does not exist. Since the Lawgiver prohibited selling the former while it does not exist, it is necessary, if

---

## Page 10362

you draw an analogy with it, that the effective cause underlying the ruling in the original case must also be present in the new case. Why, then, do you say that the effective cause in the original case is mere nonexistence? Why could it not instead be selling something while it does not exist when its sale could be postponed until it exists? On this understanding, the effective cause is restricted to a particular kind of nonexistence: that of something which can be sold after it comes into existence. Unless you establish that the effective cause in the original case is the feature shared by both cases, your analogy is unsound. This demand for proof is sufficient to halt your analogy.

But we can also demonstrate its invalidity as follows: the cause we have identified applies consistently, whereas the cause you have identified admits of counterexamples. If you explain the prohibition by mere nonexistence, certain assets and usufructs invalidate your proposed cause. But if you explain it by the nonexistence of something whose sale can be postponed until it exists, or by nonexistence involving uncertainty, the cause applies consistently. Moreover, this cause is supported by its suitability to the ruling.

For if something has both a state of existence and a state of nonexistence, selling it while nonexistent involves risk and gambling. This is the reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, gave for the prohibition when he said:

‘Tell me: if Allah withholds the fruit, on what grounds does any one of you take his brother’s wealth without right?’

This is unlike something that has only one state and is ordinarily free from harm: this does not involve risk, and there is a need for it. One of the principles of Islamic law is that when benefit and harm conflict, whichever outweighs the other takes precedence. He prohibited sales involving uncertainty only because they involve risk that harms one of the two parties, whereas in

---

## Page 10363

preventing them from engaging in sales they need causes even greater harm. He therefore does not spare them slight harm at the cost of exposing them to severe harm. Rather, the greater of two harms is averted by bearing the lesser. Thus, although he prohibited muzābana sales because they involve a form of usury or harmful risk, he permitted them in the case of ‘arāyā sales because of people’s need, since the harm of prohibiting these is greater. Likewise, although he forbade them carrion because of its unwholesomeness as food, he permitted it in cases of necessity, because the harm of death is greater. There are many similar examples.

If it is asked, “But is not all of this contrary to analogy?”

The reply is: We have already explained that the new case possesses a particular feature requiring it to be distinguished from the original case. Every valid distinction runs counter to an invalid analogy. If, however, what is meant is that the original and new cases are identical in the factors that entail the ruling and those that preclude it, yet their rulings differ, this is categorically false.

In short, when one thing resembles another in one respect but differs from it in another, assigning them different rulings on account of their distinguishing feature runs counter to treating them alike on account of their shared feature. Yet this is precisely sound analogy, in both directions: treating like cases alike and distinguishing between unlike cases. By contrast, assigning both the same ruling despite their differing in what entails or precludes that ruling is an invalid analogy. Islamic law invariably invalidates unsound analogies, such as the analogy drawn by Iblīs and that drawn by

---

## Page 10364

the polytheists who said:

“Trade is only like usury,”

and those who compared carrion to properly slaughtered animals, saying, “Do you eat what you yourselves have killed, yet refuse to eat what Allah has killed?” They thus took the determining factor in the original case to be its having been killed by a human being. Another example is the analogy drawn by those who compared the Messiah to their idols, saying, “Since our gods will enter the Fire because they were worshipped besides Allah, the Messiah should likewise enter the Fire.” Allah Most High said:

“When the son of Mary was cited as an example, your people burst into laughter.”

“They said, ‘Are our gods better, or is he?’ They cited him to you only for argument’s sake. Indeed, they are a contentious people.”

This was the basis of Ibn al-Ziba'rā’s argument when Allah revealed:

“Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell. You will enter it.”

“Had these been gods, they would not have entered it. And all will remain there forever.”

The address here is to the polytheists, not the People of the Book. The polytheists did not worship the Messiah; they worshipped only idols. What is meant by His words, “what you worship,” is the idols. Thus, the verse did not include the Messiah, either in its wording or in its meaning.

Whoever claims that the verse is general and includes the Messiah, but that clarification of his exclusion was delayed, is mistaken. Had that been correct, the polytheists’ argument would have been valid. For anyone who addresses others in general terms encompassing both truth and falsehood, without clarifying his intent, leaves himself open to objection. Yet Allah Most High said:

“When the son of Mary was cited as an example.”

That is, they were the ones who cited him as an example, as He said:

“They cited him to you only for argument’s sake.”

That is, they made him an example with which to compare their gods, drew an analogy between their gods and him, and put him forward as a counterexample

---

## Page 10365

saying:

“If our gods enter the Fire because they are worshipped, this same attribute is present in the Messiah, so he too must enter the Fire. Yet he will not enter the Fire; therefore, neither will they.”

This is a false analogy, based on their assumption that the determining factor is merely being worshipped. That is not so. Rather, the determining factor is being an object of worship that does not deserve reward, or an object of worship whose admission into the Fire involves no injustice. The Messiah, Ezra, the angels, and others worshipped besides Allah who are among His righteous servants deserve honour from Allah by virtue of His promise, justice, and wisdom.
