They are therefore not punished for another’s sin, for no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another. The purpose of casting idols into the Fire is to humiliate their worshippers, whereas those close to Allah are granted honour, not humiliation. This distinction exposes the error of basing the ruling on that shared attribute. False analogies are of this kind.

Whoever says that the Sharia runs contrary to an analogy of this kind is correct. This is part of the Sharia’s perfection and its embodiment of the justice and wisdom with which Allah sent His Messenger. Whoever does not reject such false analogies, but instead treats two things as equal merely because they share some attribute, must consequently treat every two existing things as equal, since both fall under the designation of existence. He would thus equate the Lord of all worlds with some of

---

## Page 10366

His creatures, thereby becoming one of those who set up equals to their Lord and associate partners with Him. This is among the gravest forms of false analogy. Such people say:

“By Allah, we were clearly astray
when we made you equal to the Lord of all worlds.”

For this reason, some of the early generations said: “The first to employ analogy was Iblīs, and the sun and moon were worshipped only through analogies.” That is, analogies of this kind, in which something is likened to what differs from it, as in the analogies of the polytheists. Anyone acquainted with people’s discussions of rational matters will see that most of the error of those philosophers and speculative theologians who went astray arose from such false analogies. In these, two things are equated because they share certain attributes, despite differences between them that entail the greatest divergence. Consider their discussions of the existence of the Lord and the existence of created beings: these contain inconsistencies that we have discussed at length elsewhere.

What we have said about leasing assumes, for the sake of argument, their assertion that the sale of nonexistent objects is impermissible. This is the second premise, which may be addressed in two ways.

The first is to say: We do not concede the validity of this premise. There is nothing in the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Messenger—nor, indeed, anything reported from any of the Companions—stating that the sale of nonexistent things

---

## Page 10367

is impermissible, whether stated in general terms or conveyed by general implication. Rather, there are prohibitions against selling certain nonexistent things, just as there are prohibitions against selling certain existing things. Neither existence nor nonexistence is the reason for the prohibition. What is authentically reported, rather, is:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited sales involving uncertainty.”

Such uncertainty concerns something one cannot deliver, whether it exists or not, such as a runaway slave, a straying camel, and similar things that one may be unable to deliver. Anything that may or may not be obtained involves uncertainty and may not be sold, even if it exists. A sale requires delivery of the item sold, yet the seller is unable to deliver it. The buyer is merely taking a risk and gambling: if he manages to obtain it, he has won his gamble against the seller; if he cannot obtain it, the seller has won his gamble against him.

Likewise, the sale of a nonexistent thing involving uncertainty was prohibited because of its uncertainty, not because it does not exist. An example is selling whatever offspring a particular animal will bear, or whatever produce a particular orchard will yield. It may or may not produce anything; and if it does, neither the quantity nor the characteristics of what it produces are known. This is wagering, a form of the gambling that Allah has forbidden.

The same applies if someone leases out animals that he cannot deliver, or real estate that he cannot hand over: it may or may not become available. This is a lease involving uncertainty.

---

## Page 10368

The second point is this:

On the contrary, the Lawgiver has validated the sale of nonexistent things in certain circumstances. It is established through several chains of transmission:

“He prohibited selling fruit until signs of ripeness appear.”

“He prohibited selling grain until it hardens.”

These reports are among the most authentic hadiths and are recorded in al-Sahīh from several Companions. He distinguished between the appearance of signs of ripeness and their absence, permitting sale in one case and prohibiting it in the other.

It is well known that, before signs of ripeness appear, purchasing the fruit on condition that it be harvested is permissible by agreement—as when someone buys unripe grapes to pick them while still unripe. The prohibition applies only when it is sold on the understanding that it will be left in place. This indicates that, once signs of ripeness appear, he permitted its sale with the understanding that it would remain until fully ripe. This is the position of the majority of scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others.

Anyone who permits its sale in both cases on condition that it be harvested, but prohibits it on condition that it be left in place, or without either stipulation, gives no significance to the appearance of signs of ripeness and draws no distinction between what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited and what he permitted.

The proponent of this view says: “The contract entails delivery immediately upon its conclusion, so delay is impermissible.”

The response is: “We do not concede that this is what the contract entails. Such an obligation must arise either from what the Lawgiver has made binding through the contract or from what the contracting parties have undertaken to do. Neither applies here. The Lawgiver has not required delivery immediately upon the conclusion of every sale, nor have the contracting parties committed themselves to that. Sometimes they conclude the contract on this basis, as when a specified item is sold for a price payable immediately; at other times, they stipulate deferred payment of the price

---

## Page 10369

as in a salam sale; the same applies to specified items. A seller may have a legitimate purpose in delaying delivery, as Jābir did when he sold his camel to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, reserving the right to ride it to Medina. Thus, the correct view is that any contracting party may reserve whatever use of the subject matter serves a legitimate purpose. For example, someone may sell a property while reserving the right to live in it for a period; sell his riding animals while reserving the right to ride them; give away property while reserving its use; free a slave while reserving his service for a period or for the remainder of the master’s life; or establish an endowment while reserving its income for himself during his lifetime, and so forth.

This is the expressly stated position of Ahmad and others. Some of Ahmad’s followers, however, said that anyone who reserves the use of an item he sells must first deliver it to the buyer and then take it back to enjoy that use. This rests on the unsound principle that entitlement to possession must necessarily arise immediately upon conclusion of the contract. It is a weak position.

On the same principle, some maintained that a lease is valid only for a term beginning immediately after the contract is concluded. They observed what people sometimes do and made it binding upon them in every circumstance. This is unsound analogical reasoning.

They also based their rulings concerning the sale of leased property on this principle. Some said that the sale is invalid because the right to use the property is not included in the sale, so delivery cannot take place.

Others said that this is an exclusion established by the Sharia, unlike an exclusion stipulated by contract. Yet if someone sells a married slave woman, the sale is valid by their agreement, even though the benefit of

---

## Page 10370

sexual relations belongs to her husband. Those who distinguish between the two cases have offered grounds explained in detail elsewhere.

The point here is that all these rulings derive from that weak principle: that a contract necessarily confers entitlement to delivery immediately upon its conclusion. The Sharia provides no evidence for this principle. Rather, taking possession of tangible property and rights of use is like receiving what is owed: sometimes the contract requires receipt immediately after its conclusion, insofar as possible, and sometimes it requires delivery to be delayed for a legitimate purpose.

Accordingly, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, permitted the sale of fruit once it begins to ripen, with the buyer entitled to leave it until it is fully ripe. The seller must water and tend it until then. This includes what does not yet exist and has not yet been created. Taking possession of such fruit is comparable to taking possession of leased property: it permits the buyer to dispose of it according to the stronger of the scholars’ two opinions, which is also the more correct of the two positions reported from Ahmad. Taking possession does not, however, transfer the risk of loss to the buyer. Rather, if the fruit perishes after it has begun to ripen, the loss is borne by the seller. This is the position of the scholars of Medina, including Mālik and others, and of the scholars of hadith, including Ahmad—may Allah be pleased with him—and others. It is also a view held conditionally by al-Shāfiʿī. It is authentically reported in Sahīh Muslim that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“If you sell fruit to your brother and a calamity strikes it, it is not lawful for you to take any of your brother’s money. On what grounds would any of you take his brother’s money without right?”

Those who disagree have no evidence from the Sharia that every taking of possession which permits disposal transfers the risk of loss, and that taking possession which does not permit

---

## Page 10371

disposal does not transfer the risk of loss. Rather, taking possession of leased property permits its disposal without transferring the risk of loss.

The sale of cucurbit crops falls into the same category. Some scholars permit their sale only one picking at a time, because selling them otherwise involves selling something not yet in existence. They regard this as selling fruit before it begins to ripen.

Some of these scholars further say that selling the plants together with their roots is like selling the trees themselves together with their fruit, which is permissible before the fruit begins to ripen. They cite the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in a hadith agreed to be authentic:

“Whoever sells date palms that have been pollinated, their fruit belongs to the seller unless the buyer stipulates that it is his.”

If the buyer stipulates that the fruit is included, it becomes part of the sale. Here, selling fruit before it begins to ripen is permissible as an adjunct to the sale of the trees themselves. For this reason, tending it is the buyer’s responsibility. It is well known, however, that in the case of trees, the trees themselves are what is sought, whereas with cucurbit crops, it is the produce that is sought. The two therefore cannot be treated as analogous.

Other scholars permit the sale of cucurbit crops. This is the view of Mālik and others, and one position within Ahmad’s school. This is the more correct view, since these crops cannot be sold in any other way: one picking cannot be distinguished from another. As explained above, when something can be sold in only one way, its sale is not prohibited. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, only forbade the sale of fruits whose sale could be deferred until they begin to ripen. Cucurbit crops therefore do not fall under his prohibition.

For this reason, many scholars have included orchard contracts under his prohibition. They say that if an orchard is contracted out for a specified sum to someone who tends it until it bears fruit, this constitutes a sale

---

## Page 10372

of fruit before it begins to ripen, and is therefore impermissible. Some have claimed a consensus prohibiting this, but their claim is incorrect. Rather, it is established that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, contracted out Usayd ibn Hudayr’s orchard for three years, taking the payment in advance and using it to settle a debt owed by Usayd, since he was his executor.

Ibn ʿAqīl permitted such orchard contracts alongside leases of agricultural land when the two could not be separated. Mālik permitted this as an adjunct to the land, up to one third. An incident such as this involving ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb would ordinarily become widely known, yet no objection from any of the Companions has been reported. The correct position, therefore, is what ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb did, for the distinction between a sale and an orchard contract is the distinction between a sale and a lease.

Do you not see that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade selling grain before it hardens? Yet leasing land to cultivate it is permissible, even though the lessee seeks the grain. He seeks, however, to obtain it through his own work, not the seller’s work. Likewise, someone who leases an orchard to tend and water its trees until they bear fruit is in the position of a lessee, not that of a buyer who purchases fruit while the seller bears the expense of tending and watering the trees.

If it is said:

“These are tangible goods, whereas a lease cannot have tangible goods themselves as its subject.”

The reply is:

The answer is twofold. First, these tangible goods were produced through his own work from the leased asset

---

## Page 10373

just as grain is produced through his work on leased land. If it is said, “The grain comes from his own seed, whereas the fruit comes from the lessor’s trees,” this is a distinction with no effect in Islamic law. Do you not see that fruit-sharing contracts are analogous to crop-sharing contracts? The worker tending the trees is entitled to a share of the fruit produced by the owner’s trees, and the cultivator is entitled to a share of the crops growing on the owner’s land, even when the seed belongs to the owner. The same applies when the cultivator supplies the seed, as established by the Sunnah and the consensus of the Companions. The seed is consumed and does not return to its owner.

It is established in the authentic hadith collection that:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, contracted with the people of Khaybar for half of its yield of fruit and crops, on condition that they cultivate it at their own expense.”

The land, date palms, and water belonged to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Through their work, they became entitled to a share of the fruit just as they became entitled to a share of the crops, even though they supplied the seed while the trees belonged to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It is therefore clear that this distinction has no effect in Islamic law. If it has no effect in fruit-sharing and crop-sharing contracts, where the yield is shared, then it has even less effect in a lease. Leasing land is not subject to the same degree of disagreement as crop-sharing. Thus, if leasing land is more clearly permissible than crop-sharing, leasing trees is more clearly permissible than fruit-sharing.

The second answer:

We say that this is comparable to hiring a wet nurse, leasing a well, and similar arrangements. Discussing this brings us to the second principle governing leases. We therefore say: whoever claims that hiring a wet nurse is contrary to legal analogy does so only because he believes that

---

## Page 10374

a lease can concern only intangible benefits and cannot confer entitlement to tangible things. Yet nothing in the Quran, the Sunnah, consensus, or legal analogy supports this restriction. Rather, the foundational principles establish that tangible things produced gradually while their source remains are governed by the same rules as benefits of use, as with fruit and trees, and milk in animals.

For this reason, the two are treated alike in endowments. The governing principle is to retain the underlying property and dedicate its benefit. The underlying property must therefore remain, while its benefit arises from it. Thus, the benefit of an endowment may be a right of use, such as residence; it may be fruit, as when trees are endowed; or it may be milk, as when livestock are endowed so that their milk may be used.

The same applies to “gratuitous transfers.” Loans for use, fruit grants, and milk grants all involve giving property to someone who benefits from it and then returns it. A milk grant consists in giving livestock to someone who drinks their milk and then returns them. A fruit grant consists in giving a tree to someone who eats its fruit and then returns it. A grant of residence consists in giving a house to someone who lives in it and then returns it.

Likewise, in leasing, one sometimes leases property for a benefit that is not itself a tangible thing, such as residence or riding, and sometimes for tangible things produced gradually while their source remains, such as a wet nurse’s milk or the water of a well or spring. Since water and milk are produced gradually while their source remains, they are treated like benefits of use. What justifies leasing is the feature shared by both: the gradual production of what the contract is intended to provide, whether what arises is a tangible thing or a benefit of use, since the fact that it is

---

## Page 10375

a physical substance or a quality inhering in one has no bearing on permissibility, since both share the grounds that make the transaction permissible. Indeed, contracting for tangible things is even more deserving of permissibility, for physical substances are more complete than their attributes, and a contract concerning them can only be concluded in this manner. This principle is applied more extensively to hiring a wet nurse than to hiring an animal for suckling. A wet nurse may be hired for a specified wage, for her food and clothing, or with her food and clothing forming part of her wage.

As for livestock, when a contract is concluded for their milk in exchange for payment, the milk may be purchased with the owner remaining responsible for feeding and tending the animals, or with those responsibilities falling upon the purchaser. This second arrangement resembles contracting for the produce of orchards and is more akin to a lease. The milk is given to the infant to drink and is consumed as he benefits from it, just as someone leases a spring to irrigate his land with its water. This differs from the case of someone who takes delivery of the milk itself, since he thereby takes possession of the very thing contracted for. Calling one transaction a sale and the other a lease is merely a verbal dispute; what matters is their intended substance.

Some jurists, however, hold that differences in wording affect a contract’s validity or invalidity. Some even deem a contract valid when expressed in one form but not another. Thus, some say that a salam (advance-payment sale) contract stipulating immediate delivery is impermissible, yet permit it when concluded using the wording of a sale.

Others say that sharecropping is impermissible when the cultivator supplies the seed, yet permit the arrangement when concluded using the wording of a lease. This is the view of some jurists of Ahmad’s school. It is a weak position, for what matters

---

## Page 10376

in contracts is their intended substance. If the intended meaning is the same in both cases, permitting a transaction when expressed in one wording but not another is like permitting it in one language but not another. Admittedly, if one expression entails a ruling that the other does not, that is a different matter. This is not the place to discuss these questions at length.

The purpose here is simply to draw attention to what is described as agreeing with analogy or running counter to it. When the Lawgiver treats two things alike—as He does hiring someone to breastfeed and hiring someone to provide a service—the distinction between them, namely that one involves a tangible substance and the other a benefit, has no bearing on the ruling. Conversely, when He distinguishes between two things, their shared feature cannot, by itself, be the basis of the ruling; rather, the distinguishing feature has an effect.

Section

Another example is the claim that requiring the ‘āqila (the group responsible for paying blood money) to bear blood money runs counter to analogy.

The response is this: undoubtedly, whoever causes a loss requiring compensation is personally liable for it. Scholars disagree, however, over blood money: does the ‘āqila bear it as a primary obligation, or as a liability assumed on another’s behalf? Similarly, they disagree over zakāt al-fitr that a person must pay on another’s behalf, such as for his wife or child: is it a primary obligation upon him, or one assumed on their behalf? There is a well-known disagreement about this within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere. This distinction determines the ruling when the person on whose behalf it is due pays it without the permission of

---

## Page 10377

the person upon whom it is incumbent. Those who hold that it is incumbent upon that person as a liability assumed on another’s behalf say that the payment suffices. Those who hold that it is his primary obligation say that this is like paying zakāt on someone else’s behalf.

For the same reason, they disagree over blood money when there is no ‘āqila: does it become a personal liability of the killer or not? Blood money differs from other financial obligations in several respects that warrant its distinctive ruling. The blood money payable for someone killed is a large sum. The ‘āqila bears liability for accidental killing, not intentional killing, without disagreement on the latter. There is disagreement concerning quasi-intentional killing, and the stronger view is that the ‘āqila does not bear liability for it.

A person is excused for an accident. Requiring him to pay blood money from his own wealth would therefore cause him great harm despite his having committed no deliberate sin. Yet compensation for the person killed must be required. The Lawgiver has therefore required those who owe the killer allegiance and support to help him meet this obligation. This resembles the obligation to provide maintenance for relatives, or support for the poor and needy, and the obligation to ransom a captive from enemy territory. For this person is held captive by the blood money he owes. That obligation has arisen neither by his choice nor by that of the person entitled to it, unlike debts arising from loans and sales.

Nor is blood money generally a small sum, as compensation for damaged property is. Accidentally destroying property worth as much as blood money is exceedingly rare, unlike accidentally killing a person. When the intentional act causes loss of life or property, the person responsible is a wrongdoer deserving punishment. When damage to property is accidental, the amount is ordinarily small—unlike blood money.

---

## Page 10378

For this reason, the majority hold that the ‘āqila bears liability only for substantial sums. According to Mālik and Ahmad, it does not bear liability for anything below one-third of the full blood money; according to Abū Hanīfah, for anything below the compensation due for a tooth or a wound exposing the bone. Imposing this obligation therefore belongs to the same category as the kindness the Lawgiver has enjoined towards those in need, such as stranded travellers, the poor, the needy, and relatives in need.

It is well known that this is among the foundations of the revealed laws upon which the welfare of the world rests. Allah has divided His creation into rich and poor, and their welfare cannot be secured without meeting the needs of the poor. He has also forbidden usury, which harms the poor. The command to give charity thus serves the same purpose as the prohibition of usury. This is why Allah links the two in such statements as His words, Exalted is He:

“Allah brings usury to nothing and makes charity grow.”

And His words, Exalted is He:

“Whatever you give in usury so that it may increase through other people’s wealth will not increase with Allah. But whatever you give in charity, seeking Allah’s Face—it is they who will receive a manifold increase.”

Towards the end of al-Baqarah, Allah sets out the rulings governing wealth, which fall into three categories: justice, generosity, and injustice. Justice is trade; injustice is usury; and generosity is charity. He praises those who give charity and mentions their reward, condemns those who practise usury and explains their punishment, and permits trade and the contracting of debts for a specified term.

Bearing liability for blood money thus belongs to the same category as the rights He has made binding upon people towards one another, such as the rights of a fellow Muslim, a relative, a neighbour, a slave, and a wife.

---

## Page 10379

Section

The rulings said to depart from analogy are of two kinds: those agreed upon by consensus and those subject to disagreement. Those whose rulings are undisputed have been shown to accord with sound analogy. This gives rise to the question: may such rulings themselves serve as a basis for analogy?

A group of jurists hold that a ruling established contrary to analogy cannot serve as a basis for further analogy. This position is reported from the followers of Abū Hanīfah. The majority, however, hold that it can. This is the position stated by the followers of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others.

They maintain that what matters is whether the conditions for analogy are met. Whenever the effective cause of a ruling is known, we extend that ruling to whatever shares the same effective cause, whether or not the original ruling is said to depart from analogy. The same applies when it is known that there is no relevant distinction between the original case and the new case. Linking cases through evidence indicating the effective cause is like linking them through the effective cause itself.

If, however, no evidence establishes that the new case is equivalent to the original case, analogy is impermissible, whether the original ruling is said to accord with analogy or to depart from it. Hence, the correct view is that the ruling on ʿarāyā sales extends to transactions equivalent to them in substance.

---

## Page 10380

The truth of the matter is that nothing has been prescribed contrary to sound analogy. Rather, whatever is said to depart from analogy must possess a distinguishing characteristic that sets it apart from the cases with which it is contrasted and requires a different ruling. If another case shares that characteristic, it receives the same ruling; otherwise, it is a distinct case.

As for disputed rulings, an example is when a hadith establishes something contrary to a particular rule, and some say: “This is contrary to analogy,” or “contrary to analogy based on established principles.” There are several examples of this, among the best known being the sale of an animal whose milk has been allowed to accumulate in its udder. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not allow milk to accumulate in the udders of camels or sheep. Whoever purchases an animal treated in this way has the choice, after milking it, of whichever of two courses he prefers: if he is satisfied with it, he may keep it; if dissatisfied, he may return it together with a sā‘ measure of dates.”

This is an authentic hadith. Nevertheless, some have said that it conflicts with analogy based on established principles in several respects:

One is that it permits the purchased animal to be returned despite there being neither a defect nor a failure to match its description.

Another is that entitlement to the yield follows liability for loss. Thus, the purchaser owes no compensation for milk produced while the animal is in his possession, yet here he is required to compensate for it.

Another is that milk is a fungible commodity, so compensation for it must be made with its equivalent.

Another is that anything without an equivalent must be compensated for at its monetary value, yet here compensation is required in dates.

---

## Page 10381

Another is that property for which compensation is owed must be compensated according to its actual amount, not by a replacement amount fixed by revealed law; yet here the amount is fixed by revealed law.

Those who follow the hadith replied:

Rather, what you have said is mistaken. The hadith accords with established principles. Even if it differed from them, it would itself constitute a foundational principle, just as the others do. Foundational principles must not be set against one another; rather, they must all be followed, for they all come from Allah.

As for their claim that this permits a return despite there being neither a defect nor a failure to match the description, nothing in the established principles requires that the right of return be confined to these two grounds. Rather, deceptive presentation is another established ground for return, and it falls within the category of failing to match the description. The characteristics of an item for sale may be represented either by words or by actions. If it is made to appear to have a certain characteristic when it is actually otherwise, that is deceptive presentation. Indeed:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, granted traders arriving with their goods the option to cancel the sale if they were intercepted and their goods purchased before they reached the market and learned the prevailing price.”

Neither of the two grounds applies here, but a form of deception is involved.

As for his statement:

“Entitlement to the yield follows liability for loss.”

First, the hadith concerning an animal whose milk has been allowed to accumulate in its udder is more authentic than this hadith, by the agreement of the scholars. Moreover, there is no contradiction between them. The yield is what accrues while the item is in the purchaser’s ownership. The term “yield” denotes income, such as a slave’s earnings; milk and similar produce are treated in the same way. Here, however, the milk was already present in the udder and thus formed part of the item sold. The sā‘ measure was not prescribed as compensation for what was produced after the contract, but as compensation for

---

## Page 10382

the milk that was in the udder at the time of the contract. As for compensating for the milk with something else, and fixing that compensation by revealed law, this is because the milk for which compensation is owed became mixed with the milk produced after the contract, making its quantity impossible to determine. The Lawgiver therefore fixed the compensation to prevent disputes, prescribing something of a different kind because a fixed quantity of the same kind might be greater or less than the original amount, leading to ribā (usury). This does not apply when something of a different kind is given: it is as though the purchaser bought that milk, whose quantity could not be determined, for a sā‘ of dates.

Dates were the food of the people of Medina: an edible staple measured by volume, just as milk is a staple measured by volume. Dates can also be eaten as a staple without preparation, unlike wheat and barley, which require preparation. Of the staple foods they consumed, dates were therefore the closest to milk. Hence, it is a matter open to juristic reasoning whether people in all regions must compensate for that milk with a sā‘ of dates, or whether this applies to those whose staple food is dates. This is open to juristic reasoning, just as is his command to give a sā‘ of barley or dates as zakāt al-fitr, the obligatory charity at the end of Ramadan.

Another example is the claim made by some:

“His command that someone who prays alone behind the row must repeat the prayer runs contrary to analogy, since the imam stands alone, and a woman stands alone behind the men, as established in the Sunnah.”

This is not so. There is agreement that the prescribed practice for the imam is to stand ahead, and that the prescribed practice for those following him is to form rows. How, then, can one situation be compared to the other?

---

## Page 10383

That is because the imam is followed: when he leads them, they can see him and follow him more fully. As for a woman, she stands alone when no other woman is present; the prescribed practice for her is to form a row. However, the woman’s case establishes two points. It establishes that if someone finds no one to stand beside him behind the row, and cannot enter the row, he may pray alone because of the need. This accords with analogy, for obligations are waived when need requires it. The command to stand in a row with others is one such obligation; if that is impossible, it is waived because of the need, just as other obligatory elements of prayer are waived when needed, as in the prayer of fear, in order to preserve congregational prayer.

Applying this principle consistently, if someone cannot pray with the congregation except by standing ahead of the imam, he may stand ahead of him because of the need. This is the position of several groups of scholars and one of the two views within Ahmad’s school, although they do not permit standing ahead of the imam when that can be avoided.

In short, standing alongside others in a row is no more obligatory than other duties. If those other duties are waived for a valid excuse in congregational prayer, then this duty is all the more deserving of being waived. Among the general principles of Islamic law are that an obligation ceases to be binding when it cannot be fulfilled, and that what necessity compels one to do, without sinful transgression, is not prohibited. Thus, Allah has not made obligatory what is beyond the capacity of

---

## Page 10384

His servant, nor has He forbidden what necessity compels His servant to do.

Another example is the claim made by some concerning the authentic hadith:

“A pledged animal may be ridden and milked, and whoever rides and milks it must bear the cost of its upkeep.”

They claim that this runs contrary to analogical reasoning, but that is not so. When the pledged property is an animal, it is entitled to protection in its own right, and both its owner and the pledgee have rights in it. If it is in the pledgee’s possession and he neither rides nor milks it, its benefits go to waste. We have already explained that milk is treated as a benefit derived from the animal. Thus, if the pledgee enjoys its benefits and compensates for them by paying for its upkeep, both interests and both sets of rights are upheld. The animal’s upkeep is obligatory upon its owner. When the pledgee pays for it, he discharges an obligation on the owner’s behalf, while also having a right in the animal. He is therefore entitled to reimbursement. The animal’s benefits can serve as compensation, so making use of them is better than allowing them to be lost to their owner and go to waste.

The jurists have disagreed about someone who discharges another person’s obligation without his permission, such as paying his debt. Mālik’s position, and Ahmad’s according to the well-known report from him, is that he may seek reimbursement from that person. Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī hold that he may not.

If someone pays maintenance that the other person is obliged to provide—for example, by providing for that person’s young child or slave—some scholars of Ahmad’s school say that he may not seek reimbursement, distinguishing maintenance from debt. The discerning scholars of his school, however, treated the two alike, saying that both are obligations. Even if he were to ransom him

---

## Page 10385

from captivity, he would be entitled to demand reimbursement of the ransom, even though it was not a debt. The Quran supports this view, for Allah says:

“If they breastfeed for you, give them their payment.”

He commands payment simply on account of breastfeeding, without stipulating a contract or the father’s permission. Likewise, He says:

“Mothers shall breastfeed their children for two complete years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing period. The father must provide their food and clothing according to what is reasonable.”

He makes this obligatory upon the father without stipulating a contract or permission. An animal’s upkeep is obligatory upon its owner, while the pledgee or lessee has a right in it. If he pays the maintenance incumbent upon its owner, his claim to reimbursement is stronger than that of someone who provides for the owner’s child. Suppose the pledgor says, “I did not give you permission to pay for its upkeep.” The other may reply, “That upkeep is obligatory upon you, and I am entitled to demand it from you to preserve the pledged or leased property.”

If the person who paid for the upkeep agrees to take the benefits of the pledged property in compensation, without demanding repayment of the expenditure, he has done its owner a kindness. This is an unqualified benefit to the pledgor. The same applies if someone entrusted with another person’s animal—such as a custodian, partner, or agent—pays for its upkeep from his own funds and takes the benefits of the property in compensation. This is a kindness to its owner when the owner does not provide for its upkeep.

Among the hadiths said to depart furthest from analogical reasoning is the report in the Sunan collections, narrated by al-Hasan, from Qabīsah ibn Hurayth, from Salamah ibn al-Muhabbaq: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ruled concerning a man who had intercourse with his wife’s slave woman

---

## Page 10386

: if he forced her, she is free, and he owes her mistress an equivalent slave woman; but if she consented, she belongs to him, and he owes her mistress an equivalent slave woman. Another wording states: ‘If she consented, both she and an equivalent slave woman from his property belong to her mistress.’” Some have criticized this hadith’s chain of transmission, but it is a sound hadith, and they themselves cite weaker reports as evidence. Its apparent difficulty, however, made them more inclined to grade it as weak.

This hadith accords with analogical reasoning when considered alongside three valid principles, each upheld by a group of jurists.

The first principle is that if someone alters another person’s property in a way that deprives its owner of its intended use, the owner may require him to provide an equivalent in compensation. An example is when someone alters wrongfully appropriated property so that it no longer bears its original designation. There are three views on this within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere.

The first is that it remains the property of its owner. The person who wrongfully appropriated it is liable for any decrease in its value and has no entitlement to any increase. This is al-Shāfiʿī’s view.

The second is that the person who wrongfully appropriated it thereby becomes its owner and owes compensation to its original owner. This is Abū Hanīfah’s view.

The third is that the owner may choose between taking it back, together with compensation for any decrease in value, and demanding a replacement. This is the fairest and strongest of these views. If he causes it to lose its intangible qualities, such as

---

## Page 10387

making him forget his craft, weakening his strength, or corrupting his intellect and religion, then here too the owner may choose between claiming compensation for the diminution in value and demanding a replacement. If someone cuts off the tail of a judge’s mule, Mālik holds that he must provide a replacement and becomes its owner, since, by customary standards, its owner can no longer use it for its intended purpose; alternatively, the owner is given the choice. The same applies to a ruler if someone cuts off his horse’s ears and tail.

The second principle is that all destroyed property must, as far as possible, be compensated for with property of the same kind, taking its value into account. This includes animals, just as a loan must be repaid with its equivalent. If someone borrows an animal, he returns an equivalent, as in the report:

“The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, borrowed a young camel and repaid it with a better one.”

Likewise, in the case of a man deceived concerning a slave woman, compensation for his children is made by providing their equivalents, as the Companions ruled. Similarly, if a seller reserves the head of the animal sold, but the animal is not slaughtered, the Companions ruled that a head should be purchased—namely, one equivalent to it in value. This is one of the two views within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere.

The account of David and Solomon, peace be upon them both, belongs to this category. The livestock had destroyed the people’s cultivated land, which was their orchard. They said it was an ʿayn. The term harth (cultivated land) applies to both trees and crops. David awarded the sheep to the owners of the cultivated land, apparently holding the livestock owners liable for its monetary value. Since they possessed no property other than the sheep, he awarded the sheep as compensation of equivalent value.

Solomon, however, ruled that the livestock owners should tend the cultivated land until it was restored to its former condition. He thus required them to make restitution in kind, and gave the livestock to the owners of the cultivated land so that they could benefit from it as compensation

---

## Page 10388

for the benefit lost from the time the cultivated land was destroyed until it was restored. Al-Zuhrī gave this same ruling to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz concerning someone who had destroyed trees belonging to him, saying: “He must replant them until they are restored to their former condition.” It was reported that Rabīʿah and Abū al-Zinād said, “He is liable for their value,” and al-Zuhrī spoke harshly of them.

This is what the evidence requires, for the obligation is to compensate for destroyed property with its equivalent as far as possible. Allah Most High says:

“The recompense for an evil is an evil like it.”

And He says:

“So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same measure as he transgressed against you.”

And He says:

“If you retaliate, then retaliate with the like of what you have suffered.”

And He says:

“Violations of sacred limits are subject to retribution.”

If someone destroys money, grain, or the like, compensation with an equivalent is possible. But if the destroyed property consists of clothing, vessels, or animals, an equivalent in every respect may be unobtainable.

There are therefore two alternatives: either he compensates for it by paying its value in dirhams, which differ from the destroyed property in kind and characteristics but equal it in monetary value; or he compensates for it with clothing of the same kind, vessels of the same kind, or animals of the same kind, taking value into account as far as possible, so that the replacement equals the destroyed property in value. In the latter case, monetary value is equal, just as with payment in money, but there is the additional advantage of correspondence in kind and characteristics. This therefore provides a closer equivalent than monetary compensation. Whatever provides a closer equivalent is more just, and must therefore be awarded when an equivalent in every respect is unobtainable.

A parallel to this is what is established by the Sunnah and the agreement of the Companions concerning retaliation for a slap

---

## Page 10389

and a blow. This is the view of many of the early scholars, and Ahmad explicitly affirmed it in the report transmitted by Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿīd al-Shālanjī, which al-Jawzajānī explained in his book entitled al-Mutarjim. A group of jurists said:

“Exact equality is unattainable in such cases, so recourse must be had to discretionary punishment.”

They may be answered as follows:

What the transmitted reports establish is precisely what sound analogy requires. Discretionary punishment is a penalty whose kind, manner, and degree are not fixed; these are left to the ruler’s judgment. Clearly, ordering a blow that approximates the offender’s blow—even if its exact equality cannot be established—is closer to justice and equivalence than imposing an entirely unmeasured punishment that differs from it in kind and manner.

Know that an equivalent in every respect is unattainable even for commodities measured by volume, let alone other things. If someone destroys a sāʿ of wheat and compensates for it with another sāʿ of wheat, it cannot be known that the two measures contain exactly the same quantity of grain; indeed, one may contain more than the other. Hence Allah Most High says:

“Give full measure and weight with justice. We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”

Achieving exactness in measuring and weighing may be beyond human ability. Thus, when equivalence in every respect cannot be attained, one says, “This is a closer equivalent than that,” meaning that it more closely approximates an exact equivalent.

The third principle:

If someone mutilates his slave, the slave thereby becomes free. This is the position of Mālik, Ahmad, and others. Reports to this effect have been traced back to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and have also been transmitted from his Companions, such as ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, as has been mentioned elsewhere

---

## Page 10390

in another passage.

This hadith thus accords with these three principles, which are established by evidence consistent with just analogical reasoning. If she willingly submitted to him, he has spoiled her for her owner, for by consenting she becomes guilty of fornication. This diminishes her value and prevents her owner from employing her as before, because of his aversion to her, the slave woman’s desire for the master, and the master’s longing for her—especially since this creates difficulties for her owner, so that he does not obey her as she used to obey him.

If someone deals with property in a way that diminishes its value, its owner is entitled to demand an equivalent replacement. He therefore awarded her an equivalent slave woman. Clearly, if she preferred to retain ownership of her and require him to compensate for the diminution in her value, that would not have been precluded. The ruling merely established an option available to her. This entails, however, that if a man spoils a slave woman for her owners by inducing her to consent to fornication, they may demand a replacement from him. He must then provide an equivalent slave woman, on the principle that an equivalent must be provided, as far as possible, for anything for which compensation is owed.

If, however, he forced her, this falls under mutilation, for forcing someone to submit to intercourse constitutes mutilation: intercourse is treated as a form of destruction. Hence it has been said that if a man forces his male slave to submit to sodomy, the slave thereby becomes free. For this reason, intercourse entails either compensation or punishment; it is not treated like the benefit derived from service.

Thus, since she became his property through his spoiling her for her owner, he was required to provide an equivalent slave woman, just as in the case of consent. His having mutilated her then made her free of his ownership.

It may be said that this necessarily entails that if a man forces his male slave to submit to the indecent act, the slave thereby becomes free; and if he forces another person’s slave woman to submit to the indecent act, she becomes free, and he is liable to compensate for her

---

## Page 10391

with an equivalent slave woman, unless a distinction is drawn between his wife’s slave woman and another’s. If there is a distinction between them recognized by the Sharia, it may be upheld; otherwise, analogical reasoning requires that they be treated alike. As for the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic:

“Do not compel your slave women to prostitution, if they desire chastity, seeking the fleeting gains of worldly life. But if anyone compels them, then after their being compelled, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

This prohibits compelling them to earn money through prostitution, as it is reported that Ibn Ubayy, the hypocrite, had slave women whom he forced into prostitution. This is not the same as forcing a slave woman to submit to his own unlawful intercourse with her. The latter amounts to mutilating her, whereas the former means obliging her to go and engage in illicit intercourse herself. Moreover, it might be said that emancipation on account of mutilation had not yet been prescribed when the verse was revealed, but was prescribed later.

Discussing this hadith is a particularly delicate matter. If it is reliably established, then this is the explanation that has become apparent to me and the way to account for it on the basis of established principles. If it is not reliably established, there is no need to discuss it.

In short, I know of no authentic hadith that cannot be accounted for on the basis of established principles. I have reflected on as much of the evidence of the Sharia as I could, and I have never found sound analogical reasoning that contradicts an authentic hadith, just as clear reason does not contradict authentic transmitted revelation. Rather, whenever you find an analogy contradicting a transmitted report, one of the two must be unsound. Yet much of what distinguishes sound analogy from unsound analogy eludes even eminent scholars, let alone those below them in learning. For properly understanding the attributes that determine rulings

---

## Page 10392

and knowing the rulings and meanings embodied in the Sharia are among the noblest branches of knowledge. Some of this knowledge is evident and understood by many people, while some is subtle and understood only by a select few. Thus, the analogical reasoning of many scholars is rejected for contradicting the scriptural texts, because sound analogy eludes them, just as many people fail to perceive the subtle indications of rulings contained in those texts.

Section

As for their claim that continuing with an invalidated Hajj is contrary to analogy, this is not so. Allah has commanded the completion of Hajj and ‘umrah. Thus, anyone who begins either must continue, even if he undertook it voluntarily; on this the imams agree. They disagree, however, over whether other voluntary acts of worship become obligatory once begun. By entering the consecrated state, a person becomes obliged to continue until he leaves that state, and to refrain from intercourse during Hajj. If he has intercourse during Hajj, this does not remove his obligation to complete it.

The same applies to fasting in Ramadan. Since completing the fast is obligatory by virtue of His words:

“Then complete the fast until nightfall,”

breaking it does not release a person from the obligation to complete it. Rather, he must complete his Ramadan fast even if he has invalidated it. This is because fasting has a fixed endpoint—sunset—just as Hajj has an appointed time

---

## Page 10393

, namely the Day of ‘Arafah and the days thereafter, and an appointed place: ‘Arafah, Muzdalifah and Minā. Thus, a person cannot leave the consecrated state of Hajj before reaching its appointed place, just as he cannot end the fast before its appointed time—unless, of course, he has a valid excuse, such as being prevented from completing Hajj. Such a person is like someone with a valid excuse to break the fast. This differs from prayer: if a person invalidates it, he starts it anew, because prayer can be performed again within its allotted time, whereas Hajj cannot.

Section

As for eating forgetfully, those who regard the ruling on this as contrary to analogy say: It falls under the omission of a commanded act. Whoever omits a commanded act out of forgetfulness has not discharged his obligation, as when someone forgets to pray or forgets to form the intention to fast. His worship is invalidated only by committing a prohibited act.

Those who maintain that it accords with analogy, however, say: Analogy dictates that whoever commits a prohibited act out of forgetfulness does not invalidate his worship, because someone who does so incurs no sin. This is indicated by the words of Allah Most High:

“Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake.”

It is authentically reported that Allah said: “I have done so.”

The scholars do not dispute that someone who acts forgetfully incurs no sin. They do, however, disagree over whether his worship is invalidated. The proponent of this view argues: If he incurs no sin, then he has not committed an unlawful act; and someone who has not committed an unlawful act has not invalidated his worship. Worship is invalidated only by omitting an obligation or committing an unlawful act. Thus, if what he did falls under the commission of an unlawful act, but he did it forgetfully, his worship is not invalidated.

The proponent of this view also says: Analogy dictates that

---

## Page 10394

speaking forgetfully during prayer does not invalidate it. He likewise says: Analogy dictates that whoever forgetfully commits an act prohibited in the consecrated state owes no compensatory penalty.

It has also been said: Killing game falls under liability for what is destroyed, like the blood money payable for a person killed. This differs from using perfume and wearing clothing, which fall under personal comfort. Likewise, shaving the hair and trimming the nails actually fall under personal comfort, not the destruction of something valuable, since what is removed has no value. Thus, the most balanced opinion is that no expiation is due for any of these acts, except compensation for killing game.

A consistent application of this principle means that whoever forgetfully does something he has sworn not to do does not break his oath, whether the oath involves divorce, emancipation, or anything else. This is because whoever forgetfully does what is prohibited neither sins nor disobeys; breaking an oath stands in the same relation to oaths as sin does to commands and prohibitions. Likewise, whoever forgetfully comes into contact with impurity during prayer need not repeat it, because this falls under committing a prohibited act. This differs from failing to purify oneself from ritual impurity, which falls under omitting a commanded act.

If it is said: Abstention in fasting is commanded, which is why intention is required for it. By contrast, abstention in these other cases is not commanded, since intention is not required for it.

The reply is: There is no doubt that intention is obligatory in fasting; without it, one would receive no reward;

---

## Page 10395

because reward is only earned with intention. Likewise, if someone intends to refrain from those acts for Allah’s sake, he is rewarded for doing so. If the intention to refrain from them never occurs to him, he is neither rewarded nor punished. If, however, he intends to refrain from them for Allah’s sake but does one of them forgetfully, his forgetfulness does not diminish his reward. Rather, he is rewarded for his intention to refrain from them for Allah’s sake, even though he does them forgetfully.

The same applies to fasting. What a person does forgetfully is not attributed to him; rather, Allah has brought it about in him without his intending it. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever forgetfully eats or drinks should complete his fast, for it is Allah who has fed him and given him drink.”

He thus attributed the feeding and giving of drink to Allah, because the person neither deliberately did this nor intended it. The servant is not forbidden to do what is attributed to Allah; rather, the prohibition concerns his own actions. Involuntary acts do not fall within the scope of religious accountability. Thus, the act of someone who forgets is like the act of someone asleep, someone of unsound mind, a child, and others in comparable circumstances.

This is illustrated by the fact that a fasting person who has a wet dream while asleep does not break his fast, whereas if he deliberately brings about ejaculation, he does. Likewise, if he is overcome by vomiting, he does not break his fast, whereas if he induces vomiting, he does. If what happens without his intention were treated in the same way as what happens intentionally, his fast would be broken in both cases.

If it is said: But someone who acts under a mistaken assumption does break his fast—for example, someone who eats thinking that it is still night, only to discover that dawn has broken; or someone who eats thinking that the sun has set, only to discover that it has not.

---

## Page 10396

The reply is:

This is disputed among both the early and later scholars. Those who distinguish between someone who forgets and someone who acts under a mistaken assumption say that the latter can guard against his mistake, unlike forgetfulness. They draw an analogy with someone who does not fast on the day when the beginning of Ramadan is uncertain, only to discover that it was part of Ramadan. Some of the early scholars reportedly held that the fast must be made up in the case involving sunset, but not in the case involving dawn, just as when the uncertainty persists.

Those who hold that the fast is not invalidated in any of these cases say: “Our evidence is stronger, and the Quran and Sunnah support our position more clearly.” For Allah says:

“Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make a mistake.”

Thus, He mentions forgetfulness and error together. Moreover, someone who mistakenly commits acts prohibited during pilgrimage or prayer is like someone who commits them forgetfully. It is established in the Sahīh that people broke their fast during the Prophet’s lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and then the sun reappeared. The hadith does not mention that they were ordered to make up the fast. Hishām ibn ʿUrwah, however, said: “It must be made up.” His father, who was more knowledgeable than he was, used to say: “They do not have to make it up.”

It is also established in the two Sahīh collections that a group of the Companions

“used to eat until one of them could distinguish a white thread from a black thread. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to one of them: ‘Your pillow must indeed be wide! What is meant is the whiteness of day and the darkness of night.’”

It is not reported that he ordered them to make up their fasts. They were ignorant of the ruling and were therefore acting in error.

It is established that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb broke his fast, after which it became apparent that it was still daytime. He said: “We will not make it up, for we did not intend any sin.” It is also reported that he said: “We will make it up”; but

---

## Page 10397

the chain of transmission for the former report is more reliable. It is also authentically reported that he said: “The matter is simple.” Some interpreted this to mean that making up the fast was a light burden, but the wording does not indicate that.

In sum, this view is stronger in terms of transmitted evidence and reasoning, and accords more closely with the indications of the Quran, the Sunnah, and sound analogy. This also shows that analogy dictates that someone who acts forgetfully does not invalidate his fast. The principle established by the Quran and Sunnah is that someone who does a prohibited act forgetfully does not fall under the prohibition. Thus, no act of worship is thereby invalidated. There is no distinction between intercourse and other acts, whether during the consecrated state of pilgrimage or while fasting.

Section

As for the statement, “They say this regarding what is reported from some of the Companions,” this is a broad subject. The position he maintains is that, where some Companions held one view and others held the opposite, one of the two views may conflict with sound analogy, or even with an explicit scriptural text.

What unquestionably constitutes authoritative evidence is a practice instituted for the Muslims by the Rightly Guided Caliphs when no disagreement with them on it has been reported from any of the Companions. This is undoubtedly authoritative evidence—indeed, it is consensus. This is also indicated by the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “Adhere to my Sunnah and the sunnah of the caliphs

---

## Page 10398

who are rightly guided and guided to the truth after me. Hold fast to it and cling to it with your molar teeth. Beware of newly introduced matters, for every innovation is misguidance.” An example is the decision of ‘Umar and ‘Uthmān, may Allah be pleased with them both, to retain the conquered lands rather than distribute them among those entitled to the spoils.

Whoever declares this impermissible because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, distributed Khaybar, and maintains that a ruler’s decision to retain such lands must be overturned for contravening the Sunnah, holds a mistaken view and shows audacity toward the Rightly Guided Caliphs. What the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did at Khaybar indicates only that his action was permissible, not that it was obligatory. Even if we had no other evidence that this was not obligatory, the practice of the Rightly Guided Caliphs would itself establish that. How much more so when it is established that he conquered Mecca by force, as numerous authentic hadiths report—indeed, this is established through mass transmission among scholars of the military campaigns and the Prophet’s biography?

He came after they had broken the treaty and encamped at Marr al-Zahrān. None of them came to negotiate peace with him, nor did he send anyone to negotiate peace with them. Rather, Abū Sufyān went out to gather intelligence, whereupon al-‘Abbās took him and brought him to the Prophet like a captive. At most, al-‘Abbās had granted him safe-conduct, making him a person under a guarantee of safety. He then embraced Islam and became one of the Muslims. How, then, could he conceivably conclude a peace treaty on behalf of the unbelievers after embracing Islam, without their authorization?

Further clarification comes from the fact that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made safety conditional upon certain actions, saying, for example:

“Whoever enters Abū Sufyān’s house is safe, and whoever enters the mosque

---

## Page 10399

is safe, and whoever shuts his door is safe.” Thus, he granted safety to those who did not fight him. Had they already been under a treaty, they would not have needed this. Moreover, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, called them “the freed ones,” because he released them after gaining power over them, just as a captive is released. They therefore had the same standing as those whom he released from captivity, such as Thumāmah ibn Uthāl and others. Furthermore, he authorized the killing of certain men and women among them.

It is also authentically reported from him in the collections of authentic hadith that he said in his sermon:

“Fighting in Mecca was not permitted to anyone before me, nor will it be permitted to anyone after me. It was permitted to me only for an hour of one day.”

He entered Mecca wearing a helmet, not in a state of ihrām. Had they concluded a peace treaty with him, nothing otherwise forbidden would have become permissible for him—just as concluding a peace treaty with a town outside the Sacred Precinct would not have made such acts permissible. How, then, could fighting in the Sacred City become permissible for him while its people were at peace with him and bound to him by a treaty? Moreover, they fought Khālid, and he killed a group of them.

In short, anyone who reflects on the transmitted reports cannot but recognize that Mecca was conquered by force. Yet the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not distribute its land, just as he did not enslave its men. He conquered Khaybar by force and distributed its land, and he conquered Mecca by force without distributing its land. This establishes that both courses are permissible.

There are three positions on this issue: that distributing the landed property is obligatory, as al-Shāfiʿī held; that distributing it is forbidden and retaining it is obligatory, as Mālik held; or allowing a choice

---

## Page 10400

between the two, as held by the majority, including al-Thawrī, Abū Hanīfah, and Abū ʿUbayd. This is also the apparent position of Ahmad’s school, although positions corresponding to the first two have also been transmitted from him.

Among the rulings of the Rightly Guided Caliphs that have most perplexed jurists is that concerning the wife of a missing man. It is established that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb prescribed a waiting period of four years for a missing man’s wife and instructed her to remarry thereafter. When the missing man subsequently returned, ʿUmar gave him the choice between his wife and her dowry. Imam Ahmad and others followed him in this ruling.

A group of later scholars of Ahmad’s school, however, said: “This is contrary to analogical reasoning. Analogy dictates that she remains married to the first husband, unless we hold that the separation takes effect both outwardly and in reality, in which case she is the second man’s wife.” The former is al-Shāfiʿī’s position, and the latter is Mālik’s.

Others went to excess in rejecting this ruling, even saying: “If a judge ruled according to ʿUmar’s position, his judgment would be overturned because it departs so far from analogy.”

Still others accepted part of ʿUmar’s ruling and rejected another part, saying: “Once she remarries, she is the second man’s wife; and once the second man consummates the marriage with her, she is his wife and is not returned to the first.”

Those who disagreed with ʿUmar failed to discern what he discerned, and their understanding of sound analogy did not equal his, for this is based on

---

## Page 10401

a principle concerning contracts whose validity remains pending approval: when a person acts in a matter affecting another’s rights without that person’s permission, is his action invalid, or does it remain subject to that person’s ratification?

There are two well-known positions, both transmitted from Ahmad. The first is that such an action is generally invalid, though certain distinctions are reported from him. Unconditional invalidity is al-Shāfiʿī’s position. The second is that it remains pending ratification; this is the position of Abū Hanīfah and Mālik. This applies to marriage, sale, lease, and other contracts.

The apparent position of Ahmad’s school is that, when the person acting is excused because he cannot seek permission and needs to act, his action remains subject to ratification, without dispute. If, however, he could have sought permission, or had no need to act, then the matter is disputed.

The first case is exemplified by someone holding property whose owners he does not know, such as wrongfully appropriated property, borrowed items, and the like, when he is unable to identify its owners and has lost hope of doing so. The position of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, and Ahmad is that he should give it in charity on their behalf. If they subsequently appear, they have the choice between ratifying his action and requiring compensation.

This is among the rulings established by the Sunnah concerning lost property: after publicly announcing it, the finder takes it for his own use and disposes of it. If its owner then appears, he has the choice between ratifying the finder’s action and demanding his property back. Thus, the action remains subject to ratification; here, however, seeking permission was impossible, and there was a need to act.

Likewise, when someone makes a bequest exceeding one-third of his estate, his bequest remains subject to the heirs’ approval

---

## Page 10402

according to the majority, and they are given this choice only upon his death. As for a missing man of whom no news has been received, if it is said that his wife must wait until his fate becomes known, she would remain neither unmarried nor living as a wife until she grows old and dies without learning what became of him. The Sharia has prescribed nothing of this kind. Thus, once she has been made to wait four years without any news of him emerging, he is presumed dead.

If it is said that the ruler may separate them out of necessity, this is only because he believes the husband to be dead; otherwise, if he knew him to be alive, the man would not be considered missing. This is analogous to the permissibility of disposing of property whose owners cannot be identified. When the man returns, it becomes clear that he had been alive, just as when the owner of such property appears. The ruler has acted concerning his wife by separating them, so this separation remains subject to the husband’s ratification. If he wishes, he may ratify what the ruler has done, and it then becomes equivalent to a separation he had authorized. Had he authorized the ruler to separate them, and the ruler had done so, the separation would undoubtedly have taken effect. In that case, the first husband’s marriage would be valid.

If he does not ratify what the ruler has done, the separation becomes invalid from the moment he chooses his wife, but not before that. Rather, what is unknown is treated as nonexistent, as in the case of lost property: when its owner appears, this does not invalidate what took place previously. Her marriage to him continues from the moment he chooses her, and she is thus his wife. The returning husband therefore has the choice of ratifying or rejecting what the ruler has done. If he ratifies it, he has relinquished his conjugal rights.

The loss of a husband’s conjugal rights is compensable according to the majority, such as Mālik,

---

## Page 10403

al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, according to the more explicit of the two reports from him. Compensation is assessed at the stipulated dowry, as Mālik and Ahmad maintain—the latter according to one of the two reports from him. Al-Shāfiʿī holds that compensation is assessed at the customary dowry for a woman of her standing.

Their disagreement concerns a case in which witnesses testify that a man divorced his wife and subsequently retract their testimony. One view holds that they owe nothing, on the grounds that the loss of a husband’s conjugal rights is not compensable. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa and, according to one of the two reports from him, Ahmad. Later scholars of Ahmad’s school, such as Judge Abū Yaʿlā and his followers, adopted this report. Another view holds that the witnesses owe the customary dowry for a woman of her standing. This is al-Shāfiʿī’s position and one juristic opinion within Ahmad’s school. A third view holds that they owe the stipulated dowry. This is Mālik’s position and is more widely attested in Ahmad’s explicit statements. He expressly ruled that, where a man’s marriage to his wife is invalidated through breastfeeding, he may recover the stipulated dowry.

The Quran and Sunnah support this view. In Sūrat al-Mumtahana, Allah Most High says:

“Ask for what you have spent, and let them ask for what they have spent.”

He also says:

“Give those whose wives have gone away the equivalent of what they spent.”

This refers to the stipulated dowry, not the customary dowry for a woman of her standing. Likewise:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed the husband of a woman seeking divorce in return for compensation to take back what he had given her.”

He did not instruct him to take the customary dowry for a woman of her standing. In unrestricted transactions of exchange, he commands only what is just. This is discussed at length elsewhere, and ʿUmar’s case rests on this principle.

The Companions agreed that contracts may be held in suspense when necessary. It is established

---

## Page 10404

that this was their practice in numerous cases, with no one known to have objected. Examples include Ibn Masʿūd’s giving charity on behalf of the owner of a slave girl he had purchased, using the purchase price he still owed him when he could no longer locate him; and a man’s giving away property he had misappropriated from the spoils of war when it could no longer be distributed among the army, with Muʿāwiya’s approval. There are other such cases as well. Moreover, the view that contracts may generally be held in suspense has stronger evidential support and is the position of the majority. This entails no harm whatsoever; rather, it brings benefit without detriment. A man may consider buying, selling, hiring or undertaking an obligation on someone else’s behalf, then consult him. If he approves, it proceeds; otherwise, he has suffered no harm. The same applies to arranging the marriage of a woman under one’s guardianship and similar matters.

Where there is a need, however, this position is indispensable. The case of a missing husband is one in which the ruler’s declaration is contingent upon the husband’s consent if he returns, just as the actions of someone who finds lost property are contingent upon its owner’s consent if he appears. The view that the dowry should be returned to the husband rests on his wife’s passing out of his marital authority. They disagreed, however, over which dowry he may recover:

Is it the dowry he himself gave her, or the one the second husband gave her? There are two reports from Ahmad on this. The correct view is that he may recover only his own dowry, for that is what he is entitled to. He has no right to the dowry the second husband gave her. If the first husband becomes liable to the second for the dowry, may he recover it from her?

There are two reports on this:

---

## Page 10405

According to the first, he may recover it from her, because she is the one who received it. The second husband has already paid her the dowry he owed and is therefore not liable for two dowries. The woman’s position is different: since she chose separation from the first husband and marriage to the second, she must return the dowry, because the separation originated with her.

According to the second, he may not recover it from her, because the woman is entitled to the dowry in return for the lawful intercourse he had with her, while the first husband is entitled to the dowry because his marital rights over her have ended. The second husband is therefore liable for two dowries.

Some leading jurists regard this ruling transmitted from ʿUmar concerning “the case of the missing husband” as among the views furthest removed from analogical reasoning, prompting certain leading jurists to make the remarks they did about it. Nevertheless, it is the soundest view and the most consistent with analogical reasoning; every other view advanced on this matter is mistaken.

It is mistaken to say that she must be returned to the first husband even though he neither chooses nor wants her, when they have been separated in a manner permissible under Islamic law and he has approved that separation. For even if the ruler discovers that the facts were contrary to what he had believed, the right at issue belongs to the husband. Once he approves the ruler’s action, the objection is removed.

It is likewise mistaken to hold that she remains the second husband’s wife in all circumstances, even after her husband reappears and it becomes clear that the facts do not support the action taken. He did not part with his wife; rather, they were separated on grounds that have proved unfounded. He is now seeking his wife, so how can they be kept apart? If he demanded his property or its equivalent, it would be restored to him. How, then, can his wife not be restored to him, when his family

---

## Page 10406

is dearer to him than his wealth?

If it is said, “The second husband has acquired a right over her,” the answer is: the first husband’s right precedes that of the second, and the grounds upon which the second became entitled to have her as his wife have proved invalid. What, then, requires that the second husband’s right be respected rather than the first husband’s?

The correct ruling, therefore, is that delivered by the Commander of the Faithful, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb. If the Companions are shown to be correct in difficult questions such as these, on which scholars such as Abū Hanīfa, Mālik, and al-Shāfiʿī disagreed with them, then they are all the more likely to be correct on matters in which these scholars agreed with them.

I have examined as many questions of this kind as Allah has willed, and I have found the Companions to possess the greatest understanding of the religion and the greatest knowledge in this community. This may be seen in questions concerning oaths involving vows, manumission, divorce, and other matters, as well as questions concerning divorce made contingent upon conditions, and similar issues. In my writings, I have explained that the views transmitted from the Companions on these matters are the soundest, both as legal rulings and in terms of analogical reasoning. They are supported by the Quran and the Sunnah, as well as by clear analogy. Every other view is inconsistent in its analogical reasoning and contrary to the scriptural texts.

The same applies to other questions, such as that concerning the son of a woman who has undergone mutual imprecation, and that concerning an apostate’s inheritance. In as many questions as Allah has willed, I have found no views better than those transmitted from the Companions.

---

## Page 10407

And to this very day, I know of no view held by the Companions without disagreement among them that is not supported by analogical reasoning. Yet distinguishing sound from unsound analogy is among the highest branches of knowledge. Only those thoroughly acquainted with the underlying wisdom and objectives of the Sacred Law can do so—those who understand the countless merits of Islamic law, the benefits it secures for people in this life and the Hereafter, and its profound wisdom, all-embracing mercy, and perfect justice. Allah knows best what is correct, and to Him is the return and final destination.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked: (*)

“Is it permissible to follow such imams as Hammād ibn Abī Sulaymān, Ibn al-Mubārak, Sufyān al-Thawrī, and al-Awzāʿī? A man has said of them—I mean these aforementioned imams—‘These men should be disregarded.’ What is the ruling concerning someone who says this?”

He replied:

The imams mentioned are among the foremost imams of Islam. Al-Thawrī is the imam of the people of Iraq, and most of them regard him as greater than his contemporaries, such as Ibn Abī Laylā, al-Hasan ibn Sālih ibn Hayy, Abū Hanīfa, and others. His school of law survives to this day in Khurāsān. Al-Awzāʿī is the imam of the people of Syria, who continued to follow his school until the fourth century AH. Indeed, the people of the Maghreb followed his school before Mālik’s school reached them. Hammād ibn Abī Sulaymān was Abū Hanīfa’s teacher.

> **Footnotes:**
> (*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd states (p. 172):
> Two points should be noted:
> First: This answer is excerpted from a longer question recorded at 23:393–400.
> Second: The original question concerned someone praying alone behind the row. This clarifies certain potentially confusing passages here, such as his statement at 20:584: “Nevertheless, this view is held by Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, and others. His school survives to this day, and this is also the school of Dāwūd ibn ‘Alī and his followers. Their school survives to this day, so there is no consensus today against this view; rather, many in both the East and the West hold it.”
> Thus, the expression “this act” refers to declaring invalid the prayer of someone praying alone behind the row.

---

## Page 10408

And yet this view is held by Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, and others. His school survives to this day, and it is also the school of Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī and his followers. Their school survives to this day, so people today have not reached a consensus against this view. Rather, many in both the East and the West uphold it. Neither the Quran nor the Sunnah distinguishes between individual imams qualified to exercise independent legal judgment.

Mālik, al-Layth ibn Saʿd, al-Awzāʿī, and al-Thawrī were all imams in their time. Following the legal authority of any one of them is like following another. No Muslim would say that it is permissible to follow one but not another. However, anyone who prohibits following one of these imams in our time does so for one of two reasons:

The first is his belief that no one remains who knows their schools. Following the legal authority of a deceased scholar is a matter of well-known disagreement. Those who prohibit it say, “These scholars are dead,” while those who permit it say, “There must be someone living who knows the deceased scholar’s position.”

The second is that he says, “A consensus has now been established against this view.” This rests on a familiar question in the principles of Islamic jurisprudence: if the Companions, for example, or the scholars of any other generation differed over an issue, holding two views, and then the Successors or the scholars of the following generation unanimously agreed upon one of them, would this constitute a consensus that supersedes the earlier disagreement? There is well-known disagreement on this question within Ahmad’s school and among other scholars.

For anyone who holds that, once the scholars of the second generation have reached a consensus, it is no longer permissible to adopt the other view, and believes that the scholars of that generation did reach such a consensus, the combination of these two

---

## Page 10409

beliefs leads to this prohibition. For anyone who knows that the earlier disagreement remains valid—since views do not die with those who held them—a scholar qualified to exercise independent legal judgment may adopt the other view if it accords with his judgment. As for following another scholar’s legal authority, this depends on the question of following a deceased scholar, on which there are likewise two well-known views within the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, and among others.

If, however, a view held by these imams or others has also been held by scholars whose schools survive, then there is no doubt that their agreement supports and strengthens that view. Their authority may be cited against that of their peers who disagreed: thus, al-Thawrī and al-Awzāʿī may be cited against Abū Hanīfah and Mālik. For the Muslim community agrees that when Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, al-Thawrī, and Abū Hanīfah differ, it is not permissible to declare one scholar’s view correct rather than another’s without evidence. And Allah knows best.
